22059-balthasar-and-other-works-1909:
Anatole France, the great French man of letters, wrote the tales gathered in Balthasar and Other Works. Mrs. John Lane's English translation appeared in 1909. The title story concerns Balthasar, one of the three wise men of the Christmas story. France presents him as a king in Ethiopia, learned in the stars.

Other pieces include The Curé's Mignonette, The Daughter of Lilith, and The Red Egg. France treats saints, devils, and scholars with the same gentle irony. His prose is smooth, his learning worn lightly, and his sympathy always with the weak. These short works show the humane wit that later won him the Nobel Prize.
amphitheatrvm-sapientiae-aeternae-solius:
Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae, the Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom, was published in 1609 by Heinrich Khunrath, the German physician and alchemist. Its long subtitle calls the work Christian-Kabbalistic, divine-magical, and physico-chymical at once. Khunrath meant it as a theatre in which true wisdom, found only in God, could be contemplated from every side.

The book is famed for its engraved plates, eleven double plates among them, whose allegories join the alchemist's laboratory with Christ and the cosmos. One famous circular plate shows the laboratory as a chapel of work and prayer. The preface is signed by Erasmus Wolfart, and the plates carry dates from earlier in the decade. It remains the showpiece of Rosicrucian-era alchemy.
angela-foligno-divine-consolation-1909:
Angela of Foligno told her Book of Divine Consolation to her priest. Mary G. Steegmann gave the work English dress in 1909. Angela was a rich wife in Umbria who lost her kin and turned to God. She joined the third order of St. Francis in her grief.

Step by step, she tells how God drew her from a lax life to deep pain and light. Visions of Christ in His pain crowd the mid parts. Her words are raw, bold, and free of all soft gloss. The book is a chief text of women's soul lore of the mid ages.
apuleius-apologia-florida-butler-1909:
Harold E. Butler translated Apuleius's Apologia and Florida into English in 1909. Apuleius, the Roman novelist, had been tried for practicing magic in North Africa. His defense speech survives as the Apologia.

Prosecutors claimed he won his rich wife through spells and enchantments. Apuleius answers with wit, philosophy, and ridicule of his accusers' ignorance. He discusses fish, mirrors, and poetry to show his interests were scholarly. The Florida collects showpieces of his public speaking beside the defense. Together they form the great surviving record of a Roman witchcraft trial. Butler's translation keeps the legal fireworks readable. The speech is long, bold, and full of wit from the first page to the last.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-09:
Volume nine of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, the penultimate book of the main set. Shahrazad's store seems endless even as its appointed end draws near. Kings in her tales keep meeting clever wives, lost sons, and fortunes reversed in a single night.

Burton, nearing his own finish line, still refuses every shortcut in the text. His renderings of verse stay verse, and his notes stay frank about manners and belief. The Gutenberg text of this volume is ebook 55587, set apart from its neighbors in numbering. That quirk aside, the volume matches the rest in dress. One volume more completes Shahrazad's bargain in the main series.
arxiv-2510-00409:
Corey de Wit wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the famous hat tiling and the system that generates it. The hat is a single tile shape that covers the plane only in non-repeating patterns. Smith and colleagues stunned geometers with its recent discovery. De Wit describes that aperiodic tiling as the output of an overlapping iterated function system.

An iterated function system builds a pattern by applying scaled copies of a rule again and again. The hat tiling's substitution rule is imperfect, so ordinary theory does not fit it directly. De Wit develops a theory of infinite sequences of such systems that converge uniformly, piece by piece. That theory then models the hat's substitution system faithfully. The paper connects a headline discovery in tiling theory to a classic fractal framework. It gives other researchers a new handle for proving facts about the hat.
arxiv-2510-00509:
Mingxiang Pan, Feng Liu, and Huaqing Huang published this 2025 physics paper introducing orbital altermagnetism, a new kind of magnetic order. Altermagnets hide their magnetism: opposing moments cancel, yet their bands split by direction. Known cases involve electron spin, the familiar magnetic degree of freedom. The authors show pure orbital motion can carry the same symmetry-protected order.

A minimal model on a square-kagome lattice produces the order from staggered loop currents. The currents lock orbital motion to momentum in a d-wave pattern. First-principles calculations found the order in copper bromide and vanadium disulfide, independent of spin ordering there. It can also coexist with spin altermagnetism, as in certain oxide monolayers. A large nonlinear current-induced orbital magnetization showcases the transport effects on offer. The authors pitch orbital altermagnets as a fresh platform for spintronics without net magnetization.
arxiv-2510-00809:
Karaouli and four co-authors test whether time series foundation models forget catastrophically, in this 2025 arXiv paper on continual learning. Such models forecast zero-shot across many domains, but real deployments keep fine-tuning them on fresh data. In language models, sequential fine-tuning is known to erase earlier skills, and nobody had checked the effect for forecasting models. The authors built synthetic datasets with varying structure to control the experiment.

Fine-tuning TimesFM on a new dataset improved performance there, yet accuracy on earlier datasets often fell sharply. The pattern is the classic stability-plasticity dilemma: plasticity for the new task is bought with stability of the old ones. Because time series are noisy and non-stationary, the models latch onto short-term fluctuations instead of patterns. The authors argue that robust continual learning strategies are a prerequisite for trusting these models in real-world forecasting.
arxiv-2510-00909:
Klymenko and five co-authors, from the Technical University of Munich and Google, interview European AI developers about privacy risk in this 2025 arXiv paper. The team spoke with twenty-five developers building AI systems in Europe. They asked which privacy threats the developers rank as most dangerous for users, businesses, and themselves, and which mitigations they actually use. The headline finding is disagreement: there was little consensus on the ranking of risks.

Those differences traced back to recurring reasoning patterns, many rooted in human and organizational factors rather than technical judgement. Developers knew the proposed mitigation strategies well, including privacy-enhancing technologies such as differential privacy. Yet they reported minimal real-world adoption of the advanced ones. The authors call the field not future-ready, and they argue progress needs better tooling plus cooperation among providers, users, researchers, and regulators.
arxiv-2510-01009:
Dahal, Ghimire, Murad, and Rahimi make video question answering data-efficient in this 2025 arXiv paper presenting POVQA. Long videos swamp vision-language models with frames, and even context windows hold under a minute of footage at rate. The authors compress each second of video into one temporally pooled image, using motion-blur and weighted-averaging variants. That pooled stream is all the model ever sees.

They built ReasonVQA, a dataset of two hundred thirty-nine human-annotated questions over twelve movies, each with a written rationale. Qwen2.5-VL-7B was fine-tuned with supervised training plus preference optimization on those rationales. F1 score jumped from about 0.21 to 0.54, and BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L rose as steeply over pooled baselines. Gains held across pooling schemes at test time, and zero-shot transfer to TVQA stayed competitive. The message: rationale quality and token economy can matter as much as dataset size.
arxiv-2510-01109:
Tamiti and Barua, at George Mason University, supervise speech bandwidth extension with chaos-inspired discriminators in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bandwidth extension rebuilds high frequencies lost when speech is recorded or sent at low sampling rates. Neural systems often over-smooth the fine structure of voiced sound, which leaves audio dull or buzzy. Voiced speech is genuinely chaotic, though, and the authors turn that physics into a training signal.

Their framework, NLDSI-BWE, uses two discriminators built on nonlinear dynamics. One reads recurrence patterns that capture self-similarity across time scales, and the other tracks Lyapunov exponents that measure divergence. Depthwise-separable convolutions keep both discriminators tiny. Against the prior AP-BWE model, the discriminator parameter count fell about forty-four fold, from roughly twenty-two million to under half a million. Testing used only the VCTK dataset in clean conditions, which the authors flag as a limitation.
arxiv-2510-01309:
Kumar constrains dark radiation that talks to ordinary matter only through gravity, using the sharpest cosmological data available. Hidden radiation appears in many theories beyond the standard model, in four behavioral types. Free-streaming, self-interacting, decoupling, and recoupling variants each leave different fingerprints on the sky.

Microwave background, galaxy structure, and supernova data jointly test the possibilities. No strong preference for new physics emerged from the combined fit. Intriguing trade-offs did appear, including data favoring massless dark radiation over massive neutrinos when densities vary freely. Even secluded sectors, the study shows, cannot hide from precision cosmology. Adiabatic and isocurvature starting conditions widen the search honestly. Neutrino mass bounds loosen when radiation can take the strain. No isocurvature signal appeared, despite room in the fit for one. Degeneracies among densities are mapped rather than ignored. Gravity alone betrays the hidden sector.
arxiv-2510-01409:
Cotti and co-authors turn raw security logs into structured threat intelligence graphs that follow a shared ontology. Logs capture attacks faithfully but arrive noisy, fragmented, and semantically messy. Their agent, OntoLogX, reads them with a language model guided by a lightweight log ontology.

Retrieval support and iterative correction keep the produced graphs valid in form and meaning. Session-level aggregation then links scattered events into campaigns. A final model pass maps the evidence onto a standard catalog of adversary tactics. Benchmark logs and a real honeypot deployment both yielded sound graphs. Honeypot logs are messier than benchmarks, which is why they convince. Multiple graph database backends accepted the generated output. Tactic prediction lifts log lines into adversary strategy. Ontology grounding is what makes separate graphs interoperable. Threat intelligence becomes queryable instead of archival. Noise is the native condition of logs.
arxiv-2510-01509:
Füredi, Imolay, and Schweitzer pin down how large the biggest clique can be in xor-products of Kneser graphs. These graphs encode set systems where vertices are subsets and edges join disjoint pairs, a coding-theory staple. Earlier work bounded the second power up to an unknown correction term.

The team determines that correction term's exact order of magnitude. For the complete-graph case with three or more factors, explicit constructions and an algebraic proof squeeze the clique number between two near-matching bounds. General growth in the ground-set size is trapped between two polynomial rates. The authors conjecture the lower rate is the true one. Alon and Lubetzky opened the complete-graph case as coding theory. Budapest and Stockholm anchor the author affiliations. Binomial growth sets the correction term's scale. Disjointness is the adjacency rule throughout the construction. Extremal combinatorics is the home field.
arxiv-2510-01609:
Ma and co-authors split a conversational recommender into a team of specialized language-model agents. One agent understands dialogue, another models preferences, another tracks context, and another ranks items. A coordination layer adjusts each agent's influence by learning from how conversations unfold.

Simple questions get fast answers, while tangled preferences trigger deeper joint reasoning. The tiered strategy keeps routine chats cheap and reserves collaboration for hard cases. Experiments reported better recommendation quality and shorter conversations than single-agent designs. Division of labor, borrowed from human teams, suits recommendation's many simultaneous goals. Adaptive weights shift with interaction patterns instead of staying fixed at design time. Conversation coherence across turns is an explicit design target. Multiple ranking goals compete, and the hierarchy arbitrates among them. Users feel the difference as fewer, better questions before a good suggestion. Specialization scales better than monoliths here too.
arxiv-2510-02509:
Gragera-Mas and co-authors reconstruct past and future stellar flybys of Beta Pictoris. Their 2025 astronomy paper studies a young star with two giant planets. A debris disk circles the star as well. Passing stars can stir the outer comet reservoir. Stirred comets then dive inward as visible exocomets. The team gathered stars now within eighty parsecs of the system. Gaia data plus spectroscopy supplied their motions. Orbits were integrated backward and forward in a galaxy model. Encounters closer than two parsecs were logged as events.

The catalogue holds over ninety nine thousand traced stars. Dozens of them pass within two parsecs in the full window. Forty nine stars met that close encounter test. Binary systems account for several of those visitors. The catalogue now grounds future dynamical studies. Flyby histories can be weighed against exocomet records. Planetary systems everywhere evolve under such passing traffic.
arxiv-2510-02609:
Guo and co-authors build an agent that automatically attacks code generating agents to expose their flaws. Their 2025 AI safety paper presents the RedCodeAgent system. Code agents now write, run, and debug software interactively. Those powers open real safety and security holes. Static benchmarks miss combined and boundary attacks. RedCodeAgent adapts its strategy to each target query. A memory module stores jailbreak knowledge from past attempts. The agent picks and combines tools from its own toolbox. Simulated sandboxes then judge what the attacks actually did. Execution results ground the safety verdicts.

The system uncovers vulnerabilities that fixed tests overlook. Stronger base models made the red teaming slightly sharper. Prompt injection variants lowered rejection rates in tests. Defenders gain a moving target to practice against. Code agents ship faster than their audits today. Automated red teaming helps close that gap.
arxiv-2510-02809:
Dupuy and co-authors improve a method for honest forecast ranges. Conformal prediction wraps a forecast in an interval. The interval should contain the true value at a set rate. For time series, the method must update online as data drifts. Most updaters ask one blunt question after each step. Did the truth land inside the interval or not? The threshold then jumps by a fixed rule.

The new method asks a richer question. It measures how close the truth fell to the interval's edges. That distance grades how relevant the interval was. Smooth grades prevent wild swings in the threshold. Tests on real data sets followed. The graded updates gave tighter intervals than rival methods. Coverage stayed valid over the long run. Narrower intervals with honest coverage help decision makers act. The idea fits fields like health, sport, and finance, where drift is common.
arxiv-2510-02909:
Nayal and co-authors flag unknown objects in street scenes without any special training. Self-driving cars must spot things they were never taught. A segmentation model labels each pixel by class. Objects outside its class list are called out-of-distribution. Most detectors for them need example outliers in training. This team instead leans on large vision foundation models.

Their recipe uses features from the InternImage backbone. K-means clustering groups the pixels of a scene. A confidence check on the raw output scores marks suspect clusters. No outlier data and no extra training are involved. The method scored well on two public benchmarks. It passed several supervised and unsupervised rivals on both. The authors admit the scores still trail the best systems. Their long-term aim is a recipe that turns any closed-set model into an open-world one.
arxiv-2510-03109:
Mildner, Giampouras, and Damoulas prove that generalized Bayesian updates survive bad priors. A prior can be badly wrong about the world. Standard theory may then fail to settle anywhere useful. Generalized variational inference swaps the usual divergence for others. It also searches a smaller family of candidate posteriors. Federated versions spread that work across many sites. Open questions dogged the framework's safety under misspecification.

Existence and uniqueness of the update come first. They hold on broad Polish spaces under stated conditions. The posterior then piles up near the loss minimizers. Rates for that piling come next, and they ignore the prior. Even severe prior error cannot derail the limit. Bounded divergences are the setting for the proofs. Restricting the search family is what buys the control. Decision makers gain a firmer base for robust inference. The work backs generalized methods for federated learning too.
arxiv-2510-03309:
Tupakula presents a 2025 arXiv paper on matching drugs with medical text without training a giant joint model. Large mixed models for drug search need huge data sets and heavy computing. The cheaper idea here is a thin bridge, a small learned layer placed over two frozen encoders. One encoder reads chemical fingerprints of drugs. The other reads biomedical sentences, and the bridge pulls matching pairs close together in meaning.

Training used drug and text pairs drawn from the ChEMBL database. Extra weight on hard cases taught the bridge to split drugs that share the same target. Tests split the data by chemical core, so the model faced truly new drug families. Even then, the bridge beat frozen baselines by a wide margin at telling same target drugs apart. The result offers a low cost path to drug search tools for precision medicine teams.
arxiv-2510-03409:
Viitanen and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper that fits spectral models to sources in the XMM-Newton X-ray sky catalogue. The satellite has mapped the X-ray sky for over two decades. Its DR11 release lists numbers of detections and stacked sources. The team ran fitting pipelines over those spectra inside the XMM2ATHENA project. Their goal was to release ready to use catalogues of fitted values for the whole community.

Four catalogues came out of the work. One holds absorbed power law fits for every single detection with a spectrum. Another fits both power law and blackbody models to the unique stacked sources. A third estimates spectral shape from band count rates alone. A fourth applies richer models to sources already classed as galaxy cores, stars, or binaries. The team also shows that optical and infrared colors can pick out hidden, absorbed galaxy cores well.
arxiv-2510-03509:
Topollai and Choromanska present a 2025 arXiv paper on teaching models from a few examples in ways that travel across domains. Few shot methods usually train on one data world and stumble in the next. Their idea works at the level of whole tasks rather than single images. Simple task variations create paired views, and a contrastive loss pulls matching task summaries together. The method is light and drops into existing few shot and meta learning systems without redesign.

On the MetaDataset benchmark, the approach beat rival methods in the reported tests. Gains came without knowing which domain a task belonged to in advance. Computing cost fell at the same time, which rarely pairs with accuracy gains. Clustering whole tasks seems to teach features that care about task structure, not surface style. Clinics, field robots, and other low data settings could adapt models to new jobs faster with such training.
arxiv-2510-03609:
Bae, Roh, and Choi present a 2025 arXiv paper on learning state observers for systems whose dynamics are unknown, with proofs that the observers are safe to pair with certified controllers. Controllers with safety certificates assume the state is known, but systems only offer noisy measurements. The authors learn the observer and a robustness certificate from data. The certificate is a Lyapunov function witnessing a stability property called incremental input to state stability. Under assumptions about model fidelity, the estimation error provably settles.

Because the observer carries a certificate, a controller's safety proof stays valid when it tolerates bounded estimation error. The team extends the design to interconnected systems using the small gain theorem, giving a distributed observer recipe. Tests on nonlinear systems support the theory. Safety critical machines, from robots to power equipment, need estimates with guarantees. This framework supplies the estimate and the guarantee in one learning pass.
arxiv-2510-03809:
Huang wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on why high-dimensional learning models fail suddenly when data runs short. Such models look stable until sample size drops below a sharp threshold, then collapse. Huang argues that the cause is geometric rather than a flaw in any one algorithm. The key object is the Fisher information, which measures how much data reveals about the parameters.

The paper proves a result called the Fisher Threshold Theorem. It says the smallest Fisher eigenvalue must stay above an explicit bound that depends on dimension and sample size. Below that bound, parameters cannot be identified reliably. Huang also proposes a checkable fix, the Fisher floor, that keeps models above the threshold. Tests on synthetic mixture and logistic models matched the predicted transition closely. The work gives practitioners a diagnostic for when more data is truly needed.
arxiv-2510-03909:
Nam and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on generating videos of people from a text prompt alone. Video diffusion models improved fast, but human motion remains hard because bodies bend in complex ways. Most prior work starts from a still image or covers narrow cases like dance. The authors build a two-stage pipeline that begins with motion itself.

Their framework, CAMEO, first turns text into a motion sequence with a text-to-motion model. A video model then renders that motion into frames. A camera-aware module picks viewpoints that match the prompt, reducing manual setup. The authors reworked training captions so the two stages stop conflicting. On the MovieGen benchmark and a new test set, CAMEO produced steadier bodies and fewer pose glitches than a strong baseline. Weak spots remain for finger motion and crowded scenes, but planning motion first clearly steadies results.
arxiv-2510-04009:
He and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper with a benchmark for measuring creativity in foundation models. Creativity is prized in human intelligence, yet model evaluation still centers on accuracy. Earlier creativity tests were scattered and used ad hoc scores with little grounding in theory. The authors build a unified benchmark, C2-Eval, from established social science ideas about what makes work creative.

The benchmark splits creativity into two kinds. Convergent creativity covers tasks with tight constraints, like code generation, while divergent creativity covers open-ended work like storytelling. Every output is scored on usefulness, originality, and surprise. The team tested more than twenty leading open and proprietary models. Stronger reasoning and well-designed creative instructions improved scores reliably. The two creativity kinds were related but traded off against each other in notable ways. The benchmark gives researchers a shared lens for studying machine creativity.
arxiv-2510-04109:
Jana and Basu present this 2025 arXiv paper on the rough phases of growing interfaces that conserve material. Conserved growth models describe surfaces where matter moves around rather than appearing or vanishing. The authors show sufficiently strong nonlocal chemical potentials drive these models into strong coupling phases. Between weak and strong coupling lies a roughening transition, whose character they work out in detail.

In the weak coupling phase, the dynamics and roughness exponents obey an exact relation in every dimension. At the critical dimension, scaling survives but picks up exactly computed logarithmic corrections. Below the critical dimension, the strong coupling phase is unstable and the surface crumples instead of roughening normally. That crumpled state differs from the famous strong coupling phase of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. The results redraw the phase diagram of conserved surface growth and warn against borrowing KPZ intuition too freely.
arxiv-2510-04309:
Nguyen and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper giving activation steering of language models a foundation in classical control theory. Steering methods nudge internal activations toward desired behavior, but they were developed empirically without performance guarantees. The authors show popular steering methods behave exactly like proportional controllers, with the steering vector as the feedback signal. That observation suggests upgrading the controller rather than inventing another heuristic.

Their PID Steering framework adds integral and derivative terms to the proportional one. The integral term accumulates past errors, enforcing persistent corrections across layers. The derivative term counteracts rapid activation changes, damping overshoot. The closed-loop design connects steering quality to classical stability guarantees and yields interpretable error dynamics. Across several model families and benchmarks, PID Steering consistently beat prior approaches. Control theory thus supplies both the explanation of why steering works and a principled way to make it more reliable.
arxiv-2510-04509:
Huanqing Wang and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on controlling soft robots that carry unknown loads. Soft robots bend in complex ways, so exact models of their motion are hard to build. Data driven predictive control skips the model and steers from recorded input and output data. An unknown payload shifts the dynamics, though, and the controller starts missing its target. The team recast the method in a velocity form to absorb that shift.

The velocity form works with changes in inputs and outputs rather than their raw values. Steady offsets from a payload cancel out in that view, with no need for weighted data sets or extra disturbance estimators. The team tested the method on a planar soft robot in the lab. Against standard data driven control, the new form held accuracy when unknown payloads were added. It also kept the optimal control behavior that makes the method attractive.
arxiv-2510-04609:
Shreya Chappidi and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a side effect of AI accountability rules. Oversight regimes ask organizations to keep records so that decisions can be checked. Records promise transparency, contest, and redress for people harmed by a system. The team argues that the act of keeping records reshapes the oversight it was meant to serve. They name that reshaping accountability capture. A survey of one hundred practitioners tests the idea in practice.

The survey found record keeping problems that match the capture pattern across many workplaces. Staff juggle clashing demands between review needs and reporting duties. Some employees resist or work around record practices they see as imposed from above. Records built for accountability can drift into tools for watching workers themselves. Privacy and data protection stakes rise as logs grow richer. The authors urge designers of accountability regimes to plan for these effects from the start.
arxiv-2510-04709:
Saeed Fakhry, Maryam Shiravand, and Antonino Del Popolo wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on the surprisingly bright early galaxies seen by the Webb telescope. The standard model predicted fewer galaxies in the first era than the telescope found. Many took that gap as a threat to the model. The authors revisit how dark matter halos collapse and grow. Their halo counts include angular momentum, dynamical friction, and collapse barriers that shift with redshift.

Those refinements predict many more halos at early times than the classic formula. One of their models, called DP2, then matches the observed brightness counts from redshift seven to fourteen. It does so with moderate star formation efficiency, a sane demand. The model needs implausibly high efficiency to reach the same counts. The authors conclude the problem lies in simplified collapse physics, not in new cosmology. That reading protects the standard model while sharpening its small scale machinery.
arxiv-2510-04809:
Davide Buoso and Riccardo Molinarolo wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the tone of a vibrating plate over a ring shaped domain. The biharmonic operator governs plate bending, and its eigenvalue sets the tone. For drum like problems the first tone is known to be simple, with one shape. Plates break that rule on domains, where the tone can repeat. The authors study rings, punctured disks, and balls in higher dimensions.

With two edge conditions, clamped or hinged, they prove the tone is always simple in dimension three and up. That means the vibration has a unique shape, up to scaling. In two dimensions the answer depends on the hole. A big inner radius again forces the tone to be simple. A small hole can make it double, and one threshold ring makes it triple, as earlier work showed. Knowing when the mode is unique matters for resonance analysis in engineering.
arxiv-2510-05009:
Thomas Pawlaschyk works in complex analysis in this 2025 arXiv paper. He studies tube domains, which are regions in complex space built over a real base set. A classical result by Lelong links smoothness properties on the tube to convexity on the base. Pawlaschyk asks how far that link extends to weaker notions of convexity.

He introduces real q-convex functions, a graded weakening of ordinary convexity. His main theorem says a rigid function on a tube is q-plurisubharmonic exactly when it is real q-convex on the base. A companion result characterizes when tube-like cylinders are q-pseudoconvex. He applies both results to complements of graphs of affine maps and to Reinhardt domains. The work extends the Lelong-Bochner picture to the Hunt-Murray setting.
arxiv-2510-05209:
Ethan Huecker and Yuxuan Wang study a superconductor whose current is carried by electron quartets in this 2025 arXiv paper. Ordinary superconductors pair electrons into Cooper pairs. In pair-density-wave materials, pairs also arrange into a spatial wave. When that wave melts, a leftover vestigial order can survive at higher temperatures.

Earlier work used an artificial mean-field theory to predict quartet superconductivity from this melting. Huecker and Wang go further by including phase fluctuations and topological defects. The fluctuations strongly favor a d-wave charge-4e order at intermediate temperatures. A rival charge-density-wave vestige fails to develop, because its stiffness is suppressed. The analysis points to the layered cuprate LBCO as a candidate material for the effect.
arxiv-2510-05409:
Paulo L. Dattori da Silva and André Pedroso Kowacs test whether a refined inequality survives beyond the torus in this 2025 arXiv paper. Steinerberger's directional Poincaré inequality sharpens the classical one along a chosen direction. On the torus it holds only for a thin, uncountable set of directions. Compact Lie groups are the natural next setting.

In the same formulation, the answer turns out negative for non-torus groups. If the inequality holds, the group must actually be a torus. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions through eigenvalue estimates on the vector field's global symbol. A refined version holds exactly when the left-invariant vector field is globally solvable. They extend that equivalence to tube-type fields on products with a circle.
arxiv-2510-05609:
Chen and colleagues ask whether a language model alone can detect human-object interactions. The task finds people, objects, and the actions linking them in images. Standard pipelines bolt detectors and vision-language priors together in complex stacks. Their 2025 HOI-R1 framework drops the detector entirely.

HOI-R1 solves the task in pure text through an explicit reasoning process. Training runs in two stages, supervised fine-tuning and then reinforcement learning. Instruction templates and data augmentation shaped the fine-tuning stage. Custom reward functions score the model's interaction answers during the second stage. Reinforcement learning then tuned the model directly for the task's metrics. On the HICO-DET dataset, accuracy reached twice the baseline level. The model also generalized well beyond its training interactions. The authors present it as the first pure language-model framework for this task. Simpler stacks could make interaction detection easier to extend.
arxiv-2510-05709:
Llewellyn and colleagues make language-model security tests trustworthy. Teams compare designs for prompt-injection weakness before use. Current tests mix up design with training data and ignore output randomness. Their 2025 work fixes both the design and the analysis stages.

Two user cases guide fair tests: train your own model, or deploy a pretrained one. A Bayesian hierarchical model then studies the attack results. Grouping prompts by embedding-space closeness handles prompts that resemble each other. The model measures uncertainty despite chance-driven outputs and limited compute. Counting output spread often makes headline findings less firm. A case study pits Transformer against Mamba architectures. Matched training data or math skill sharpened that head-to-head test. Some attacks show both kinds more at risk than point guesses hinted. Honest uncertainty helps users choose designs with open eyes.
arxiv-2510-05909:
Reedi and colleagues test whether optimizing for persuasion generalizes better than optimizing for truth. Truth-trained language models overfit, producing brittle reasoning that fails on new data. Debate offers a controlled arena for comparing the two objectives. Their 2025 DebateQD algorithm evolves diverse debate strategies through tournaments.

Two models debate while a third judges each exchange. Quality-diversity evolution maintains strategies spanning rationality, authority, and emotional appeal. The protocol stays fixed while only the fitness function swaps. Persuasion fitness rewards convincing the judge regardless of correctness. A single model hosts all strategies through prompts, not separate populations. Across three model scales, persuasion-optimized strategies show smaller generalization gaps. Test performance matches or exceeds the truth-trained strategies throughout. The gap shrinks by up to about fourteen percent relative to truth optimization. The effect strengthens in low-data regimes especially.
arxiv-2510-06109:
Mazanik and three co-authors design a magnetic switch run by superconducting phase in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Their device is a Josephson junction built from two bilayers, each pairing a ferromagnetic insulator with a diffusive superconductor. An insulating barrier separates them, and the two magnetizations form the switch state.

Computing the free energy reveals two competing contributions. Driving a supercurrent costs work, while the condensate couples the insulators antiferromagnetically across the barrier. For phase differences in a broad window around pi, the balance tips and the magnetizations flip between parallel and antiparallel settings. The effect survives at finite temperatures when the insulators have strong easy-plane anisotropy. With realistic parameters, half-flux-quantum voltage pulses or magnetic field pulses trigger switching within microseconds. Europium sulfide and aluminum heterostructures offer a route toward controllable superconducting memory.
arxiv-2510-06309:
Balasubramanian, Chan, and Murdia show how to detect which microstate an AdS black hole occupies in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Black holes with identical mass and charge can hide enormous numbers of quantum microstates. Ordinary probes see only thermal averages, so telling microstates apart seemed impossible.

The authors use the Euclidean two-point function of a carefully chosen probe. The probe must be tuned state-dependently, matched to the microstate being tested. With that tuning, a new gravitational saddle dominates the usual thermal saddles. The correlator then carries a fingerprint of the specific microstate. They reproduce the gravitational result in the dual boundary theory, assuming eigenstate thermalization. They also give a binary search protocol identifying the microstate from a candidate list. If microstates are detectable in principle, the information paradox becomes a measurement problem.
arxiv-2510-06909:
Ze-Tong Li and Xin Wang turn a hard quantum design problem into a geometry problem they can optimize. Their 2025 paper works on LOCC protocols, where distant parties act locally and talk classically. Such protocols power entanglement distillation and state merging. Designing good ones by hand is very hard, especially with few communication rounds.

The authors show that fixed-round LOCC operations form a smooth curved space called a product Stiefel manifold. That shape lets them run solvers that climb along the surface itself. The search returns protocols that are fully usable, not just abstract bounds. Applied to entanglement distillation, the method produced improved protocols. Some of them match upper bounds computed by a standard relaxation technique. State merging gained new protocols and sharper achievable bounds as well. The framework also covers two useful subclasses with post-selection. Manifold search may become a general tool for entanglement work.
arxiv-2510-07009:
Takahiro Matsumoto leads a team beaming live stage performances into venues, touch included. Their 2025 paper presents a tele-immersive entertainment system built on 3D point clouds. Performers are captured as point clouds under shifting stage lighting. Their footsteps are sensed as vibrations by wearable accelerometers.

Both streams travel to a venue in real time. There, a large 3D LED wall shows the performers, and a haptic floor replays their footsteps. The pipeline runs with under one hundred milliseconds of latency. A trial at Expo 2025 linked two sites twenty kilometers apart. Visitors watched a live dance show and chatted with the dancers naturally. The floor covered ninety square meters and used one hundred twenty-eight actuators. End-to-end delay measured eighty-one milliseconds in that deployment. The trial was the first stage-scale fusion of live 3D video and touch. Remote audiences gain presence that streaming cannot offer.
arxiv-2510-07509:
Pan and Woodard supply the missing theory for multimodal co-training, a scheme where models trained on different data views teach each other. Their 2025 paper addresses learning when labels are scarce and conditions shift. Two classifiers, say one reading images and one reading text, label unlabeled data for each other and retrain on the confident cases. Practitioners use the loop widely, but guarantees lagged behind. The authors derive conditions under which unlabeled data and enforced agreement between views genuinely improve generalization.

Their new generalization bound is the first in this setting to itemize the gains. It separates the contributions of unlabeled data volume, inter-view agreement, and conditional independence of the views. Knowing which ingredient pays lets practitioners design view pairs deliberately instead of hoping.
arxiv-2510-07809:
Ding and five coauthors wrote this 2025 security paper on attacks against AI agents that operate smartphones. Such agents read the screen and tap through apps for the user. Earlier attacks needed obvious overlays or special permissions, which limited their realism. The authors show a stealthier route that hides inside an app's interface text. The hidden prompt stays inert for users and wakes only when an agent drives the phone.

A touch-based trigger tells agent taps from human ones by their traits, exposing the payload only during agent operation. A search procedure then trims the payload so it slips past on-device safety filters at once. Across model backends and three Android apps, hijack rates ran. For GPT-4o, over eighty percent of planning attempts and three quarters of executions were hijacked in one shot. The study exposes a weakness in how mobile agents perceive content.
arxiv-2510-07909:
Chen, Lin, Li, and Ding wrote this 2025 paper on audio backdoors that hide inside watermarks. Data owners plant triggers in training audio so a trained model reveals its origin later. Older audio triggers degrade sound quality, and listeners can notice them. The authors ask whether ordinary watermarking, designed to be imperceptible, can serve as the trigger instead. Their framework, Bloodroot, tests exactly that idea.

An adversarial fine-tuning step sharpens the watermark trigger's effect. On speech recognition and speaker identification data, the poisoned audio kept high perceptual quality. Trigger success and clean-sample accuracy both ran higher than with conventional backdoors. The attack also survived acoustic filtering and model pruning. The authors present the work as both an ownership tool and a warning. Watermarking, usually a defensive technology, can be turned into a stealthy poisoning channel that defenders should watch.
arxiv-2510-08309:
Michael Gorczyca and co-authors fix a bias in how daily body rhythms are measured, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Gene activity, hormones, and body temperature all rise and fall on a roughly twenty-four-hour cycle. Studies link odd rhythms to cancer, metabolic syndrome, and sleep disorders. But peak times differ from person to person, which standard fits often ignore.

The standard tool, trigonometric regression, fits sine-like curves to rhythm data. When individual peaks shift, group-level amplitude estimates shrink toward zero, a flaw called attenuation bias. The authors propose a refined two-stage method that first fits each person's curve alone. It then combines transformed individual estimates into population values for inference. Simulations showed their method cut bias and raised statistical power over the standard two-stage approach. It also kept error rates at the correct level in repeated trials.
arxiv-2510-08409:
Yu-Han Wu and co-authors show that stopping diffusion generation early can be the right move in a 2025 arXiv paper. Latent diffusion models create images by denoising in a compressed latent space, not pixel space. Conventional wisdom holds that more final steps mean better samples, aside from numeric concerns. The authors find the last steps can actually degrade sample quality.

They trace the effect to the dimensionality reduction built into latent models. In a Gaussian framework with linear autoencoders, they characterize when early stopping minimizes distance to the target distribution. Lower-dimensional latent spaces benefit from earlier termination, they prove. Higher-dimensional spaces need later stopping times to reach their best quality. Latent dimension also interacts with other settings, like constraints in score matching training. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets confirmed the pattern, they report.
arxiv-2510-08709:
Maxwell Rosenthal ranks experiments without assuming any prior beliefs in a 2025 arXiv paper in decision theory. Blackwell's classic order compares experiments by their value to every Bayesian decision maker. Rosenthal's decision maker instead observes the whole signal distribution of a known experiment, under an unknown state distribution. She judges experiments by worst-case, maxmin expected utility.

An experiment counts as robustly more informative when the other one can be written as a linear transformation of it. Equivalently, the more informative experiment's null space sits inside the other's null space. Blackwell's order implies this prior-free criterion, while the reverse implication fails. An example shows the new ranking compares strictly more pairs of experiments than the classical one. More experiments become rankable, at the price of a coarser notion of informativeness. The result reframes experimental comparison for ambiguity-averse decision makers.
arxiv-2510-08809:
Anwar and colleagues shine light on the boundary where a solid meets a liquid and watch its electric state change, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such boundaries drive devices that turn sunlight or water motion into energy. Probing them without disturbing them is hard, because the signal from a single surface layer is faint. The team uses a light-doubling effect, boosted by tiny structures carved into silicon, to listen in.

Their nanostructured surface amplified the signal more than a hundredfold, giving live optical access. Gentle light charged the surface as light freed charge carriers that then got trapped. Stronger light instead heated the surface, and the heat shifted chemical reactions that set its charge. Saltier liquid also failed to behave as a classic theory predicts, showing a rise and fall tied to the surface geometry. The readings even showed the surface charge reshaping the silicon's own electronic response.
arxiv-2510-08909:
Zhang and colleagues show that gravity can switch on a counterintuitive heat effect in fluids, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The effect is negative differential thermal resistance: push a bigger temperature gap across a fluid and, past a point, less heat flows. It could power thermal switches and logic devices, much as its electrical cousin powers electronics. In fluids the effect was known only for weakly interacting systems, which limits designs.

Simulating a fluid of colliding particles, the team first derives the heat flow formula for a case they can solve exactly. Adding gravity along the driving direction greatly lowers the temperature gap needed to trigger the effect. Gravity also lets the heat-bath mechanism behind the effect work in strongly interacting fluids, where it previously failed. The behavior survived even in mixed fluids. The authors offer the results as a foundation for fluid-based thermal devices that exploit gravity.
arxiv-2510-09009:
Wang, Yurechko, and Zhang put users in charge of tuning the prompts that filter their own content, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models let anyone build a personal classifier from a plain description, but raw descriptions usually perform poorly. Automatic optimizers can sharpen them, yet they ignore how a person's goals for a filter shift between first setup and later use. They also return prompts the user cannot read or steer.

Promptimizer keeps the user in the loop at the points where preferences can be expressed, and it hands back a final prompt that stays interpretable. In a lab study, users significantly preferred it over a fully automatic optimizer. The team then built it into Puffin, a tool for YouTube creators filtering their comments. During a three-week deployment, ten creators built varied filters to understand their audiences and shield their communities.
arxiv-2510-09609:
K Mahesh Krishna, the sole author, extends a celebrated theorem of signal processing into abstract spaces in a 2025 arXiv paper. The sparsity theorem, proved independently by Donoho and Elad, by Gribonval and Nielsen, and by Fuchs in the early two thousands, gives good news about hard problems. It says the unique sparse solution of an NP-hard minimisation problem can be recovered from the unique solution of an easier companion problem.

Krishna carries that result from Hilbert spaces, the familiar geometry of signals, into general Banach spaces, a broader class of spaces where length still exists but angles may not. The key step is noticing that the normalised condition used in the Hilbert space proof can be generalised much further in the Banach setting. The paper presents the extension as a functional version of the theorem, widening the range of problems where sparse recovery guarantees apply.
arxiv-2510-09809:
Romain Allart and a large team of co-authors watch a giant planet's atmosphere escape into space in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ultra-hot Jupiters orbit so close to their stars that irradiation drives their atmospheres away, shaping their evolution and composition. The escaping gas is traced through a near-infrared helium line, which has measured mass loss for tens of planets but rarely mapped the outflow's extent.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope, the team monitored WASP-121b continuously over a full orbit, the first such helium phase curve. Helium absorption appears for nearly sixty percent of the orbit. The outflow separates into two tails, one trailing the planet and one leading it. The leading tail is denser and moves toward the star, while the trailing tail is pushed away and blue-shifted by the star's radiation pressure. Their velocity shifts suggest both tails stay collisional far from the planet.
arxiv-2510-10009:
Shu Zhao and co-authors train a search agent to expand its own queries in this 2025 arXiv paper on information retrieval. Reasoning search agents loop through thinking, searching, and answering. Even so, their scores on multi-hop question answering, which needs several linked facts, stay far from satisfactory.

The bottleneck, the authors argue, is reliance on a single query at each step. Their agent learns query expansion through reinforcement learning, widening a question into several searches that cover compound or complex needs. Better coverage of the question raises the chance that the needed facts are retrieved. The trained capability is native to the agent, rather than a fixed rule bolted on outside.
arxiv-2510-10209:
Merouani, Afif Boudaoud, and Riyadh Baghdadi release LOOPerSet in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning for compilers. The polyhedral model optimizes loop nests, the nested loops at the heart of scientific code, by reasoning about their geometry. Learning-based optimizers for it are starved of public performance data.

LOOPerSet is a large-scale dataset built to remove that bottleneck. Without shared data, each research group pays for its own costly measurement campaigns, and results cannot be reproduced. A common dataset lets learned optimizers be trained and compared fairly. The authors aim to speed up innovation in data-driven compiler optimization, where the quality of training data often decides which method wins.
arxiv-2510-10509:
Zihan Zhang and six co-authors rethink sound separation as a learning problem driven by meaning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Universal sound separation aims to pull one target sound out of a mixture. Models tuned only on signal level metrics often leave behind interference that sounds similar to the target, so the output stays semantically contaminated. Their system, MARS-Sep, instead learns separation through reinforcement learning, treating each masking choice as a decision.

MARS-Sep learns a mask policy and updates it with a clipped trust region method, a cautious style of policy improvement, plus rewards drawn from an encoder that links audio, text, and vision. Those rewards favor outputs that match the query in meaning, whether it comes as text, audio, or an image. A progressive alignment scheme sharpens the encoder itself. Across benchmarks, the system improved signal metrics and semantic quality for text, audio, and image queried separation.
arxiv-2510-10609:
Yiting Lu and ten co-authors build a single reward model that judges images on several kinds of quality at once, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Existing visual evaluation splits into separate tasks: technical quality for distortions, aesthetic quality for appeal, and text to image alignment for matching a prompt. Reward models guide generative systems, so a unified judge is valuable. Their framework, OmniQuality-R, turns multi task quality reasoning into continuous, interpretable reward signals.

To train it, they built a dataset of reasoning trajectories gathered by rejection sampling, forming chain of thought data for supervised fine tuning. They then applied a reinforcement method, Group Relative Policy Optimization, with a Gaussian based reward for continuous scores. Standard deviation filtering and entropy gating kept training stable. Tests on aesthetic, technical, and alignment tasks showed gains in robustness and generalization. The model can also guide image generation at test time with no retraining.
arxiv-2510-10709:
Kyla Chasalow, Skyler Wu, and Susan Murphy handle missing data in reinforcement learning that must act in real time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In online learning, an agent imputes missing values and acts at every step. Imputation cannot wait until enough data accumulates for a stable model. Worse, today's imputations shape tomorrow's data and learning. The team proposes fully online imputation ensembles, which keep several imputation pathways running at once.

Maintaining multiple pathways may balance two needs: capturing uncertainty about what is missing, and staying efficient enough for online use. The authors consider several ways to fold the pathways into learning and action selection for tabular Q-learning. In a Grid World experiment with various types of missingness, they find preliminary evidence that multiple imputation pathways help. They present the approach as a useful framework for simple, efficient online learning with missing data.
arxiv-2510-10909:
Daoyu Wang and six co-authors benchmark AI agents on real research work across many papers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reading and reasoning over the scientific literature is a key test for language model agents. Existing benchmarks mostly use tool free tasks inside single papers. Their benchmark, PaperArena, instead poses questions that require integrating information across multiple papers while using external tools. Agents must plan, interact with the papers, and invoke tools to produce a grounded answer.

The team provides an execution platform with a modular tool environment covering multimodal parsing, context retrieval, and programmatic computation. The results are humbling. Even the leading language model inside a well established agentic workflow reached only 38.78 percent average accuracy. On the hard subset, accuracy fell to 18.47 percent in their experiments. They also analyze reasoning traces to diagnose where agents go wrong.
arxiv-2510-11009:
Jiamin Liang and five co-authors propose listening for gravitational waves with spinning nuclei, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Detectors have opened gravitational wave astronomy, but high frequency waves, from kilohertz to gigahertz, remain undetected. The team derives how spins respond to a passing wave and identifies three effects: the known Gertsenshtein effect, a metric induced interaction, and a gravitational spin Hall effect. Nuclear spins are attractive sensors because they stay coherent for long times and can be highly polarized.

The scheme reads the spins out with nuclear magnetic resonance, a mature laboratory technique. Their small gyromagnetic ratio, usually a drawback, here helps tune the response. The projected sensitivity reaches about ten to the minus twentieth in strain noise units across the kilohertz to gigahertz band in their estimates. That band is almost completely unexplored: interferometers excel at low frequencies, and no instrument currently covers these high tones.
arxiv-2510-11509:
Rooms change: chairs move, objects vanish, and an assistant that cannot notice gives stale directions. Ruiping Liu and co-authors build a dataset for teaching multimodal language models to understand such changes in 3D scenes in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. Situat3DChange frames change understanding as three situation-aware tasks following a perception-action model: answering questions, describing what changed, and issuing instructions to rearrange a scene back.

The dataset holds 121 thousand question-answer pairs, 36 thousand change descriptions, and 17 thousand rearrangement instructions, built from 11 thousand human observations of real environmental changes. Observations mix egocentric and allocentric viewpoints with categorical and coordinate spatial relations. Because comparing two point clouds of the same scene with minor differences is hard. The authors also propose SCReasoner, a 3D multimodal model that compares point clouds with minimal extra parameters and no extra decoder tokens.
arxiv-2510-11609:
Screening experiments test many factors at once with fractional factorial designs, and choosing a good design means minimizing aliasing, the confusion between effects that the fraction cannot separate. Xietao Zhou and Steven G. Gilmour prove a theorem about the generalized word count in this 2025 arXiv statistics paper. The generalized word count pattern is a sequence of numbers summarizing aliasing between effects of each size, and it underlies criteria such as minimum aberration used to rank competing designs.

Their theorem concerns unreplicated two-level designs, the workhorse setting where each treatment combination is run once.  The payoff is explanatory: a phenomenon about optimal designs that had been observed in the recent literature, without a theoretical reason, follows from their theorem. The paper sits in design theory alongside the older minimum aberration criterion for regular designs and the G2-aberration generalization for non-regular ones, .
arxiv-2510-11709:
Edward Stevinson, Lucas Prieto, Melih Barsbey, and Tolga Birdal offer a new explanation for adversarial attacks on neural networks. These attacks are tiny, carefully chosen changes to an input that flip a network's answer. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that the weakness comes from superposition. Superposition means a network stores more features than it has dimensions, so features overlap and interfere with each other.

The team shows that attack patterns can be predicted from how features are arranged in that overlapping code. In synthetic setups where they control the overlap exactly, they prove that superposition alone is enough to create the vulnerability. The same effects then appear in a vision transformer trained on the CIFAR-10 image dataset. Their framework also explains two known puzzles: why attacks transfer between similar models, and why some classes fall more easily. Vulnerability, they conclude, can be a side effect of efficient compression.
arxiv-2510-11809:
Miguel G. Echevarria, Raj Kishore, and Samuel F. Romera calculate how J/psi particles are produced when electrons strike protons. The J/psi is a heavy particle made of a charm quark and its antiquark. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in the regime where the produced particle drifts sideways only slightly. There, a framework called transverse-momentum-dependent factorization splits the process into simpler pieces.

The team computed the hard function, one of those pieces, to next-to-leading order, meaning with one layer of quantum corrections included. They also analyzed the shape function, which encodes how the charm pair binds, from its operator-level definition. The paper shows how this shape function combines with the gluon distribution inside the proton. Finally, the authors predict the full production rate for the future Electron-Ion Collider, a machine now being built in the United States. The predictions target exactly that region.
arxiv-2510-12109:
Zhao Zhang and Na Ou push uncertainty through porous rock without drowning in dimensions. Models of flow in porous media depend on random parameters, and forward uncertainty accounting asks how that randomness infects the forecasts. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends the stochastic finite volume method by grouping samples in parameter space instead of gridding it.

Classic versions lay a structured grid over the parameters, which explodes in combinations as dimensions grow. Grouping replaces the grid with data-driven clusters, extending the method to spaces with more dimensions. The authors construct schemes for the standard trio of parameter equations: elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic, all in Darcy flow settings. They supply error analysis for the new version, then show and check it on typical reservoir test cases. For engineers forecasting oil, water, or contaminant flows, the payoff is uncertainty estimates that stay cheap as models gain realistic complexity.
arxiv-2510-12509:
Liu and colleagues plan the movements of a robot arm that prunes fruit trees, a task where branches block every path, in a 2025 arXiv robotics paper. Pruning keeps orchards healthy, but it needs seasonal skilled labor, motivating automation. Earlier robotic pruning research focused on perception, seeing the tree, while guiding a cutter through tangled branches got less attention.

The authors formulate behavior planning for a high dimensional arm in the pruning setting, where planning and control must work in both joint and Cartesian space. They investigate the system's intrinsic redundancies, the extra ways a many jointed arm can reach the same pose, and propose a full workflow integrating perception, modeling, and holistic planning. Experiments show that fuller planning greatly improves the manipulator's performance. The workflow was also implemented on a real world robot, and the authors present the work as a complement to perception focused efforts.
arxiv-2510-12609:
Heesterbeek and colleagues reconstruct tissue stiffness from internal motion alone, without needing to know what happens at the tissue's boundary, in a 2025 arXiv medical imaging paper. Elastography images mechanical properties of soft tissue, which disease often changes. The standard magnetic resonance approach uses dynamic shaking, but tissue's viscoelastic nature makes results depend on the shaking rate.

Their framework instead uses quasi static displacement fields captured on the time scale of body motion, with squashing induced by a pneumatic pressure cuff. The method needs no boundary information, which is hard to obtain inside the body, and avoids spatial slopes of the displacement field, which amplify noise. Computer tests on a numerical phantom checked the method. Tests on a volunteer's thigh showed the rebuild repeats reliably. As an application, muscle stiffness changes during knee flexion came out meaningful for the body, supporting the approach as a rate independent option.
arxiv-2510-12809:
Max proposes a taxonomy for artificial general intelligence in this 2025 arXiv paper, arguing that policy debates blur two very different kinds of systems. Some AGI would be built for open commercial use, while other systems would serve sovereign, security-focused states. Treating both under older dual-use ideas, which only ask whether a tool has civilian and military uses, misses the different social worlds that produce them.

His scheme separates low-AGI from high-AGI, borrowing the high and low politics distinction from international relations and viewing it through construal-level theory, a psychology framework about mental distance. By placing AGI inside power structures and securitization theory, the study of how issues become security matters, the taxonomy aims to sharpen risk assessment. Max argues it can help policymakers anticipate security dilemmas and other technical-political spillovers.
arxiv-2510-13309:
Arimoto proves that the canonical actions of the Thompson groups are not strongly ergodic in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The Thompson groups, introduced in nineteen sixty-five, act naturally on the Cantor set, and strong ergodicity is a rigidity property saying almost invariant sets must be almost trivial. Whether these actions have it bears on the operator algebras built from them.

Arimoto shows the canonical actions of Thompson's group V and its generalizations fail strong ergodicity. A direct consequence is that the crossed-product von Neumann algebras attached to them are not full, meaning they admit nontrivial central sequences, a structural weakness with classification implications. The paper also extracts a result ruling out certain embeddings of the Thompson groups themselves. The work complements earlier results on inner amenability, together painting a detailed picture of how these groups sit between amenability and its strongest failures.
arxiv-2510-13409:
Ahuja, Chowdhury, and Mohapatra speed up the QR method for eigenvalues of square matrices. Their 2025 arXiv paper deals with non-Hermitian matrices, whose eigenvalues can be complex. Plain QR methods converge slowly on such matrices and waste many steps. For Hermitian ones, fast and stable QR methods already exist. Eigenvalues anchor tools across physics and engineering.

Their version adds smarter shifts and early deflation, which drops finished parts from the work. On random test matrices of many sizes, it converges faster than prior QR methods and keeps accuracy high. The gains held in all test cases the team ran. Mid-to-large matrices gain the most, even at fifty rows and columns. Fewer steps also cut the cost of each run, the authors note. They aim at fast, exact eigenvalue work for real-world use.
arxiv-2510-13509:
Fumagalli and the Euclid Consortium examine how systematic effects distort cosmology from galaxy cluster surveys. Their 2025 arXiv paper supports the Euclid space survey, which counts clusters and maps their clustering. Both probes can pin down the matter density and the clumpiness of the universe. Errors in observing and modelling can bias those answers if left unchecked.

The team built one thousand Euclid-like cluster catalogues to stress-test the analysis. They tracked how uncertainties shift cluster statistics and their covariance structure. A likelihood analysis then measured the damage to cosmological constraints. Combining clustering with number counts sharpened constraints greatly, more than tripling the figure of merit over counts alone in their tests. The two probes proved essentially uncorrelated, which strengthens the joint result. The paper also gives model recipes for analysing both probes together.
arxiv-2510-13709:
Ellis and co-authors train language model assistants to empower their users instead of replacing them. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that helpful agents should act, yet also step back at key decisions. Standard training, by imitation or reward tuning, pushes agents to finish tasks solo. It also leans on costly explicit human feedback for its signal.

Their method, Empower, instead maximizes the human's own ability to change the environment. It fine-tunes models on offline text alone, with no fresh human labels or checkable rewards. In an eighteen-person study, users preferred the empowerment assistant in most head-to-head comparisons. They accepted its suggestions more often while receiving fewer of them overall. A new simulated coding environment tests multi-turn help with a fake human programmer. There, Empower-trained agents raised the simulated user's success rate on hard coding questions sharply over supervised baselines.
arxiv-2510-14409:
Tatsuru Kikuchi builds a framework that treats treatment effects as continuous fields flowing over space and time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The fields obey the same equations as fluid dynamics. Econometrics estimates treatment effects at points. Interventions like pollution controls spill across boundaries. The author wants language for how effects spread, where their boundaries sit, and how exposure accumulates.

With treatment intensity as a function over space-time, the framework builds on self-similar solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations, yielding scaling laws for how effects decay with distance and time. Validation uses forty-two million observations of nitrogen dioxide around United States coal plants, finding strong exponential decay with effect boundaries hundreds of kilometers out. Monte Carlo simulations show the approach beats discrete methods at boundary detection and false-positive avoidance. Analysis confirms the diagnostics behave near the plants.
arxiv-2510-14709:
Robinson and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a practical way to find whales in satellite images without first training a detector. Counting whales matters for conservation, but ship and aerial surveys are costly and hard to scale. Whales do appear in very high-resolution satellite imagery. The catch is searching enormous archives by eye, with almost no labeled examples to train on.

Their approach uses statistical anomaly detection to flag spatial outliers, points that look unusual against the ocean background. Experts then check only those flagged points in a web interface built for fast labeling. On three benchmark scenes with known whale positions, the system recalled between 90.3 and 96.4 percent of the whales in the reported tests. It shrank the area needing expert inspection by up to 99.8 percent, in some cases from over a thousand square kilometers to under two. The whole pipeline is open source.
arxiv-2510-14809:
Wallström and a large team of co-authors release, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the first batch of carbon monoxide observations from the Nearby Evolved Stars Survey. Dying low- and intermediate-mass stars return gas and dust to space, enriching the material between stars. Measuring that return for a fair sample is the survey's goal: about 850 evolved stars within three kiloparsecs, observed with several telescopes.

This release covers 485 sources observed with the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, reduced with a new pipeline built for uniformity. It is one of the largest homogeneous samples of its kind, with carbon isotope ratios, early mass-loss rates, and gas-to-dust ratios. Detection rates reached about four-fifths of sources in the main carbon monoxide line. Older samples over-represent stars with high mass loss, especially carbon-rich ones. This survey reaches far more quiet stars, including fifty-nine first-time detections.
arxiv-2510-15409:
Azalea Gui and colleagues at Sony AI and the University of Toronto clean corrupted training data for music separation models without knowing what the corruption is. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles datasets where songs bleed into the wrong tracks or labels are wrong, flaws that teach models bad habits. Cleaners built for one specific flaw fail when the damage type is unknown.

The team tests two noise-agnostic cleaners. One uses data attribution via unlearning, scoring each training sample by how much removing it would help, then drops the least helpful samples. The other measures how unlike a small trusted clean set each sample sounds and removes the outliers. On a dataset dosed with simulated real-world noise, the unlearning cleaner won. Its model beat training on the dirty data and even on the small clean set alone, closing about two-thirds of the gap to a contamination-free model.
arxiv-2510-15609:
Inflation theory usually treats the inflaton as a single scalar field driving early cosmic expansion. Lin-Hong Sui and three co-authors study a version where a fermion field couples to it directly. The coupling is a Yukawa interaction, the same kind that links particles to the Higgs field. Working in the slow-roll regime, the team solves the Dirac equation for fermions during inflation. Their fermion pair density formula shows the coupling controls how far the system departs from adiabatic behavior.

For heavy effective masses, the predicted ratio of gravitational waves to density ripples drops sharply. That regime also shows strong backreaction on the expanding background. For light masses, predictions match standard cold inflation results.
arxiv-2511-00109:
Karl Dilcher and Christophe Vignat extend classes of infinite series involving central binomial coefficients. Starting from a known family depending on a positive integer setting, they first extend identities to all complex settings. Exponential Bell polynomials and integral representations then push the results further, with extensive use of gamma and polygamma functions.

Special functions readers get new evaluations and identities for series that appear across combinatorics and analysis. Central binomial coefficients sit at many crossroads, from probability to number theory, so each closed form can simplify calculations elsewhere. The paper's method mix shows how several standard tools combine on one series family.
arxiv-2511-00409:
Sourendu Gupta, Pritam Sen, and Rishi Sharma write an effective field theory for hot quantum chromodynamics just below the crossover temperature, where quarks and gluons settle into ordinary matter. Effective theories trade fine detail for a few constants that capture long-distance behavior. The team fixes those constants from lattice simulations of pion screening masses at two temperatures, using realistic quark masses for the three-flavor case and a heavier pion for the two-flavor case.

The theory then predicts other static pion properties where lattice results exist, and it matches them well. For the three-flavor case it offers predictions not yet measured, an excellent account of the phase diagram, pressure estimates, and a real-time quantity called the kinetic mass. The work shows a simple long-distance theory can organize a strongly interacting system.
arxiv-2511-00609:
Shengqi Xu and eight co-authors tackle personalized image preference: judging what one specific user will like, given only a few reference images. General preference models train on large data for well-defined tasks, but personal taste is scarce in data, diverse, and complex. Their bridge is a common preference profile, a shared description format that lets large-scale user data train a profile predictor usable for individuals.

The framework follows a predict-then-assess pattern. First it predicts a user's profile from the reference images, then it scores candidate images across several dimensions with interpretable reasoning. A large chain-of-thought dataset with diverse profiles supervises the reasoning, and two-stage training, supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, sharpens it further. A similarity-aware reward improves profile prediction, and experiments show the method beating rivals.
arxiv-2511-00809:
Yang Xu, Haibin Kan, and Guangyue Han revisit two classic questions in coding theory, but for a weighted version of the Hamming metric. In this setting each coordinate carries its own positive weight, so errors in different positions can count differently toward a code word's weight.

Using only elementary linear algebra and two identities proved by double counting, they characterize when weight preserving maps between codes can be extended to the whole space. They also describe all constant weight codes under this metric. Setting every weight to one recovers two known results for the ordinary Hamming case, including the fact that constant weight codes are repetitions of the dual of the Hamming code.
arxiv-2511-01009:
Fabricio Olivetti de Franca and Gabriel Kronberger aim to cut wasted work in symbolic regression, the search for formulas that fit data. Genetic programming, the standard search method, spends much of its time re-evaluating expressions that are equivalent to ones already tried, because neutral plateaus in the search space must be crossed.

Their algorithm, SymRegg, is built around an equality graph, a structure that stores many equivalent expressions compactly. Candidate solutions are sampled from the graph and perturbed; a result is evaluated only if it is genuinely new, then inserted with its equal forms. Across data sets, SymRegg kept accuracy in line with the standard approach while searching more efficiently, and it needs only a small set of hyperparameters.
arxiv-2511-01209:
Sophia Adams improves thermal bootstrap methods for matrix quantum mechanics, a technique that bounds a system's energies using only symmetry and self consistency conditions. The targets are anharmonic oscillator models with one and two large matrices, studied in the large N limit.

Using a conic optimization solver, she bounds the thermal energies without the logarithmic relaxation earlier work relied on. Stricter bounds apply to the one matrix model. At low temperature it can be read as a theory of long strings. The bounds pin the first long string excitation energy to within a tiny fraction of a percent of its physical value. The same equations yield the first estimate of the first long string coupling coefficient obtained from symmetry and self consistency alone.
arxiv-2511-01909:
Ethan Abraham dissolves a decades-old contradiction in electron transfer chemistry. Marcus theory predicts that once the driving force for an electron hop exceeds the reorganization energy, the transfer rate should fall, the famous inverted region. Yet many measured systems instead show Rehm-Weller behavior, the rate leveling off rather than dropping.

Abraham shows both patterns emerge from one microscopic model, a two-state quantum Hamiltonian, as opposite physical limits. In the normal region the model reproduces both behaviors. In the inverted region it gives Marcus's falling rate in the nonadiabatic limit but Rehm-Weller saturation in the adiabatic limit. The model uses realistic reorganization energies and electronic couplings. It quantitatively reproduces the original Rehm-Weller data, with no ad hoc patches. The paradox is reframed as a question of which limit a given system lives in.
arxiv-2511-02009:
Everett McArthur, Martin Millon, Meredith Powell, Risa Wechsler, and dozens of DESI collaborators search for quasars that act as gravitational lenses, their gravity bending light from galaxies behind them. Such systems let astronomers weigh the quasar's host galaxy from the Einstein radius and trace how black hole and host masses grew together.

From about 812,000 quasars in DESI's first data release, the team hunted background emission lines hiding in quasar spectra. A convolutional network trained on mock lenses built from real quasar and galaxy spectra reached near-perfect classification, and a regression network estimated the background galaxy's redshift. The pipeline found seven high-quality lens candidates, each showing a strong oxygen doublet from beyond the quasar, four with hydrogen and oxygen lines as well. The haul significantly expands the known candidate sample beyond the dozen found previously.
arxiv-2511-02109:
Joshua Ashkinaze, Hua Shen, Saipranav Avula, Eric Gilbert, and Ceren Budak introduce a benchmark that asks whether language models learn people's deep values or only their surface preferences. The distinction matters for alignment: a system keyed to surface patterns may behave badly when situations change.
