Their design deliberately entangles the two during training, pairing moral principles with shallow features such as writing style in human preference data.

At test time the pairings are reversed, forcing a choice between the deep value and the shallow feature. Across nine models, the rate of generalising by deep value averaged only 0.30, below chance for every model tested, and larger models scored slightly worse than smaller ones. The dataset was checked through three human validation studies.
arxiv-2511-02309:
Aman Sharma and Paras Chopra challenge the standard recipe for squeezing better reasoning out of language models at test time. The dominant approach spends extra computation on many independent attempts run in parallel, then takes a majority vote, a method called self-consistency. The alternative is sequential: fewer chains, where each new attempt builds on the previous ones and refines them. The authors compared the two at exactly matched token budgets and compute.

Across five leading open-source models and three hard reasoning benchmarks, sequential scaling won in 95.6 percent of configurations, with accuracy gains reaching 46.7 percent. They also introduce inverse-entropy voting, which weights each answer by how confident its reasoning chain was, and show it improves sequential scaling further. Their conclusion is that refinement, not repetition, should be the default way to spend inference-time compute.
arxiv-2511-02409:
Saumyajit Das, Tuhin Ghosh, and Susovan Pramanik solve an inverse problem. Can the shape of a closed surface-like space, and a potential, be recovered from boundary-style readings of waves? This is the Calderón problem, here made harder by anisotropy and by a nonlocal logarithmic Schrödinger operator of order above two. It is built from the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a Riemannian manifold of dimension at least two.

The authors show that the Cauchy data of the operator determine both the metric and the potential, a result holding without extra conditions when both manifolds share the same space. For distinct manifolds, measurements on a nonempty region pin down the manifold up to isometry and the potential up to a gauge freedom. That holds without conditions when the potential lives inside the observed region, and under geometric assumptions otherwise. Results of this strength are rare for nonlocal operators.
arxiv-2511-02509:
R. Alberich and five co-authors build a method for picking out the microbes that distinguish one health state from another, in data with a statistical trap. Sequencing a microbiome sample yields shares, not absolute amounts, and standard tools mislead on such data. Their framework classifies samples with a multinomial model built on log-ratio regression with a penalty, after screening every pair of taxa, called OTUs, for separability.

Each taxon's discriminative power is scored by the area under the receiver operating curve for all its pairwise log-ratios. The scores are then aggregated into a global separability index with confidence intervals, giving an interpretable ranking. Re-checking a colorectal adenoma dataset, the method recovered the core discriminant taxa found by an earlier ranking-based study. Adjusting for age, gender, and diabetes medication sharpened the index and promoted extra taxa, suggesting part of the original signal was confounding.
arxiv-2511-02809:
Matteo D'Anna, Jannes Nys, and Juan Carrasquilla present a new algorithm for simulating how fermion systems evolve in real time. Such dynamics are a frontier problem: classical methods struggle, yet the behavior matters for chemistry, materials, and quantum technology. Their 2025 method works in the Heisenberg picture, evolving the observables rather than the state.

Observables are written in a Majorana-string basis and trimmed by a truncation scheme that keeps Trotter accuracy. For quadratic Hamiltonians the method is exact, staying inside a fixed low-weight sector set by the observable. Interacting cases use controlled truncations, and varied starting states are allowed. Benchmarks on Fermi-Hubbard quenches in one and two dimensions match tensor network methods and recent experiments, holding accuracy on par with the best variational tools.
arxiv-2511-02909:
Conny Aerts measures how fast nearly three thousand middling stars spin, using the stars' own vibrations as the probe. Spectroscopic spin measures blur because the tilt of each star is unknown, and surface turbulence adds extra widening. In a 2025 study, Aerts uses asteroseismology on 2,937 gravity-mode pulsators of B, A, and F types across the Milky Way. Their masses run from one point three to eight point eight times the Sun's mass.

The sample spins from nearly zero up to periods just above a third of a day. Between two point three and two point seven solar masses, the spin per unit mass shows a clear break. Lighter stars share one smooth pattern, while heavier ones show extra structure. Near-core spin slows as stars age, pointing to very efficient transport of angular momentum inside. The catalog gives modelers firm targets.
arxiv-2511-03109:
Abraham Khan, Chao Chen, Vishwas Rao, and Arvind Saibaba speed up kernel matrices whose settings must be tuned again and again. Kernel matrices appear across machine learning and computing, and hierarchical matrices already compress them by splitting near parts, stored densely, from far parts, stored in low-rank form. But standard builders ignore that the kernel depends on hyperparameters, as in Gaussian processes, so each tuning step pays full price.

Their parametric hierarchical matrices split the work in two. An offline stage approximates the blocks with polynomials and tensor compression, once. An online stage then assembles the matrix for any chosen settings with no new kernel evaluations, and cheaper far-field blocks. Tests showed speedups over one hundredfold against existing techniques, at similar offline cost.
arxiv-2511-03509:
Davood Momeni and Ratbay Myrzakulov work out how black hole entropy changes in a broad family of modified gravity theories. Those theories blend curvature with torsion and non-metricity, the ways a geometry can twist and fail to preserve lengths. Wald's classic entropy formula is derived anew for each subclass with a frame-based method.

Extra geometric freedom adds systematic correction terms to the entropy, the authors show. The corrections arise while keeping the theory's core symmetry intact, so the thermodynamics stays consistent. Such results refine how physicists think about heat and information in gravity beyond Einstein's picture. They also give model builders a check: any new theory must yield a sane entropy story.
arxiv-2511-03709:
Nick Dorey and Paul Luis Roehl examine the giant graviton expansion for three-dimensional superconformal field theories with a high level of supersymmetry, working in a simplifying limit. Their focus is the hidden mathematical content of the expansion coefficients for theories tied to M2-branes on a particular cone geometry.

Coefficients turn out to connect with Hilbert series of quiver varieties and with representation theory for vertex algebras. For the brane setup studied, the authors derive an explicit formula using affine fermionic forms. Those coefficients match characters of a direct sum of parafermionic W-algebras. The link ties a counting problem in physics to concrete structures in algebra and geometry.
arxiv-2511-04009:
Chenzui Li, Yiming Chen, Xi Wu, Giacinto Barresi, and Fei Chen present a posture optimization method for two-armed human-robot co-carrying that pursues ergonomics and force manipulability together. Earlier work usually stressed human safety or handling efficiency alone, leaving a gap when grasp postures and object shapes vary.

Joint angles of a simplified human skeleton are optimized with a cost function that rewards safer, more capable postures. Robot end-effector targets then guide the person toward that posture, and a model predictive impedance controller recalibrates motion along planned paths. Tests in human-human and human-robot carrying showed clear improvement in target muscle activation after optimization.
arxiv-2511-04209:
Monica Conte, Rene van Roij, and Marjolein Dijkstra present a brain-like microfluidic network that learns physically instead of digitally. Nodes are joined by conical, electrolyte-filled channels acting as memristive iontronic synapses, whose conductance responds to electrical, chemical, mechanical, and geometric changes alike.

Forward passes happen through ionic easing in the fluid itself. Training adjusts channel shape or applied stimuli while numeric gradient descent guides the updates from outside. Input-output mapping and linear regression with bias are shown in theory. The vision is soft, adaptive materials that compute and learn without standard electronics, using the same multi-way sensitivity that makes the channels useful as sensors.
arxiv-2511-04509:
Christoph Kopper and his co-author relate triviality to perturbation theory in four-dimensional phi-four theory. The model, with O(N) symmetry, is a mean-field test case for quantum field theory. In earlier work they built its trivial solution using renormalization group flow equations.

Here they connect that solution to plain perturbation theory order by order. With an ultraviolet cutoff kept in place, a renormalized coupling can be defined cleanly. They prove the resulting series is locally Borel-summable. It also matches the non-perturbative solution as an asymptotic series, settling how the two views of the theory fit together.
arxiv-2511-04609:
Mladen Dimitrov and his co-author generalize a classic Manin bound to abelian three-folds. Fifty years ago, Manin showed uniform limits on cyclic isogenies between non-CM elliptic curves. The bound depends only on the number field and the chosen prime.

The pair treats two-dimensional families of abelian three-folds of Picard type. These varieties carry multiplication by an imaginary quadratic field. Uniform irreducibility of the Galois action on the prime-primary part is the core result. Such uniformity controls how symmetries of torsion points can vary across a whole family, a central question in arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2511-04709:
Sébastien Aumaître and his co-author model a granular phase change from the particle level up. Shaken grains in tight spaces can split into solid-like and liquid-like zones. Reports differ on whether that change is sharp or smooth.

In the solid patch, grains move together with the shaking cell, like a collect-and-collide damper. The authors model that patch as one effective particle with zero restitution. Mechanics of that single body then drives the coexistence picture. A microscopic origin story like this helps explain why similar shaken systems show both kinds of transition.
arxiv-2511-05509:
Joel Valdivia Ortega and co-authors tackle a flaw in DINOv2, a vision model used on both medical scans and normal photos. The model often leans on weak image patches, which makes its focus maps hard to read and hurts trust. Shifts between hospitals or data sets can make the problem worse.

Their fix, called Randomized-MLP regularization, is added while fine-tuning the model. It pushes the model toward features that line up better with real meaning in the image. Tests on medical and natural images show equal or better scores and clearer attention maps. The team also gives a math analysis of why the method helps.
arxiv-2511-06209:
Jingwei Ni and colleagues present ReProbe, a light way to check each step of a language model's reasoning as it is produced. Checking steps can raise accuracy, but standard reward models are costly and need large amounts of labeled data. ReProbe instead reads the model's own internal states while it generates text.

A small transformer probe, trained on those internal states, estimates how credible each reasoning step is. Labels can come from a larger model or from the model itself in a self-supervised way. With under ten million parameters, the probes matched or beat reward models up to eight hundred ten times larger across math, planning, and question answering.
arxiv-2511-06509:
Alexander Bratus, Sergei Drozhzhin, and Artem Novozhilov model consumers and resources that each split into subspecies that affect each other. Think predators and prey, where each side also competes or cooperates within its own ranks, while the consumer harms the resource it feeds on. Most models ignore those within-side effects, yet they can change who wins.

Ecology runs fast and evolution runs slow in their framework, with evolutionary steps chosen by the opposing fitness goals of consumer and resource. Simulations show the expected victories for either side, but also a near-steady coexistence where both fitnesses keep growing. Within-group ties, the authors argue, can underwrite long-term ecological stability.
arxiv-2511-06809:
Feng Wang and four co-authors study what happens over long times when salty water freezes in a closed, convecting system. The ice that forms is mushy and porous, trapping brine inside it. Their work combines lab tests with theory to follow the coupled flow, heat transfer, salt movement, and phase change.

A mushy layer forms quickly, then slowly gives up its salt, and as it desalinates its pores shrink and the ice can slowly thin. Weaker convection inside the layer feeds back on further desalination. The team shows a one-dimensional model with suitable global parameters predicts this long-term behavior accurately, and they use it to explore wider conditions, with sea ice aging as a natural application.
arxiv-2511-07809:
Sara Kangaslahti, Danny Ebanks, and Jean Kossaifi scale topic modeling to billions of political documents. Classic topic models choke long before that size. Tensor Latent Dirichlet Allocation recasts the model so parameters can be identified and recovered with guarantees, and so computation grows only linearly with corpus size.

The online tensor method runs three to four times faster than parallel predecessors while using modest memory. An open-source graphics processor implementation accompanies the theory. At billion-document scale, scholars can track themes across entire news or social archives rather than samples. The team demonstrates the method on political text, where scale changes which questions are askable.
arxiv-2511-07909:
Hengjun Xu and Takashi Goda scatter points evenly over triangles, a basic need in graphics, simulation, and integration. Quasi-uniform sets keep points from clumping or leaving holes, measured by the mesh ratio. Their Voronoi-guided greedy packing repeatedly adds the candidate point farthest from the current set.

After finitely many steps the mesh ratio reaches at most two, which is provably optimal. Two existing low-discrepancy triangle sets are also shown to have bounded ratios, certifying their uniformity. Constructive guarantees beat empirical point sets because simulations inherit the worst gap, not the average one. Triangular domains tile everything from terrain to finite elements.
arxiv-2511-08109:
Yuxuan Liu, Haim Dubossarsky, and Ruth Ahnert measure how science fiction loosens the groups human, animal, and machine. Literary theory calls this estrangement, following Darko Suvin, but the effect is hard to measure. The team uses masked language modelling on science fiction and general fiction sets to turn the idea into numbers.

RoBERTa proposes swap words for masked terms, and the swaps are classified to track category crossing. Retention, replacement, and entropy scores show science fiction has higher conceptual permeability, above all around machine terms. Human terms stay more coherent and anchor the substitutions, suggesting estrangement works as a controlled shake up of semantic norms.
arxiv-2511-08509:
Xueqi Guo and co-authors propose a fast framework for segmenting many organs at once in three dimensional CT scans, a basic step in clinical automation pipelines. Running a neural network over every voxel of a full volume is slow and memory hungry, while point classifiers trade away accuracy. Their method samples the volume hierarchically and sparsely, keeping context at several resolutions while skipping most of the volume.

A residual transformer network then merges information across those levels at low computational cost. On an internal set of more than ten thousand CT images and the public TotalSegmentator data, segmentation quality improves over the current fast organ classifier. Speed reaches about two seconds per scan on ordinary CPU hardware.
arxiv-2511-09009:
Jakkapat Seeyangnok, Udomsilp Pinsook, and Graeme Ackland compute what hydrogen does to a family of layered superconductors built from metal tetraboride sheets. The parent compounds, with beryllium, magnesium, calcium, or aluminum between boron sheets, were already predicted to carry current with no loss, calcium's version most strongly at about thirty-six kelvin.

Adding hydrogen to make trilayer stacks keeps the materials metallic, with boron orbitals dominating the states at the Fermi level, while reshaping the bands and Fermi surface. Phonon math confirms dynamical stability and strong electron-phonon coupling, yielding more than one gap in three of the four compounds. Calcium's hydrogenated version couples most strongly, reaching a predicted sixty-four kelvin, while the aluminum one is weakest at twenty-two kelvin. The spread shows how swapping elements tunes these layered superconductors.
arxiv-2511-09209:
Tianle Pu and seven co-authors aim to speed up mixed-integer linear programming, a workhorse of combinatorial optimization, with graph neural networks. These networks predict good solutions, but the authors find two mismatches with how such problems really work. Standard training treats variables independently, and standard message passing smooths variable features together.

Their system, CoCo-MILP, adds a contrastive loss that separates the embeddings of variables set to one from those set to zero. A new competitive network layer also sharpens, rather than blends, the features of variables competing inside one constraint. On standard benchmarks, CoCo-MILP beats earlier learning-based methods by a wide margin. The authors report solution gaps reduced by up to about 68 percent against traditional solvers.
arxiv-2511-09409:
A. C. S. Readhead leads a 26-author team reporting firm evidence for two linked rhythms in a distant blazar's radio light. The object, PKS J1309+1154, is a candidate pair of supermassive black holes orbiting each other. Forty-six years of monitoring from Michigan and Owens Valley observatories trace its brightness at radio frequencies.

The light curve shows a period of about eighteen years, plus a first harmonic near nine years. The authors argue both periodicities are real, the first watertight case of a fundamental and harmonic together in a blazar. That strengthens the binary interpretation considerably. They expect observatories like Vera Rubin to reveal hundreds more candidates for gravitational-wave searches.
arxiv-2511-09609:
Yini Li, Louis Forster, David Bull, and Nantheera Anantrasirichai brighten low-light videos without any paired training examples. Collecting matched dark and bright video is impractical because lighting and camera settings keep shifting. Their unsupervised approach, TempRetinex, builds on the Retinex idea that an image separates into illumination and reflectance.

A preprocessing step aligns brightness profiles across exposures, making the model robust to varied lighting. A multiscale time loss and occlusion-aware masking keep consecutive frames consistent, while reverse inference repairs unstable frames. A self-ensemble step further denoises across textures. The authors report state-of-the-art perceptual quality on their tests, making TempRetinex fit real footage shot under uncontrolled, diverse lighting.
arxiv-2511-10309:
Xiaomei Yang and six co-authors match people across visible-light and infrared cameras, a re-identification task where the two image types differ wildly in character. Their network, CLIP4VI-ReID, uses text as a bridge: a generation module writes identity-related text semantics for visible images only, aligning visible and text features first. An embedding module then corrects infrared features using that text, injecting identity semantics into the shared image encoder.

A final alignment stage refines the text so it carries only identity information, sharpening cross-modal matching and the distinctiveness of the shared representations. Because the infrared side aligns to visible images indirectly through language, the physical gap between spectra is sidestepped. Experiments on widely used visible-infrared re-identification datasets beat prior state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2511-10409:
Kayla Boggess, Sarit Kraus, and Lu Feng study how to explain the behavior of decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning systems. In these systems, several learning agents act on local information, so their joint choices can be hard to predict or audit. Most explanation tools assume a central controller, which decentralized settings do not have.

Their methods summarize a policy by showing task ordering and how agents cooperate with each other. They also answer user questions of three kinds: when something happens, why an alternative did not, and what would change an outcome. Tests span four domains and two learning algorithms, and user studies found the explanations improved people's answers and their sense of understanding.
arxiv-2511-10509:
Alexander Logunov and Dmitrii Zakharov contribute a construction to the minimal distance problem, a question in discrete geometry about how points and lines can be arranged while keeping unwanted close approaches away. Their setup places pairs of points and lines inside the unit square.

For any number n, they build a collection of n points and n lines such that each point lies on its own line. Its distance to every other line stays above a bound that decays more slowly than simple constructions achieve. The improvement over the trivial construction is a polynomial factor. The arrangement has a fractal-like structure, built so that the separation property repeats across scales inside the square.
arxiv-2511-10709:
Apoorva D. Patel examines when quantum machine learning can truly beat classical methods at unsupervised learning, the task of finding the probability distribution that best describes data and using it to predict observables. Classical models usually fit Boltzmann distributions of Hamiltonians with many tunable parameters, while quantum versions replace those distributions with density matrices.

Patel argues an advantage appears only when a method uses features of density matrices that classical probability laws simply do not have. Whether such features matter depends on both the input data and the observables being targeted. Through explicit examples, the paper brings out the constraints that limit possible quantum advantage, with effects for data analysis and for sensing uses.
arxiv-2511-10809:
Jiazhou Liang, Hassan Khurram, and Scott Sanner improve linear predictive clustering, a technique that groups samples by shared linear relationships between features and a target, with uses from marketing to medicine. The greedy algorithms in common use alternate between clustering and regression but carry no optimality guarantee, and they falter when clusters overlap.

An exact mixed-integer formulation exists but scales poorly. Building on it, the authors derive two near-optimal approximations with provable error bounds by exploiting theoretical properties of separability, sharply cutting the formulation's complexity. A further approximation recasts the problem as quadratic pseudo-Boolean optimization for still larger computational gains in some settings. On synthetic and real datasets, their methods matched near-optimal quality with much lower error than greedy optimization and far better scaling than the exact program.
arxiv-2511-11109:
Natalia Gorobey, Alexander Lukyanenko, and A. V. Goltsev propose a model of a two-sheeted universe in quantum gravity. They ask how CPT symmetry works there. CPT is the joint flip of charge, mirror image, and time. Their base is a shared proper time for the whole closed universe, defined through a special operator on spinor fields. Equivalent frames of reference are fixed by that operator's spectrum.

By analogy with flat-space field theory, they define the three flips one by one in the two-sheeted setting and state a CPT rule for it. They build a matter theory that respects charge flip and construct a symmetric state step by step, starting from the no-boundary wave function.
arxiv-2511-11209:
Piero Romare, Farzaneh Karegar, and Simone Fischer-Hübner work toward privacy controls that users of trigger-action automation platforms can actually manage. Such platforms link services with if-this-then-that rules, but their permission controls are coarse, and fine controls overwhelm users with choices. Grouping users by privacy stance could let platforms suggest sensible defaults instead.

The team built and validated a survey on concerns about confidentiality, control, and transparency, then ran it online with about three hundred informed participants. Users clustered into basic, medium, and high privacy groups. Vignette tests on data type, recipient, and purpose turned those groups into three distinct sharing profiles.
arxiv-2511-11409:
Cyril Houdayer and Amine Marrakchi introduce selfless W-star probability spaces and study how the notion connects with Connes' bicentralizer problem. A W-star probability space pairs a von Neumann algebra, a large algebra of operators, with a faithful normal state that plays the role of an expectation. The bicentralizer problem asks about operators that commute with everything the state fixes, a subtle structural question for such algebras.

Their main result gives a clean sufficient case. If an algebra is a separable factor of type three-one with trivial bicentralizer, then the paired space is selfless for every faithful normal state. That link ties the new notion to a central problem in operator algebra theory.
arxiv-2511-11809:
Sebastian Miles and three co-authors derive compact models for holes in special nanowires. The wires have a germanium core wrapped in silicon. They are candidates for quantum devices. A full band-structure treatment is unwieldy for design work. Device designers need small models of the lowest energy bands.

Higher-order perturbation theory is carried to fifth order. It yields models that can be read and reused. The models cover growth directions used in real labs. Cross terms are included, such as how effective mass depends on magnetic field. Low-symmetry directions show orbital inversions of the lowest bands. They also weaken the direct Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Compact, accurate models speed the design of nanowire qubits.
arxiv-2511-11909:
Jiacheng Wu models financial systemic risk as a diffusion process. A logistic growth term is added. Default stress spreads between linked firms like heat through a material. It also feeds on itself locally. Stability analysis asks when the healthy state can hold.

A stabilizing controller is built in three steps. First, a Riccati equation for the linearized system gives an exponentially stabilizing law. Second, the nonlinear term is treated as a forcing input. Third, a contraction mapping argument gives existence and uniqueness. Control theory becomes a language for financial rules here. Interventions can be designed with the rigor of engineering feedback.
arxiv-2511-12009:
Guangchao Yao and Yali Li attack the N-Queens counting problem on graphics processors. Solution counts are rigorously verified only up to twenty-six queens. The problem's cost grows brutally with board size. The twenty-seven case fell to an FPGA effort in 2016. It took about a year, and the result still awaits independent checks. Recent GPU estimates suggest seventeen months for the same task.

An iterative depth-first search is their core contribution. It is engineered for zero shared-memory bank conflicts. The GPU's memory system is squeezed instead of stalled. Faster exhaustive search is the only route to confirming the twenty-seven count. It is a small trophy with an outsized name in parallel computing.
arxiv-2511-12109:
Felipe Fujita and Hideyuki Takada test how to improve English to Japanese translation when training data are scarce. They start from a baseline model. Then they try two low-cost ideas on small Japanese text sets. One is backtranslation, which makes training pairs from Japanese text alone. The other is fine-tuning on a small set of real pairs.

Backtranslation alone gives a modest gain, while fine-tuning on news and literary pairs gives a much larger jump. Using both, first adding synthetic pairs and then fine-tuning, gives the best score in their tests. The result offers a light strategy for language pairs that lack large parallel datasets.
arxiv-2511-12209:
Akshay Chandran and four co-authors present a multiscale solver for turbulent flow near walls. Accurate treatment matters because near-wall instability helps trigger the shift to turbulence, yet a fully kinetic method lacks the power to cover both the wall layer and the bulk flow at once.

Their solver couples two levels: a kinetic particle method handles the thin layer near the wall, while a high-order lattice Boltzmann method handles the bulk. They validate the pair on standard channel and sliding-wall flows far from equilibrium. With the coupled solver they report early evidence of the regeneration cycles of flow structures that appear above a critical Reynolds number.
arxiv-2511-12609:
Yunxin Li and eleven co-authors present Uni-MoE-2.0-Omni, a fully open-source large model that understands and generates across many modalities, including text, images and speech. It grows out of an earlier series and is built from scratch around a language model core. Three contributions carry the design.

A dynamic-capacity mixture-of-experts layout uses shared, routed and null experts to balance cost and skill across ten kinds of cross-modal input, with a three-dimensional position scheme that aligns space, time and modality. Training follows a progressive path from cross-modal pretraining to supervised fine-tuning that activates modality-specific experts, steadied by a reinforcement method and balanced, curated multimodal data.
arxiv-2511-13209:
Nandana Ghosh and Ankush Acharyya solve a terrain geometry problem exactly. A one-and-a-half-dimensional terrain is a polygon whose top edge is a single x-monotone chain over a horizontal base. The authors ask for the largest-area convex quadrilateral that fits inside such a terrain with n vertices, allowing the optimum to degenerate to a triangle when no quadrilateral does better. Assuming no three terrain vertices are collinear, they give a deterministic exact algorithm running in near-quadratic time with linear working space.

The algorithm returns a genuine quadrilateral whenever an optimal one exists, and otherwise the maximum-area triangle. As a bonus, they prove that the largest axis-parallel rectangle inside the terrain is a tight one-half approximation to the quadrilateral optimum and can be computed faster.
arxiv-2511-13309:
Kaiwen Cai and 9 co-authors present DriveLiDAR4D, a system that generates LiDAR scenes in sequence with control over cars and background. Realistic point clouds help build and test self-driving software, but older generators lacked sequence output and placed foreground objects poorly. The new pipeline accepts several kinds of guiding input at once.

Its LiDAR4DNet model predicts noise step by step to keep scenes steady over time while staying editable. The authors call it the first end-to-end method for sequential LiDAR generation with full scene control. On nuScenes and KITTI data it beat the prior best method by large margins on their realism scores.
arxiv-2511-13609:
Marianne Rakic and 5 co-authors present AtlasMorph, a learning framework that builds brain MRI templates matched to a chosen population. A template, or atlas, is a prototypical anatomy image used for registration and segmentation across studies. Building one is costly, so researchers often settle for atlases that fit their subjects poorly.

AtlasMorph trains convolutional registration networks to output a template conditioned on traits such as age and sex, with anatomical label maps when segmentations exist. The same network can register new scans to its templates. On a pooled set of 3D brain datasets, conditional labeled templates registered better than unconditional ones and beat other construction methods, giving studies atlases that truly mirror their populations.
arxiv-2511-13709:
Lawrence Hollom and Benedict Randall Shaw give counterexamples to several conjectures on strong maximality and minimality in infinite graphs and hypergraphs. Strongly maximal matchings and strongly minimal covers were expected to exist broadly, under conjectures tied to names such as Aharoni and Tardos. Their constructions show those expectations fail in clean cases.

In particular, they build three-uniform hypergraphs with no strongly maximal matching and others with no strongly minimal cover. From the cover construction they derive a graph with no strongly minimal coloring. Refinements of the original problems are treated as well, so the paper closes a cluster of open questions rather than a single one.
arxiv-2511-14009:
Halle C. Braun, Kushin Mukherjee, Seth R. Gorelik, and one co-author study how colormaps can carry feelings as well as data. Color strongly shapes a chart's emotional tone, and lightness drives much of that effect: light reads positive, dark reads negative. But maps that encode values with color need lightness contrast to show fine spatial detail, which seems to block a clear mood.

The team found colormaps can do both: keep strong contrast for structure while still signaling a clear emotional tone. The tone depended on the color scales chosen and on how often each color appeared, which the underlying data controls. Their results argue for data-aware design that plans emotion and legibility together.
arxiv-2511-14109:
Zhenyu Li and Tianyi Shang improve visual place recognition, the task of matching a photo to a known location. Top methods compress deep image features into one global descriptor, often by solving an optimal transport assignment between features and cluster centers. The standard solver treats both sides symmetrically, which hurts when features and centers follow very different distributions.

Their method, A2GC, normalizes rows and columns separately and calibrates the two margins independently, allowing genuinely asymmetric matching. Learnable coordinate embeddings add geometric constraints that push nearby features into the same cluster. On the MSLS, NordLand, and Pittsburgh data sets the approach beat prior methods in matching accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2511-14609:
Niklas Knobel studies stability of three dimensional magnetohydrodynamic flow near Couette flow with a steady magnetic field. Couette shear mixes the fluid, while a field across the shear plane stabilizes modes that vary along it. At the same time the averaged magnetic field can grow algebraically. Knobel asks how viscosity and resistivity set sharp stability thresholds.

He finds a nonlinear transient growth regime with an optimal exponent range. Small initial data below the threshold stay stable in a nonlinear sense. Other data depart from linear behavior at a stated rate through instability. The threshold exponent cannot be improved in Sobolev spaces without new mechanisms. The analysis sharpens understanding of transition in magnetized shear flows.
arxiv-2511-14909:
Amit Lavon introduces Izzy, a fast simulator for metagenomic reads designed for current data scales. Modeled microbial communities benchmark abundance estimators and other bioinformatics tools. Modern studies need many large modeled samples, so slow simulators become bottlenecks. Izzy builds on existing error models rather than inventing new ones.

The new implementation delivers up to sixty times speedup over prior tools. Its interface stays simple and easy to use. Speed at scale lets scientists test new methods more thoroughly. Benchmarks can include larger and more numerous communities without prohibitive wait times. Lavon presents Izzy as a drop in accelerator for a routine but critical step in metagenomics research.
arxiv-2511-15609:
Rodrigo Alonso, Christoph Englert, Wrishik Naskar, and Shakeel Ur Rahaman propose a way to estimate theory errors in effective field theories, simplified models that add small corrections for unknown high-energy physics. Any such model must cut its expansion off somewhere, and that cut is tangled with the freedom to redefine fields without changing physics. Judging the size of the neglected terms has often rested on community habit.

Their idea uses that redefinition freedom as a check: different valid descriptions should give consistent error estimates. They compare equation-of-motion replacements with full field redefinitions as a data-informed validation. A case study on Higgs effective theory, focusing on shared Higgs properties, shows how process-specific expectations can mislead.
arxiv-2511-15709:
Violeta Kastreva, Philip Whittington, Dennis Komm, and Tiago Pimentel prove that optimal tokenization stays hard even over tiny alphabets. Tokenization splits text into reusable chunks before a language model processes it, and the goal is a chunk set that compresses a data set best. Earlier hardness results assumed alphabets of unlimited size, unlike real byte or character alphabets used in practice.

For two natural variants, choosing merge steps in order or choosing a vocabulary directly, they prove the problems are not just NP-complete but also hard to approximate, even with a binary alphabet. Direct tokenization stays NP-complete even over a one-letter alphabet. The results explain why practical tokenizers rely on heuristics and point research toward approximation methods.
arxiv-2511-16109:
Tony Puthenpurakal studies curvature of modules over Cohen-Macaulay local rings and the obstructions it imposes. Curvature measures growth of minimal free resolutions through their Betti numbers. The residue field's curvature is a key invariant of the ring itself. Puthenpurakal asks what follows if one module has curvature strictly between one and that of the residue field.

Under mild hypotheses, such a single module constrains both curvatures at once. Vanishing of higher Tor modules between two modules likewise constrains both of their curvatures. These links turn isolated curvature values into structural information about the ring. The results serve commutative algebraists who use resolution growth to detect singularity type and homological complexity of local rings.
arxiv-2511-16209:
Huseein Jawad and Nicolas Brunel harden system prompts against extraction attacks by adding an optimized protective shield text. System prompts often hold proprietary logic or sensitive instructions. Adversarial queries can elicit those hidden prompts, creating security and privacy risks. Heuristic defenses are brittle, heavy, or unusable through black box application interfaces.

Prompt hardening is formalized as utility constrained tuning. A language model acts as optimizer, searching shield texts that minimize leakage across a suite of attacks. Utility of the original prompt must be preserved at the same time. Shield adding is lightweight and API compatible. The approach offers deployers a principled way to trade a small text addition for measurably lower prompt leakage.
arxiv-2511-16509:
J. Sirker writes a comment challenging a recent claim that dynamical quantum phase transitions survive noise. Those transitions are sharp non-analytic points in a system's return probability after a sudden quench. The criticized work reported they persist after averaging over noise in a two-band model, using a pure-state approximation for the noisy state.

Sirker proves that approximation fails exponentially badly in the thermodynamic limit. With the correct distance measure, the echo between two density matrices can reach zero only when both are pure, which rules out the transitions at any nonzero noise. A reinterpretation as an interferometric protocol is possible but blind to decoherence, so it cannot test noise effects. Other natural noise averagings also smooth the transitions away.
arxiv-2511-17109:
Fei Hu proves that the eigenvalues of polarized endomorphisms, maps from a variety to itself that respect a polarization, obey parity and symmetry patterns on cohomology. These patterns were predicted by the standard conjectures of algebraic geometry and were earlier known only for Frobenius endomorphisms, the special maps available in positive characteristic. Hu's result extends them to the general polarized case.

Besides the hard Lefschetz theorem, the proof leans on a recent Riemann hypothesis style result by J. Xie about such eigenvalues. Hu also proves a Newton over Hodge comparison for abelian varieties and Grassmannians. The paper strengthens the evidence that the standard conjectures' predictions hold broadly, and hands geometers new tools for studying self-maps of varieties.
arxiv-2511-17209:
Cris Claessens and four co-authors introduce SPECTRE, a foundation model for volumetric computed tomography, the three-dimensional scans central to modern medicine. Training a general model on such scans is difficult: volumes produce huge token counts, voxel spacing is uneven, and clinical labels are weak or noisy. Standard transformer and contrastive recipes fail out of the box under these conditions.

SPECTRE pairs a local transformer, which extracts high-resolution features, with a global one that models whole-scan context, making three-dimensional attention affordable. Pretraining blends self-distillation in the style of DINO with vision-language alignment against paired radiology reports. Notably, training used only openly available datasets. Across CT benchmarks, in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, SPECTRE beat earlier CT foundation models. The authors offer it as proof that open data suffices for strong, general 3D medical representations.
arxiv-2511-17309:
David Nordström and three co-authors present MuM, a self-supervised model that learns visual features built for three-dimensional understanding. Most image pretraining optimizes semantic recognition, not geometry, leaving features weak for tasks like reconstruction and camera pose estimation. MuM extends masked image modeling, where parts of an image are hidden and predicted, to arbitrarily many views of the same scene at once.

All views are masked uniformly, and a lightweight decoder with attention between frames reconstructs what is missing, forcing the features to encode how views relate geometrically. The design is simpler and more scalable than its main predecessor, CroCo. On downstream tests covering feedforward reconstruction, dense image matching, and relative pose estimation, MuM outperformed strong general encoders, including DINOv3, and the earlier CroCo v2. The work pushes self-supervised learning toward truly spatial representations.
arxiv-2511-17609:
Linh Van Ma and four co-authors reconstruct 3D ground truth about tracked objects from the 2D annotations of several cameras. Accurate 3D ground truth underpins autonomous navigation, surveillance, and robotics, yet it is usually expensive to capture directly. Their method takes human-annotated 2D bounding boxes or pose keypoints from multiple calibrated cameras and fuses them with an unscented Kalman filter. It projects image coordinates into the world through homographies and lets the filter reconcile the views.

The algorithm estimates each object's position and full shape while coping with occlusion, a step beyond approaches that report only ground-plane positions. Evaluations on three multi-camera datasets, including Wildtrack and Panoptic, showed high localization accuracy against the 3D reference data. The pipeline runs on its own and scales, needing only the 2D labels that labeling teams already produce.
arxiv-2511-17709:
Haedam Im leads a team of twelve authors re-examining Kepler-1624b, a sub-Saturn planet orbiting a small red star. Earlier work found its transits arriving early or late by about two minutes, a wobble that hinted at a hidden companion planet. Such resonant pairs are rare and prized, since they constrain how planets form and drift. The team reworks the archived Kepler transits and stretches the record by eleven years.

New data from the TESS satellite and from telescopes at Palomar and Las Cumbres are fitted together with the old record. The wobble comes out far weaker than first reported, and a formal model comparison favours a single planet over two. The authors stress the care needed before claiming companions from small timing shifts in faint systems.
arxiv-2511-17809:
Cuong Pham, Hoang Anh Dung, Cuong Nguyen, Trung Le, Gustavo Carneiro, Jianfei Cai, and Thanh-Toan Do improve quantization of large language models, a way to shrink models for cheaper running. Outliers in weights and activations cause large quality losses, and prior fixes apply the same transformation to every layer.

Their framework picks a transformation type layer by layer, guided by a simple measure of weight spread that replaces a costly search. Tests on Llama models beat fixed settings, with clear gains in text quality and in zero shot task accuracy. The work shows that layers differ enough to need different treatment.
arxiv-2511-18109:
Onofre Rojas explains pseudotransitions, sharp changes in one dimensional materials that look like phase transitions even though true transitions are forbidden there with short range interactions. The behavior is analytic, a steep crossover rather than a genuine singularity, and several models show it.

Rojas traces it to transfer matrices that cannot be split into blocks yet are nearly block diagonal at low temperature, because off diagonal weights are tiny. Two weakly coupled sectors then compete, producing the abrupt crossover, with residual entropy bounded between the sectors' values. Case studies cover a degenerate Ising chain, where exact formulas follow, and a large nanowire model reduced by symmetry.
arxiv-2511-18309:
James C. Hateley builds a math frame that ties the zeros of the Riemann zeta function to the tones of a quantum style operator. The Riemann zeros mark key points in number theory, and a long held hope seeks an operator whose tone list matches them. Hateley works on a space built from the adeles, which join all prime based views of the numbers.

He places a wave operator in a split, mirror form to get a global Dirac type operator with an exact flip symmetry. Prime linked terms, built from Hecke operators, then shift the tones while the mirror form holds. Shifted tones show as jumps in a spectral count, and a trace formula splits into a wave part and a prime part. The frame is offered as a path toward the spectral view of the zeros.
arxiv-2511-18409:
Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Hanjie Chen, Najoung Kim, Hosein Mohebbi, Aaron Mueller, Gabriele Sarti, and Martin Tutek report the findings of a shared task on opening up language models. Mechanistic interpretability tries to say which internal parts cause a model's behaviour, but measuring progress needs shared tests. The task builds on a standard benchmark and turns it into a community-wide, reproducible contest with two tracks.

One track grades methods that locate the circuits, the components and links that drive a behaviour. The other grades methods that map internal activations onto interpretable variables. Three teams with eight methods took part in the circuit track, gaining ground through ensembles and regularisation. The report gives the young field a common yardstick and a record of what worked.
arxiv-2511-18609:
David Krakauer, Gülce Kardeş, and Joshua Grochow use the Rubik's Cube as a window on how groups of experts learn. Hard data on long-term skill growth are scarce, and the cube sits at a crossing of puzzle solving, cultural transmission, and group theory, with a large competitive community to study. The authors find a shared pattern in how that community improves, in both sighted and blindfolded solving.

Expert performance follows smooth exponential progress curves, whose shape reflects the delayed uptake of algorithms that shorten solutions. Blindfolded solving forms its own class, limited not only by knowledge but by the memory bottleneck of holding the cube in mind, a constraint it shares with blindfold chess. The study argues such cultural artefacts reveal universal features of collective learning.
arxiv-2511-18809: Yezheng Gao compares two ways to measure the slopes of a solvable differential module over the punctured open unit disc. The formal slope comes from the module's algebraic form. The p-adic slope comes from p-adic analysis. Gao establishes several inequalities between the two. The proofs rest on a close study of Newton polygons and on the log-convexity of generic radius functions. Those functions track how solutions behave near the puncture. The results tie a formal invariant to an analytic one.
arxiv-2511-18909:
Atila Poro and five co-authors model the light curves of eight totally eclipsing contact binary stars in full detail for the first time. In a W Ursae Majoris system two stars touch and share an envelope, and total eclipses give clean reads of their traits. Ground data in four color bands came from an observatory in Mexico, joined by space time series from TESS.

New eclipse times feed a study of period change: some systems drift in a line, some in a curve that shows a steady period shrink. Light curve fits with the PHOEBE code and a companion app yield the system traits. The team also revisit the link between period and the hot star's temperature, where they find a clear break. Contact pair physics gains eight firm cases.
arxiv-2511-19709:
Lukas Molnar and five co-authors control a legged robot that must walk and handle objects at the same time. Loco-manipulation needs the whole body to cooperate, balancing locomotion while the arm applies the right forces. Their controller plans directly in joint torques using full inverse dynamics inside one predictive layer.

Built with the Pinocchio and CasADi tools and a fast interior-point solver, the system runs in real time at eighty cycles per second. The test platform is a Unitree B2 quadruped carrying a Z1 arm. It pulls heavy loads, pushes boxes, and wipes a whiteboard, showing fine position and force control together.
arxiv-2511-19809:
Rahul Gulia, Feyisayo Favour Popoola, and Ashish Sheikh model vehicle-to-everything radio links with formulas a person can read. Neural networks predict block error rates accurately but hide their logic and cost too much for real-time embedded use. Symbolic regression instead searches for a compact equation.

A stabilized version of that search trains on realistic driving simulations. The final expression, with only about one hundred sixty nodes, captures how error rate depends on signal strength, relative speed, coding choices, and line-of-sight conditions. Inference is fast enough for embedded deployment, giving engineers an interpretable tool for robust vehicle communication design.
arxiv-2511-19909:
Haoxuan Wang and five co-authors present Motion Marionette, a framework that copies rigid motion from a video onto a still image. Earlier methods lean on outside geometric, generative, or simulation guidance, which trades broad use against smooth timing. Their approach instead builds guidance from inside the source video itself.

Both the video and the target image are lifted into one three-dimensional space, and motion paths are drawn from the video. Those paths form a prior that records relative movement over time, free of the object's shape or meaning. Joined with the target, it yields a controllable velocity field, refined with position-based dynamics to cut artifacts. Tests show consistent motion across many kinds of objects.
arxiv-2511-20009:
Yulong Deng, Zheng Guan, Min He, Xue Wang, Jie Liu, and Zheng Li address cold-start knowledge tracing across school subjects. When students move to a new discipline, little interaction data exists there, so their knowledge state is hard to model. Older transfer methods lean on entities shared between subjects, but such overlap is scarce and simple mappings miss complex links.

Their framework pretrains a model on a source discipline and clusters student knowledge states into groups. Those group traits guide a mixture-of-experts network through a gating mechanism, forming a bridge between subjects. An adversarial discriminator pulls features of like students together and pushes unlike ones apart, easing the small-sample problem. The method is validated across twenty extreme cross-disciplinary cold-start scenarios.
arxiv-2511-20409:
Kafi, Moni, and Banshal warn that shrinking words can silently destroy meaning. Their 2025 paper evaluates text normalization in language processing pipelines. Stemming chops words down to a root form. It reduces vocabulary size and can speed up tasks. But judges rarely check whether aggressive stemming harms meaning. The team built a three-part evaluation framework.

One score measures stemming effectiveness through word reduction. A second tracks downstream task performance changes. A third measures meaning distance between stemmed and original words. Two stemmers were compared: Bangla's BNLTK and English's Snowball. The Bangla tool scored 1.67 on effectiveness, the highest mark recorded. Its compression ratio reached 1.90 across the test corpus used. Yet its meaning distance of 0.26 in the same tests exposed harmful over-stemming. Downstream performance dropped accordingly in those runs. Snowball scored 1.31 on effectiveness with a safer distance overall, 0.14 in the final comparison table. The lesson: check meaning safety before chasing compression.
arxiv-2511-20509:
Hudişteanu, Kalinin, and Cyffers train neural networks privately without the usual memory blow-up. Their 2025 paper proposes DP-MicroAdam, a differentially private optimizer. Private training normally relies on DP-SGD, which clips gradients and adds noise. That method demands heavy compute and endless tuning. Adaptive methods like Adam promise faster, stabler learning.

Clipping and noise bias Adam's moment estimates in private settings. DP-MicroAdam updates only the largest gradient coordinates each step. Sparsity plus error feedback counteracts the bias that clipping creates. Memory use shrinks because most coordinates stay untouched. Convergence at the optimal rate is proven theoretically. The rate matches the best possible up to privacy constants. Experiments spanned CIFAR-10 and large-scale ImageNet training. Private fine-tuning of pretrained transformers was also tested. The method beat other adaptive private optimizers consistently. It matched or topped DP-SGD accuracy with minimal tuning.
arxiv-2511-20609:
Wang and colleagues argue memory lookup should ask which stored pattern most likely spawned the query. Their 2025 paper rethinks similarity in associative memory. Hopfield-style networks retrieve the stored pattern nearest the cue. Nearness, though, does not guarantee the true source. A query is better seen as a warped variant of one memory.

The right score is the chance each pattern generated the query. That generating process, the variant distribution, shifts with context. No fixed similarity can track an unknown, shifting process. Their adaptive similarity learns it from context samples instead. Optimality is proven for three common variant families. Noisy, masked, and biased corruptions are all covered. The mechanism powers a new adaptive Hopfield network, A-Hop. It set state-of-the-art results among Hopfield networks in tests. Tasks spanned memory retrieval and two kinds of classification. Gains grew largest when variant types were mixed.
arxiv-2511-20709:
Abhijeet Pathak and colleagues present in 2025 DualGauge, a benchmark that grades AI-written code on security and correctness at the same time. Scoring them apart hides a real tension: a model can patch a hole while breaking the program, or ship working code riddled with flaws. Studies cited by the authors find that 30 to 60 percent of code suggestions from modern language models contain exploitable flaws.

DualGauge pairs each coding task with checked test suites covering what the code must do and what it must never allow. An agent-based executor runs programs inside sandboxes, sealed environments, while a language-model evaluator judges behaviour against expectations. The team applied the framework to ten leading language models across thousands of test scenarios. The scores exposed gaps that separate testing had missed: models failed to be correct and secure together. The system and benchmark suite are open source, for reproducible, scalable evaluation.
arxiv-2511-20909:
Anil K. Saini and colleagues test in 2025 whether evolving training-data weights with a genetic algorithm beats fixed recipes for fairer models. Reweighting gives some training examples more influence, softening biased predictions. The rivals were weights computed from dataset characteristics alone, and the default of equal weights for all. Performance was scored jointly on predictive quality, accuracy and ROC area, and on fairness: demographic parity difference, plus false-negative fairness across subgroups.

Across eleven public datasets, two of them medical, evolved weights often produced better fairness-accuracy trade-offs than the alternatives. But the size of the win depended heavily on which metric pair the evolution optimised. Pairing accuracy with demographic parity difference yielded the most datasets where evolved weights were significantly better on both goals. The lesson is practical: the objective choice, not the evolution itself, decides whether reweighting helps.
arxiv-2511-21109:
Mudi Jiang and colleagues make in 2025 fair clustering explain itself. Clustering people or cases can disadvantage protected groups, and existing fair methods are black boxes, a poor fit for high-stakes decisions. Their Interpretable Fair Clustering Tree, IFCT, builds fairness constraints into a decision tree that partitions the data. Every cluster assignment can be read off as a path of if-then splits. A variant, IFCT-P, prunes a tree grown without fairness constraints, removing the need to tune a fairness hyperparameter by hand.

Experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets showed competitive clustering quality with improved fairness over rival methods. The comparison table makes the gap plain: among fair clustering algorithms, only IFCT combined interpretability with support for multiple sensitive attributes, multiple groups within one attribute, and mixed-type features. The authors pitch the method for settings like lending or healthcare triage, where an unexplained grouping is not acceptable.
arxiv-2511-21409:
Wouter Visser and Jelmer Wolterink study how medical image representations forget, and how to stop them, in 2025. Neural fields store a scan as a continuous function inside a small neural network, prized in biomedical imaging for being lightweight and differentiable. Unlike voxel grids, they cannot simply be extended: train the network on new anatomy or a longer scan, and the old content degrades, a failure called catastrophic forgetting.

Visser and Wolterink test several neural field designs on cardiac cine MRI, heart movies, under two growth scenarios, enlarging the space-time domain and adding signal dimensions. Forgetting varied widely by architecture. Knowledge distillation, where the updated network is trained to mimic its earlier self on old territory, substantially reduced the loss in both scenarios. The finding suggests continual learning is practical for biomedical neural fields, letting one model grow with a patient's record instead of being rebuilt.
arxiv-2511-21509:
Dirk Beyer, Gidon Ernst, Martin Jonáš, and Marian Lingsch-Rosenfeld propose a common language for software verification tools in 2025. Two decades of work produced strong verifiers, programs that prove code meets its specification, but each is welded to one programming language like C or Java. Many of the underlying algorithms are language-agnostic, so the field reinvents the same machinery repeatedly for lack of a shared task format.

Their answer is SV-LIB, an exchange format and intermediate language covering programs, specifications, and verification witnesses, the evidence files a verifier produces. Expressions borrow the established SMT-LIB syntax, so existing solver-based tools can adopt it cheaply. Version 1.0 also standardizes witnesses for both correct and incorrect programs, plus validation tasks, letting independent checkers re-verify another tool's claims. Formal semantics and concurrency support are planned next, decoupling language front-ends from verification back-ends for good.
arxiv-2511-21709:
Blessed Guda and four coauthors tackle selection bias in multiple-choice testing of large language models, in 2025. Models often pick answers based on position or option symbols rather than content, which quietly corrupts benchmark scores. Existing bias measures need answer labels and miss how predictions shift when choices are reordered.

The team offers three tools. Their Permutation Bias Metric is label-free and directly measures how inconsistent predictions become across answer orderings. BaQCKV makes majority voting across orderings cheap by caching question context. A LoRA fine-tuning strategy, trained using the metric itself, then reduces the bias without labels. Experiments across several datasets and models show the combined approach cuts bias while staying computationally light, giving evaluators a more trustworthy multiple-choice scorecard.
arxiv-2511-21909:
Labat and colleagues build a dataset for teaching AI to read emotions in customer service chats, using a Wizard of Oz setup where humans secretly play the chatbot. Emotion datasets are usually scraped from other domains and labelled only after the fact. Here, wizards were instructed to steer each conversation toward a target ending mood, positive, neutral, or negative, across aviation, e-commerce, travel, and telecom scenarios.

The resulting bilingual Dutch-English corpus, EmoWOZ-CS, holds 2,148 dialogues from 179 participants, with emotions and valence-arousal-dominance scores on customer turns and strategy labels on operator turns. Neutral messages dominated, with desire and gratitude commonest, and self-reports diverged from third-party labels except for neutral, gratitude, and anger. Objective strategies like explanations tended to earn gratitude, while irony and miscomprehension raised anger and annoyance. Steering worked, most clearly for negative targets; predicting future emotions proved hard.
arxiv-2511-22109:
Hoang, Ransom, Stephens, and colleagues blend psychological theory with large language models to predict when an online message will actually change someone's belief. Classic persuasion models were built for face-to-face conversation and describe rather than predict, while purely data-driven detectors ignore why messages work. The team has language models rate messages on eight features drawn from psychological experiments, then trains a random forest classifier on those ratings to forecast belief change in social-media style discourse.

Of the eight features, epistemic emotion, curiosity, confusion, and surprise that push people to think harder, and willingness to share the message ranked as the top two predictors of successful persuasion. Beyond the ranking itself, the hybrid design shows how language models can operationalize theory-derived features at scale. The authors point to applications in influence detection, misinformation mitigation, and measuring how effective online narratives really are.
arxiv-2511-22309:
McBride, Gorce, Douspis, and colleagues forecast what the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich signal reveals about the first galaxies. As cosmic microwave background photons cross the epoch of reionization, moving electrons in ionized bubbles Doppler-shift them, imprinting a patchy kSZ power spectrum that encodes how reionization proceeded. The team repurposes the LoReLi II simulation suite into 6,796 mock kSZ spectra, trains a neural-network emulator for fast Bayesian inference, and forecasts constraints for current and upcoming CMB surveys.

The escape fraction comes out with about 14 percent average relative error across a thousand test forecasts. The same data independently measure the CMB optical depth with uncertainty near 0.0012 in their forecasts, below the cosmic-variance limit of large-scale surveys, a fivefold improvement over current constraints, with emulator error the dominant remaining limitation. Emulator reconstruction error, reducible with a larger simulation training set, currently dominates the error budget.
arxiv-2511-22409:
Giannouris and Ananiadou present NOMAD, a team of language-model agents turning written software requirements into UML class diagrams. Such diagrams are blueprints showing a system's main concepts and how they relate, and drawing them by hand is slow and error-prone. NOMAD splits the job into roles, such as extracting entities, classifying relationships, and assembling the diagram, mirroring how a human engineer works.

Tested on the Northwind case study and human-written modelling exercises, NOMAD beat every single-agent baseline, reaching near-perfect class identification and much better relationship reasoning. Fine-grained attribute extraction stayed hard, which the authors link to ambiguity in the requirements themselves. The paper also gives the first systematic taxonomy of errors in machine-generated UML diagrams, sorted into structural, relationship, and semantic kinds. The paper tests a verifier agent, finding that checking improves completeness and consistency, though with mixed effects.
arxiv-2511-22809:
Xu and colleagues test whether AI summaries atop search results move public opinion. In a preregistered randomised experiment, 2,004 participants viewed mock search pages about four debated health topics: raw milk, water fluoridation, artificial sweeteners, and GMO foods. Pages varied in whether an AI summary appeared, its placement at top or middle, and its framing around benefits or harms, against a no-summary control.

Exposure worked: participants seeing AI summaries reported attitudes, intentions, and policy support shifted toward the summary's stance, versus controls. Placement mattered for attitudes, top-of-page summaries shifting them more than middle placement, though not intentions or policy support. Effects were moderated by issue familiarity and trust in AI, hitting hardest where familiarity was low and trust high. Harm-emphasising summaries were also perceived as more useful than benefit-framed ones. AI summaries act as persuasive cues, the authors warn, calling for transparent, accountable design and regulation.
arxiv-2511-22909:
Yamagami and colleagues built a faster way to map the electronic structure of materials, the pattern of electron energies inside a solid. Their tool is soft X-ray ARPES, a technique that knocks electrons out of a sample and measures them to reveal its three-dimensional bulk structure. It is installed at the BL25SU beamline of the SPring-8 synchrotron in Japan.

The method is normally slow because soft X-rays produce few electrons. So the team added a deep prior denoising system, a neural approach that cleans data using patterns it learns from the data itself. It removes grid and spike noise in about 30 seconds of computing. On a crystal of CeRu2Si2, the team gathered good data in roughly 40 seconds of measurement. The team reached an energy resolution of 51.6 meV in separate tests on gold, which opens shorter and sharper experiments on other materials.
arxiv-2511-23109:
Eraşcu tackles cloud deployment planning: assigning the components of an application to virtual machines rented from cloud providers. Cost must be minimized, and every interaction and capacity constraint must hold. The problem is NP-hard and exact solvers bog down as instances grow. So the paper asks whether a neural network's guesses can safely steer an exact solver instead of replacing it.

The framework trains a graph neural network on small deployment instances, recasting placement as an edge-classification task on a graph of components and machines. It then feeds its predicted assignments into the Z3 solver as soft constraints, preferences the solver may override. Across realistic case studies, including multi-tier WordPress deployments, the guidance usually made the solver converge faster while still returning cost-optimal deployments, even when the network's predictions were imprecise. Soft constraints can speed the search but cannot corrupt the answer.
arxiv-2511-23209:
Wang and colleagues add randomness to eco-evolutionary game dynamics, the framework where players' payoffs and the environment reshape each other in a two-way feedback loop. Deterministic versions say where the system settles, but real populations jitter. So the team applies a systematic noise expansion to a two-strategy game whose payoff matrix depends on population size, asking how large the fluctuations around equilibrium are.

They show each strategy's population fluctuates around the deterministic interior equilibrium. When that equilibrium is asymptotically stable, its variance settles to a constant proportional to the environment's carrying capacity, neither growing nor vanishing over time. Simulations confirm the expansion approximates the true stochastic process well. So the deterministic stability conclusions carry over to the noisy regime whenever the carrying capacity is sufficiently large, a reassuring result for applying the theory to real ecosystems and social systems.
arxiv-2511-23409:
Abbas and colleagues redesign physics-informed neural networks, which solve partial differential equations by training a network to satisfy the equation and its boundary conditions at once. In this setup, the two goals often fight during optimization. Their dual-network framework splits the solution into an interior part and a boundary part. The two networks are softly specialized by distance-weighted priors that fade in and out on a cosine schedule during training.

Boundary conditions are enforced by an augmented Lagrangian method that removes manual penalty tuning, and training runs in two phases, uniform sampling first, then focused sampling near the boundary. On Laplace and Poisson benchmarks the method cuts error by 36 to 90 percent, improves boundary satisfaction by 21 to 88 percent, and lowers mean absolute error by a factor of 2.2 to 9.3 against a single-network baseline, with ablations crediting each design piece.
arxiv-2512-00209:
Bayesian networks lay out how random variables depend on each other, which makes reasoning under uncertainty manageable. Bart Jacobs, Márk Széles, and Dario Stein study compositional inference for such networks and for causality in 2025. Inference means updating some variables with evidence and computing outcomes elsewhere.

When a joint distribution is represented by a network, its structure lets inference proceed piece by piece, with great benefits. Compositional methods scale better and are easier to verify than one global computation. The approach matters for medical, legal, and engineering reasoning, where transparent probability updates are essential. Causal reasoning adds direction to those updates, asking what changes when a variable is forced. For teams who build tools for doctors, judges, or plant staff, the gain is speed with care. Fast sums that still show how each fact moved the end result.
arxiv-2512-00309:
Biao Dong and Bin Cao study distributed sensing joined with edge artificial intelligence in 2025. In their system, scattered devices sense a target and send locally estimated features to an access point. The access point then performs collaborative inference from those features.

Performance is set at two levels: how well the devices sense, and how well they communicate. Exploiting prior information is the lever the authors use to improve the combined system. Such integrated designs matter for surveillance, environmental monitoring, and smart infrastructure, where sending raw data from every device would flood the network. Prior information is the resource the design exploits at both sensing and inference levels.
arxiv-2512-00409:
Josephson junctions carry supercurrents between superconductors, and their behavior depends on phase coherence. Polevoy and a team of co-authors report a multiterminal ballistic Josephson effect in monocrystalline gold in 2025. They built a planar junction array inside a micron-sized single crystal of gold.

The system shows a nonlocal effect: the supercurrent between any two superconducting leads is governed by phase coherence across the entire crystal. Such multiterminal devices interest physicists building novel superconducting circuits and probes of quantum transport. A single clean crystal hosting the whole array reduces the disorder that usually clouds these effects. Phase coherence across a whole crystal is the striking feature the array demonstrates.
arxiv-2512-00509:
Non-orthogonal multiple access lets several users share the same channel, which makes separating them difficult. Sumita Majhi and co-authors improve channel estimation for such systems using Gold sequences in 2025. Superimposed signals on shared subcarriers are the core obstacle.

Gold sequences have orthogonality features that may enhance user separation and channel estimation. The proposed approach uses fractional power allocation and partially decoded data symbols to refine estimates. Better estimation in shared-channel systems means more users served on the same spectrum, a direct concern for crowded wireless networks. Partially decoded symbols recycle information the receiver already has, improving the estimate cheaply. The comparison includes a conventional V-BLAST receiver design. For folks who build phone nets, the gain is more calls on the same band. There is less fuzz in the link when crowds of phones share one base site.
arxiv-2512-00609:
Wireless users sharing a channel interfere with each other, and outage probability measures how often service fails. Fernando Almeida García and co-authors analyze outage in transmit-antenna-selection NOMA systems with multi-antenna users in 2025. The fading channel follows a flexible distribution with two shape parameters.

The analysis covers maximal-ratio and equal-gain combining at the receivers. Imperfect successive interference cancellation is modeled explicitly, since real receivers never cancel perfectly. Outage formulas like these guide the design of dense wireless networks that stack users onto the same spectrum. The fading model used is flexible enough to cover many real channel conditions. Antenna selection is a cheap diversity trick, using the best antenna rather than all at once.
arxiv-2512-00809:
Zhanna Kuznetsova and Francesco Toppan build a new algebraic frame for quantum systems in a 2025 paper. They introduce color Heisenberg-Lie superalgebras, graded by small abelian groups. Grading sorts the algebra's parts by labels, and the color version adds twists to how parts combine.

Working at the third root of unity, they study the multi-particle quantum paraoscillators tied to these algebras. Paraoscillators are cousins of the oscillators used across quantum physics, with richer rules. The framework connects to Majorana qubits, a kind of quantum bit prized for stability. New algebra like this can suggest fresh ways to build and control quantum states.
arxiv-2512-00909:
Alireza Javanmardi and a team from a German AI research center present TalkingPose in a 2025 computer vision paper. Diffusion models can now animate a character from one still image plus a set of driving poses, with strong realism. Faces and gestures must move together for the result to feel alive.

Long videos remain hard, since motion can drift and lose coherence over time. TalkingPose adds feedback guidance to the diffusion process to keep face and gesture animation efficient and consistent. Better long-form animation could help virtual presenters, sign language avatars, and film pre-visualization, where a single photo must carry a whole performance.
arxiv-2512-01209:
Yadan Duan and seven coauthors resolve a solar reconnection event in fine detail in a 2025 paper. Interchange reconnection happens where open and closed magnetic field lines in the Sun's corona swap partners. It is thought to play a significant role in producing solar jets and the solar wind.

The dynamics in the low corona may be more complex than recognized, especially at the higher time and spatial resolution now available. Using Solar Orbiter observations, the team studies an event in a fan-spine-like magnetic topology. Resolving such events helps explain how the corona feeds the wind that fills the solar system.
arxiv-2512-01509:
Patrick Odagiu and co-authors shrink data so quantum classifiers can use it. Quantum methods stall when data has too many traits. Most real sets do. Cutting traits first is the plain fix. The cut must keep what the quantum step needs.

The team learns reduced forms of the data for that step. A good form keeps class gaps while traits drop. That opens quantum learning to larger real sets. It also cuts circuit size, which helps today's noisy quantum hardware run deeper tasks with fewer errors. Feature cuts learned once can be reused across classifiers, which spreads the cost of the quantum-ready form over many later tasks.
arxiv-2512-01709:
Eyal Buks studies a ferrimagnetic sphere resonator under parametric drive. The sphere's response to a pumped signal is measured in the lab. A theoretical model predicts that response. Its base claim is that disentanglement occurs spontaneously in quantum systems.

Measurements are set against those predictions. Agreement or gaps both teach something. A match would back the spontaneous disentanglement claim. A gap would bound where the model fails. Sphere resonators serve in magnon and quantum sensing work, so their drive response matters broadly. Sphere resonators couple to microwaves cleanly, so the same setup links this test to magnon devices used in hybrid quantum systems.
arxiv-2512-01809:
Chaoyi Pan and co-authors probe why flow and diffusion policies work well in robotics. Generative policies have become popular and effective for robot control. Their edge is often credited to multimodal action capture. Complex behavior expression is another claimed cause. Hard evidence for each claim is thin.

The team runs controlled tests to separate those factors. Knowing the true driver guides policy design choices. If multimodality is key, data collection should stress diverse demos. If not, simpler policies may match at lower cost. Controlled factors include data scale and policy class, so the verdict states which knob matters under which robot task family.
arxiv-2512-01909:
