Why a large language model gives one answer rather than another is hidden inside its calculations, and wrong answers, or hallucinations, are hard to diagnose. Lihu Chen, Xiang Yin, and Francesca Toni introduce a framework in 2025 that reads a model's prediction as the outcome of an inner debate.

Called latent debate, the framework treats the model's internal activity as implicit arguments for and against possible answers. Making those hidden arguments visible gives researchers a handle on where a prediction came from and why it may have gone wrong. The approach adds a new tool to the effort to make language models interpretable rather than opaque.
arxiv-2512-02109:
Cosmic chronometers date the cosmos by the ages of old, calm galaxies seen at unlike ranges. The method gives the rate of expansion in a direct way. E. Tomasetti and a large team stretch the method in 2025 to whole clusters of galaxies. They gauge the past expansion near the mid-point of cosmic history.

They use fine spectra from the MUSE tool on the Very Large Telescope. Three clusters sit in close redshift bins. Cluster galaxies give many clocks in one field of view, all under shared terms. A fresh, free measure of expansion counts for much, since the main methods still clash on the rate.
arxiv-2512-02209:
The muon, a heavier cousin of the electron, wobbles in a magnetic field at a rate theory predicts with extreme precision. Dinko Počanić reviews in 2025 the experimental status of that wobble, the muon magnetic anomaly, and the prospects for sharpening it further.

The past five years brought major new measurements, and the dominant uncertainty now comes from hadronic vacuum polarization, a strong-force contribution that is hard to compute. Any lasting gap between measurement and prediction would point to unknown particles. The review gathers where the field stands in one of particle physics' longest-running and most sensitive tests of the Standard Model.
arxiv-2512-02609:
Shengkai Wu and nine co-authors teach robots to grasp one chosen object when several valid targets sit in view. Imitation learning copies human demonstrations, but demonstrations may grasp different objects in the same scene. Averaging those conflicting lessons yields one blurred, invalid action.

Their SAM2Grasp method uses prompts to say which object is meant, then predicts the grasp over time. Conditioning on the prompt resolves the multimodal confusion instead of averaging it away. Robots that grasp the intended item reliably are safer and more useful in homes, warehouses, and care settings. A prompt that names the goal turns a vague reach into the right reach, time after time.
arxiv-2512-02809:
Etienne Granet and Michael Levin test whether topological qubits survive long range forces between particles. Topological ground states are prized because their degeneracy can store quantum information robustly. Known stability theorems cover short range forces, or long range ones that fade fast.

Slowly decaying forces, falling like a power law weaker than the space dimension, escape those theorems. The authors study robustness exactly in that uncovered regime. The answer matters for quantum memory designs, where stray long range coupling is hard to remove from real materials and devices. Slow tails are the norm in real stuff, so a proof that owns them is worth more than one that bans them.
arxiv-2512-03009:
Ava Shahbazi Sooraki and Ahmad Sheykhi use the universe's matter surplus to bound a smallest possible length. String theory and quantum gravity suggest a zero point length, a minimal scale of spacetime. That length modifies the entropy tied to cosmic horizons, which feeds back into the Friedmann equations of expansion.

Gravitational baryogenesis, one story for why matter beat antimatter, depends on that expansion history. Requiring the story to match the observed surplus constrains the zero point length. Cosmology thus becomes a tool for testing quantum gravity ideas far beyond any collider. Sky based bounds reach scales no lab can touch. A tight sky bound on a small length is news worth the ink it gets.
arxiv-2512-03109:
AI agents act step by step, so each step needs a check. Shuvom Sadhuka and co-authors study verifiers for agent work in this 2025 work. Verifiers, such as model judges and process reward models, score how good each action is.

Weak scores can let bad steps pass or block good ones. The authors build a verifier method based on sequential hypothesis testing, which checks evidence step by step. Their tool is called E-valuator. More reliable checks could make agents safer to use in research and business tasks where errors compound fast. Sequential testing also lets a verifier stop early when evidence is already strong enough.
arxiv-2512-03209:
A star system with hot dust may hide a small companion star. T. A. Stuber and a large team report a detection in this 2025 work. The system, kappa Tuc A, sits inside a group of five stars and shows a changing infrared glow.

Using interferometry, which merges light from separate telescopes, the team found a subcomponent. They model its orbit and describe it as a low-mass star on an eccentric path. A companion could explain the hot dust near the main star. The finding sharpens the picture of this complex system. A companion on a wide, eccentric path can stir dust and gas around the main star over time.
arxiv-2512-03309:
Earth system models drift from reality over time. Aniruddha Bora and co-authors propose a way to correct them while they run in this 2025 work. Coarse grids, imperfect sub-models, and uncertain starting states all limit predictions.

Classic bias correction helps when data constrain the run, but less once models run freely. The authors train a neural operator that maps model states to correction tendencies. Those corrections apply online during integration, at a limited cadence. The approach could improve climate forecasts without rebuilding the whole model. Online corrections differ from after-the-fact fixes, since they steer the run while it unfolds.
arxiv-2512-03609:
Active proteins stir the membranes they sit in. Sneha Krishnan and Rickmoy Samanta model that stirring in this 2025 work. Membrane-bound motors exert force dipole flows along fluid interfaces and lipid bilayers.

The authors build a unified hydrodynamic and Hamiltonian framework. It covers pusher and puller dipoles in an incompressible two-dimensional membrane over a shallow viscous layer. Membranes govern how cells eat, signal, and move. A sound theory of active membranes helps explain those life processes. Pusher and puller dipoles stir flow in opposite senses, shaping patterns on the membrane that hosts them and their neighbors.
arxiv-2512-03909: Yuan Xiang Chew and Frédérique Oggier study a special family of lattices in this short 2025 algebra preprint. A lattice is well rounded when its shortest nonzero vectors span the whole space in a balanced way, a property prized in coding and cryptography. The authors build such lattices from ideals inside totally definite quaternion algebras. They prove results on when these lattices exist and classify the possibilities, illustrating the methods with worked examples.
arxiv-2512-04009:
Shoppers on platforms like Airbnb rarely book the first listing they see; they compare several side by side before deciding. Jie Tang and colleagues argue in a 2025 information retrieval preprint that search rankings ignore that behaviour. Standard rankers score each item alone, while shoppers judge items against the alternatives visible on the same page.

Their Learning to Comparison-Shop system models comparison behaviour directly inside the ranking architecture. Offline tests and live experiments support the design, with ranking quality and booking conversion both improving by small but statistically significant margins in A/B testing. The model also beat state-of-the-art baselines the authors compared against. The gains matter because they come from aligning the ranker with how users decide, rather than from a bigger model.
arxiv-2512-04209:
Weak gravitational lensing maps the dark universe, but two astrophysical nuisances blur the map: gas feedback reshaping matter, and galaxies aligning intrinsically. Leah Bigwood and colleagues revisit the Dark Energy Survey's third-year cosmic shear analysis in a 2025 cosmology preprint, asking how much precision those nuisances have been costing.

Their approach calibrates both effects with outside data instead of self-calibration alone. A star-forming blue galaxy sample carries alignment parameters fixed by direct spectroscopic measurements. A feedback model draws on X-ray gas fraction measurements and on kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich profiles, spanning wide ranges of halo mass and redshift. The payoff is a two-percent constraint on the clustering amplitude, twice as tight as the survey's fiducial analysis. The central value shifts upward, landing closer to the cosmic microwave background result. The authors offer the recipe as a blueprint for next-generation lensing surveys.
arxiv-2512-04309:
Teaching a computer to write captions for photos usually takes huge sets of photos paired with human-written lines. Rui Fonseca, Bruno Martins, and Gil Rocha present TOMCap, a 2025 method that learns from text alone, with no paired photos at all. Their aim is to cut the cost of building caption tools while closing the gap with fully trained systems.

TOMCap prompts a ready-made language model with clues drawn from a vision-and-text model, after steps that shrink the gap between how text and images are stored inside the model. It also pulls in sample captions fetched from a store of text to guide each new line. In wide tests, TOMCap beat other methods that train on text alone or skip training, and the authors check which parts of the design help most.
arxiv-2512-04509:
Reon Ogawa, Masaki Gen, Kazuyuki Matsuhira, and co-authors report a first test of measuring heat effects inside magnetic fields far stronger than any steady magnet can reach. The magnetocaloric effect is the warming or cooling of a material as a field ramps up or down. Their 2025 arXiv paper pushed pulsed fields to one hundred twenty tesla, a realm where the magnet destroys itself in each shot. The test material was a spin-ice compound of holmium, titanium, and oxygen.

A thin-film thermometer made of gold and germanium tracked the sample's temperature through radio-frequency readings. The team caught a giant heat effect at low fields. They also caught a sharp temperature jump at high fields, tied to a crossing of crystal-field energy levels. The authors discuss a possible lag in the temperature response. The work opens a path to finer heat studies inside destructive pulsed fields.
arxiv-2512-04709:
Clément Bled and François Pitié improve a family of image restoration solvers by training their denoiser inside the solving loop itself. Solvers for tasks like inpainting, super-resolution, and demosaicing often borrow a denoiser as a stand-in for natural image rules. A classic result links a denoiser's leftover noise to the slope of the image prior, which powers gradient-based methods. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on that link, following Kadkhodaie and Simoncelli's gradient solvers.

Instead of a frozen, general denoiser, they fine-tune it end to end across the solver's steps. Training spans several restoration tasks at once. One versatile denoiser comes out, tuned for inverse problems rather than plain cleaning. The team shows the tuned denoiser lifts restoration quality across tasks. A shared, solver-aware denoiser could simplify pipelines in photography, microscopy, and medical scans.
arxiv-2512-04909:
Youla Yang introduces PVLS, a method that uses a graph neural network to pick strong starting parameters for variational quantum linear solvers. Such solvers aim to solve linear systems on near-term quantum hardware. In practice they stall: flat training landscapes, called barren plateaus, and poor starting guesses make optimization crawl as systems grow. Her 2025 arXiv paper teaches a network to read the problem's matrix and predict where the solver should begin.

The graph network exploits the matrix's structure, so its guesses scale with problem size. Tests span matrices from small to more than a thousand rows. Predicted starts cut optimization time by up to about two and a half times and lowered the iteration count, while solution accuracy held steady. Warm starts learned from structure could decide whether variational solvers stay toys or become tools.
arxiv-2512-05009:
Seyed Farid Taghavi and Seyed Mohammad Ali Tabatabaee Mehr ask how fluid-like the matter made in oxygen-oxygen collisions really is. When two oxygen nuclei collide at the Large Hadron Collider, they create a droplet far smaller than those from heavy nuclei. Whether such a droplet flows like a liquid or streams like loose particles is an open question. Its in-between size, plus good control over the starting state, makes it a sharp test case.

The team models the collisions with a hybrid setup that follows the droplet from its first moments through a fluid stage to the final spray of particles. Comparing the model with fresh collider data, they gauge the droplet's opacity — how its size stacks up against the distance particles travel between hits. They find that the more glancing collisions gradually stop behaving like a fluid, marking where the liquid picture breaks down.
arxiv-2512-05109:
Christopher Leong, Daniel Salib, and Bitan Roy chart the phase diagram of electrons on a hyperbolic lattice — a tiling that curves like a saddle, unlike any normal crystal. On these two-dimensional lattices, electrons near half-filling behave like relativistic particles with a vanishing density of states at zero energy. The question is what dirt does to them: sprinkle in dirt, and does the relativistic behavior survive, turn metallic, or freeze into an insulator?

Using a polynomial method on lattices with huge numbers of sites, the authors track two measures of the zero-energy density of states as disorder grows. Weak disorder leaves the Dirac-like behavior intact. Moderate disorder triggers a smooth transition into a metal, and stronger disorder ends in an Anderson insulator. Checking against the flat honeycomb lattice shows the hyperbolic result stems from the negative curvature, giving a phase diagram with no flat-space counterpart.
arxiv-2512-05309:
Adam Alami and four co-authors study how engineers engage with code review when the reviewer is a language model instead of a colleague. Code review is social as much as technical, and how feedback feels shapes whether it gets used. In a two-phase study with twenty engineers, participants exchanged peer reviews and were interviewed about their emotional responses. They then reacted to model-generated review prompts tuned to their preferences.

Peer review, they find, runs on self-regulation: engineers reframe criticism, talk it through, avoid it, or get defensive, and engagement is calibrated to team climate and norms. Model review lowers emotional costs and the need for self-regulation; when the feedback matched expectations, processing felt easier and adoption likelier. The authors conclude model review shifts engagement from managing feelings to managing mental effort, and that AI serves best as a supportive partner, with humans keeping accountability.
arxiv-2512-05509:
Xing Jin and four co-authors build an ultra-stable laser reference the size of a lunchbox. Optical resonators that pin a laser's frequency are cornerstones of precision science, but the best ones live in laboratories. Navigation, portable clocks, and remote sensing need that stability in the field, in ambient conditions. Their device is a whispering-gallery resonator carved from magnesium fluoride, in which light circles the rim with a high quality factor, packaged with fiber coupling that survives ordinary handling.

Stabilizing a laser to the resonator yields a linewidth of only a few hertz. It also yields fractional frequency stability at a level usually associated with national standards instruments. The device can be manufactured quickly and carried out of the lab. Phase noise stays low at offsets. The work makes a case that hertz-class optical references can become portable hardware rather than room-sized installations.
arxiv-2512-05709:
R Datta and four co-authors model a hazard inside SPARC, a compact, high field fusion device. When the hot plasma cools in a disruption, electrons can be accelerated into a runaway beam carrying heavy current. Using an extended magnetohydrodynamics code with a runaway fluid model, the team simulates this coupled system for the first time in SPARC.

They vary the tactic: neon gas alone, or neon mixed with deuterium. Neon alone still left runaway plateaus, with current above five million amperes. The mixed injection held the beam far lower, under two million amperes. In the mixed case a vertical drift of the cooling plasma then killed the beam before any plateau formed. The runs trace the full story, from instability boosting growth, through losses in tangled fields, to surfaces healing and trapping what remains. Such maps guide the design of protection for high current machines.
arxiv-2512-05809:
Saurav Jha and four co-authors stress test a popular trick for helping vision language models reason about space. Models struggle with multi-view scenes and new viewpoints. A system called MindJourney answers by dreaming: a world model imagines views along possible actions, and a verifier scores which imagined views help. The team examines whether the verifier's scores can be trusted.

Their uncertainty analysis is deflating. The verifier barely calibrates its picks, and random scoring often cuts answer uncertainty just as well, exposing biased action choices and unreliable rewards. They then build a better verifier, ViSA, which grounds rewards in small, checkable claims pinned to specific frames. ViSA improved reasoning on one benchmark and balanced the exploration. But on a harder benchmark, no verifier, theirs included, scaled consistently. The imagined views seem to be the bottleneck: detail free dreams cannot sharpen reasoning.
arxiv-2512-05909:
Dakshesh Kololgi, Krishna Naidoo, Amélie Saintonge, and Ofer Lahav teach a network to read a galaxy's address in the cosmic web. Galaxies live in voids, sheets called walls, filaments, or dense clusters, and their dark matter neighborhood shapes how they grow. The team builds a three stage pipeline on the IllustrisTNG simulation, where the true environment is known from the matter field itself.

First, galaxies are labeled by that hidden truth. Their positions are woven into a Delaunay triangulation, and ten graph measures summarize each galaxy's local geometry. A graph attention network learns from those measures to predict the environment label. For galaxies above a billion solar masses in stars, the best model reaches about eighty five percent accuracy, beating both plain networks and other graph designs. The plan is to aim the system at real DESI survey data.
arxiv-2512-06109:
Ajinkya Bhole, Mohammad Mahmoudi Filabadi, Guillaume Crevecoeur, and Tom Lefebvre draw one map for a scattered family of control theories. Optimal control steers systems toward goals under noise. Its variants multiply: classical, risk sensitive, and soft policy versions. A central problem separates the two penalties, and the familiar problems fall out as special cases.

Two results give it teeth. The soft versions majorize the originals, so iterating their solutions recovers the true objectives. In a synchronized case, the soft problem yields linear Bellman operators and path integral solutions. Solvers transfer across problems. Solvers can now be marched toward harder problems.
arxiv-2512-06209:
Andreas Erik Gejl Madsen and Jesper Glückstad report a first working run of a printing method that builds solid objects with light alone. Their setup shines patterned light into a spinning vial of liquid resin, and the light hardens the resin into a full three dimensional shape. What is new is that no lenses or mirrors shape the beam on its way in.

A chip that shifts the phase of light forms the patterns on its own, using a tiling scheme the group built in past work. With a plain resin mix and a short light path, the team printed complex shapes again and again with good control of the dose. The result shows that a compact, lens free printer can do volume printing, which could make such machines cheaper and easier to adapt to new tasks.
arxiv-2512-06409:
Matthew Bate, Mark Hutchison, and Daniel Elsender build a computer code that follows dust as stars and their planet forming discs take shape. Planets start as tiny dust grains that stick together and grow. The grains also drift through the disc under gas drag and get stirred by turbulence. Growth, mixing, and drift must be modeled together. No code had done that from the first collapse of a cloud.

The team merges a grain growth method with a multi grain dynamics scheme inside a three dimensional fluid simulation. Fresh implicit methods keep the stiff drag forces and the turbulent spreading stable. When they ran the code, a surprise emerged. Turbulence inside the disc feeds small and mid sized grains into the zones where the largest grains grow. That speeds growth a great deal. The code opens a way to trace how the seeds of planets form inside young discs.
arxiv-2512-06609:
Tongda Xu and six co authors find a shortcut to a kind of model that squeezes images into discrete tokens. Such tokenizers, VQ-VAEs, are useful for generation, but their discrete step makes them notoriously hard to train. The team's method, Gaussian Quant, trains a smooth Gaussian version of the model first, under set constraints, then converts it into the discrete form with no further training at all.

The conversion uses random Gaussian noise as the codebook and matches each smooth code to its nearest noise vector. Theory backs the trick: once the codebook is large enough relative to a coding rate of the smooth model, the error from the swap is provably small. A training heuristic, the target divergence constraint, makes the smooth model convert cleanly. In tests the converted models beat established discrete rivals on two backbone designs, and the heuristic also improved earlier conversion methods.
arxiv-2512-06709:
Sadia Ruhama tests whether a patient's genetic profile alone can predict which drugs their leukemia will answer to. Acute myeloid leukemia is a fast, aggressive blood cancer with poor survival, so picking the right drug early matters. Cancer genomics now lets doctors tailor treatment to a tumor's genetic features, but how far those features alone can forecast drug sensitivity was unclear.

Ruhama used a public data set from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer project. She trained a support vector regression model on it. That method fits a tolerant band around the data rather than a single line. The model picked out the genetic features that most sway drug response. Its scores on held out data were strong, close to the truth on both validation and test sets. The study supports genetic screening as a real input to personalized leukemia care.
arxiv-2512-06909:
Qiankai Shen and co-authors build a touch-free way to spot bruxism, the teeth grinding and clenching that damages teeth and ruins sleep. Current checks often mean wearing gear in the mouth or sleeping wired to sensors, which disturbs the very sleep being studied and can feel intrusive. The team instead points millimeter-wave radar at the sleeper. Radar echoes shift subtly as the jaw moves, and grinding has a pattern of its own.

From the echo signals the authors extract eleven features that capture that pattern. A random forest classifier, trained on a data set the team built with the same radar, sorts grinding episodes from other motion. The authors see radar as a private, non-invasive option for home screening, while noting wider testing is still needed.
arxiv-2512-07009:
Saeid Ghafouri and co-authors present a case study in speeding up video analytics, using a poultry welfare monitoring system as the test bed. Farms film chickens at high resolution and want near-real-time readings on the flock, which piles up heavy computing work. The pipeline watches the birds through detection, tracking, clustering, and behavior analysis stages. The team tunes every stage rather than swapping in bigger models.

Their fixes are practical engineering: running work in parallel at several levels. Moving hot code from the processor to the graphics card, grouping birds with vectorized math, and trimming memory use in post-processing. On real farm footage, the combined changes delivered up to twice the speed with no loss in model accuracy.
arxiv-2512-07109:
Miguel Ingram and Arthur Merritt diagnose why transformer models stumble on abstract reasoning puzzles, using the ARC benchmark of grid tasks. They first sort all four hundred tasks in a reissued set into a nine-category taxonomy, validated by rule-based code analysis. A vision network trained on raw grids confirms the categories capture something visually real. Turned on the main test set, the taxonomy exposes a bias: a large share of tasks have low neural affinity for transformers.

Fine-tuning a small transformer across most of the tasks reveals a stark compositional gap. On most tasks the model gets individual cells largely right, mastering local patterns, yet almost never completes the whole grid, failing at global synthesis. An independent study with hundreds of specialist models trained on a million examples each confirms the pattern: low-affinity tasks hit hard ceilings no amount of data lifts.
arxiv-2512-07209:
Masato Ishii and co-authors keep sound and picture in step when a video is edited. Cut or transform the visuals of a clip and the original audio suddenly lies: footsteps land early, new objects arrive in silence. Their pipeline edits the video first with state-of-the-art tools, then generates replacement audio that follows the edited picture. A new video-to-audio model takes three inputs at once: the source audio, the target video, and a text prompt describing the edit.

The architecture is extended to accept that conditional audio feed, and a data augmentation strategy makes training more efficient. The model also meters how much the source audio should influence the result according to how complex the edit is, preserving the original sound's structure wherever the picture allows.
arxiv-2512-07609:
Nikita Vaibhav Pavle, Rakesh Kumar Sahoo, and Manoranjan Sinha wrote this 2025 robotics paper. It addresses how drones can dodge moving obstacles in crowded airspace on their own. The classic method for this, the artificial potential field, has two known flaws.

A potential field steers a drone like a ball rolling away from repelling hills. But the drone can get stuck in a hollow, and the classic field ignores how obstacles move. The authors add a bounded weighting that scales the push by each obstacle's direction and relative speed. They then embed the improved field inside model predictive control. That pairing plans smooth paths while respecting how the drone can actually turn and accelerate. In simulations, the drone escapes the old stuck spots and swerves early around movers. Paths stay clean and safe, which supports the method for real cluttered flight.
arxiv-2512-08109:
Yubo Zhang, Johannes Froch, Jinlin Xiang, and colleagues, researchers in optics and machine learning, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is optical neural networks, which use light based hardware to do part of a computing task with far less energy. A flat metalens placed before a sensor can pre process images, but such fixed front ends often fail to generalize beyond one narrow task.

The team tests a single layer broadband metalens working across visible light. It matched the classification accuracy of high end sensor limited optics and beat a standard hyperboloid lens across sensor sizes and digital back ends. They also designed a full metasurface for ImageNet classification, tuned end to end. The tuning tended to balance how sharply the lens passes detail across colors. Keeping spatial detail across wavelengths, they argue, is a key factor in optical network performance.
arxiv-2512-08309:
Alexander Goslin, a computer graphics researcher, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about generating endless virtual terrain. Classic procedural noise is fast and infinite, but its landscapes look fake and lack large scale coherence. Diffusion models make far more realistic terrain, yet they normally work only on fixed size canvases.

His method, InfiniteDiffusion, reshapes diffusion sampling so terrain can be produced lazily, only where needed, without bounds. It keeps the traits that made procedural noise essential: seamless extent, consistency from a seed, and quick random access to any spot. A stack of diffusion models links planetary context down to local detail, and a compact encoding keeps outputs stable across Earth scale height ranges. The system runs faster than orbital velocity on a consumer graphics card, allowing interactive exploration. Goslin presents diffusion as a practical base for the next generation of infinite game and simulation worlds.
arxiv-2512-08509:
Ashutosh Prajapati, Prathapasinghe Dharmawansa, Marco Di Renzo, and Italo Atzeni, wireless researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is holographic MIMO, a future antenna technology using very large apertures instead of many spaced elements. Working so close to the antennas, signals arrive both by direct line of sight and by scattered paths, and the two need one consistent physical model.

The team extends a framework called wavenumber division multiplexing, built for line of sight channels, to a unified electromagnetic model covering both parts. For the scattered part, the framework yields an angular domain picture. They derive closed form results for uniform and non uniform scattering, recovering a classic model as a special case. Finally, they count the usable degrees of freedom and capacity. Adding the scattered component substantially improves performance over the line of sight only picture.
arxiv-2512-08809:
Yi Liu and coauthors present PrivTune, a framework for fine tuning large language models with private data while protecting that data. Providers now let users fine tune custom models from uploaded data sets, which creates a risk of sensitive information leaking. Earlier privacy methods in split device cloud setups often either weaken protection or hurt model quality.

PrivTune uses split learning and adds carefully crafted noise to token representations from the part of the model that runs on the device. The noise makes each token resemble its indirect neighbors, which blurs private content. An optimization step sets the best noise direction, and token importance scales how much noise each token receives. Tests on five data sets, against embedding inversion and attribute inference attacks, show a sharp drop in attack success. Utility falls only slightly, beating prior baselines on the privacy and quality trade off.
arxiv-2512-08909:
Ramin Babaee, Shahab Oveis Gharan, and Martin Bouchard study output glitches in current steering digital to analog converters caused by unequal rise and fall responses in the switches. Such converters are widely used in high speed settings such as optical communication. Their glitches depend on the input and degrade dynamic performance, so reducing them matters for signal quality.

The authors focus on glitches that arise specifically from rise fall asymmetry. They formulate a glitch metric that captures overall converter performance under that effect. That metric is then used to design a new weighting scheme for the converter architecture. Numerical simulations show the proposed design can offer a significant performance advantage over the standard segmented structure. The work gives converter designers a targeted way to attack one concrete glitch source, rather than treating all dynamic errors as a single undifferentiated problem.
arxiv-2512-09109:
W David Wick studies islands of instability that can appear in wavefunction models with nonlinear evolution, a type proposed in the context of the measurement problem in quantum theory. Such islands form a new scenario for chaos in Hamiltonian systems. Criteria for their presence were derived in earlier papers and shown to hold in finite dimensional models, then generalized to continuum models.

The only continuum example before was a model whose linear equation could be solved exactly. Exact solutions of many body problems are rare, so that limit blocked wider use. Wick shows the instability criteria can instead be checked by inserting test functions into computable expressions, bypassing the need for an exact solution. The method can handle realistic potentials between molecules. That opens a possible link to instabilities in fluids and gases, where similar nonlinear dynamics may arise in practice.
arxiv-2512-09209:
Shipeng Cen and Ying Tan work on automated algorithm design, where computer systems invent optimization methods instead of humans writing them by hand. Recent frameworks let large language models evolve algorithms, but they leave untouched the prompts that steer the model. Cen and Tan argue that swarm intelligence, methods modeled on flocks and colonies, gives this design work a firmer base.

Their framework evolves swarm optimization algorithms and their guiding prompts together, using a single language model. They also add a simple way to judge prompt templates, so the process stays understandable. On a range of hard NP problems, the paired evolution beat leading automated design systems. Tests with several different language models produced very different prompt histories, which the authors take as proof that prompt evolution needs structure. The approach also kept its lead without the strongest models, lowering the cost of use.
arxiv-2512-09309:
Zihao Ding and colleagues tackle a privacy problem in mobile vision. Phones and wearables increasingly use vision transformer models, but those models need more computing power than small devices have. Sending images to the cloud solves the power problem while exposing private pictures during transfer and server-side processing.

Their framework splits the work. A trusted local edge device, such as the user's phone, acts as orchestrator and cuts the visual data into pieces. The pieces go to several independent cloud servers, so no single server ever holds the whole image. Only the trusted device merges the results at the end. The team demonstrates the design on the Segment Anything Model for image segmentation. Their tests keep segmentation quality near the normal cloud baseline while sharply reducing the chance that anyone can rebuild the user's content.
arxiv-2512-09409:
Kyle Habib and three co-authors propose Proof of Trusted Execution, a new way for blockchains to agree on blocks. Today's main paradigms have known costs. Proof of Work burns computation and confirms slowly, while Proof of Stake risks stake concentration and long-range attacks, and its speed is capped by slot times and committee voting rounds.

In their design, validators run inside trusted execution environments, hardware enclaves on varied virtual machines, all executing the same recorded program. Each validator produces a vendor-backed attestation tying the enclave's code measurement to the block's contents. Because execution is deterministic and the proposer is picked uniquely from public randomness, blocks can commit in a single round of verification, with no forks and no bottleneck. The paper presents the design of a consensus client, describes a reference implementation, and evaluates it against the throughput needs of a decentralized exchange called Trillion.
arxiv-2512-09609:
Rafael Abreu and Chahana Nagesh introduce the Fréchet interaction density, a quantity for sensitivity analysis of wave equations. Kernels tell modelers how a measurement responds to changes in a medium. The authors extend the adjoint method, the machinery behind such kernels, to equations with complex solutions.

They define the interaction density as the object from which Fréchet sensitivity kernels can be derived. They compute and analyze it for four equations: the second-order wave equation and the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, both real-valued, plus the complex transport equation and the Schrödinger equation with zero potential. Across all four, the interaction shows a structure, with a waveform set by the conditions. For the Schrödinger equation, choosing the adjoint field as the conjugate of the wavefunction makes the interaction density reduce to the Born probability density. That is a bridge between sensitivity theory and quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2512-09709:
Kanchan Meena, Souvik Ghosh, and P. Singha Deo argue for a reinterpretation of electrical conductance in mesoscopic devices, with claimed consequences for quantum mechanics. Their work builds on a quantity called the local partial density of states, which describes how electronic states are distributed in space and can turn negative in the quantum regime. They treat it as a hidden variable that quantum mechanics does not display but experiments can infer through clocks.

Using this idea, they re-derive the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, the phenomenology for conductance in such samples, aiming to ground it as a bridge between classical and quantum behavior. They argue the calculated quantum time dilates like relativistic proper time. They argue measured conductance is a deterministic outcome of the state superposition, which in their view resolves the quantum measurement problem. The three-probe conductance formula is analyzed as the test case for the claim.
arxiv-2512-09809:
Di Zhu, Jianxi Chen, and Hyojoon Kim propose ACORN, a system that runs machine learning classification directly inside network hardware. Doing the classification on the device itself keeps delay low and steady. Existing attempts, though, are squeezed by strict hardware limits and are hard to use. ACORN automates the whole path: it takes Python models and spreads them across network devices using an optimized plan from an integer programming planner.

To fit larger models onto limited hardware, the team designed a new way to represent decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines in the data plane. The design leaves room to reprogram at runtime. They built a prototype in the P4 language and ran it on real programmable hardware. In tests ACORN handled models with several times more features than leading alternatives, while adding negligible drag on network traffic. The authors plan to release their code publicly.
arxiv-2512-09909:
Andrew Elashkin and Orna Grumberg present STACHE, a tool that explains why a reinforcement learning agent chose a particular action. Agents often behave in unexpected ways, especially where rewards are sparse or safety matters, so debugging tools are in demand. STACHE explains one decision at a time, without opening the agent's internals. Each explanation has two parts. One is a robustness region: the connected set of nearby states where the agent would do the same thing. The other is minimal counterfactuals: the smallest changes to the state that would flip the decision.

The method exploits factored state spaces, where a state splits into separate variables. That structure allows an exact search based algorithm, avoiding the accuracy gaps of surrogate models that merely imitate the agent. Tests on standard Gymnasium environments show the explanations track how policy logic evolves during training, from erratic early behavior to stable, robust strategies.
arxiv-2512-10109:
Nizar Riane models Morocco's public procurement market as a strategic game and asks whether stable outcomes exist. Firms bidding for government contracts interact with payoffs that are discontinuous and not quasiconcave, awkward features that break the usual equilibrium theorems. Riane first shows the game has no equilibrium in pure strategies: no fixed profile of bids is stable against unilateral deviation. The analysis then narrows to two players. For that case, explicit mixed strategy equilibria are derived, both for the symmetric game and for a weighted version where players carry unequal weights.

Finally comes the general many player result. Using an extended version of a theorem by Dasgupta and Maskin, Riane proves a symmetric equilibrium in mixed strategies does exist for any number of players, despite the payoff discontinuities.
arxiv-2512-10309:
Jiayu Weng and colleagues teach neural networks to track the probabilities of large chemical reaction networks, including their rarest events. Reaction networks model stochastic processes inside cells, but their exact description, the chemical master equation, explodes: the state space grows exponentially with the number of species. Rare transitions between stable states, often the events that matter most biologically, are the hardest to capture. The authors represent the full joint probability distribution autoregressively with a neural network. Training uses second order optimization, natural gradient descent and the time dependent variational principle, which follow the distribution's geometry rather than fighting it.

Enhanced sampling resolves the rare regions; demonstrations include a genetic toggle switch and a MAPK cascade. Spatially extended Schlögl models on one and two dimensional lattices push the method to state spaces of astronomical size, far beyond exact enumeration.
arxiv-2512-10509:
George Willis studies flat groups of automorphisms, symmetries of totally disconnected, locally compact groups, the kind of groups that arise for number systems built over local fields. A group of symmetries counts as flat when a single compact open subgroup is moved by every symmetry so that a certain index is minimised. That tidy anchoring condition unlocks a great deal of structure.

Flat groups carry a rank, read off from a free abelian quotient. And the paper shows they mimic their best-known examples, such as Lie groups over local fields and symmetry groups of buildings. Analogues of roots appear, and the anchoring subgroup splits into analogues of root subgroups. Willis presents new proofs of improved versions of these results, tightening a theory that organises a wide family of otherwise unruly symmetry groups.
arxiv-2512-10709:
Yizhou Fang and co-authors present disperon QED, a method for feeding measured data into loop calculations inside Monte Carlo event generators. Precision particle physics needs hadronic vacuum polarisation inside two-loop corrections, but that ingredient comes from experiment, not from clean theory, and wiring data into automated codes is delicate. Dispersion relations offer the bridge.

The method combines those relations with automated tools such as OpenLoops, effective field theory reasoning. And a threshold subtraction to keep the numerics tame. The authors apply it in the McMule code to electron-positron annihilation into two pions. The method handles the hadronic insertions in two-loop terms. It also handles the pion's vector form factor, within a scalar QED scheme. They stress the method's generality for harder processes. The thirty-four page paper appears in SciPost Physics.
arxiv-2512-10909:
Filippo Gaggioli, Pierre-Antoine Graham, and Liang Fu let a neural network explore how electrons arrange themselves inside a semiconductor quantum well. The homogeneous electron gas underpins much of condensed matter theory, but for strongly interacting electrons in a realistic three-dimensional well, theory has lagged. Their variational method, driven by a neural network and starting from first principles, scans electron densities and well thicknesses without assuming the answer.

Metallic and crystalline phases appear, with the charge settling into either a single layer or a bilayer depending on conditions. In the bilayer regime the method found something new. An electronic quasicrystal, a pattern with the long-range order of a crystal but no repeating unit, made purely of electrons. The authors present the phase as a discovery enabled by the unbiased search, the kind of structure a method that only tests guessed candidates would never propose.
arxiv-2512-11009:
Nikhil Raghav and fellow authors report their team's entry to a national Indian AI challenge on language independent speaker work. The task combined identifying who is speaking, separating speakers in recordings, transcribing speech, and translating it. Such tools matter for multilingual and code-mixed audio, where people switch languages mid sentence.

Their process bettered speaker separation first, using robust voice action spotting and fine tuned speaker embeddings for low resource settings. A multi-kernel clustering setup they had proposed earlier raised separation scores across the training recordings. Modules for speaker and language identification, speech spotting, and machine translation completed the system, with post processing steps added to make the output more reliable in real use.
arxiv-2512-11309:
Claudia Lagos and the COLIBRE simulation team trace a fundamental galaxy law across thirteen billion years of cosmic history. The Kennicutt Schmidt relation links how much gas a galaxy has per unit area to how fast it forms stars there. Their simulations follow non equilibrium chemistry, dust evolution, and cooling to very low temperatures, so atomic and molecular gas can be predicted directly.

For the present day universe the simulations reproduce the observed relations for both kinds of gas, including their scatter, which the team ties to stellar density, star formation intensity, and metal content. Looking back, the time galaxies need to use up molecular gas shrinks dramatically toward early epochs, mainly because early gas held fewer metals. Galaxies forming stars more intensely also hold more molecular gas and use it faster. Predictions match observations across a wide span of cosmic time.
arxiv-2512-11509:
Mohor Banerjee and fellow authors test whether methods that stop language models from hallucinating also dull their creativity, a trade off that matters for discovery in science. Assistants must be factually reliable, yet hypothesis generation needs divergent, exploratory thinking. The team weighed three popular fixes: a self verification method, a decoding method that contrasts internal layers, and retrieval augmented generation.

They tested several model families at sizes from small to very large on two creativity benchmarks. The three fixes pulled in varied directions. Self verification in fact enhanced divergent creativity, the decoding method suppressed it, and retrieval changed little. The findings give researchers concrete guidance: the right anti hallucination tool depends on whether the use case prizes being right alone or being right with creative range. Workflows in science, the authors argue, should choose on purpose rather than by habit.
arxiv-2512-11809:
Youssef Azouzi proves a completeness result for a family of function spaces built on vector lattices. Vector lattices, or Riesz spaces, order their elements like functions while allowing limits. The spaces Lp(T) arise when a conditional expectation operator T, an averaging map, supplies the size measure.

Azouzi first builds a general convergence theory that unifies order, norm, and weak convergence, with simpler proofs than before. With that frame he shows the Lp(T) spaces are strongly complete for all p, settling a question open for years. The universal completion is covered too. A final payoff is a new ergodicity result for systems that preserve the averaging operator.
arxiv-2512-12009:
Marc Uphues, Sebastian Thöne, and Herbert Kuchen draft a reference architecture for putting quantum software inside business systems. Quantum hardware can accelerate certain hard business problems, but enterprise software has strict needs for modularity and audit that quantum code rarely respects.

Their design splits the system into loosely coupled services. Some services are quantum free, handling business logic, while others wrap the quantum steps. An executable BPMN process model conducts the whole flow, giving a stable reusable pipeline. Two case studies from operations research, both combinatorial problems, show the pattern in action. The blueprint lets firms add quantum parts without rebuilding their core systems around them.
arxiv-2512-12109:
Allen Daniel Sunny and Ido Sivan-Sevilla build a framework that holds public sector AI to the law. Auto eligibility systems decide who gets vital benefits like CalFresh, California food aid program. Their stated reasons often drift from the statutes that authorize the decisions, leaving wronged applicants with little to contest.

The framework encodes eligibility rules from the state policy manual into a formal ontology. A pipeline turns statutory logic into checkable form, and a solver tests whether each system explanation obeys the law. Case studies show it catching explanations that break real rules and naming the rule broken. The goal is decisions that stay traceable and contestable by design.
arxiv-2512-12209:
Zahra Dehghanian and three co-authors present CineLOG in a 2025 paper on film style video generation. Text prompts give weak control over camera moves and genre, two things viewers notice at once. Old data sets also have uneven labels, noise, and a gap between fake and real footage.

CineLOG is a data set of 5,000 high quality, uncut clips with balanced coverage. It covers 17 camera movements and 15 film genres, each clip with scene notes and camera orders. A four stage pipeline builds the clips, plus a module that smooths joins between shots. Human judges rated its videos above top end to end models on following camera and script orders.
arxiv-2512-12809:
Junbo Jacob Lian and seven co-authors present OPAL, a system that learns an optimizer program for each black box problem, in a 2025 paper. Black box optimization tunes inputs when only outputs can be seen, and standard evolutionary algorithms vary wildly by problem. OPAL views an optimizer as a short program over a small set of search operators, like explore, restart, and local search.

A small design budget probes the landscape with a differential evolution baseline, and sampled points form a nearest neighbor graph encoded by a graph neural network. A meta learner then outputs a phase wise schedule of operators for that instance. On the CEC 2017 test suite, one meta trained policy was statistically competitive with top adaptive differential evolution variants, with modest overhead.
arxiv-2512-13409:
K. Decker French, Brenna Mockler, Nicholas Earl, and Tanner Murphey estimate how well the Vera Rubin Observatory will measure black hole masses from tidal disruption events. In such events, a star shredded by a black hole flares brightly. Rubin should find thousands per year, a flood compared with today.

They model how Rubin's sampling and noise affect fits to simulated light curves. Black hole masses in their tested range were recovered with typical errors of 0.26 dex, and early coverage removed the worst outliers. The disrupted star's mass proved hard to recover, tangled with accretion efficiency. Only 57 percent of cases correctly told full disruptions from partial ones.
arxiv-2512-13509:
Rodrigo F. Saliba and Raphael C. Drumond study the quantum Mpemba effect in open quantum systems. In this odd effect, a system far from balance can settle to balance faster than one that starts closer. Their 2025 paper looks at systems that lose memory of past states as they evolve, a case called Markovian.

The authors offer a cause based on parts of the system that stay free of decoherence. They show the decay rate can grow fast with system size, giving an extreme form of the effect. They also test strong forms through Davies maps and build a small model of the heat bath around the system.
arxiv-2512-13609:
Shweta Mahajan and co-authors introduce Do-Undo, a task and benchmark for action understanding in vision-language models. A model must show the outcome of a real-world action on a scene, then reverse it back to the first state. That forward and reverse demand tests true cause-and-effect grasp, not just style edits.

The team built a curated benchmark of reversible actions from real-world scenes. Their tests show current models struggle with reversibility in image generation. The gap shows why action understanding needs its own tests, apart from prompt-based editing scores. Do-Undo gives a plain testbed for judging and improving models that must reason about how the physical world changes.
arxiv-2512-13909:
Frank M. Abel and co-authors train machine learning models to predict magnetization of iron oxide nanoparticles from X-ray diffraction alone. High-throughput materials work needs property checks from a single measurement. Their route builds the training data from physics-based simulation rather than from large lab campaigns.

Simulated diffraction patterns, generated from crystallographic files and modulated, are linked to a simple magnetic model to give magnetization at a set field. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models train on that simulated data. The team then synthesized real nanoparticles and measured diffraction and magnetization curves to tune the models. Best models reached an R squared above 0.9 for maximum magnetization at 2.8 T on five tuning samples, and predicted full magnetization curves reasonably well.
arxiv-2512-14009:
Yadikaer Maitiniyazi, Christof Wetterich, and Masatoshi Yamada discuss scaling solutions for gauge invariant flow equations in dilaton quantum gravity. Asymptotically safe gravity seeks an ultraviolet fixed point that keeps quantum gravity well behaved at very short distances. The dilaton version differs from the Reuter fixed point because the Planck mass depends on a scalar field.

They use the gauge invariant functional flow equation in a general approximation with up to two derivatives. That strengthens the argument that this fixed point exists. The quantum effective action from the scaling solution can describe inflation in early cosmology. It can also describe dynamical dark energy for late cosmology, linking one quantum gravity scenario to both ends of cosmic history.
arxiv-2512-14109:
Peter Athron and the GAMBIT Collaboration review global fits in a 2025 paper on the hunt for physics beyond the Standard Model. Global fits combine many experiments at once to test a theory against all the data, rather than one result at a time.

Early fits focused on simple supersymmetric models, which add partner particles to known ones. The review traces how fits grew to cover axion like particles, larger Higgs sectors, dark matter models, and effective field theories. It also covers the shift from hunting signals to judging whole models after null results. The authors close with machine learning, faster sampling, and shared software as next steps.
arxiv-2512-14409:
Michelle Döring, Jannes Malanowski, and Stefan Neubert study the River method, a newer voting rule related to Ranked Pairs. Both rules build a margin graph from voter preferences and remove majority cycles to pick a winner. Ties in the graph force a tiebreaker, which breaks neutrality because the rule then favors some options in advance.

Counting a candidate as a winner whenever any tiebreaker would elect them restores neutrality, but for Ranked Pairs that task is NP-complete. For River, the authors give a fast algorithm instead. Their Fused-Universe method runs all tiebreakings in one pass and produces certificates explaining each winner.
arxiv-2512-14509:
Andrei Tokovinin measures the orbits of twelve multiple-star systems, where stars orbit each other in nested pairs. He combines sharp speckle imaging with radial velocity data to pin down both the tight inner orbits and the wide outer ones. Masses and brightnesses of the individual stars are estimated along the way.

Four systems hold four stars arranged as a triple plus a distant single, while the rest are triples. Two triples turned out nearly flat, with similar-mass stars on mildly stretched orbits. One inner pair circles in just a quarter of a day, two stars nearly touching. Another compact system, first spotted by the Gaia mission, gained a newly confirmed wide companion.
arxiv-2512-14709:
Transformer language models reason well on many tasks, yet they stay brittle when a task needs stable handling of symbols. A vector-symbolic view is developed here to explain both sides of that behavior in one frame.

The reading treats self-attention and the residual stream as a rough form of vector symbolic architecture, a scheme where symbols are bound by vector operations. On this view, reasoning works when the binding stays clean and fails when it degrades. The view gives researchers a shared language for diagnosing transformer failures, and for building models that handle symbols with more care.
arxiv-2512-14809:
Tinglong Feng, Jesse Moes, and Tomislav Prokopec study how unstable quantum states decay over time. Such decay is mostly a steady exponential drop, but it starts with odd early behavior and ends with a slow tail. The team gives a full study of simple one dimensional models of this process, called resonance models.

They split the math into a pole part and a branch part, and use the split to define two key times. Dawn time marks when the steady decay takes over, and twilight time marks when the tail wins out. The twilight time has a neat closed form using the Lambert W function. Their formulas cover square and curved barriers, and the picture may extend to vacuum decay in field theory.
arxiv-2512-14909:
Wyatt Gibbons and five coauthors boost a quantum effect that lets current flow one way more easily than the other. The setting is a superconducting diode effect inside a SQUID, a loop device that is exquisitely sensitive to magnetic fields. The effect comes from interference between the wavy current patterns of the loop's branches.

Their device uses two loops, and each branch holds two gate tunable Josephson junctions in series. The gates let them tune both the shape and the strength of three interfering patterns on their own. With careful tuning, the diode efficiency passed 50 percent. Wiggles in the response as flux changed matched a simple model of the device well. Strong, tunable diodes of this kind are sought for superconducting circuits that waste less energy.
arxiv-2512-15309:
Kai Zhang and seven coauthors present GuangMing-Explorer, a four legged robot that explores on its own. Autonomous exploration fuses perception, planning, control, and motion, and it serves indoor search, mapping of extreme places, and resource scouting. Progress on single parts has been strong, but a full, practical system description covering hardware and software together is rare.

The paper walks through the whole platform: the hardware design, the software stack, how algorithms are deployed, and the experimental setup. Real world trials then show the robot carrying out exploration tasks effectively and efficiently. The authors aim to give builders a working blueprint, not just a lab demo. Their results suggest the platform can handle complex, unstructured environments, the kind where exploration robots earn their keep.
arxiv-2512-15409:
Hector Ariza, Carmen Fernandez, and Antonio Galbis study composition operators on weighted modulation spaces in a 2025 math paper. A composition operator reshapes a function by feeding its input through another function first. Modulation spaces measure a function by both its size and its frequency content, with weights that stress some parts over others.

The authors look at operators whose symbols are suitable small changes of the identity map. They study how these operators act between different weighted modulation classes. The work covers spaces built from tempered distributions and also spaces of ultradistributions defined with a subadditive weight. The results clarify when such reshaping stays well behaved across these settings.
arxiv-2512-15609:
Antonio Galvan and co authors test whether hadronic processes drive high energy emission in quasars seen by the Fermi space telescope in a 2025 paper. Most models credit leptons, such as electrons, for quasar gamma rays. Hadronic processes, involving protons, would also produce neutrinos, giving a cross check.

The team models the full spectral energy distributions of a sample of flat spectrum radio quasars with both lepton and hadron parts. The fits suggest a hadronic contribution is needed to explain the observed spectra. Even so, the share of the IceCube neutrino flux these quasars supply stays modest. The paper is accepted in Revista Mexicana de Astronomia y Astrofisica.
arxiv-2512-16109:
G Abellan, N Bolivar, and I Vasilev construct model universes from electric fields in an arXiv paper published in 2025. They ask how gravity responds when the only source is a classical electrostatic setup, like the field of a charged ball. Their spacetimes are static and spherically symmetric, written in Painleve-Gullstrand-like coordinates.

Inside each charged region the geometry comes out flat, while outside it is shaped by the field. The authors work through several cases: point-charge-like fields, screened Yukawa fields, dielectric layers, and a Hulthen-type field. For each they derive the pressures the Einstein equations require and test the classical energy conditions. They also check for singular behavior where regions join. The models offer a clean, solvable setting to study gravity from simple, well-understood sources.
arxiv-2512-16409:
Hao Tang and four co-authors generalize neural PDE solvers in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. Neural operators learn maps between functions, solving whole families of partial differential equations quickly. Most designs stumble on signals that do not repeat, on transient responses, and on domains with irregular shapes.

Their framework expands solutions in a pole-residue form enriched with exponential basis functions, which naturally captures aperiodic and decaying behavior. The Geometric Laplace Neural Operator then places that representation in the eigen-basis of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, extending it to curved surfaces of any shape without grids or periodicity. A companion network, GLNONet, makes the scheme grid-invariant in practice. Across PDE and ODE benchmarks and real-world data sets, the method proved more robust than leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-16509:
C Morin and seven co-authors demonstrate an elusive state of matter in research shared on arXiv in 2025. A supersolid is both a crystal, with atoms locked in a pattern, and a superfluid, flowing without friction. Real examples are rare and fragile, limited to weakly interacting gases.

The team confines dipolar excitons, bound electron-hole pairs with long-range interactions, in a lattice with long-range hopping. At fillings of one quarter, one third, and one half, crystals of about 100 sites form on their own, breaking the lattice's translation symmetry. Coherent hopping across the lattice gives the same crystals off-diagonal long-range order, the mark of superfluidity. Numerical calculations confirm quantitatively that supersolidity builds in the ground state. The framework reaches the strong interaction regime earlier work could not.
arxiv-2512-16709:
Didier Barret and Simon Dupourqué improve fast X-ray spectrum fitting with simulation-based inference, in the third paper of a series. The method learns likely parameter ranges from simulated spectra, giving near-instant fits for data from the future newAthena X-IFU instrument.

An auto-encoder first squeezes each spectrum into a small code, trained with a custom loss tied to fit quality. A density model then learns ranges from those codes over several rounds, each round zooming in near the observed data. A final importance sampling step corrects the learned ranges to exact ones. On test data the results match slow nested sampling, at ten times the speed on a laptop.
arxiv-2512-16809:
Davide Racco and Alfredo Stanzione revisit how dark matter froze out or froze in when the early universe went through supercooling, a stage of fast expansion during a phase switch. The changed expansion and the heat dumped at reheating can shift the final dark matter share.

Past work counted only a plain dilution factor. The pair show extra effects when dark matter making ends during supercooling itself. For WIMP-like candidates, zones once ruled out can open up for direct searches, and freeze-in candidates move closer to test reach. The linked gravitational wave background gains a distinct low-tone shape from a slow reheating stage, tying lab searches to wave astronomy.
arxiv-2512-16909:
Yuanchen Ju and coauthors introduce MomaGraph, a scene graph format for household robots that must both move and handle objects. A good scene record must say where things are, what they do, and which parts can be grabbed, and it must update as states change.

MomaGraph merges spatial and functional links with part-level detail in one task-aware graph. The team also built MomaGraph-Scenes, a large annotated data set, and MomaGraph-Bench, a test suite over six reasoning skills. Their 7 billion parameter vision-language model, trained with reward learning, predicts such graphs and plans from them. It hit 71.6 percent on the bench, 11.4 points past the best rival, and transferred to real robots.
arxiv-2512-17009:
João Barata and coauthors show how jet substructure can probe the first instants of heavy-ion collisions, when quark-gluon matter sits far from equilibrium and strongly directional. Those early stages set later flow, yet soft measures barely see them.

Using classical Yang-Mills runs and kinetic theory for the jet quenching parameter, they compute the energy-energy correlator for mid-rapidity jets in the BDMPS-Z frame. Split into celestial blocks, the result isolates terms that encode the directional shape of the young medium. A named observable couples straight to spatial anisotropy. Checks with the JEWEL Monte Carlo, tuned to a directional medium, agree in kind, and higher-point correlators could sharpen the view.
arxiv-2512-17209:
Keisuke Toyama and coauthors test whether foundational audio encoders understand music structure, the sections and repeats that organize a song. Such encoders, pre-trained on large audio corpora, lift many music tasks, but structure analysis was barely explored.

Eleven encoder types were compared, varying learning method, training data, and context length. Encoders trained by self-supervised masked modeling on music data proved best for structure analysis. Other mixes lagged, showing that what an encoder learned from matters more than size alone for this task. The findings chart how future encoders should be built and picked for music structure work.
arxiv-2512-17309:
Asil Kaan Bozcuoğlu and Ziyuan Liu revisit RoboEarth, an early project that let robots share what they know about actions, objects, and places through one shared knowledge graph. Engineers once wrote that knowledge by hand in a formal web language, a slow process that kept the library small. The authors ask whether a large language model can do much of that writing now.

Their planner, RecipeMasterLLM, takes a user prompt and drafts action descriptions that fit the RoboEarth format. The model was fine-tuned for that format, and at run time it pulls facts about the setting from the graph to ground its answers. The goal is a robot knowledge base that can grow on its own.
arxiv-2512-18309:
Harsh Rathva, Ojas Srivastava, and Pruthwik Mishra sketch a way to build safety into learning agents rather than bolting it on after. In multi agent training, guardrails usually come as outside rewards or late checks. Their ESAI frame grows an inner alignment signal inside each agent, a learned code that forecasts harm from roads not taken and steers updates away from it.

Four parts work together: soft what if penalties, attention weighted by alignment, a memory that links cause to later credit, and a graph spread that tempers bias. The authors prove when the inner codes stay bounded and weigh fairness against raw performance. No lab tests are included; the paper is a blueprint with open questions named.
arxiv-2512-18509: V. R. Shaginyan and A. Z. Msezane wrote this two-page comment, posted to arXiv in December 2025, answering an earlier paper on the future of the correlated electron problem (arXiv:2010.00584). They argue that some of the very difficult problems that paper raised have in fact been successfully solved, and that the field should focus on those resolved problems. Quoting the original authors' hope that their topics inspire progress, the comment concludes there is no need to mislead potential researchers about how open the problems remain.
arxiv-2512-18909:
Anshika Bansal, Jack Jenkins, and Daniel Winney refine predictions for rare kaon decays, prized tests of the Standard Model. The decays of a charged kaon into a pion plus a lepton pair, or a pion plus a neutrino pair, are described by nonlocal form factors that are hard to compute directly. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds dispersive representations grounded in unitarity.

The representations lean on the P-wave amplitude for kaon-pion scattering into two pions. That amplitude is parameterized in the Khuri-Treiman framework and pinned by data from kaon decays into three pions, plus the pion vector form factor. Relations from the operator product expansion tie the charged-lepton and neutrino modes together, adding constraints. The payoff is a sharper theoretical grip on the neutrino mode's spectrum and rate, exactly where new physics could hide.
arxiv-2512-19509:
Shangbo Yun, Xiaodong Gu, Jianghong Huang, and Beijun Shen sort programming languages into families, for the benefit of code language models. Trainers usually just pool code from every language together. Whether languages help or hinder each other, and which are truly kin, has gone mostly unasked.

Twenty-one linguistic traits, from variable definition to control flow, anchor the study. A model writes trait-matched snippets in nineteen languages, and embeddings of those parallel samples form a similarity map. Hierarchical clustering then reveals clear language families. The authors argue such kinship should shape how multilingual code data is mixed for training and inference, replacing blind pooling with structured sharing.
arxiv-2512-19609:
Route tracing on maps turns out to be a weak spot for multimodal language models, the systems that reason over images and text together. Artemis Panagopoulou and four co-authors note that models often break basic path rules, partly because pixel-accurate route annotations are costly to collect by hand. Their answer, MapTrace, generates that training data synthetically instead.

MapTrace builds synthetic map images and parses them at pixel level to produce exact path labels automatically. From it the team assembled 23 thousand path samples spread over 4 thousand maps, then fine-tuned open and proprietary models with the data. On the MapBench benchmark, success rates rose by up to 6.4 points and path-tracing error fell, showing spatial skills can be taught with synthetic supervision.
arxiv-2512-19809:
Shashwat Chakraborty and Taylor Hughes describe a skin effect that lives in state space, not in real space. In non-Hermitian systems, states can pile up at a boundary. Here the pile-up is across Fock space, the space of many-body setups. The stage is a quantum dimer model, where atoms pair up under strict rules. They name the effect the Fock space skin effect. They map it with both math and computer runs.

The payoff is state preparation. The effect can steer a system into a gapped quantum spin liquid state. Such states are prized for their long-range entanglement, and hard to make. A Rydberg-atom layout is shown to do the job. It uses blockade tricks to enforce the pairing rules. One-way reservoirs supply the non-Hermitian drive. The layout reaches an exact spin liquid ground state on a square grid.
arxiv-2512-20009:
Ahmed Elezaby and Artem Abanov bound how hot a superconductor near a quantum critical point can stay superconducting. At such a critical point, soft collective bosons mediate strong interactions that simultaneously create non-Fermi-liquid behavior and unconventional pairing, breaking textbook BCS and Eliashberg theory habits. Their playground is the gamma-model, where the effective interaction falls off as a power of frequency.

A recent reformulation recasts the Eliashberg equations as a classical infinite spin chain with nonlocal interactions, and free-energy Hessian analysis turns that picture into algebra. From it they derive rigorous closed-form lower and upper bounds on the transition temperature for every positive gamma. The new upper bound is significantly tighter than the literature's and converges quickly toward earlier numerical results, while their route independently confirms known lower bounds.
arxiv-2512-20209:
Ya-Min Quan and co-authors model the magnetic compound CoNb2O6 as a twisted Kitaev chain. Kitaev interactions are prized because they can host exotic fractional excitations, but they are hard to detect in real materials. The team fixes the model's twist angle by matching the measured specific-heat phase diagram of the compound.

They then predict what terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy should see in this material. The simulated signals show diagonal peaks and a grid of split rephasing peaks. A projection analysis traces these features to excitations made of two and four spinons. The message is practical: even weak Kitaev interactions should be visible with this spectroscopy, giving experimentalists a concrete detection route.
arxiv-2512-20309:
Xuegang Li and co-authors design a dark matter detector built from arrays of superconducting qubits. Light dark matter particles would deposit only tiny amounts of energy, far below what conventional detectors notice. The team's quantum parity detector aims to sense single phonons, the smallest packets of lattice vibration, with high resolution.

A two-chip layout reduces signal loss between the absorber and the sensing qubits. Full simulations of phonons and quasiparticles show the device catching energy deposits of roughly thirty milli-electronvolts with near-perfect efficiency. Projected sensitivity to dark matter scattering improves by orders of magnitude for both light and heavy mediators. Similar gains are expected for axion and dark photon absorption in a stated low mass range.
arxiv-2512-20409:
Junho Yoon, Jaemo Jung, Hyunju Kim, and Dongman Lee align room cameras with ambient sensors to recognize human actions. Wearable-based systems work, but they burden users, raise privacy worries, and scale poorly. Fixed exocentric video plus room sensors is a gentler alternative, provided the two streams can be aligned well.

Global alignment, the standard trick, washes out subtle motions and confuses actions with similar timing but different meaning. DETACH instead decomposes alignment into spatial and temporal parts. New sensor-spatial features, found by online clustering, ground the alignment in context. Mutual supervision sets spatial correspondence first; a weighted contrastive loss then handles time. On two public data sets, the method improves substantially over adapted wearable-based benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-20509:
Sanjay Pant, Himanshu Parihar, and Pradeep Kumar Sharma use holography to measure a subtle kind of quantum link. Entanglement negativity detects mixed-state links that entropy measures can miss. Their bulk setting is a deformed anti-de Sitter black hole, backreacted by a cloud of strings, dual to a hot gauge theory with heavy quarks.

The authors establish a first-law-like relation for the heat-like rules of entanglement at small backreaction, taking the zero-temperature black hole as ground state. Pen-and-paper expansions in cold and hot limits yield negativity for adjacent, bipartite, and disjoint regions. Backreaction enhances distillable links at both extremes of heat. Compared with the usual entropy measure and mutual information, negativity reads the tug-of-war between thermal and quantum correlations more sharply.
arxiv-2512-20709:
Władysław Sokołowski, Huma Jamil, and Karol Makuch extend a theory of diffusion to particles shaped like rods. In complex fluids, how fast a particle spreads resists the classic Stokes-Einstein rule. A fruitful line of work ties that spreading to the fluid's viscosity function, which says how thick the fluid feels at each length scale. The authors widen that line from round probes to long ones, using linear response theory.

Their test rod is a dimer, two beads joined as one. Neat closed forms give its spread rates along its axis and sideways to it, both read straight off the viscosity function. The same forms cover near-round wandering and strongly one-way, snake-like motion. For lab workers who track rod-like tracers in polymer solutions, the result is a handy tool, with its limits for gels stated plainly.
arxiv-2512-21009:
S. M. Shovan, Arindam Khanda, Sanjukta Bhowmick, and Sajal Das build the missing data structure for networks whose connections join groups, not pairs. Hypergraphs capture those higher-order interactions, and counting their triads reveals group patterns ordinary graphs miss. Real hypergraphs are large and constantly changing, and no specialized tooling existed for tracking them. ESCHER is a graphics-processor-centered structure designed to store an evolving hypergraph and update triad counts without recomputing from scratch.

The update framework trims redundant work for hyperedge-based, vertex-based, and temporal triads alike. On large real and synthetic datasets it outruns prior methods by factors reaching into the hundreds, with the largest gain above four hundred seventy times on vertex-based triads. Dynamic hypergraph analysis becomes something researchers can run interactively rather than overnight.
arxiv-2512-21109:
Chen Liang and Daniel Rakita speed up the derivative bottleneck inside a popular robot-control library. MuJoCo MPC plans robot motion by repeatedly rolling out the MuJoCo physics simulator and optimizing. It prices candidate actions with finite-difference derivatives, a costly nudge-and-measure routine. That routine scales badly with a robot's degrees of freedom. The authors swap in Web of Affine Spaces derivatives, a recent technique that reuses information across related derivative computations to produce accurate approximations faster and more stably.

The fit with predictive control is natural, since each planning step needs derivatives only slightly changed from the last. Across a suite of tasks and robot bodies, the new backend integrates seamlessly, runs up to twice as fast with gradient-based planners, and beats the library's sampling-based planners on efficiency and reliability. The integrated implementation is open source.
arxiv-2512-21809:
Vitthal Bhandari, in a term paper for a course on the societal impacts of language technologies, examines how researchers study cross-cultural bias in language models. Large models can adjust answers to cultural context, but they also overgeneralize across cultures.
