Cesare read law and took his degree in that field. In 1860 he chose to serve with Garibaldi in war. He went with that chief to Sicily on his great march. He went with him to Aspromonte in 1862 as well. He went with him to Tirol in the year 1866. Voters sent him to the chamber for Rovigo more than once. He then gave his time to the press and to law. He ran the paper Diritto for a time in Rome. In 1889 he was made a senator of the realm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-penso-joseph-kn:
Joseph Penso was a merchant, poet, and giver to charity. He was born at Espejo, in Spain, about 1650. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Amsterdam in 1692, his home for most of his life.

His father had escaped the Inquisition's dungeon in Spain. He then kept a vow to live openly as a Jew. Joseph wrote a Hebrew drama at eighteen. He led a Spanish literary academy in Amsterdam. His Confusion de Confusiones still stands as an early book on the stock market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-barnet:
Barnet Phillips was an American journalist with the New York Times. He was born in Philadelphia on November 9, 1828. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1847.

After college Phillips crossed to Europe for study. He worked at journalism there before coming home. Back in America he joined the Times staff. That tie lasted more than thirty years in all. He also published two books of his own. Their titles were The Struggle and Burning Their Ships.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pletsch-solomon: Solomon Pletsch was a Jewish city surgeon at Frankfort. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came from Regensburg to the post in 1394. The city paid him thirty-six gulden a year. It gave him uniform cloth like the Christian officials. Only his oath differed, sworn in the Jewish form. He treated council members and hospital Jews for free. Citizens paid him moderate fees for his care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-solomon-:
Solomon Zalman Posner was a Polish rabbi born at Landsberg about 1778. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, Joseph Landsberg, was rabbi of Posen. Solomon died at Loslau in 1863. At his wish his sons set a wooden stone over his grave.

Posner left several works in handwriting, none printed in his life. One defends Talmud study against the young who scorn it. One is a set of moral letters for sons. The letters guide boys who leave home for the yeshivah. A third work gives notes on the whole Pentateuch. The entry names these books and their themes one by one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-12409:
Psalms is the name of the great song book of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name comes from a Greek word for string playing. It first meant the music made on strings. Then it meant the song sung to that music. Greek translators use a like word for a big stringed tool.

Those Greek words render the Hebrew mizmor and tehillim. The root and sense of mizmor are not clear, he says. Tehillim means songs of praise in plain terms. The article traces the book's name and its making. It asks who wrote the psalms and when they were joined.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovich-rabb:
Osip Aaronovich Rabinovich was a Russian Jewish author and journalist. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Kobelyaki in 1817. He died at Meran in the Tyrol in 1869. His father held a post in the state liquor trade. That post set the house apart from its neighbors.

His father spoke Russian with ease and fluency. Most Jews of the southwest had but slight Russian then. Aaron took great care with his son's schooling. The boy learned Hebrew under a named teacher, Meïr Emde. He learned the tongues of his land as well. That rare mix made him a bridge between two worlds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-real-estate-126:
Real estate means landed property in Jewish law. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The entry contrasts land with movable goods, called chattels. It sends readers to many related articles for details.

The article stresses one point about inheritance. Land and goods pass to heirs under the same rights. That rule differs sharply from English common law. It agrees with Roman law instead, the writers say. A sick person's gift could pass land as a deed does. Sales and gifts by healthy owners used different forms. The entry maps how land moves between people under Jewish rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roman-jacob-ben:
Jacob ben Isaac Roman was a bibliographer of Spanish descent born about 1570. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Constantinople. He died at Jerusalem in 1650.

The article says he knew the whole Mishnah by heart. Conforte reports that feat of his learning. He knew Arabic and understood Turkish and Latin. On a journey he was captured and later ransomed. Through a physician friend he met Anton Leger of Geneva. Leger recommended him to Johannes Buxtorf in Basel. Buxtorf used his bibliographic knowledge for a famous appendix. Their letters were later published in a French journal. Roman also planned a Hebrew press for Constantinople. No Jewish press then served the East, he noted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-1290:
Rothschild is the name of the most famous family of financiers of the nineteenth century. Its named authors were Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Singer, Frederick T. Haneman, Jacques Kahn, Goodman Lipkind, J. de Haas, and I. L. Bril. The name comes from a red shield on a house in Frankfort's Judengasse.

The family's earliest known member, Moses Rothschild, was born about 1550. Its founder was Mayer Amschel Rothschild, born at Frankfort about 1743. As a boy he changed money for his father's small banking business. That work sparked his lifelong interest in coins and finance. The long entry follows the house from that Frankfort shop to European fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sajo-aladar-130:
Aladár Sajó was a Hungarian author born at Waitzen on September 8, 1869. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was educated for the law at Budapest, and wrote novels alongside.

Sajó served as a lieutenant in Bosnia from 1892 to 1894. That service gave him his great subject: army life in barracks and field. His books Among the Soldiers and Secrets of the Barracks made him popular. Recruits and Other Soldiers and the novel Ezredes Boriska followed in 1897. He also wrote for the Budapesti Hirlap, a leading daily paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco: Samuel ben Jacob of Capua was an Italian translator of the late thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He may have been father of the physician Solomon of Capua, if Steinschneider guessed right. Samuel turned into Hebrew a work of Mesue the Elder, written first in Arabic. It treats the choice and correction of purgative medicines for doctors. The translation, in two parts, still survives only in manuscript copies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-midrash-:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Midrash to Samuel. The work, Midrash Shemu'el, retells the Books of Samuel with stories and moral teaching. Rashi quotes it as early as his notes on First Samuel. It also went by the name Agadat Shemu'el. Printers once gave it the wrong title, Shoḥer Ṭob, by mistake.

The book holds thirty-two chapters of homilies. Each one opens with a verse from some other part of the Bible. The compiler gathered his material from the Mishnah, the Talmuds, and many older midrash collections. Almost every sage named in it lived in Palestine. Zunz dated the compiler to the first half of the eleventh century. The article closes with the book's printing history, from Constantinople to Buber's edition of 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarsino-sarcino:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Jacob ben Joseph Sarsino. He was an Italian rabbi of the seventeenth century. Sarsino studied under Ẓebi Hirsch ben Isaac in Cracow. He became a rabbi in Venice. There he worked alongside Leon of Modena. Much of his labor went into the printed books of his day.

Sarsino corrected several books printed at Venice. He supplied them with notes of his own. He printed the notes of his teacher Ẓebi Hirsch on Jacob Weil's rules for slaughtering. He added his own notes to that work. In 1692 he published Seder ha-Niḳḳur at Venice. That book gives the rules for porging, the removal of forbidden fat and sinews. It is said to be only an extract. The full work belonged to his teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schott-schottla:
Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Benedict Schott. He was a German educationist. Schott was born in Danzig on March 11, 1763 or 1764. He died at Seesen on July 21, 1846. Orphaned early, he wandered Germany as a young scholar. In Berlin he tutored in the home of Herz Beer, Meyerbeer's father.

In 1804 Schott joined the new Jacobsonschule at Seesen as a teacher. Two years later he became its director. In 1806 Jacobson sent him to Paris. There he urged Napoleon's Sanhedrin to back better schooling for Jews. He retired on July 1, 1838, in his seventy-fifth year. His books include a reader for Jewish schoolchildren. He also wrote an open letter on a Jewish consistory for Westphalia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semahot-joys-13:
Semahot, meaning Joys, is the soft name for Ebel Rabbati, a tract on mourning for the dead. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The tract counts among the small, later treatises printed after the fourth order of the Babylonian Talmud.

Much of the entry asks whether this tract matches an older collection cited in the Talmud. The authors compare quoted lines and note that only some match well. They also report an early gaon's account of a large and a small version. Readers get a careful lesson in telling similar rabbinic texts apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shatzkes-moses-:
Moses Aaron Shatzkes was a Russian Hebrew author born at Karlin in 1825. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He had both Hebrew and general schooling and chose literature. Writing earned him little, and he lived in straitened means.

His chief work, Ha-Mafteah, applied modern inquiry to Talmudic tales. Printed at Warsaw from 1866 to 1869, it stirred Orthodox readers with bold views. It marked a fresh turn in Hebrew writing at the time. Shatzkes also wrote a satiric sketch of Jewish life in Judeo-German. That piece was reprinted often for common readers. He spent his last twenty years at Kiev and died there in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shomron-kol-tit:
Shomron Kol Titten is a dramatic elegy by Solomon ibn Gabirol for the fast of Ab. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the poem. Polish ritual sings it at the close of the lamentations. It is sung at both evening and morning services.

Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two faithless sisters in it. Ezekiel's image of sister cities stands behind the poem. The sisters take turns bewailing their sins and punishments. Verses two and three give each her grieving voice. In verse four the poet begs pity for both. He prays for their Lord to return in forgiveness. Sephardim add the poem to prayers for the fast of Tebet. The entry shows two ruined cities speaking their sorrow aloud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-nano:
Simeon ben Nanos was a tanna of the second generation, peer of Ishmael and Akiba. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He often debated points of law with those two giants. He is often mentioned simply by the name Ben Nanos.

Simeon won high fame for knowing Jewish civil law deeply. Ishmael said whoever would study civil law should learn from him. Several of his civil law sayings survive in the Mishnah. They appear in Bava Batra and Shebu'ot among other tractates. Opinions of his on other legal topics survive too. Neither his teachers nor his pupils are known today. The entry honors a specialist whose subject was money, property, and fairness between neighbors in daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-small-and-large:
Small and large letters are odd-sized letters in the Masoretic Bible text. Crawford Howell Toy and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. About one hundred such letters occur in all. Many of them stand in the Pentateuch. Scribes always copied them with care. Printed editions still show them today.

Examples include the cut waw in the word peace in Numbers. An inverted nun appears in nine passages in all. Large letters often point to a Talmudic or midrashic teaching. They also guard the text against copying errors. The first letter of Genesis must be large, the lists say. The waw in gahon is the middle letter of the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-somekh-abdallah:
Abdallah Abraham Joseph Somekh was rabbi of Bagdad, born there in 1813. Joseph Jacobs and N E B Ezra wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was educated by Jacob Joseph ha-Rofe and Moses Hayyim. He was looked on as spiritual head of Bagdad Jewry. His legal decisions were accepted as conclusive across Asia.

Through his influence about twenty yeshivot were founded. The Sassoon family and Calcutta Jews helped fund that work. He left a work on ritual in manuscript at his death. Parts of it were published at Bagdad in 1900. It bore the title Zibhe Zedek, sacrifices of righteousness. A riot broke out at his funeral over his burial place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinberg-joshu:
Joshua Steinberg was a Russian Jewish writer and educator born in Wilna in 1839. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinberg trained at the rabbinical school in Wilna and served briefly as a rabbi at Byelostok. In 1861 he was called back to Wilna as a rabbi.

Steinberg became head teacher of Hebrew and Aramaic at the Wilna rabbinical seminary in 1867. He later served as its inspector until 1904. His efforts led the Russian government to open seven elementary city schools for Jewish children in 1863. From 1863 he also worked as censor of Jewish publications. He wrote major dictionaries, including a complete Russian-Hebrew dictionary in 1880. His work shaped Jewish schooling across Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulzer-salomon-:
Salomon Sulzer was an Austrian cantor and composer born in 1804. Isidore Singer and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Hohenems, Tyrol, on March 30. His family had moved there from Sulz in 1748. He died at Vienna on January 17, 1890.

Sulzer trained for the cantorate and traveled with his teachers. In 1820 he became cantor at Hohenems and added a choir. Vienna called him as chief cantor in 1826. There he kept old chants but harmonized them anew. His two-volume Shir Zion set models for synagogue music. It covers Sabbaths, festivals, weddings, and funerals. Nearly every synagogue in the world adopted parts of it. The entry honors the man who modernized Jewish song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tallage-14209:
Tallage was a tax a ruler could impose at will. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. The whole community owed the entire sum together. English kings levied it on Jews again and again. The 1100s and 1200s saw the heaviest demands.

The Saladin tallage of 1189 demanded 60,000 pounds. Its stated purpose was a crusade against Saladin. King John tallaged the Jews for 60,000 marks in 1210. Henry the Third levied smaller sums in 1225 and 1270. Edward the First added repeated tallages of his own. These came atop fines, fees, and many other claims. One claim says losing Jewish income changed royal tax rights. Edward then gave up tallaging Englishmen in general. The entry shows a tax used as a royal squeeze.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-the-seco:
The Second Temple in Jerusalem, from ruin to rebuilding, is traced here. George A. Barton wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Nebuchadnezzar had burned Solomon's Temple in 586 B.C. The site stayed a place of worship through the Exile.

Cyrus let the Jews return and rebuild in 538 B.C. Little building seems to have happened at first. Real work began under Darius in 519 B.C. The preaching of Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people. Within three years the new Temple stood finished. The article tests the Book of Ezra against other evidence. It shows how scholars weigh claims about Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-title-page-1440:
The title-page of Hebrew books grew out of the printer's colophon. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Early Hebrew books, like manuscripts, carried titles in colophons. The Soncino Berakot of 1483 followed that pattern. Kimhi's grammar of 1491 set its title on page one.

By the early 1500s titles moved to the first page. Bomberg's Talmud of 1520 gave its title five small lines. Soon titles filled whole pages with rich borders. Flowers, angels, deer, and Bible heroes framed the words. Prague printers copied the look of lit manuscripts. Temple gates formed a favorite design. Amsterdam's 1666 Tikkun used a fully engraved title-page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-ernst-joh:
Ernst Johannes Trier was a Danish educator who founded a famed folk high school. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Copenhagen in 1837, he died at Vallekilde in 1893. He took his theology degree in 1863. He fought in the war with Germany in 1864.

In 1865 he became a follower of Grundtvig. At Grundtvig's urging he founded a school at Vallekilde in 1866. It soon led all Danish schools of its kind. Courses covered navigation and branches of trade too. It first brought Swedish gymnastics into Danish schools. His memoirs of twenty-five school years stayed unfinished. Overstudy hastened his death, the article says. Trier was a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-urim-and-thummi:
Urim and Thummim were objects in the high priest's breastplate used as a divine oracle. Emil G. Hirsch, W. Muss-Arnolt, Wilhelm Bacher, and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Greek translators rendered the names as revelation and truth. Others gave lights and perfections instead. The Bible itself gives no basis for those renderings.

Exodus describes the breastplate as four-square and double. Twelve stones sat on its outside, not inside. Moses placed the Urim and Thummim within it at Aaron's consecration. Deuteronomy blesses Levi with God's Thummim and Urim. First Samuel shows Saul asking God through the oracle. Wellhausen and Driver restored that passage from the Greek text. The article weighs every clue to a lost practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-virtue-original:
Original virtue, in Hebrew zekut abot, means the merit of the fathers. Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The term was coined as a contrast to original sin. It names a Jewish idea about ancestors. God rewards children for the goodness of their parents.

The doctrine rests on Bible verses. The second commandment promises mercy to thousands of generations. Isaac was blessed because Abraham kept God's commands. The first blessing of the daily Amidah prayer recalls the fathers. The entry adds a key limit. The merit helps only when children keep their parents' piety. It ties family memory to present duty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weaving-14809:
Weaving was a basic craft of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the nomadic age, families spun camel and goat hair. Sheep's wool served the same purpose. From these they wove rough cloth for tents and clothes. Their looms were simple sticks and threads.

In Palestine the methods grew somewhat better. Egypt's weaving was praised as highly developed. Yet Egyptian looms stayed primitive too. Herodotus says Egyptians wove at an upright loom. They began their work at the bottom, unlike others. Stone carvings show horizontal looms as well. The entry compares tools, terms, and cloth across the region.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wieniawski-jose:
Joseph Wieniawski was a Russian pianist and composer. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lublin on May 23, 1837. He was the brother of Henri Wieniawski. He studied at the Paris Conservatoire under Zimmerman and Alkan. Harmony teachers included Marmontel and Leccoppey.

After 1850 Joseph often toured with his brother Henri. In 1856 he studied under Liszt at Weimar. He later studied theory under Marx in Berlin. In 1866 he settled in Moscow as a professor. He then opened a private piano school there. His works include two orchestral overtures. A string quartet and a piano concerto followed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-albert-ed:
Albert Edward Woolf (born 1846) was an American chemist and maker of new tools. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in New York, he was schooled in its public schools. He also studied at the College of the City of New York.

His best work dealt with clean water and clean wounds. In 1876 he brought in a bleach for fine feathers. That same bleach served as a germ wash as well. In 1889 he found a new germ kill in sea water. Electric force split the sea water to make the wash. Town crews used it on water, waste, and sewage. In 1899 it helped fight yellow fever at Havana. He held seats in two learned groups in two lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-ze-e: Yizhak ben Zeera was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He read one verse of the Psalms in a rare way. The set sun, he said, is like a drop of blood. That drop is no more wide than a seed of mustard. One note on the Song of Songs bears his name too. Some books give a like name in its place there. The short entry rests on the tale study of Bacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuzim-15309:
The Zuzim were an ancient people named once in Genesis, east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Genesis says Chedorlaomer smote them at Ham. The storyteller seems to assume readers already knew the name well.

Greek and Syriac translators read the name as a word meaning the strong or the mighty. On that reading, the Zuzim match the Rephaim, giants of the district. The Ammonites called those giants Zamzummim, a name close to Zuzim. The entry weighs whether the two names are one, split by copyists' errors. Sayce even traced the split to alike letters in Babylonian writing.
journal-of-discourses-vol-09:
War's middle years fill Volume Nine of the Journal, issued in 1862. The Saints prosper in their valleys while the Union fights for life. Young presses self-sufficiency in nearly every discourse of this span.

Home industry, grain reserves, and new settlements lead his public counsel. Converts keep gathering from Europe to swell the kingdom's towns. The discourses build Zion's workshops as Babylon tears itself apart. That sharp contrast gives Mormon Utah its odd, proud edge here. Faith, thrift, and defiance blend in the Tabernacle's weekly public voice. The volume shows prosperity preached as proof of divine favor.
kawaguchi-three-years-in-tibet-1909:
Ekai Kawaguchi lived in Tibet disguised as a Chinese pilgrim, and Three Years in Tibet, from 1909, tells how he did it. Kawaguchi, a Japanese Zen monk seeking true texts of his faith, spent 1897 to 1903 reaching Lhasa and studying in its great monasteries. Detection meant death, and his road ran through years of cold, hunger, and fear.

His account, the first by a Japanese traveler, shows daily life in the closed capital as few books ever have. Temples, markets, medicine, and monks all pass under his patient, observant eye along the way. The narrative stands as a primary witness to the old Lhasa on the edge of change.
kepler-astronomia-nova-1609:
Johannes Kepler published Astronomia Nova in 1609, the fruit of his long war with the orbit of Mars. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in Latin. Kepler worked from Tycho Brahe's superb records, the best naked-eye data ever gathered.

From those numbers Kepler forced out his first two laws of planet motion. Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. They also sweep equal areas in equal times. The laws broke the ancient rule that heavenly motion must be circular. Kepler told the story of his false starts in the book itself. It stands as a founding work of modern astronomy.
khunrath-amphitheatrum-sapientiae-1609:
Heinrich Khunrath was a German physician and Hermetic philosopher whose Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae appeared in 1609. The title means Amphitheater of Eternal Wisdom, and the book is built like its title: a theater of engraved visions. It is the great Christian-kabbalistic alchemical emblem book.

Nine large engravings show the alchemist at prayer and at the furnace, angels, gates, and the stone as Christ-like figures of renewal. Khunrath joins laboratory work to devotion, holding that the adept must be reborn along with his matter. Collectors prize the plates, and scholars mine the book for the period's union of faith and furnace.
kropotkin-great-french-revolution-dryhur:
Peter Kropotkin told the French Revolution from below in his history of 1789 to 1793. N. F. Dryhurst translated the work for Heinemann in 1909. The full English text runs to sixty eight chapters. Kings and assemblies share the stage with the Paris sections and village communes.

Peasant risings against feudal dues drive much of Kropotkin's story. He argues that common people, not leaders, made the Revolution's real gains. His anarchist sympathy shapes the telling without hiding the facts he gathered. The work rests on years in French archives. It remains a standard anarchist history of the event. Readers get the Revolution as a people's movement.
kuprin-yama-1909:
Yama, also called The Pit, is Alexander Kuprin's novel of life in a brothel district of a southern Russian city. Kuprin published the first part in 1909, and Bernard Guilbert Guerney translated the book into English in 1922. Kuprin called it the first and last honest book on its subject.

Inside the houses of Yama, Kuprin follows the women, their keepers, their clients, and the students who debate their fate. He shows routine, humor, cruelty, and sudden violence without flinching. The book was banned in places, devoured everywhere, and argued over for years. Kuprin meant it as protest, not titillation, and its frankness still startles.
les-sept-livres-de-l-archidoxe-magique-t: A 1909 French printing presents the Seven Books of the Magic Archidox, a work ascribed to Paracelsus, the Swiss physician and alchemist who died in 1541. The title page says these books were translated for the first time in this edition. The hosted sample survives only as garbled scan marks, so nothing beyond the title facts can be checked here. The entry is kept brief for that reason.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The February 1875 Lippincott's concludes Following the Tiber. Six Months Among Cannibals offers rougher travel reading. Mary E. Blair tells of an American girl and her lovers. W. E. Griffis describes a Japanese marriage in high life.

William Black's Three Feathers advances through chapter twenty-five. Not the last word ends that installment of the serial. H. C. Wood Jr. writes a medical piece on fever. Trollope recalls sculptor Hiram Powers from personal recollection. Corn, by Sidney Lanier, and Gentleman Dick vary the number. A singular family and the lost baby complete the fiction.
lister-collected-papers-vol1-1909:
Joseph Lister was a British surgeon who changed hospital care by fighting wound infection. He built on Pasteur's germ theory and began treating wounds with carbolic acid in the 1860s. His key papers were gathered after his death, and this first collected volume appeared in 1909.

The papers set out the antiseptic principle: kill germs in and around a wound, and patients stop dying of hospital gangrene. Lister reports operations, compares results before and after his method, and answers his critics. Death rates in his wards fell sharply. These writings mark the start of safe modern surgery.
lister-collected-papers-vol2-1909:
Joseph Lister, the British surgeon behind antiseptic surgery, published research across a long career. His collected papers were issued in two volumes in 1909. This second volume holds his later scientific work rather than the first antiseptic reports.

The papers study inflammation, the clotting of blood, and related questions in surgery and physiology. Lister describes experiments on animals and patients, and he refines the methods behind his wound care. Readers can watch a careful scientist test each claim step by step. Together with volume one, the set records how modern surgery was built, step by tested step, over one working lifetime.
lodge-ether-of-space-1909:
Oliver Lodge, an English physicist, gave the ether its last great public defense in this book of 1909. He wrote for lay readers, in clear and warm terms. By then the new work of Einstein had made the ether look like a needless prop.

Lodge sets out what the ether does in his scheme, from light to the pull of worlds. He holds that space must be full of a real stuff that bears all waves and forces. The book shows the old view at its peak, just as its age came to a close.
lodge-survival-of-man-1909:
Oliver Lodge, a chief of the science of waves and wires, made his case for life past death in The Survival of Man, out in 1909. Lodge held high posts in the schools of Britain. He turned their tools on the dark room: notes, tests, and checks for fraud, weighed with a calm, fair hand through years of sittings.

He claims some notes from the dead pass all fair tests. His rank gave the claim a weight no mere fan could match. The book took the theme to the heart of science. Its calm tone is its force.
london-martin-eden-1909:
Jack London published Martin Eden in 1909, his tragic Künstlerroman of a working-class sailor who educates himself. A sailor educates himself into a famous writer, then discovers success is hollow, in London's most bitter novel. He protested that Eden was an individualist, not a socialist, and that the book indicted Eden's creed, not society's alone.

Martin loves Ruth Morse, a bourgeois student, and remakes himself by savage study in Oakland libraries. Rejection slips pile for years until the magazines suddenly pay fortunes for the work they once returned unopened. The same world that starved him now begs his company, and he sees the welcome is for fame, not for him. Ruth returns too late, and Martin sails for the South Seas and slips, at last, into the sea. The novel is the classic anatomy of literary success in America.
lorentz-theory-of-electrons-1909:
Hendrik Antoon Lorentz, a Dutch sage, gave these talks at Columbia in New York, and they came out in book form in 1909. His theme is the electron, the tiny charged part he had helped to place at the heart of physics. The talks sum up his life's work.

Lorentz shows how swarms of electrons can give light, heat rays, and the split hues of the Zeeman effect. He sets out the shrink of fast bodies that bears his name, tied to a still ether. The book is the old scheme in its last strict, fine form, by its chief maker.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol1-1909:
Max Arthur Macauliffe spent years in India studying the Sikh faith with Sikh scholars. His six-book account, printed in 1909, was the first full one in English. The first book gives scripture in English dress beside the lives of the Gurus. It opens with Guru Nanak, the founder.

Nanak's travels, hymns, and talks with Hindus and Muslims fill these pages. Macauliffe aimed to let Sikh texts speak in their own voice, not through hostile reports. He quotes the hymns at length and adds notes on custom and belief. The whole set still stands as a base text for the study of Sikhism.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol2-1909:
Work on the second book of Macauliffe's Sikh Religion keeps to the same plan as the first. Scripture in English dress stands beside the lives of the Gurus. The years run from 1909, when the whole set came out. This part takes up the line after Guru Nanak.

Four Gurus lead this book: Angad, Amar Das, Ram Das, and the years between them. Their hymns come with tales of how each man held the young faith firm. New towns, new rites, and a growing flock mark the age. Readers see how a small group became a lasting faith.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol3-1909:
Part three of Macauliffe's Sikh Religion, from 1909, turns to Guru Arjan. Arjan was the fifth Guru and a poet of great gifts. He built the Golden Temple at Amritsar. He also made the choice that fixed Sikh scripture for all time.

Arjan drew the hymns of the first Gurus and of holy men into one book, the Granth. Macauliffe gives long extracts in English and tells how the work was done. Arjan's death at the hands of the Mughal state closes the tale. The book shows the faith gaining a scripture and a martyr.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol4-1909:
Gurus from Har Gobind to Teg Bahadur lead the fourth book of Macauliffe's 1909 Sikh Religion. Har Gobind took up the sword beside the prayer book. The faith now had to guard itself in a hard age. Temples and troops both grow in these tales.

Life stories of each Guru come with hymns in English and notes on the times. Teg Bahadur gave his life to shield the faith of others, a deed Sikhs still honor. Macauliffe keeps his aim of fair, full telling from Sikh sources. The book traces the turn from peace to arms.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol5-1909:
Guru Gobind Singh fills the fifth book of Macauliffe's Sikh Religion, printed in 1909. He was the tenth and last human Guru of the Sikhs. His great act came in 1699, when he formed the Khalsa. That order of devoted Sikhs still shapes the faith today.

Pages tell of Gobind Singh's wars, his court of poets, and his loss of his sons. In 1708 he named the Granth, the holy book, as Guru after him. Macauliffe gives the Guru's own hymns in English with the tales round them. The human line of Gurus ends here in high drama.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol6-1909:
Last of Macauliffe's six books on the Sikh faith, from 1909, turns from lives to the holy book itself. The Granth Sahib holds the hymns Sikhs treat as their living Guru. Macauliffe gives its chief parts in English dress. The set that began with Nanak ends with his words.

Hymns of the Gurus stand beside songs of the Bhagats, holy men from Hindu and Muslim paths. Long notes explain hard lines, old words, and points of faith. Macauliffe also sums up what sets Sikh belief apart. The book closes the first full English account of Sikhism.
marett-threshold-of-religion-1909:
R. R. Marett published The Threshold of Religion at London in 1909, with Methuen. Marett, an Oxford anthropologist, challenged E. B. Tylor's famous claim that religion began in animism, the belief in spirits. He argued that something earlier and simpler stands at the threshold: awe before a vague, potent force like the mana of Pacific belief.

Taboo, dance, and ritual feeling, on his account, precede any doctrine of souls. The book founded the mana-taboo school in the early anthropology of religion. Marett writes with unusual grace for a theorist, and his examples range worldwide. Later scholars revised his scheme, yet his question still organizes the field. What comes first in religion, belief or feeling, is his lasting problem.
marx-capital-vol-3-1909:
Book Three of Capital came out in the dress of Ernest Untermann in 1909. Friedrich Engels built the book from Marx's notes after his death. The full title calls it the tale of the whole scheme of wealth and trade. With it, the three books of Capital stand done.

Profit, rent, and fees on loans split the gains of trade in this book. Marx shows how the parts hide the source of the gains in work. Falls in the rate of gain form a grave theme of the text. The book is the cap of the most weighty work of its school.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-09: For volume nine, Gutenberg's catalogue gives etext 3559 and a 2002 release. Bourrienne, who served Napoleon as private secretary, is the named author. The file head also carries a date label, 1807, beside the title. The sample itself stops at appeals for the Gutenberg fund. It holds no chapter, no anecdote, and no memoir text at all. Grounding rules leave only the bibliographic facts above to report for this volume.
monro-digest-justinian-vol2-1909:
Monro's English Digest of Justinian reached a second volume in 1909. The Digest itself, Justinian's sixth-century gathering of Roman jurists, runs to fifty books, so translation was a long labor. Monro, a fellow of a Cambridge college, worked through it with the patience of a practicing lawyer.

Volume 2 continues through the early books of the Digest, where the jurists treat actions, contracts in their first forms, and the protection of property. The decisions are concrete: real disputes about sales, loans, and guardianship, answered in a few exact lines. Readers meet Roman law as working law, not as marble. The classical law of Rome becomes available book by book to the English bar and to students who lack Latin. Monro's two volumes remain a standard doorway into the Digest.
my-novel-volume-09:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's ninth book turns to public life. The narrator admits his cast now crowds him like poor kin at Christmas. The Caxtons have been pushed out of their own rooms. New faces need space, and the tale must make room.

He asks if the reader has known public life at all. Not just Parliament counts, he says, but vestry and town hall too. Busy local men shape the world most folk live in. Riccabocca, Randal Leslie, and Dick Avenel press forward here. The volume widens the novel from one family's hall to the clash of ambition in open life.
nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-1909:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Beyond Good and Evil in 1886, a sharp attack on the philosophy and morals of his age. The English text here is Helen Zimmern's translation of 1909. Nietzsche questions dogmas about truth, free will, and the good. He sorts morals into master and slave types with different roots.

Aphorisms and short essays carry the argument, often with stinging wit. Nietzsche praises the free spirit who thinks beyond the herd. He also attacks nationalism, anti-Semitism, and shallow modern culture. The book states his mature views in compact form. It is a fine first Nietzsche for bold readers.
nietzsche-zarathustra-common-1909:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Thus Spake Zarathustra between 1883 and 1885, his most famous book. The English text here is Thomas Common's translation of 1909. Zarathustra is a prophet who leaves his mountain cave to teach mankind. He announces that God is dead and calls for the overman, a higher human type.

The book mixes sermons, songs, parables, and wild humor in biblical style. Zarathustra scorns herd morals and praises those who create their own values. He also teaches the hard thought of eternal recurrence. Nietzsche called it his deepest work. Its images and phrases have spread through modern culture worldwide.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume nine of Penzer's Ocean of Story, issued from 1924, brings Tawney's Kathasaritsagara within reach of its close. Somadeva's ocean begins to gather its streams: the hero's long foretold destiny as emperor of the Vidyadharas stands near. Yet the tales refuse to thin out, and fresh wonders crowd the road to the throne.

Penzer's notes here lean on Indian custom, ritual, and law to gloss the tales' assumptions. Tawney translated with a schoolmaster's clarity, scene by scene, across thousands of verses. The Penzer edition remains the form in which English reads the whole Ocean. Volume nine is the last deep water before the shore. Its stories show no wear from the long voyage.
odes-of-solomon-harris-1909:
J. Rendel Harris translated the Odes of Solomon into English in 1909. The Odes are forty-two hymns composed around the year 100. They had been lost for centuries until a Syriac manuscript surfaced.

Harris recognized the manuscript's importance and published the hymns quickly. The songs celebrate divine love, living water, and spiritual rebirth. Their roots are Jewish, their tone mystical and joyful throughout. Scholars rank the Odes as the earliest Christian hymnbook known. Questions about their original language and community still occupy researchers. Harris's translation gave English readers a forgotten treasure of early worship in 1909.

The team tested thirty-two sesame accessions with DNA markers. The plants came from five world diversity centers. They recorded hundreds of markers, most of them varied. Large genetic variability appeared within the whole collection. Plants grouped into two main clusters by similarity. Origin region did not match the genetic grouping closely.
openalex-w2002202509:
Roger Prichard, Maria-Gloria Basanez, Boakye Boatin and colleagues set out a research agenda for worm diseases. Their review appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2012. Worm infections place a heavy burden on poor communities. Large control programmes were already under way. The authors asked what research is still needed.

The paper covers major worm diseases targeted by control work. These include river blindness and elephantiasis. They also include gut worms, schistosomiasis and cysticercosis. The authors reviewed tools for control and elimination. They named gaps in drugs, tests and field methods. Their agenda aims to guide funders and research teams. It stresses work that helps programmes finish the job.
openalex-w2059302109:
Marcio Nucci, Flavio Queiroz-Telles, Tito Alvarado-Matute and colleagues surveyed bloodstream Candida infections in Latin America. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Candidemia patterns differ between world regions. Latin American data were scarce. The team ran a laboratory survey to fill the gap.

Twenty centres in seven countries took part. The survey ran for twenty-four months. It recorded hundreds of candidemia episodes. Children made up a large share of cases. Candida albicans was the leading species overall. Other species ranked differently in different countries. Most isolates responded well to standard antifungal drugs. Fluconazole was the most used first treatment. The data guide treatment choices in the region.
openalex-w2271393109:
Ana Betrán, Jianfeng Ye, Anne-Beth Moller, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2016. They charted caesarean section rates worldwide from 1990 to 2014. Rates keep rising almost everywhere, with no agreement on the right level, and surgery carries extra risks and costs for mothers and babies.

Nationally representative data were gathered and regional averages weighted by population. The latest figures cover one hundred fifty countries. About nineteen in a hundred births worldwide now arrive by caesarean. The share ranges from about six percent in the least developed regions to over twenty-seven percent in the most developed. The authors track each region's pace of increase over the twenty-four years.
openalex-w2604487509:
The ATLAS Collaboration described its particle flow jet method in this 2017 paper in the European Physical Journal C. Jets are sprays of particles created when quarks and gluons burst from a collision. Measuring them well is central to almost every ATLAS analysis. The paper uses data from Run 1 of the Large Hadron Collider at eight TeV.

Particle flow combines two detector views instead of trusting the calorimeter alone. For charged particles it uses the precise momentum measured by the inner tracker. Calorimeter readings then cover only neutral particles, avoiding double counting of energy. The team compared these jets with calorimeter-only jets on real data. Particle flow jets showed better energy resolution and stayed steadier when many collisions overlapped. The method became a standard tool for later ATLAS running.
openalex-w2900536309:
Maria Kyriakidou, Helen H. Tai, and Noelle Lynette Anglin, with colleagues, reviewed polyploid genome assembly in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2018. Polyploid plants carry more than two chromosome sets in every cell. Wheat, potato, strawberry, coffee, and banana all evolved this way. Extra genome copies create new traits and adaptation routes, but they tangle DNA sequencing badly.

Assembling a polyploid genome means separating near-identical copies that differ subtly. Standard tools built for diploids collapse them into mosaics. The review surveys current strategies for doing better. It covers how assembly choices affect linking genes to traits. Polyploid cells must also coordinate expression among their genome copies. Progress here unlocks the genetics of humanity's staple crops. The authors chart where methods stand and what breeders still need.
openalex-w2909240409:
Aldenor Gomes Santos, Gisele O. da Rocha, and Jaílson B. de Andrade measured two potent mutagens in city air for Scientific Reports in 2019. The compounds, 2-nitrobenzanthrone and 3-nitrobenzanthrone, rank among the strongest mutagens found in airborne particles. They form from traffic-related aromatic chemicals. The team sampled fine particles at a bus station and an outdoor coastal site.

Buses at the station burned a diesel-biodiesel blend, while cars used varying ethanol-gasoline mixes. Average concentrations stayed under about fifteen micrograms per gram for one compound. The other averaged under four and a half micrograms per gram. Statistical source analysis fingered diesel and biodiesel exhaust at the station, plus resuspended floor dust. At the coast, vehicle emissions, photochemistry, and wood burning dominated. The study also estimated lifetime cancer risk from breathing these particles.
openalex-w3016939709:
Zuzana Kos, Elvire Roblin, Rim Kim, and colleagues published this article in npj Breast Cancer in 2020. It warns of pitfalls in scoring stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, immune cells found inside breast tumors. Such scores help predict outcomes in triple-negative and HER2-positive breast cancers.

Standard scoring guides exist and are widely used, but pathologists still disagree more than they should. The team re-examined three earlier ring studies, in which many readers scored the same slides. Uneven spread of the immune cells within a tumor drove most disagreement, joined by slide faults and scoring beyond the proper area. They also tested how such gaps shift outcome estimates for early triple-negative disease.
openalex-w3094812309:
R. Abbott, T. D. Abbott, S. Abraham, and colleagues of the LIGO and Virgo groups published this catalog in Physical Review X in 2021. GWTC-2 lists gravitational-wave events from merging compact objects found in the first half of the third observing run, from April to October 2019.

Applying a strict false-alarm threshold, the team presents thirty-nine candidate events, with expected contamination below ten percent. Twenty-six had already been announced in near real time; thirteen appear here for the first time. Most sources are black hole mergers, some seen across vast cosmic distances. A few events have parts that cannot be cleanly classed. The catalog doubles as the field's census of colliding black holes and neutron stars.
openalex-w3123340709:

Complex forests support rich wildlife and strong ecosystem functions, from boreal to tropical zones. How climate change will shift that complexity is a pressing question. Climate shapes which species live in a forest and what they do, and those traits in turn build its structure. The authors join worldwide measurements to show where complex forests stand and which climate traits favor them. The map is a base for forecasting forest change.
openalex-w4416290809:
Julie Helms, Kenta Kondo, Kunihiko Nagakari, and Toshiaki Iba review the diagnosis and management of heat-related illness. Their review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. These illnesses arise when the body cannot shed excess heat. Heatwaves are making them more common.

The elderly, children, outdoor workers, and people with chronic disease face the highest risk. Diagnosis has long rested on clinical signs alone. The review adds new laboratory tests and molecular markers to that picture. It sets out a fuller diagnostic approach and reviews management. Early recognition matters most: severe heatstroke kills and damages organs. Combining bedside judgement with modern biomarkers should sharpen both speed and accuracy of care.

Florin Scarlatescu, a neurologist in Bucharest, Romania, led a 2026 study of brain dysfunction in adults who arrive at an emergency department with sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to infection. About four fifths of patients showed neurological dysfunction, and about a quarter had the pure sepsis-linked form. A blood measure of red cell size variation independently predicted the pure form, and shrinkage of the frontal brain region on scans was its only imaging link. Both conditions came with much lower survival to discharge. The authors suggest these early markers could speed risk sorting.
openalex-w7171565009:

The team reviewed forty-two patients to see how the two signals move together across surgery.

The two signals correlated positively, though only weakly to moderately, in some muscles and phases, and not consistently in others. In three patients the main signal plunged during correction; in one the reference signal stayed normal, warning that the drop might be technical, while in two both fell together. All recovered without lasting deficits. Watching both, the authors argue, helps interpret alarms.
openalex-w7204863209:
Roberto Kennedy Ferreira da Silva de Queiroz led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on self-medication and its impacts on population health, read through collective health. Searching three sources for full papers from 2021 to 2026 in three languages, the team identified over two hundred studies and selected fourteen. The practice proved frequent across populations and contexts, shaped by social, economic, and individual factors and by access to health services, the review finds. Analgesics, anti-inflammatories, and antibiotics were the most used drugs, with risks including adverse effects, interactions, poisonings, and antimicrobial resistance. The authors call self-medication an important collective health problem requiring health education, professional guidance, and pushing sensible drug use.

Vanusa Freitas Carvalho de Paniagua led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on maternal immune activation and the risk of autism spectrum disorder in offspring. Autism's causes are complex, and immune imbalance has gained ground for unusual brain growth. Using a standard review method across four sources, the team included thirty-three studies from 2004 to 2023, checking quality and grading the evidence.

A positive, consistent link appeared between maternal autoimmune diseases and higher autism risk, the review finds, strongest for rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren's syndrome. Atopic problems such as asthma and allergies were key risk factors when present or treated in the first two trimesters, and male offspring were markedly more vulnerable. Proposed pathways involve inflammatory signals and brain-reactive antibodies crossing the placenta. The authors urge careful prenatal care of inflammatory and allergic problems.

Forty grown folk with neck pain took part, in a fore-and-aft study of three rounds. Each time they scored their pain on a plain scale, from no pain to worst pain.

Pain fell round by round. Mean scores fell hard in the first round and kept their fall. By the third round's end, close to nine in ten told of no neck pain at all. The rest kept a slight pain. The team shows the yield as a kind cast for the Yamamoto way. They frame the study as ground work: firm plans are still need to prove the gain holds.

Kenta Kondo and three colleagues at Juntendo University in Tokyo write a perspective on a dangerous clotting disorder that rides along with sepsis. In sepsis-induced coagulopathy, infection throws the blood-clotting system off balance: clots form in small vessels, platelets and white cells activate, vessel linings are injured, and organs begin to fail. A 2025 international definition now describes the condition as a progression from a quiet early phase to overt, full-blown clotting failure.

Naming the early stage matters, the authors argue, because it opens a window for treatment before organ damage becomes permanent. Current options include heparins, natural anticoagulant proteins, and a lab-made form of thrombomodulin, though benefits vary and bleeding is a risk. Newer ideas, from factor XI blockers to drug-carrying nanoparticles, aim to stop clots without causing bleeding. The future they sketch rests on earlier diagnosis and careful staging.
openalex-w7213451509:

The extra step, they argue, is to ask how relations shape the very ways of life of each species. They separate three kinds of question: interaction, systemic interdependence, and relational formation. No new classroom method is proposed. Instead, teachers gain a wider set of questions for making ecological events intelligible, while keeping core concepts, mechanisms, and systems in place.

Anomic aphasia, the trouble finding names, should not be read as a simple speech fault, they argue. It sits at the centre of self-concept, behaviour control, and obsessive pattern persistence. Gut microbes, mitochondrial problems, and atypical sensory processing are discussed as amplifiers. New medical concepts are set out, including parental emotional anomia and a growing inner void. The matrix aims to guide clinicians who meet language and behaviour together.
openalex-w7213784009:

Strict blood sugar control is the base of treatment, with the clearest benefit in type one diabetes. Alpha-lipoic acid stood out as the antioxidant with the strongest backing. For nerve pain, older antidepressants, duloxetine, and gabapentin-type drugs remain first choice, while opioids are discouraged. A nerve impairment score and corneal microscopy show promise for early diagnosis. Care must join metabolic control, pain relief, and prevention of complications.
openalex-w7214050009:

Burnout is defined by exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy.

Surgeons face high technical responsibility, critical in-operation decisions, on-call duty, and sleep loss. Burnout rates are high yet vary widely across studies, the review finds. Workload, life-work imbalance, low autonomy, conflict, and adverse event exposure all associate with it. Burnout also links to more reported medical error and poorer safety perception. Lower professionalism and patient satisfaction complete a picture that ties surgeon welfare to patient outcomes.
openalex-w7219781809: Francisco Cesino de Medeiros Júnior led a seven-author study, published in Brazil in 2026. Most participants saw the theme's relevance for academic formation and for more inclusive teaching practice. Gaps in training persist, however, in how sexual and gender diversity is taught in higher health courses, and part of the teachers felt insecure about building inclusive teaching strategies for it. Training teachers better and deepening this debate, the authors conclude, are needed for safer, more coherent teaching aligned with today's demands and human rights.

Their bibliographic and documentary research reads legal doctrine, national legislation, and recent statistics. It stresses the Maria da Penha law's protective measures and the femicide law that wrote the crime into the penal code.

Brazil's legal framework has advanced a lot, they find, with urgent protective measures and stricter criminal accountability for aggressors. Femicide rates nonetheless remain high. Whether laws work depends on more than written norms, they conclude. It requires public policy put in place, integrated action by justice and public security institutions, and stronger prevention strategies. The study measures the gap between a law on paper and protection in daily life.

The city recorded several thousand cases, with a record peak in 2022. People aged eighteen to twenty-nine made up just over half of all reports and faced the highest incidence by far. Cases concentrated among young men, brown-skinned residents, and people with less schooling. The authors read the pattern as a sign of uneven access to testing and care, and a warning for local prevention work.

Their review collects the functional evidence on each side of a long-running surgical argument, where the fracture's shape and the patient's needs usually decide.

Their title frames the tension: workers hired to care are themselves falling ill, under chronic overload, constant exposure to suffering and death, and thin organizational support.

Twelve studies from 2022 to 2025 named workload, wrong staffing levels, and weak support as the main stressors. Anxiety, depression, and burnout appeared at notable rates, worst in high-complexity units. Personal coping strategies helped but could not carry the load alone. original-short-stories-volume-09:
Toine, the fat innkeeper nicknamed Burnt-Brandy, gives volume nine of Maupassant's Original Short Stories its opening and its earthiest comedy. Fourteen tales follow in the contents. They include Madame Husson's Rosier, The Adopted Son, and A Coward. Sundays of a Bourgeois in Paris and The Love of Long Ago are also there, all in the standard English translation.

Antoine Macheble made famous the hamlet of Tournevent, a cluster of ten Norman cottages tucked into a valley niche above the sea. The place hides from the salt ocean wind that burns like frost, and the whole village reads as Toine's property. Maupassant loves such rooted, excessive figures, and the volume alternates their broad peasant humor with some of his sharpest studies of shame, vanity, and quiet cruelty.
petrie-arts-crafts-ancient-egypt-1909:
W. M. Flinders Petrie shows how Egypt made its goods in The Arts and Crafts of Ancient Egypt, out in 1909. Stone work, glaze, glass, wood, and metal each get a part. Petrie had dug up the shops and tools in his years on site. He tells how each craft grew, what tools it used, and how fine its best work could be.

His eye for how a thing was made sets the book apart. Fine ware and rough ware both get fair words. The book is a shop tour of a lost world. Crafts folk still learn from it.
plaw-111-1-2009: Public Law 111-1 is a joint resolution from the 111th Congress on the pay of the Secretary of the Interior. For a person on the board on September 30, 2009, the cap is lifted to three terms. No other part of the board's rules changes.
plaw-111-115-2009:
Public Law 111-115 is the No Social Security Benefits for Prisoners Act of 2009. The 111th Congress amended titles II and XVI of the Social Security Act.

The act bars back payments to a person for spans when that person is a prisoner. The bar also covers fugitive felons and people who break probation or parole terms. Under the new clause, no payment is made for any such span. The rule stops catch-up checks from covering time spent in prison or on the run. Titles II and XVI are the two benefit titles the act amends.
plaw-111-116-2009:
Public Law 111-116 is the Fiscal Year 2010 Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act, Part II. The 111th Congress amended the tax code to extend funding for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund.

For fuel taxes, the act moves the end date from December 31, 2009 to March 31, 2010. Ticket taxes gain the same new date. The act also extends the fund's spending power and the clearances for the airport improvement program under title 49. The short extension keeps airport and air traffic funding in place. Part II in the title shows an earlier extension came first that year.
plaw-111-117-2009:
Public Law 111-117 is the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2010, a major spending act of the 111th Congress. It gathers funding for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2010 into one law.

Division A covers Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and related agencies. Its titles fund the Department of Transportation and the Department of Housing and Urban Development in turn. Division B covers Commerce, Justice, Science, and related agencies. More divisions follow in the same joined form, each with its own titles and general rules. Joined spending acts are how Congress funds many agencies at once.
plaw-111-118-2009:
Public Law 111-118 is the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2010. The 111th Congress used it to fund the Department of Defense for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2010.

Division A holds the defense funding titles. Title I covers military personnel, and Title II covers operation and maintenance. Later titles cover buying of gear, research and testing, and other defense programs. Title IX covers overseas contingency operations, the funding line for war work abroad. Division B covers other matters outside the main titles. General rules in Title VIII govern how the defense money is used.
plaw-111-119-2009:
Public Law 111-119 is the Airline Flight Crew Technical Corrections Act, from the 111th Congress in 2009. It amends the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 to clear up who among airline flight crews may take leave.

A new part of the leave law deals with airline flight crews by name. It covers flight attendants and flight crewmembers, as the Federal Aviation Administration defines those jobs. A crew member meets the hours of service test under the stated test, even though airline hours do not match a normal work week. The fix fits leave rights to flight work.
plaw-111-12-2009:
Public Law 111-12 is the Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act of 2009. The 111th Congress amended the tax code to extend funding for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund.

For fuel taxes, the act moves the end date from March 31, 2009 to September 30, 2009. Ticket taxes on persons gain the same new date, with a like edit for property. The act also extends the fund's spending power. It extends clearances for the airport improvement program under title 49 as well. The same March-to-September shift runs through each tax part. The fund pays for airport work across the nation.
plaw-111-120-2009: Army permit work funded by others gains a year. Public Law 111-120, from the 111th Congress in 2009, extends one Army permit power through December 31, 2010. The Secretary of the Army may accept and spend funds given by non-federal public bodies to speed the handling of permits. The act does this by changing 2009 to 2010 in section 214(c) of the Water Resources Development Act of 2000. That date swap is the whole law.
plaw-111-121-2009: Public Law 111-121 is a one-line joint resolution from the 111th Congress. It appoints the day for the opening of the second session of the One Hundred Eleventh Congress. The second regular session shall begin at noon on Tuesday, January 5, 2010. Nothing else is in the resolution. The date is set in the resolution's single operative line.
plaw-111-122-2009:
Public Law 111-122 is the Human Rights Enforcement Act of 2009, passed by the 111th Congress. It sets up a new section inside the Criminal Division of the Department of Justice to enforce human rights laws.

The new office must be set up not later than 90 days after enactment. The act adds section 509B to chapter 31 of title 28 for that office. It also repeals an older part of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Small fixes to criminal and immigration laws tied to human rights breaches round out the act. A home inside the Justice Department gives the work a clear base.
plaw-111-123-2009: Debt room for the government is raised once more. Public Law 111-123, from the 111th Congress in late 2009, bears the plain title of an act to permit continued financing of Government operations. It amends section 3101 of title 31, the debt limit law. The act strikes the dollar amount in that section and inserts $12,394,000,000,000. In short, it raises the public debt cap to about 12.4 trillion dollars so the government can keep borrowing. That single swap is the whole act.
plaw-111-124-2009:
Public Law 111-124 extends two trade programs, as the 111th Congress voted in late 2009. They are the Generalized System of Preferences and the Andean Trade Preference Act.

For the first program, the act moves the end date from December 31, 2009 to December 31, 2010 in the Trade Act of 1974. The Andean program gains the same new date in two places. The act also lengthens the run for certain apparel goods, from seven yearly periods to eight. A third part deals with customs user fees. Both programs give poor nations favored access to United States markets.
plaw-111-125-2009: Public Law 111-125, from the 111th Congress in 2009, extends the commercial space transportation liability regime. It amends section 70113(f) of title 49, United States Code. The act strikes December 31, 2009 and inserts December 31, 2012. That three-year extension of the space launch liability rules is the whole law. The regime it extends governs who bears loss after a launch accident.
plaw-111-13-2009:
Public Law 111-13 is the Serve America Act, also titled the Edward M. Kennedy Serve America Act. The 111th Congress passed it in 2009 to renew and reform the national service laws.

Title I amends the National and Community Service Act of 1990. One part deals with Learn and Serve America, covering school-based grants, higher education rules, and Campuses of Service. It also covers new programs, research, and a study of service-learning effects. A later part amends the National Service Trust Program, the system that rewards service with aid for schooling.
plaw-111-14-2009: A new courthouse in Rockford gains a judge's name. Public Law 111-14, passed by the 111th Congress in 2009, names one courthouse in Rockford, Illinois. The United States courthouse then under construction at 327 South Church Street shall be known as the Stanley J. Roszkowski United States Courthouse. Any mention of that courthouse in a law, map, rule, or other federal record counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-111-15-2009:
Public Law 111-15 is the Special Inspector General for the Troubled Asset Relief Program Act of 2009. The 111th Congress amended the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 to give that watchdog more power.

Section 2 covers audit and investigation powers. The Special Inspector General may carry out, oversee, and coordinate an audit or probe within the stated scope. That power sits on top of the duties already listed in the 2008 act. Section 3 covers personnel powers. The office watched the large bank rescue program known as TARP. A named watchdog can follow rescue money in a way broad offices cannot.
plaw-111-16-2009:
Public Law 111-16 is the Statutory Time-Periods Technical Amendments Act of 2009. The 111th Congress made small fixes to laws that set time periods for court cases.

Section 2 amends title 11, the bankruptcy code, point by point. In section after section, a five-day period becomes a seven-day period. Section 3 turns to title 18 in the same way. The pattern gives courts and parties a full week where the old text gave five days. Such fixes keep deadlines in line with court counting rules. Seven days also matches how courts count short spans of time.
plaw-111-17-2009: Public Law 111-17 is a joint resolution of the 111th Congress naming one citizen regent of the Smithsonian Institution. It appoints David M. Rubenstein of Maryland to the Board of Regents. He fills the vacancy left when the term of Anne d'Harnoncourt of Pennsylvania ended. The seat is in the class other than Members of Congress. The appointment runs for a term of six years from the date the resolution took effect.
plaw-111-18-2009: A freeze known by one man's name is repealed. Public Law 111-18, from the 111th Congress in 2009, is one of the shortest laws in this set. Its single section repeals section 10(f) of Public Law 93-531. That part of the older law is commonly known as the Bennett Freeze, as the act itself states. The repeal strikes that subsection from the older law. The text states no further terms, findings, or dates, so the act does only that one repeal and nothing more.
plaw-111-19-2009:
The Civil Rights History Project Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-19, passed by the 111th Congress. It directs the Librarian of Congress and the head of the Smithsonian to run a joint project. The project sits at the Library of Congress and the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

Its job is to collect video and audio oral histories from people who took part in the civil rights movement. Congress cites events like the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the March on Washington, and the march to Selma. The act notes famous leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks, but it stresses the many less known people whose own stories also shaped the movement.
plaw-111-2-2009:
The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-2, one of the first laws of the 111th Congress. It amends four civil rights laws, among them Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act.

Congress wrote it after the Supreme Court ruled against Lilly Ledbetter in her pay bias suit in 2007. The court had strictly limited the time a worker has to file such a claim. The act states that a biased pay decision counts as a fresh wrong each time a paycheck based on it is paid. That rule gives workers more time to bring a claim.
plaw-111-20-2009: Public Law 111-20 of 2009 has the long title Protecting Incentives for the Adoption of Children with Special Needs Act. Its one change strikes a limit written into the 2009 spending law. With the limit gone, states get their fiscal year 2008 adoption bonus payments in line with the Fostering Connections Act of 2008, the rule Congress had set the year before.
plaw-111-21-2009:
The Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act of 2009, or FERA, is Public Law 111-21. Congress passed it in May 2009 to sharpen the fight against fraud tied to federal aid and relief programs. It covers mortgage fraud, stock and commodity fraud, and bank fraud.

One early change widens the legal meaning of a financial institution in the fraud laws. The term now reaches mortgage lending firms, not just banks. A mortgage lending firm is defined as a group that funds or refinances debt backed by real estate and whose work affects trade across state or national lines.
plaw-111-22-2009:
Public Law 111-22 of 2009 opens with Division A, the Helping Families Save Their Homes Act of 2009. Congress passed it in May 2009, in the depths of the housing crash. Its stated aims are to prevent home foreclosures and to keep mortgage credit flowing.

The division's first title covers changes to rural housing loans, veterans' housing loans, and loan change data. A second title gives loan servicers a safe harbor when they modify a mortgage. It also revises the HOPE for Homeowners Program and sets rules for lenders approved by the FHA. The division also adds funds for HUD programs that help people weather the mortgage crisis.
plaw-111-23-2009:
The Weapon Systems Acquisition Reform Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-23. It aims to improve how the Department of Defense buys major weapon systems. Congress passed it in May 2009 after years of cost overruns on big arms programs.

Title I reshapes the buying offices, with new posts for cost review, test and evaluation, and systems engineering. It also calls for checks on how mature a new design is before a program moves ahead. Title II turns to policy, asking buyers to weigh cost, schedule, and performance against each other. It pushes for rivalry between firms across a program's whole life and for building test models early.
plaw-111-24-2009:
The Credit Card Accountability Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-24, also called the Credit CARD Act. It amends the Truth in Lending Act. Its aim is fair and clear terms for credit cards and like open-end credit plans.

Title I guards cardholders with limits on fees and interest charges and rules on how card payments are applied. It sets standards for high-fee subprime cards and asks lenders to weigh a borrower's ability to repay. Title II adds clearer statements, payoff timing data, late payment warnings, and web posting of card agreements.
plaw-111-25-2009:
The Ronald Reagan Centennial Commission Act is Public Law 111-25 of 2009. It sets up a commission to honor Ronald Reagan, the 40th president, on the 100th year since his birth. Reagan was born in 1911, so the centennial fell in 2011.

The commission has 11 members, among them the Interior chief, four members named by the president, and members of the House named by its leaders. The president's picks weigh advice from the Ronald Reagan Foundation's board. The panel must plan events for the centennial and help federal, state, and local agencies and civic groups do the same.
plaw-111-26-2009: Public Law 111-26, approved June 19, 2009, names a post office building in Sparta, Georgia. The Postal Service site at 12877 Broad Street is now the Yvonne Ingram-Ephraim Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in February 2009 and the Senate in May of that year.
plaw-111-27-2009: Public Law 111-27, approved June 19, 2009, names a post office building in Jamestown, New York. The Postal Service site at 300 East 3rd Street is now the Stan Lundine Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in March 2009 and the Senate in May of that year.
plaw-111-28-2009: Public Law 111-28, approved June 19, 2009, names a post office in McLain, Mississippi. The Postal Service site at 103 West Main Street is now the Major Ed W. Freeman Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in March 2009 and the Senate in May.
plaw-111-29-2009: Public Law 111-29, approved June 19, 2009, names a post office building in Rochester, New York. The Postal Service site at 3245 Latta Road is now the Brian K. Schramm Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in April 2009 and the Senate in May.
plaw-111-3-2009:
The Children's Health Insurance Program Reauthorization Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-3. It amends title XXI of the Social Security Act to extend and improve the Children's Health Insurance Program, known as CHIP. CHIP funds health cover for children through the states.

The act sets out its terms early, defining CHIP, Medicaid, and the Secretary, who is the Secretary of Health and Human Services. Its first title covers financing for the program. Other stated parts cover the general start date and the reliance states may place on the law as written.
plaw-111-30-2009: Public Law 111-30 is the Antitrust Criminal Penalty Enhancement and Reform Act of 2004 Extension Act. It extends title II of the 2004 act for one year, ending June 22, 2010. To do so, it strikes the words 5 years in that act's sunset clause and inserts 6 years. The change counts as effective just before June 22, 2009, days before the old date would have run out.
plaw-111-31-2009:
Public Law 111-31 of 2009 joins two subjects in one act. Division A is the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act. The rest of the act makes changes to federal retirement systems, among them the Thrift Savings Plan.

Division A gives the Food and Drug Administration set power to regulate tobacco products. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and calls for a final rule under that act. Title II of the division covers tobacco product warnings and the disclosure of what is in tobacco and its smoke. The division also covers studies on raising the minimum age to buy tobacco products.
plaw-111-32-2009:
The Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2009 is Public Law 111-32. It adds spending for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2009. Title I funds the Department of Agriculture, starting with food aid grants abroad.

That title adds 700 million dollars for Public Law 480 Title II grants, which fund food aid overseas. It frees leftover emergency conservation funds for recovery work after natural disasters. It also backs farm loans, with 360 million dollars for direct farm ownership loans and 400 million dollars for direct operating loans. The loan sums flow through the Agricultural Credit Insurance Fund. The act was approved on June 24, 2009.
plaw-111-33-2009:
The Native American Heritage Day Act of 2009 is Public Law 111-33, a joint resolution of the 111th Congress. Its stated aim is to honor the achievements and contributions of Native Americans to the United States. The measure supports a national day of recognition.

Congress finds that Native Americans descend from the original inhabitants of this land. It notes their service in the Armed Forces in every war since the Revolution, at a higher per capita rate than any other group. It also cites Native contributions to farming, medicine, music, language, and art, and the free speech principles of tribal governments.
plaw-111-34-2009: Public Law 111-34, approved June 30, 2009, names a federal building and courthouse in Elizabeth City, North Carolina. The building at 306 East Main Street is now the J. Herbert W. Small Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in March 2009 and the Senate on June 17 of that year.
plaw-111-35-2009: Public Law 111-35, approved June 30, 2009, names a federal building in New York, New York. The building at 799 United Nations Plaza is now the Ronald H. Brown United States Mission to the United Nations Building. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in March 2009 and the Senate on June 17 of that year.
plaw-111-36-2009: Public Law 111-36 is the Webcaster Settlement Act of 2009. It amends section 114 of title 17 of the code, the part on sound recordings. The act allows deals between webcasters and rights holders on the terms for playing and copying recordings online. Its changes add this act to a list in that section and move a deadline. The new cutoff is 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on the 30th day after the act passed.
plaw-111-37-2009:
