Their 2026 single-center study assigned eighty-six patients to one of two arms. One arm used standard pressure settings. The other used individualized settings guided by electrical impedance tomography. That is a bedside imaging belt that watches air move through the chest, region by region.

The guided strategy combined imaging, recruitment maneuvers, and gradual pressure titration. It lifted blood oxygen levels more over the first three days. Lung stiffness trajectories looked similar between groups. The trial was sized for these physiological measures rather than survival. The authors position imaging guidance as a promising way to personalize ventilation, where one pressure plainly does not fit all.
plos-pone-0356009:
Hui-ling Yan and colleagues reviewed tools that predict poor bowel cleaning before a colonoscopy. Dirty bowels can hide disease and waste the procedure, so clinics want to flag risky patients early. Their 2026 systematic review gathered studies from eight databases and pooled how well the prediction models performed.

The review covered thirty-one studies describing forty-six models. Common risk factors included constipation, diabetes, older age, body weight, and past bowel surgery. On average the models sorted patients moderately well, both in their own samples and in outside tests. But most studies carried a high risk of bias, and few checked whether predicted risks matched real rates. The authors call for bigger, independent validation studies.
plos-pone-0357009:
Maria Emfietzoglou leads a team of eight checking whether a broken cellular recycling gene reshapes the gut microbiome, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gene, Lamp2, is needed to fuse recycling sacs with the cell's digestion chambers; its loss causes Danon disease in people. Male mice lacking the gene, and their normal littermates, gave fecal samples across their first year of life. Some cages held one genotype, others mixed both. The samples underwent deep shotgun sequencing of microbial DNA.

The headline is restraint. By the primary measures, the two groups' gut communities looked alike: similar diversity, similar overall composition. Whatever differences emerged were limited, as the paper's own framing stresses. Housing arrangement and cage effects loomed as the usual confounders to control. The careful negative matters: not every dramatic gene knockout echoes into the gut, and microbiome claims built on shallow sequencing deserve this study's deeper skepticism.
plos-pone-0357109:
Wei-Jia Kong and colleagues searched for a shared culprit between two conditions. One is sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. The other is the delirium that often follows surgery. The two can feed each other. Their 2026 study merged gene activity datasets for both conditions. It carefully corrected a badly inflated sepsis dataset. It then looked for genes moving in the same direction in each.

Forty-four candidate genes overlapped, and twenty-two agreed in direction. Network analysis elevated one gene in particular, MAPK14. It is a stress and inflammation switch. It rose across sepsis and delirium cohorts alike. Computer docking further suggested the common blood pressure drug losartan interacts with it. The authors stress this is computer evidence only. It is a lead for experiments, not a treatment yet.
plos-pone-0357209: Fino and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on judging how well the kidneys filter blood. That rate, called GFR, is usually estimated from blood tests for creatinine or cystatin C, plus age and sex. The team studied how much estimates vary under this approach. Variation matters because one estimate can label a person healthy while another flags kidney disease.
plos-pone-0357309:
Zhiping Deng and coauthors published a 2026 engineering study in PLOS ONE on a greener concrete column. The column is a steel tube filled with concrete partly made from lithium slag, an industry waste, wrapped in carbon fiber polymer rings. Twenty short columns were crushed in the laboratory while the team varied lithium slag content, fiber ring spacing, and fiber layer count.

The columns failed gradually, ending with the steel tube buckling outward. More lithium slag raised load capacity but made behavior more brittle, with a middle replacement level performing best overall. Adding fiber layers improved both strength and ductility more than tightening the ring spacing did. The team distilled the tests into a strength formula and verified its accuracy against their data. Designers gain a tested recipe for using lithium waste in load-bearing columns rather than landfilling it.
plos-pone-0357409:
Yuichi Ninomiya and colleagues followed 752 adults in Japan who quit smoking. They tracked heart tracings over six years for signs of an enlarged left ventricle. Their 2026 retrospective study used annual health checkup records from people without hypertension. It compared the electrical voltage that signals heart enlargement at quitting and six years later.

The voltage eased downward. The share of people meeting the enlargement threshold fell too. That happened even though quitters gained weight and their blood pressure rose. Both of those usually push the heart the other way. Blood pressure medication independently predicted improvement. The findings add a concrete heart benefit to quitting. The overworked heart muscle can partly recover its normal electrical pattern over time.
plos-pone-0357709:
Andreea Cislaru led a team of eight authors studying sugar tags on blood proteins in liver failure, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In decompensated cirrhosis, the liver can no longer keep up, and the sugar patterns on serum and antibody proteins change. The team linked those changes to the standard severity score, MELD-Na.

Cislaru's group mapped how the sugar profile shifts as cirrhosis worsens. Such signatures could sharpen forecasts for patients waiting for transplants, where timing is life or death. Blood sugar tags are cheap to read once the patterns are known, so a validated signature could spread widely. The study joins a growing field that reads protein sugars as early warnings of organ failure.
plos-pone-0357909:
Guanyu Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the state of behavioural research in the United Kingdom. That is the science of how people act, and it now informs policy on health, crime, climate, and more. Five workshops brought together close to sixty researchers and research users from universities, government, charities, and business. Using structured framework analysis, the authors mapped the field's strengths, its obstacles, and the fixes participants proposed.

Participants praised how visible behavioural research has become and how deeply it is embedded in some organizations. But they also listed public misunderstandings, thin funding, findings that fail to reach practice, teams working in silos, uneven training, and weak leadership backing. Remedies included making the research more accessible, reforming how it is funded, and training across sectors. Sustained investment, they conclude, is needed so behavioural evidence serves public priorities rather than sitting in journals.
plos-pone-0359109: Ranjan and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on dementia in Bangladesh, called the CARED study. They recorded the age at which people were diagnosed and which dementia subtype they had. Brain scans helped separate one subtype from another. In a country where dementia is often missed, such basic facts guide clinics and family support.
plos-pone-0359209:
Yeser Eroglu Eskicioglu and colleagues developed a measurement scale in 2026 for why people in Türkiye practice yoga. Consumer motivation matters to studios and instructors, but it also reveals how a practice imported from elsewhere takes on local meanings. Their scale development study builds and tests a questionnaire that can measure those motivations reliably.

A validated scale turns impressions about yoga's appeal, health, calm, fitness, community, or spirituality, into data that researchers and businesses can compare across groups and over time. The study also documents, through its items, the reasons Turkish practitioners themselves give. Work of this kind gives the young field of yoga research a firmer footing in a country where the practice is still spreading.
plos-pone-0359409:
Yixin Feng and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on city transit. It forecasts short-term metro passenger flow, how many riders stations will see in the near future. The modeling is decoupled spatio-temporal, treating patterns across places and across time as separate pieces before recombining them.

The design pairs a diffusion-convergence graph with a Swin-Enhanced LSTM, two machine learning components the authors credit for the forecast. Accurate short-term forecasts let metro operators add trains before platforms crowd. Transit planners in large cities are the audience for forecasting methods tested on metro data.
plos-pone-0359509: Chen and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what wins bouts in elite amateur boxing. They compared winners and losers in matched pairs, so each pair was alike in most ways. The focus was on technical and tactical signs, such as punch patterns and ring control. Knowing which signs truly track with winning can sharpen coaching beyond raw punch counts.
plos-pone-0359809:
Rashid Mehmood and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a case-control analysis of end stage renal disease, kidney failure requiring dialysis or transplant. The authors test the impact of polymorphisms, common gene variants, in two genes, GST and TP53, on susceptibility to the disease.

TP53 is famous as a guardian gene against cancer, while GST genes help clear toxins from the body. Comparing patients with healthy controls shows whether certain variants cluster in kidney failure. Nephrologists and genetic researchers can use susceptibility evidence like this to understand why kidney disease strikes some families harder.
pmc-13177909: Michael Edwards, Alexandra Lee, and Simon Thompson discuss federated data linkage in a 2024 article. Federated systems let analysts work securely across several institutions without moving sensitive data, using trusted research environments. Real-world linkage across such systems is still early, and sharing the information that shows two records match, while preserving privacy, is hard. The article examines these challenges for population-scale linkage, including how links shift as providers join or leave, and explores privacy-preserving approaches across multiple research environments and their governance needs.
pmc-13197109:
Chidimma Doris Azubuike and colleagues describe a 2026 protocol called MOMitor for blood pressure after birth. High blood pressure after delivery affects about one in five women. Phone-based checks could catch rises early in this risky window, so the team set out a tracking plan.

Enrolled women answer brief phone prompts over the first six weeks after birth. Prompts ask whether pressure topped a set limit and whether warning symptoms are present. A subset also reports home pressure readings. The team will model change within and between women across the six weeks. Data gathering ran from late 2021 to mid 2025. Results are not yet reported, since analysis was still to come.
pmc-13198509:
Daniel Verscharen and colleagues review electron travel in tangled magnetic fields in a 2026 paper. Space magnetic fields are rarely smooth; plasma flows and turbulence twist them. Electrons spiral along field lines, so their measures can map how fields connect across space.

The review lays out the basics of that travel, then covers how turbulence tangles fields in the first place. It treats trapping in field dips, escape from traps, and drift across field lines. Waves hitting particles can speed or scatter electrons too. No single tool can untangle the full picture. The authors call for joint use of spacecraft data, remote views, theory, and simulation.
pmc-13199209:
Seyit Bilal Ozdemir and Busra Ozdemir tested how heat aging affects the X-ray visibility of tooth fillings in a 2026 lab study. Fillings must show on X-rays at least as clearly as tooth tissue, so dentists can spot gaps and decay. Heat cycling in the lab mimics years of hot and cold drinks.

Seven universal filling materials were shaped into discs at two thicknesses. X-ray brightness was measured against an aluminum scale. All materials met the standard minimum at the thinner size. Thicker discs read brighter across the board. After ten thousand heat cycles, two materials lost brightness at the thicker size. Material type and thickness both shaped readings, a point for dentists judging old fillings.
pmc-13237809:
Bhuiya and colleagues lay out a plan to strengthen prevention of respiratory syncytial virus in young children. The virus is the leading cause of serious chest illness and death in children under five, with the heaviest toll in poorer countries. In 2023, two new shields were approved in rich countries: a vaccine given in pregnancy and a long-acting antibody for babies.

Using Bangladesh as the model case, the authors map how low and middle income countries can actually deliver such tools. Cold chains, cost, clinic reach, and parent trust all decide uptake. A blueprint that faces those barriers gives health ministries a route from approval on paper to protection in villages.
pmc-13237909:
Berg-Warman and colleagues review the first six years of Israel's dental reform for older adults. In 2019, dental care for seniors entered universal health coverage, aiming to open access, cut money barriers, and narrow gaps in who gets treated. Such reforms are often announced loudly and then tracked poorly, leaving their real reach unknown.

The study examines how dental care among elderly Israelis changed across those six years. It asks who gained visits and treatment, and whether old inequalities shrank or merely shifted. The findings give policymakers a rare long look at a national dental reform, useful far beyond Israel as populations age everywhere.
pmc-13238709:
Chen and colleagues model a slow-motion mismatch between an oil crop and the wild bees it depends on. Camellia oleifera, a woody oil plant native to China, cannot pollinate itself and relies wholly on insects to set seed. It flowers from late October into December, when cold already keeps most bees home, leaving two specialist bees to do nearly all the work.

Those bees, Colletes gigas and Andrena camellia, are its most efficient pollinators. The team's ensemble models project how crop and bees shift range as the climate warms. If the plant moves one way and its bees another, harvests fail without any field being ploughed. Naming that risk early gives growers and conservationists time to respond.
pmc-13239709:
Jiang and colleagues find a way to make breast tumours more visible to the immune system. Triple-negative breast cancer cells wear a surface signal, CD47, that tells macrophages 'do not eat me'. Drugs blocking that signal can restore the attack, but tumours often evade them. So the team hunted for what controls the signal itself.

They show that the enzyme LSD1, which edits chemical marks on DNA packaging, keeps the signal's levels up. Blocking LSD1 lowered the signal and made signal-blocking therapy work better. The effect held across cell lines and mouse models. Pairing the two blockers could give immunotherapy a firmer grip on a stubborn cancer.
pmc-13241409:
Liakouli and the Italian GIRRCS network measured metabolic syndrome inside a large systemic sclerosis cohort. Six hundred thirteen patients from eleven top centers enrolled at one point in time. Five hundred seventy had complete data for the study. Syndrome status followed the shared global definition from 2009.

Under nine percent met the syndrome bar, a modest share. Those patients skewed older, with far more active disease and mild lung restriction. Heart involvement, lung pressure, and advanced nailfold capillary damage all ran higher. Active disease and lung stiffness stayed linked after adjustment. Hypertension was the commonest single part.
pmc-13241509:
Bråhn and co-authors at Linköping University compare experiences of public violence among Swedish youths with and without a refugee background. Young people helped shape the questionnaire used in the study. Responses came from seventy-nine youths with refugee backgrounds and one hundred five Swedish-born peers. Data collection ran from 2019 through 2022 across Sweden.

About one third of all respondents reported facing violence in public places in Sweden. Direct exposure did not differ significantly between the two groups. Refugee-background youths, though, felt less safe and restricted their daily lives more. Participants suggested more education, more surveillance, and a stronger adult presence in public spaces.
pmc-13242109:
Fadaei and colleagues in Tabriz handed stroke nurses a phone app and timed the race to thrombolysis. Sixty emergency nurses implemented the Code Sama mobile decision-support tool. Sixty stroke patients treated with the app were compared against sixty routine-care patients. Trained observers clocked every milestone around the clock.

Door-to-needle time fell from about forty-eight minutes to forty-three after the app arrived. The effect size was very large by conventional standards. Baseline times had matched almost exactly between the two groups. Fadaei calls for a randomized trial to confirm the workflow gain.
pmc-13242409:
Bohye Kim and Ju Young Yoon studied how health literacy shapes quality of life for adults with physical disabilities in South Korea. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. They analyzed survey data from 441 adults in the 2021 Korea Health Panel. Using a model that links personal, social, and health-system factors, they traced direct and indirect paths between literacy and well-being.

About forty-four percent of participants had inadequate health literacy, and another share had problematic skills. Needing more care was tied to both lower literacy and lower quality of life, while having a job and stronger literacy were tied to better quality of life. Unmet health needs also pulled scores down. Literacy partly carried the effect of care needs onward. The authors argue that services and jobs matter as much as teaching individuals.
pmc-13242509:
Gerard Breaden Madden and colleagues surveyed orchestral musicians about breathing problems and the cleanliness of their instruments. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Wind instruments can harbor microbes that players inhale again and again, and case reports link dirty instruments to lung trouble. The questionnaire went to players in German orchestras and other professional institutions, covering 245 wind players and 43 string players as a comparison group.

Asthma and diagnosed respiratory disease were reported far more often by the wind players than by the string players. Symptom patterns otherwise overlapped, and playing time and smoking did not explain the gap. The authors name microbial contamination of instruments as one plausible cause worth direct testing. They also found hygiene habits and hygiene teaching inconsistent across the profession. Standard cleaning routines, they argue, should become part of musical training for woodwind and brass players alike.
pmc-13244509:
Yong Zhang and co-authors traced how a sulfur-handling enzyme defends the heart against iron overload. Their study appeared in Redox Report in 2026. Iron overload cardiomyopathy kills patients whose bodies accumulate iron, largely through oxidative damage. The enzyme CSE runs a pathway that produces cysteine and hydrogen sulfide, the raw materials of the cell's antioxidant shield. The team deleted or boosted it in mice and in heart cells bathed in iron.

Mice lacking the enzyme suffered worse heart enlargement, weaker pumping, and more scarring under iron overload. Their cells imported less cysteine, made less glutathione, and silenced a chain of protective genes. Restoring the enzyme reversed the pattern, stabilizing the cysteine transporter and cutting reactive oxygen. The pathway thus guards both cysteine supply routes at once: making it and importing it. The authors nominate it as a drug target for iron-loaded hearts.
pmc-13245409:
Macesic, Harris, and Mo review carbapenemases, the enzymes that defeat medicine's last-line antibiotics, in this 2026 JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance article. Bacteria carrying these enzymes now span the major Gram-negative groups, their genes hitchhiking worldwide on plasmids inside high-risk clones. The review classifies the enzyme families, maps their regional patterns, and traces One Health drivers linking hospitals, communities, animals, and the environment.

Practical guidance follows: a stepwise diagnostic framework from screening swabs through rapid molecular tests to genome sequencing. Naming the exact mechanism early guides both infection control and drug choice. Treatment is organized by mechanism, with newer combination drugs central for some enzyme types. Harder workarounds are needed for the metallo-enzymes, whose rise the authors flag as the landscape's most worrying shift.
pmc-13248109:
Rodgers and Pace report a single unusual case in Case Reports in Urology in 2026. Their patient was a healthy fifty-year-old man who tore the lining of his penis during sex, an injury doctors treat as an emergency. Standard care calls for surgery at once, but the man also tested positive for COVID-19.

Because operating carried extra risk, the team waited ten days until he tested negative, then repaired the tear. At checks four and twenty months later he had no scarring or bending, and his erections were normal and painless. The authors argue that a short delay to make a patient safer can still end well.
pmc-13249709:
Feiteiro and colleagues review how a brain injury can end up harming the heart, in a 2026 Metabolic Brain Disease article. Traumatic brain injury strikes millions yearly, and survivors carry raised cardiovascular risk. The review traces the molecular chain: the autonomic nervous system falls out of balance, inflammation smolders, oxidative damage builds, and the hormone axis linking brain and body is disturbed.

Against that chain, the authors weigh physical exercise as therapy. Exercise can calm inflammation, restore autonomic balance, and support brain rewiring, all at once. What nobody yet knows is the right dose: when to start, how hard, and how long. The authors call for standard protocols tested in trials.
pmc-13250109:
Sender and co-authors test whether lung artery CT scans can use far less radiation without losing image quality. Their 2026 Scientific Reports paper compares a new low-dose protocol, rebuilt with deep learning software, against standard-dose scans using an older reconstruction method. A phantom study, using model bodies of two sizes, came first.

In the phantom, deep learning reconstruction allowed dose cuts of up to about seventy percent at equal image clarity. The team then reviewed scans from just over three hundred patients treated before and after the switch. Patient dose fell by roughly two fifths, while image quality in the main lung artery improved. The authors conclude the low-dose approach is not worse than standard care.
pmc-13251009:
Radwan and co-authors test two cell-death genes as early warning markers in acute myeloid leukemia. Their 2026 BMC Cancer study compares samples from one hundred newly diagnosed patients with forty healthy volunteers. Five-year survival in this leukemia stays poor, and relapse often grows from cells that dodge normal death programs.

One gene, NFS1, ran high in patients, while GSDMD ran low, and both patterns reversed after treatment. Worse starting patterns, high NFS1 with low GSDMD, marked patients with poorer outlooks and lower one-year survival. The genes tie to two newer death routes, ferroptosis and pyroptosis, that cancer cells often suppress. The authors propose the pair as diagnostic and prognostic markers and as possible treatment targets.
pmc-13253609:
Amirhossein Zarei, Marsa Gholamzadeh, and Fatemeh Asadi review digital twins in chronic disease care in this 2026 paper. A digital twin is a live virtual copy of a patient that can simulate how an illness will unfold, promising earlier and more personal treatment.

Searching four databases, the team found twenty studies that fit. Most appeared in 2023 and 2024, and the United States contributed the most. Training and education led the uses, ahead of personalised care and drug development. Clinicians were the top audience, then patients. Data analytics and machine learning powered most twins, with body modelling and sensors behind. The authors see the field moving from theory into clinics.
pmc-13253909:
Vilmar Machado and co-authors present a computer workflow in a 2026 study of a pest-control bacterium. Bacillus thuringiensis is widely used to kill crop pests, but many of its proteins are labeled hypothetical, meaning their jobs are unknown. The team screened such proteins from three strains of the bacterium.

Step-by-step filtering cut 2,052 proteins down to 11 strong candidates backed by several lines of computer evidence. Six had traits suited to deeper structural study. The candidates included enzymes and proteins tied to stress survival and host contact. The authors offer the workflow for other bacteria, not firm claims about protein jobs.
pmc-13254309:
Jeremy Eudaric and co-authors map malaria risk in flood zones in a 2026 study of Sub-Saharan Africa. They combined flood maps from 2000 to 2018, malaria data, and population data across 492 flood-prone zones in 38 countries. Flood water left standing after floods gives mosquitoes ideal breeding grounds.

Malaria risk was higher in flood-prone regions of East and West Africa than national baselines. About 12 million people diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria were exposed to flooding, one-third of all flood-affected people. Flood exposure stood out as a main driver of malaria burden in these zones, guiding hotspot targeting.
pmc-13255209:
Taoran Chen and co-authors build a bird flu vaccine for chickens in a 2026 study. H5 avian influenza of one fast-spreading clade has caused huge poultry losses and poses a risk to people. The team designed three versions of a trimeric hemagglutinin antigen, the virus surface protein, using mammalian cell systems.

One version, S836-Trimer, performed best in expression, stability, and immune response. A single 10-microgram dose gave chickens complete protection against a lethal challenge, matching a commercial vaccine. A stable CHO cell line made about tenfold more antigen, which the authors say supports large-scale production.
pmc-13255309:
Kiana Kiani and co-authors interview key actors about patient involvement in health research in a 2026 study. Patient involvement is widely praised but applied unevenly across research and development. The team held semi-structured interviews with 29 people: patient representatives, clinicians, researchers, industry staff, and public officials, all linked to a European patient academy in Sweden.

Five themes covered culture and power shifts, clear structures, role expectations, trust and communication, and shared understanding. Different actors read the same barriers and aids in clashing ways, creating tensions that must be negotiated. The authors suggest grounding involvement in a person-centered ethic of partnership and shared responsibility.
pmc-13255409:
Xu and a multicenter team lay out the protocol for a year-long randomized trial in people with moderate to severe COPD at high risk of flare-ups. Four hundred ten adults will be assigned to digital inhaler management, inspiratory muscle training, both together, or usual verbal education. The digital platform trains technique, monitors adherence objectively, and feeds results back in real time.

The primary outcome is the rate of moderate-to-severe exacerbations over twelve months, with follow-up visits at three, six, and twelve months. Secondary measures include symptom scores, lung function, breathing muscle strength, and walking distance. The trial is registered and ethics approved, with analysis by intention to treat.
pmc-13258009:
Marion E Cahill leads a 2026 gene therapy study in mice bred to model blue cone monochromacy, an inherited eye disorder that removes red and green color sensing. The disorder often comes from a mutation called C203R in the opsin genes, the genes for light-sensing proteins in cone cells. The mouse model carried the matching mutation and had only cone cells in its retina, like the center of the human eye.

Untreated mice showed no light response in electrical eye tests and had shortened cone outer segments. The team injected a virus carrying a healthy human opsin gene at one month and at five months of age. Treated mice regained cone function and rebuilt outer segments, and the rescue lasted at least five months. The authors say even late treatment worked, which supports testing gene therapy for patients.
pmc-13258109:
David Milewski and co-authors probe why targeted drugs stop working in medullary thyroid carcinoma. This cancer is often driven by mutations in the RET gene, and RET-blocking drugs work well at first. Their 2026 study models how resistance emerges and how it might be beaten.

Resistant cells gained extra copies of RET and a secondary mutation already seen in patients. A genome-wide knockout screen pointed to loss of the NF1 gene, which switches on a backup growth pathway. Drug screening agreed, favoring blockers of that pathway. Pairing a RET drug with a MEK drug proved synergistic in mouse tumors.
pmc-13260109:
Sofia Damian and colleagues wrote a 2026 engineering study of tension in plates with circular holes, using a modeling approach called peridynamics. Peridynamics is a nonlocal theory, meaning each point in a material interacts with neighbors across a small distance, which helps model cracks. The team used a reduced version of the model to cut computing costs. They compared two microstructures, each set by a different horizon, the model's internal length scale, while keeping overall stiffness the same.

As the horizon grew, the peak stress moved farther from the hole. The stressed area also spread out more, and the stress concentration factor, the ratio of peak to average stress, went down. The damage surface, where the material separates, likewise became more diffuse at the higher horizon. The authors say microstructure choice measurably changes predictions for this classic fracture problem.
pmc-13261009:
Abiyie Bitew Godie and colleagues present a 2026 case-control study of pneumonia risk in adult asthma patients in Awi Zone, northwest Ethiopia. Pneumonia is a frequent, life-threatening complication in asthma, yet local evidence on its determinants is limited. The study enrolled 359 adults with asthma from public hospitals between August 20 and October 25, 2025: 120 with pneumonia and 239 without. Data came from interviewer-led questionnaires and medical records, analyzed with logistic regression.

Cases were older than controls, with mean ages of 60.25 years for cases and 44.85 years for controls. Prior hospital admission for an acute asthma attack showed the strongest association with pneumonia, with an adjusted odds ratio of 13.22, the highest in the study. Inhaled corticosteroid use, loss of follow-up, current alcohol use, and increasing age also raised the odds. Controlled asthma was strongly protective, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.06 for those patients. The authors recommend strengthening follow-up.
pmc-13261309:
Yang Yang and co-authors present a 2026 global study of depression and obesity occurring together. Both are major health burdens, yet their combined patterns across countries were poorly mapped. The team set out to chart co-occurrence, trends over time, and social correlates, and to forecast the combined prevalence to 2035.

They drew on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, and World Bank data for 199 countries and territories. The consistently low-prevalence group clustered in Asia, while the consistently high group sat in the Americas. The depression-dominant group was mainly in Africa. Combined prevalence rose globally, with a median average annual percentage change of 4.66%. East Asia, Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa had higher growth despite low current levels. The team also compared seven social indicators across trend groups.
pmc-13262609:
Shuliang Chen and co-authors examine how cells clear parts of their own endoplasmic reticulum, the folded membrane network that builds proteins, in a 2026 journal article. In this cleanup, called ER-phagy, a receptor named Atg40 gathers membrane proteins, or cargo, into vesicles for breakdown. A partner protein is normally needed for cargo capture.

Working in yeast cells lacking neutral lipids, stored fats, the team saw Atg40 reach the breakdown compartment without its partner or cargo. Chemical analysis showed a changed ratio of two membrane fats, which is expected to alter how easily the membrane bends. Their reading is that membrane fats control whether the receptor couples to its cargo at cleanup sites.
pmc-13262709:
Douglas E Vaughan writes a 2026 tribute to Eugene Braunwald, whom he calls the most influential cardiologist of the modern era. Braunwald was born in Vienna in 1929 and escaped Nazi Austria with his family in 1938, settling in New York. He trained at New York University and Johns Hopkins, then joined the National Heart Institute in 1955.

The tribute traces landmark work that defined thickened-heart disease, now called hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, as a distinct condition. It also covers his 1968 survival curve for aortic stenosis, which set when valve surgery should begin, and his 1971 finding that heart attack damage can be limited. That idea, that time costs heart muscle, underlies modern heart attack care.
pmc-13265009:
Shahad Aljebeli and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition of high blood pressure, at a large Saudi care center. They reviewed five years of cases, from 2019 to 2024, and compared four subtypes for mother and baby outcomes. The subtypes were mild, severe, after-birth, and layered on prior high blood pressure.

Of 271 patients, 43.2 percent had the mild form and 37.6 percent the severe form. The mean age was 32 and mean body mass was high at 31.2. The layered subtype, though only ten women, linked to earlier preterm birth and more emergency cesarean sections. Stillbirth occurred in 5.5 percent of cases, all in the severe group, though group differences were not significant. The authors urge care in reading the small subgroup and call for prospective studies.
pmc-13266409:
Emanuele Marzetti and colleagues report a 2026 study of a one-year exercise plan for older adults in Brazil. The group followed 132 people living at home who showed early signs of sarcopenia, meaning age-related loss of muscle strength. The plan mixed strength, balance, and movement drills twice a week for a full year.

After the year, timed walking and chair-stand tests improved, and balance rose by more than half. Normal walking speed also rose, while grip-based signs of likely sarcopenia fell from about 89 percent to 67 percent. The authors argue that such training in basic care could cut falls, disability, and hospital stays.
pmc-13267709:

The team measured emissions from 111 milking cows under normal feeding, then read the full gene content of their rumen microbes.

High and low emitters differed in how their microbes supplied hydrogen, the fuel for methane making. Starch-breaking, lactic acid, and fatty acid pathways fed that supply unevenly. Tiny one-celled animals called ciliates were common in all high emitters, while methane makers varied more. Six nutrient pathways shaped output. A learning model picked 34 microbe groups as markers of methane level. The authors offer these as targets for cutting livestock emissions.
pmc-13267809:
Yingying Cai and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of mismatched mind and body burden in chronic lung disease. In COPD, lasting airflow blockage, distress often fails to match symptom severity. The team profiled 306 patients at one large hospital in Shandong, China, using measures of anxiety, low mood, lung function, symptoms, and breathlessness.

Four patient types emerged. The largest group, about 47 percent, carried low burden on both sides. About 22 percent formed a mismatch type, with mental burden far above their physical symptoms. That group reported the worst quality of life of all. It also faced more hospital stays than the low and middle groups. Differences in self-care and coping were small. The authors urge routine mental health checks in COPD care.
pmc-13268109:

The mark sits on the BRCA1 gene, a gene whose inherited faults raise cancer risk. Unlike a mutation, this mark is a methylation tag present from early development in normal tissues, including blood. The team measured it in 473 women with ovarian cancer and 476 controls.

The mark appeared in about 9 percent of patients and about 5 percent of controls. At high levels, the link to cancer grew much stronger. Women carrying the mark were diagnosed younger, at a median of 54 against 60. Half of the tumors showing the mark traced back to this body-wide form. The authors call it a robust marker of personal ovarian cancer risk.
pmc-13268409:
Seyda Dogantan and colleagues present a 2026 study of iron-linked cell damage markers in children with familial Mediterranean fever. This inherited condition causes repeated short fever attacks. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, might play a role. The team measured two related blood markers in 30 affected children during quiet periods and 30 healthy children.

Within each group, the two markers moved together closely, most strongly in the fever patients. The authors read this tight link as a hint that iron imbalance and oxidative stress interact in the disease, and call for larger studies including children mid-attack.
pmc-13268709:
Tadahiko Kamegaya presents a 2026 interview study of powered wheelchair users in Japan. Under Japan's long-term care insurance, people can rent powered wheelchairs cheaply, yet uptake stays low. Kamegaya interviewed five users of the rental service about daily use and feelings toward their chairs, organizing answers with a structured grouping method.

Users had chosen their chairs themselves, based on personal values, and grew attached to them. They saw the chairs as tools for independent living and accepted their drawbacks alongside their benefits. Still, daily use felt difficult: the driving is complex, real-world safety worries persist, and public awareness of powered wheelchairs is low. The author concludes rentals serve independence-minded users well, and that these practical barriers, not the chairs themselves, limit wider adoption.
pmc-13269509:
Shokhrukh-Mirzo Jalilov, Robert Maltsbarger, and Haluk Gedikoglu published a journal article in 2026 on farm flood losses in a county in the United States Midwest. Standard models tie damage to flood size alone. Their model adds crop growth stage, since a standing crop is worth more at some stages than others.

Frequent, mild floods caused the largest share of yearly losses. Two-year and 25-year floods together made up about 45 percent of expected annual damage. Rare extreme floods caused bigger single losses but often fell outside the growing season. Mild floods hurt most because they likely strike when crops are sensitive and water lingers longer. The authors say timing can outweigh flood size in farm risk pricing.
pmc-13269609: A correction notice from 2026, for a paper led by Timo Sonntag on exercise therapy built into routine cancer care, replaces one figure. The original article, reporting eight years of an integrated oncology exercise program, displayed an out-of-date version of Figure 1, which sets out the program concept. The notice shows the updated figure and states that this is its only change.
pmc-13269809:
Kyung Hee Han and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on radiation therapy after surgery for early-stage womb cancer. Patients were grouped by risk using European guidelines, without gene profiling. Records covered 131 patients treated from 2004 to 2020 and followed to 2023.

Seventy-two patients were intermediate risk and 59 were high-intermediate risk. Radiation was given to 98 patients, more often in the higher group, at 89.8 percent. Cancer returned in 12.5 percent of the lower group and 8.5 percent of the higher group. Radiation was tied to significantly better freedom from disease growth in the high-intermediate group only. Older age over 60 also shaped outcomes there. The authors support radiation for the higher risk group.
pmc-13270209:
Asmamaw Habtamu, Lamenew Fenta, and Pengfei Cai published a journal article in 2026 surveying summer degree students at Debre Markos University in Ethiopia about malaria. A structured questionnaire reached 366 students from July to September 2025. It measured knowledge, attitudes, prevention habits, and self-reported malaria.

Most students, 70.5 percent, came from rural areas, and 16.7 percent reported testing positive for malaria between April and June 2025. Satisfactory malaria knowledge stood at 75.4 percent, and 82.8 percent named the cause correctly. Knowledge of treated bed nets and proper care seeking was weaker. About 74.86 percent saw malaria as serious, yet only 71.58 percent used nets consistently and 39.07 percent sought facility care.
pmc-13270409:
Amirhassan Rabbani and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 47-year-old woman with mild to moderate leg swelling and weakness. Evaluation found a rare cancer, leiomyosarcoma, growing in her inferior vena cava, the body's main vein to the heart. The tumor reached the liver veins, with clot forming above the liver.

Standard removal was not feasible in place, so the liver was removed, operated on outside the body, and reimplanted. The vein was rebuilt with a synthetic Dacron graft. She had no complications after surgery. The authors say such extreme procedures, though aggressive, can be viable when they are the only route to complete tumor removal.
pmc-13271209:
Jesuély Spieckert de Souza is lead author of a 2026 study of hospital spending on headache disorders in Brazil's public health system, the SUS, from 2008 to 2023. The authors used national hospital data, adjusted costs for inflation, and modelled what drives the average cost per hospital stay.

Total spending reached about 77.6 million Brazilian reais. Women accounted for 65.7 percent of stays and people aged 19 to 59 for 66.1 percent. Patients aged 60 and older cost 21 percent more per stay, and the South region cost 73.7 percent more per stay even after adjustment. The costliest diagnoses included vascular headache and status migrainosus, a severe prolonged migraine state.
pmc-13271409:
Pengkhun Nov is lead author of a 2026 analysis of the global burden of cervical cancer caused by sexually acquired human papillomavirus infection. It uses Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for people aged ten to 54. The study tracked deaths and years of healthy life lost, called DALYs, from 1990 to 2021. It also forecast trends to 2050.

In 2021, this cause accounted for 117,060 deaths and about 5.57 million DALYs worldwide in that age group. Total counts rose roughly 24 percent since 1990, yet age-standardised rates fell to 2.31 deaths per 100,000. India and China carried the largest totals, southern sub-Saharan Africa the highest rates, and the Middle East and North Africa the lowest.
pmc-13272609:
Hilal Simsek and Asli Ucar wrote a 2026 scoping review on weight-loss drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists in older adults with obesity. These drugs aid weight loss, but lost weight can include muscle. That matters because low muscle mass and strength, called sarcopenia, can combine with obesity in older people.

The review finds that muscle loss is common with these drugs, and data on muscle size and strength are still thin and mixed. Some signs point to better muscle metabolism and less inflammation. The authors advise pairing the drugs with strength exercise, diet advice, and protein at 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram per day.
pmc-13272809:
Samah El-Debaiky leads a 2026 greenhouse study of eco-friendly ways to control onion white rot, a soil fungus disease that can persist for years. The team combined a helpful fungus, Trichoderma asperelloides, with silver nanoparticles made by biological methods, and with a silver-chitosan mix. Chitosan is a natural material from shells and fungi.

The combined silver-chitosan plus Trichoderma treatment worked best, cutting disease severity by 94.3 percent compared with infected controls. Treated plants also had heavier bulbs, longer leaves, and more leaves, plus higher activity of protective enzymes and lower markers of cell damage. The authors say field trials are still needed before farm use can be recommended.
pmc-13272909:
Christoph Bender leads a 2026 study showing that photoacoustic imaging devices leave fingerprints that can bias deep learning models. Photoacoustic imaging is a newer method that uses light and sound, and data for training models are scarce. The team analyzed images from four devices used in two studies of artery disease in the legs.

Models could tell which device made an image with up to 100 percent accuracy. When device and health status were linked in the training data, disease models used the device fingerprint as a shortcut, giving biased and misleading results. The authors warn that ignoring such confounding can inflate reported performance, and urge bias checks in multi-center studies.
pmc-13274309:
Valid Mwalukuku and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on squeezing more power from dye-based solar cells indoors. Such cells excel under dim artificial light, suiting them for powering small internet-connected sensors. The best indoor versions use copper chemistry that may not last, while sturdier iodine chemistry gives disappointing voltage.

The team redesigned the light-absorbing electrode to cut wasted charge, then let machine learning steer the recipe search. A support vector model plus Bayesian optimization pushed efficiency past twenty-three percent under bright indoor light. Voltage reached 713 millivolts at that brightness, among the highest reported for iodine-based cells indoors. The authors offer the pairing as a faster route to better indoor solar recipes.
pmc-13274609:
Rui Wang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on measuring flying particles from the rainbow their scattered light forms. Reading the size and makeup of particles in free flight is hard because they blur past detectors in a blink. The team propelled tiny particles through hollow-core optical fibers and caught their near-field scattering with a strong lens.

Each scattering fringe carried its own Doppler shift, the pitch change caused by motion, spread out like a broadband rainbow across the beam. That angle-by-angle shift converted the particle's spatial pattern into frequencies that computers can read precisely. Within a millisecond window, they could pin down a single airborne particle's diameter and refractive index, its light-bending power.
pmc-13275509:
Nolan Neville and a large team report a 2026 journal article solving how a bacterial defense machine uses scrambled DNA as a weapon. Certain bacteria fight invading viruses, called phages, with reverse transcriptase enzymes that write DNA without a template. How the resulting semi-random DNA helps defense was unknown. The team studied one system, DRT1, with cryo-electron microscopy and lab tests.

DRT1 starts DNA synthesis from its own protein, producing random-ish DNA tags stuck to itself. Making DNA switches on its second enzyme domain, while the tags drive the proteins to stack into long filaments locked in a dormant state, their active sites tucked away. Mutant phages that escaped pointed to a phage helicase the system needs, revealing how the trap is sprung.
pmc-13276309:
Qian Wang and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how the main urinary infection bacterium invades the bladder. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli causes most urinary tract infections. It uses hair-like type 1 fimbriae to enter bladder lining cells, a key step in starting infection.

The team found a two-part bacterial switch, called RstAB, that the strain needs to colonize mouse bladders. Without it, invasion during early infection faltered. The switch works by turning on the fimbriae: one part binds directly to a DNA flip switch that sets fimbriae production to on. Mice infected with bacteria lacking the system fared better, showing its role in virulence. The authors say this pathway could offer a new angle for treating urinary infections, which often recur despite antibiotics.
pmc-13276809:
Yao Zheng leads a 2026 study that builds a computer model to predict death in hospital for very ill kidney patients. The patients had sepsis, a severe infection response, plus acute kidney injury and were on a continuous blood-cleaning treatment. Records came from large United States databases and a Chinese intensive care unit.

The team compared eight machine learning models, meaning programs that learn patterns from data, using records for 1,549 patients in all. A gradient boosting model performed best and beat older severity scores in the outside test group. Urine output, a kidney blood marker, and age mattered most. The authors say the tool could help doctors sort risk early, not replace judgment.
pmc-13277009:
Preethi Sheshadri leads a 2026 cell study of Parkinson's disease linked to changes in a gene called GBA1. The gene helps lysosomes, the cell parts that break down waste, stay acidic enough to work. The team grew nerve cells from patient stem cells and measured waste cleanup and energy production.

Mutant nerve cells had weak lysosome acidity, poor cleanup of worn-out mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, and low energy output. A faulty pump that should acidify lysosomes sat behind the problem. Two treatments, rapamycin and acidic nanoparticles, restored acidity and rescued energy function. The authors present that repair route as a possible new treatment direction for this form of Parkinson's.
pmc-13277609:
Qinyue Zheng leads a 2026 modeling study of the 2025 chikungunya outbreak in Guangdong province, southern China. Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes fever and often long-lasting joint pain. Strict public health action controlled each center within about two months. Genetic analysis tied the virus to recent strains from Réunion and Mayotte, suggesting an imported start. Their model found that vaccinating before an outbreak could avert most infections at high coverage. A fast campaign during an outbreak could also cut cases sharply, supporting vaccine readiness plans.
pmc-13278409:
Bernice M Hoenderboom leads a 2026 mixed-methods study in the Netherlands on a possible test that predicts fertility risk after chlamydia, a common sexually transmitted infection. Control programs might target those most at risk of reduced fertility. The team ran five focus groups with sexual health center visitors, then built a questionnaire answered by 426 young adults.

Willingness to take such a risk test was high, at seventy-eight percent. Most expected relief from a no-added-risk result, and preparedness from a high-risk result, though worry was also expected. Accuracy, easy access, blood sampling burden, and follow-up care mattered to respondents. Test builders should weigh mental burden alongside benefit, the authors advise.
pmc-13278609:
Nao Taguchi leads a 2026 study of what happens after an AI symptom checker flags a possible HIV or sexually transmitted infection. Early HIV testing is a public health goal, yet many at-risk people never test. The team used data from the Ubie symptom search engine in Japan, covering more than four hundred thousand flagged episodes.

About a quarter of episodes led to a medical consultation, but HIV testing followed in only a few hundred cases. Older users were more likely to seek care than people in their twenties. Awareness information inside the checker was tied to seeking care. Among people who first had no plan to test, about twenty-nine percent said they would test after using the checker.
pmc-13280309:

Grade three endometrioid cancer is a high grade gland cancer of the womb lining. Node spread rates were alike in both groups. Five year progress free survival ran much lower for carcinosarcoma, near thirty six versus sixty three percent.
pmc-13281809:

Coated onto a glass fiber filter sheet, it still caught most mercury in dusty, sulfur-rich gas. Such sheets fit the bag filters factories already use. The authors say bond crafting at surfaces is a broad recipe for better traps.
pmc-13282309:

pmc-13282709:

pmc-13283209:

Lack of disease specificity does not kill its value, the authors argue. It may flag shared brain faults tied to mood, thought, and body symptoms. Such shared markers could guide prevention, tracking, and brain stimulation across disorders. Care can target shared processes, not labels alone.
pmc-13283409:

pmc-13283709:
How strong is a graft built from only half of an ankle tendon? Christopher Kleimeyer and colleagues tested that question in a 2026 lab study for knee ligament repair. Surgeons increasingly use this tendon, yet half-grafts in short four-strand form lacked strength data.

pmc-13284009:
Reward can pull attention to a chosen memory item even when color pop-out is removed, show Allison N Marino and colleagues in 2026. Working memory holds a small focus in a highly active state. Earlier proof always used red for the high-reward item, inviting doubt.

pmc-13284509:
Ning Feng and co-authors report a 2026 blood study in primary angiitis of the central nervous system, a rare illness with severe brain vessel inflammation. The authors call the work exploratory and urge larger multi-center checks.
pmc-13284609:
Maciej M. Mrugala and Michelle Monje introduce a 2026 special issue on thinking problems that follow modern cancer treatment. The issue gathers four articles from leaders in this field.

Editors note that harm was once tied mainly to brain radiation and classic chemotherapy, but immune therapy now shows like effects as well. Up to a third of survivors may be affected, with real costs for work and daily life. Causes likely mix direct nerve harm with immune shifts, oxidative stress, and mitochondria faults. pmc-13285709:
Qi Xiao, Chen Wang, and Chuang Yang present a 2026 pharmacovigilance study of drug-linked gum disorders. Their aim is to flag which drugs deserve closer watch in dental care.

pmc-13285909:
Ghazunfer Abbas leads a 2026 study of a family planning push in urban Pakistan, run with government health departments. Records ran from mid-2020 to mid-2025, drawn from the national supply tracking system for contraceptives. The gap-in-gaps method found about 3,673 extra monthly clients tied to the program across the sites studied. Health department sites alone showed an even larger net gain, and trend checks agreed with the main result. pmc-13288609:
Ngoualem Kegah Franklin and Ndjouenkeu Robert review starch in yoghurt in 2026. Most past work just added starch to milk. Few studies swapped milk fat for starch. Low-fat yoghurt leads shop sales worldwide. Claims for its health edge lack firm proof.

Added starch raised carbohydrate in yoghurt. It lowered moisture at the same time. Mineral, fat, and protein effects went all ways. Thickness rose and whey loss fell. Acidity also rose with starch. Taste and texture peaked near a two percent dose. That held for all starch sources. In storage, acidity kept climbing. Taste held steady and flow traits stayed the same.
pmc-13288909:
Chengwei Shao and colleagues scan virus changes for antibody escape. Their 2026 study maps the JN.1 Omicron line and its child XEC. They test each single change in the spike tip. Safe lab virus copies stand in for the real virus. Two strong antibodies anchor the escape tests.

pmc-13289009:
Eva Hernandez-Garcia and colleagues plan a 2026 trial series on clean bedroom air. The BREATHS trials deal with cancer survivors. These adults face high heart risk from past treatment. Dirty air can raise body-wide swelling. Night filters can cut fine dust in air.

Blood swelling marks lead the outcomes. Blood sugar and blood pressure will also be tracked. Air monitors will log dust in and out. Non-responders will move to open filter use.
pmc-13289309:

Findings needing more workup appeared in 34 athletes, and Holter caught more fleeting rhythm events than the resting tests alone.
pmc-13289409:
Isabelle Pearson and a large team offer a 2026 scoping review on protecting migrant workers from climate-driven job health risks. Two reviewers screened records on their own, with a third path for disputes. The map shows where programs exist and where blind spots remain for worker safety planning.
pmc-13290109:
What living with acne feels like, drawn from posts by users in the United States and United Kingdom, is examined by John Barbieri and colleagues in 2026. Acne mostly strikes teenagers and young adults but often persists, affecting self-esteem, body image, and mental health.

The team collected public posts from 2024 and processed them with natural language processing, machine learning, and topic modeling. From 646,809 messages by 432,234 users, the biggest topics were skincare routines and product advice, acne scars, and general treatment information. Just over half of users described at least one quality-of-life impact, most often symptoms, social functioning, mental health, and cost. Annotated messages pointed to unmet needs, above all working answers for hormonal acne and clearer guidance on triggers.
pmc-13290609:
Adults with hearing loss who lack vitamin D face notably higher depression risk over the long term, Wan-Jung Cheng and colleagues report in 2026. Hearing impairment already raises depression risk, and the team asked whether vitamin D status, a fixable factor, adds to it.

Deficiency came with a hazard ratio of 1.57 for new depression over 12 years, with similar elevations for depressive episodes, recurrence, self-harm, and death. Milder insufficiency also raised risk somewhat, tracing a gradient, while a control outcome showed nothing. Cheng and colleagues stress that observation alone cannot prove that correcting the deficiency would prevent depression.
pmc-13291009:
Public fitness facilities in China, and why some regions supply far more than others, are studied in a 2026 policy analysis by Ziwen Zhang, Shun Wang, and Xunling Wang. Instead of judging single policies alone, the team asked which mixes of policy tools tend to go with a high level of provision.

No single tool proved necessary on its own for high supply. pmc-13292109:
Abdallah Al Ghnaimat and a large team weigh a 2026 question in a systematic review and meta-analysis: can diabetes drugs called SGLT-2 inhibitors drain ascites in liver cirrhosis? pmc-13292309:
Huanhua Wu and co-authors pair a 2026 genetics method with clinic data to probe whether frailty helps cause diabetic kidney complications.
