pmc-13292509:
Justus Tönnies and co-authors lay out a 2026 study protocol, SalusTransform, for judging whether integrated urban development plans actually improve health, fairness, and sustainability in Germany. Such plans bundle housing, infrastructure, green space, and social measures, yet most past research tested single interventions. Three German cities will contribute one intervention district and one matched control district each.

Because the protocol describes work to come, it reports no findings yet. Planned data include resident surveys, focus groups, stakeholder interviews, air quality readings, site visits, and observations of walking, cycling, and green space use. Municipal records will add population and health indicators. A difference-in-differences analysis should separate plan effects from background change. The authors aim to guide municipalities on whether these bundled plans deserve institutional backing.
pmc-13293809:
Reduced watering plans go on trial in a 2026 field study by Luciana Gentili and colleagues, set in a young super high-density olive orchard in western Argentina. Dense hedgerow orchards yield early and suit machines, yet thirst heavily and suffer under long water stress in dry regions.

Three cutback plans were compared with full watering over the first three fruiting seasons in Arbosana trees. Steady watering at 70% of full need saved 30% of water, a saving the authors report, kept tree water status balanced, and lifted fruit and oil yield by the third season. Timed harsher cuts saved more water but knocked yield down in the second season.
pmc-13294109:
Celia Brown and coauthors track ethnic patterns in UK medical specialty destinations in a 2026 repeated cross-sectional analysis. General Medical Council data covered entry to specialty training across 12 specialties from 2012 to 2022, and completion awards across 11 specialties from 2007 to 2021. Groups compared were White, Asian, and other ethnicities among UK-qualified doctors.

Samples held 64,995 doctors at entry and 62,380 at completion. Gaps appeared in nearly every year and grew over time at both stages. Asian doctors were over-represented in ophthalmology at both levels, while White doctors were over-represented in acute care and emergency medicine at set points. Systemic influences on choice and selection need study.
pmc-13294409:
Sandra Fuest and colleagues test a glass solder coating for zirconia dental ceramics in a 2026 lab study. Alumina toughened zirconia samples were grit-blasted and spray-coated, then exposed to mouse fibroblasts and human dental pulp cells in direct and indirect contact. Live-dead staining, growth checks, bone-forming differentiation, and whole blood tests covered safety angles.

No toxic effects appeared for coated or plain samples in any assay. Bone-forming steps proceeded normally, and blood tests showed no red cell bursting or shifts in standard counts. Cells spread and grew well on the coating. The layer looks suitable for improving implant surfaces, pending animal work.
pmc-13295309:
Diyi Feng and Liqin Ge review heat-based cancer platforms built from metal-organic frameworks in a 2026 article. These porous, programmable materials can convert light, microwaves, or magnetic fields into tumour-heating energy. They can also carry drugs and reshape the tumour surroundings at the same time.

Simple frameworks offer stable, tunable shells, while metal-rich versions add chemical attack, magnetic response, and energy handling. Pairing heat with chemotherapy, immune therapy, or imaging guidance helps against regrowth and heat tolerance in tumours. The authors stress that standard making rules, breakdown behaviour, metal safety, and heat dosing must be settled before clinic use.
pmc-13295509:
Michael Kainz and colleagues combine printed frames with self-building peptide gels for cartilage repair in a 2026 study. Cartilage heals poorly on its own, and printed plastic frames give strength but little welcome to living cells. Filling the frame pores with a fibre-forming gel was meant to supply that welcome.

Two printed materials were used, one stiff light-cured network and one flexible silicone, both with linked pores near a millimetre wide. Gels named RADA16 and IEIK13 assembled inside the pores into fibre nets resembling natural tissue surroundings. Both gels improved cell settling and growth, with RADA16 best at supporting cartilage-like matrix formation in the hybrid builds.
pmc-13296009:
Anna Brugulat-Panés and colleagues argue, in 2026, for including grey literature, material outside commercial publishing, in global health reviews. Their case study covers food sources in Small Island Developing States, where local knowledge often sits in reports rather than journals.

Grey sources added rich detail on varied food sources, regional data and country comparisons, and often reflected partnerships with local groups. The authors give practical guidance on searching and screening such material openly. They warn that journal-only reviews risk missing voices from under-resourced places and deepening knowledge gaps in global health evidence.
pmc-13299509:
A brain-vein sampling test worked even when the patient's hormone levels looked deceptively normal on the day, recount Heraldo Mendes Garmes and colleagues in a 2026 case report. A 26-year-old woman with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome needed to know whether the source was her pituitary gland or a tumor elsewhere.

Using desmopressin to stimulate the sampling, the team found pituitary-side hormone patterns confirming Cushing disease despite calm blood cortisol at the time; surgery later verified a corticotroph adenoma. The authors reason that desmopressin targets receptors concentrated on the tumor rather than healthy gland tissue, so the test may stay informative outside high-cortisol windows. They call for confirming studies.
pmc-13300309:
Boys who carry two different copies of certain DLK1 variants tend to start life heavier, Olga Pomares and colleagues report in a 2026 genetic study. The team genotyped five variants in or near DLK1, a paternally expressed growth gene, in 949 participants whose birth weights came from official certificates.

Three variants tracked with birth weight in males only, with no signal in females. Heterozygous boys averaged more than boys carrying two identical copies, and they clustered above the population mean of 3.4 kg. The pattern fits polar overdominance, where mixed copies outweigh either matched pair. DLK1 thus joins the factors worth weighing in unusually high or low birth weight.
pmc-13300609:
A teenager's daily migraines trace back to squeezed nerves around the brow and temple in a 2026 case report by Ruben Sanchez Eligio and colleagues. The 15-year-old girl had suffered posttraumatic occipital neuralgia for years, and medicines had failed. After standard occipital decompression, her remaining trigger points called for a staged, smaller approach.

Surgeons released both supraorbital nerves through 1 cm cuts hidden along the brow's lower edge, ending her frontal migraine at once. Temporal pain was later eased by freeing the zygomaticotemporal nerve through similar pretrichial incisions. One year on, occipital and frontal symptoms had fully cleared and temporal attacks had eased markedly, with no loss of feeling or movement.
pmc-13302909:
Latvian men smoked less over a decade while women smoked more, Peteris Apinis and colleagues chart in a 2026 population study. Stratified random samples of adults aged twenty-five to seventy-four answered surveys in 2009 and 2019, over thirty-eight hundred and four thousand respondents respectively. Daily smoking was modeled against education and, in the later wave, physical activity.

Men's daily smoking fell from about forty-four percent to thirty-six percent; women's rose from fifteen percent to just over eighteen percent. Higher education roughly halved or better the odds of daily smoking in both sexes. Activity level differed across groups but predicted nothing on its own. Prevention should aim hardest at less-educated groups, the authors argue, to trim the cardiovascular toll.
pmc-13303909:
Yecheng Tan and co-authors introduce CODA, a 2026 software framework for comparing spatial gene maps across tissue slices. Spatial transcriptomics records where genes are active, but slices from different machines distort and overlap only partly.

CODA first places slices in a shared low-dimension feature space, then applies rough alignment, smart matching of shared regions, and fine local warping. Tests across platforms showed strong accuracy with modest computing cost. Staining checks and pathway analysis confirmed that genes flagged by the tool mark real tissue differences. The method should help labs merge spatial data from mixed sources with more confidence.
pmc-13305509:
Elizabeth Wojtowicz and co-authors review how long-term care homes talk about future serious illness with residents who have dementia in a 2026 integrative synthesis. Such talks often happen in crisis and center on forms, leaving residents themselves out.

Thirty-one strong studies from 2015 to 2025 were sorted by talk content, delivery style, setting, and outcomes. Most talks were biomedical, form-led, and aimed at family partners at admission or during emergencies. Plain wording, warm tone, and early chats about imagined future scenarios built trust and readiness. Inviting residents in and asking what matters most aligned care with personal values.
pmc-13306009:
Qingyu Wang coated surfaces with layered high-entropy films to capture sunlight as heat in a 2026 study. Films stacked chromium, a nitride layer and an oxide layer were laid down with an ion-assisted sputtering method.

Three versions varied by how long the main absorbing layer grew, yet all absorbed nearly all incoming light, with rates from 0.9847 to 0.9888 in reported figures. Microscopy showed clean borders and a gradual shift from mixed crystal forms toward more crystal content near the surface. Chemical checks tied high-valence oxides to heat stability and mixed chromium states to stronger visible light capture.
pmc-13306809:
Natalya Chulikova irradiated wheat seeds with electrons and X-rays before sowing in a 2026 two-year study. Lab and field trials, backed by Geant4 simulation, sought doses that lift yield while cutting Septoria fungal disease.

Seed batches received 2 to 1000 Gy in lab work, where doses above 30 Gy cut germination in reported results. Field plots then tested 5 to 30 Gy, narrowing the useful window toward 5 to 15 Gy in early findings. Germination, plant measures and fungal counts on seed guided the dose choice for growers. The dose map may help farms cut spray use while still guarding the crop each year.
pmc-13307309:
Shuo Zhang fermented a discarded herbal distillation water with a golden flower fungus to improve flavour and function in a 2026 study. Ligusticum chuanxiong hydrosol normally goes to waste for harsh medicinal smell and strong bitterness.

At best settings of 39°C, pH 6.7 and 7% inoculum, total phenolics reached 71.25 mg/L in reported figures. Electronic nose and tongue tests showed bitterness falling from 8.0 to 4.0 in the given scores, with harsh compounds removed and pleasant scents enriched. Sugar-enzyme blocking reached 80 and 79 percent in lab checks. The scent shift came with less harsh bite, a key gain for a drink or skin use.
pmc-13308309:
Jeyanthi Suppiah and co-authors review in 2026 why the lead dengue serotype swaps over time in lands where the virus is common, a shift often tied to big outbreaks. Four serotypes cycle, and past views blamed virus change alone for which one leads in a given season.

The review instead puts group immunity at the centre, as past spread shields people from one type and leaves room for others to grow. Short cross cover and a process that can worsen later illness add to that push and pull. Virus variety, mosquito skill, weather swings, crowding, and travel all feed in as well. Forecasts and vaccine plans must weigh the whole web, not one cause.
pmc-13310209:
Nudrat Jabeen and co-authors raise citric acid output from a fungus by pairing a bred strain with enzyme blocking in a 2026 study. Citric acid is a bulk food and industry chemical made by Aspergillus niger fermentation. Raising yield without costly inputs is a standing industry goal.

A mutant strain bred to tolerate a growth-limiting chemical was tuned across broth volume, acidity, starter size, time, and heat. Under tuned settings it made 26.35 g/L of citric acid, well above the parent strain in the reported runs. Partly blocking aconitase, an enzyme that drains the acid cycle, pushed output to nearly 49 g/L with two cheap additives. Yield math backed the gain, and the authors propose the paired strategy for scale-up tests.
pmc-13310409:
Yanting Zhang and co-authors test whether an anti-nausea drug lowers blood pressure drug needs during anesthesia in a 2026 trial. Blood pressure often dips right after anesthesia starts in older patients, and norepinephrine is infused to hold it up. Granisetron is given before gut surgery to prevent nausea, and it may also steady pressure.

Sixty-four patients aged 60 to 74 having keyhole gut surgery were randomly given granisetron or salt water before anesthesia, with neither side knowing which. The dose of norepinephrine that kept pressure steady in half of patients ran about 24 percent lower with granisetron in the trial results. A second statistical method backed the gap. The authors suggest a dual benefit worth confirming at larger scale.
pmc-13310909:
Jianrong Zhao and colleagues test fertilizer timing and heat effects on a potent greenhouse gas from grassland soil in a 2026 study. Nitrous oxide leaks from soil through germ paths that respond to nitrogen and warmth. In dry grassland, one path dominates, yet joint effects of dose pattern and heat were poorly known.

Loess soil jars got no nitrogen, small doses every three days, or one large dose, at cool or warm settings. Large doses spurred germ growth and gas release at both heat levels. Small steady doses kept gas low without boosting germ counts. Warmth raised gas on its own. Steady feeding in cool seasons may cut losses.
pmc-13311109:
Nicole Laurent weighs barriers to talk therapy in bipolar disorder and a diet based add on in a 2026 analysis. Cognitive behavioral therapy helps as an add on, yet value depends on starting, staying, and doing home practice. Uptake is low and dropout early in routine care, which caps the dose patients get.

Early reports link ketogenic metabolic therapy to steadier mood, sleep, energy, and thinking, all traits that may aid therapy turnout. No study has yet tested whether the diet lifts therapy turnout itself. A staged frame sets when to add the diet and which turnout signs must be tracked in trials.
pmc-13311209:
Gurumurthy and colleagues present a flower removal method to screen chickpea heat tolerance in fields in a 2026 methods paper. Late sowing, the usual heat test, also stunts early growth, which muddies results. Removing early flowers delays breeding by about two weeks, so flowering meets peak heat while plant vigor stays normal.

Across two seasons and mixed types, removed plants kept leafy growth but lost pollen life, pod set, and yield under heat above 33 °C in the test window. Hardy types lost far less yield than tender types. The cheap, simple method cleanly splits heat tolerance for breeding under warming climates.
pmc-13311309:
Davoud AmirKashani and colleagues report a 2026 case of Griscelli syndrome type 1 in a toddler with a gene change never seen before. The rare inherited disorder usually lightens hair and skin color.

The patient was a 27-month-old girl from Afghanistan whose parents are related. She showed slow development and weak muscles without the classic silvery hair. Full gene sequencing found a new homozygous change in the MYO5A gene, confirming type 1 disease. A hair check under the microscope still showed the odd pigment pattern. The case widens the known range of this condition and backs gene testing when signs are atypical.
pmc-13311709:
Austen El-Osta and co-authors survey views on lifestyle medicine in England in a 2026 study. The field treats food, movement, sleep, and habits as core care, and the team asked whether the public and staff trust it.

The online survey drew 733 adults, including 58 health professionals, in January 2026. Only 26.3 percent of the public knew the term, against 62.1 percent of professionals in this sample. Despite low awareness, support for offering such services through the NHS ran broad. Training, confidence, time, and system blocks shaped how much advice staff gave. The study gauges readiness for wider rollout.
pmc-13311809:
Mohammed Turky and Paul MH Dummer write a 2026 article on embodied artificial intelligence as a coming frontier for dentistry. Most dental AI today only reads data and advises; embodied systems sense and act in the physical world.

The authors note early signs in guided implant surgery and robot-assisted implant placement. Embodied systems join sensing, spatial awareness, adaptive learning, and real-time action, much as in surgical robots elsewhere in medicine. Dentistry has barely studied this shift. The piece argues the field should prepare for tools that do not just plan care but help carry it out beside the clinician.
pmc-13311909:
Ashley E. Choi, Megan E. Chung, and Louise Y. Sun present a 2026 study testing whether image generators picture critical care doctors as they really are. Three text-to-image systems were compared with real workforce data.

The team generated 300 images of adult and child critical care attendings and trainees using DALL-E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion, each in a recent version. Two reviewers classified each face. For adult care, real female share was 27.3 percent, while the systems showed 78.3, 9.3, and 19.7 percent female faces across the three tools in this study. Non-white faces were also over-shown. Training with skewed pictures could mislead students.
pmc-13312809:
Nowel Tan and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of vitamin D status and outcomes in critically ill newborns. Vitamin D helps regulate immunity, and deficiency is common among babies admitted to intensive care, but whether low levels on arrival actually predict worse courses had not been pooled before.

Searching four databases yielded 18 studies covering 1,981 babies. Deficient newborns faced more than double the odds of sepsis compared with babies with sufficient levels. They stayed in hospital about four and a half days longer on average, and more often needed mechanical ventilation. The sepsis link held in both preterm and term subgroups. Mortality and the lung condition bronchopulmonary dysplasia showed no difference between groups. The authors note the studies defined deficiency differently, limiting how far the results can be pushed.
pmc-13313009:
Shanthi Krishnaswami and colleagues measure, in a 2026 real-world study, the year of care that follows emergency angioplasty for STEMI, the most dangerous kind of heart attack, in the United States. Drawing on the Premier Healthcare Database plus mortality and claims records, they followed 180,691 patients treated at 633 hospitals between 2016 and 2021.

The typical patient was 62 and male, and the index hospital stay carried a median cost of $17,582 with 5.5 percent dying in hospital in the reported figures. Within a year, 17.4 percent were readmitted and 13.4 percent developed heart failure, pushing the median total cost to $21,010. A heavy load of other illnesses at arrival, a Charlson score of 4 or more, dwarfed every other risk marker, quadrupling death risk and raising costs by about three quarters.
pmc-13314509:
Si Li and colleagues report a 2026 case of a rare skin cancer on the forearm. Primary cutaneous adenoid cystic carcinoma is a slow-growing tumor of skin glands, first described in the 1970s, and it seldom shows on a limb.

Their patient was a 63-year-old man with a slow-growing lump on his right forearm. Tissue study proved the diagnosis, and the report walks through the tissue, skin-surface, and scan traits of the lump. Wide local cutting removed it with success, the standard approach to cut the risk of local return. The authors stress that skin-surface viewing can hint at the diagnosis, but only tissue study settles it, and long follow-up is a must since this tumor can come back late. The case urges doctors to weigh this rare cancer for odd, slow lumps.
pmc-13315509:
Ferehiwot Bekele Getaneh and colleagues report in 2026 a case of ovarian twisting in a woman past menopause, with gas inside the tumor and very high tumor marker levels. A 65-year-old woman with long-standing belly swelling came in with sharp pelvic pain, early fullness when eating, and constipation.

Scans showed a twisted pelvic mass measuring 20.6 by 16.5 centimeters, with bleeding, gas, and fluid, and no blood flow on contrast images. Blood markers CA 125 and CA 19-9 were markedly raised, which can mimic cancer. Surgery found a twisted, blood-starved left ovary, and removal of the uterus and both ovaries and tubes led to quick recovery with no cancer features.
pmc-13316109:
Hana Camelia and co-authors used coral skeletons in 2026 to read decades of reef temperature in the Andaman Sea, a known refuge where cold water intrusions can spare corals from heat. Upwelling and internal waves bring cooler water, but how protection varies over time was poorly observed in place.

Monthly records from coral chemistry showed subsurface cooling shifting over years to decades, driven by large-scale wind and thermocline change. Cooling was strongest during the combined positive Indian Ocean Dipole and El Niño event of 1997 and 1998. Carbon signals showed corals shifting feeding style during most bleaching events, except that strongly cooled 1998 event.
pmc-13316209:
Xia Qiu and co-authors analyzed resting brain scans in 2026 to test whether functional wiring becomes more linear with development, and whether that path differs in autism. Data came from the ABIDE collection, with 188 males with autism and 216 typically developing males of matched age.

For each person the team estimated both linear and nonlinear coupling and built an index of how fully linear links explain the nonlinear ones, at whole-brain level and within seven large networks. Group and age checks, corrected for multiple testing, probed where autistic development departs from the usual linearization trend.
pmc-13319009:
Donghan Xu and co-authors review, in 2026, a classic Chinese herbal formula, Banxia Xiexin Decoction, as an add-on candidate against stomach cancer. The formula has long treated gut disorders. Chemotherapy benefits are limited by toxicity and resistance. The review gathers evidence on its active compounds and mechanisms.

The formula slows cancer cell growth and triggers death through cell-cycle and growth pathways. Key routes include Wnt/β-catenin and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling. Active compounds such as berberine and baicalin reverse drug resistance in tumour cells. They raise sensitivity to standard drugs including cisplatin and paclitaxel. The formula may also curb abdominal spread and lift anti-tumour immunity. Gaps include weak study of immune surroundings and missing standard drug-level data.
pmc-13320109:
Yunxiao Yang and co-authors run an umbrella review of needle care for knee wear pain in a 2026 article pooling past reviews. Knee joint wear is a top cause of ache and stiff motion in older adults, and needle care is widely offered as a low drug option. Six databases were swept for past pooled reviews, and the best proof was picked after quality scoring.

Twenty three past reviews were pooled in the overview, and most needle types eased pain and lifted motion in their counts. Gains beat fake needle care, plain care, and wait lists by clear margins, and matched common pain drugs, while hand massage worked faster. Side harm was mostly mild and local, and gains held best in the first three months after care.
pmc-13320409:
Mathew Mendoza and co-authors study recovery after knee replacement across the mental health range in a 2026 records review. Knee replacement rates climb as worry and low mood also climb, yet how those states shape healing was murky. A ten item global health form with a mental score was also tested as an extra sorting lens beyond diagnosis alone.

Records covered 624 first knee replacements from July 2023 to October 2024, split near evenly by worry or low mood diagnosis. That group stayed longer, used more pain drugs before going home, and hurt more early on, and scored lower on global health forms all year. When split by mental score alone, the lowest band fared worst on all counts in both diagnosis groups, while the top band fared best.
pmc-13320509:
Sukeina Baouia and co-authors review the place of radiotherapy in a 2026 article on Hodgkin lymphoma that has returned or resisted first treatment. Standard care for fit patients still pairs rescue drug therapy with a stem cell transplant using the patient's own cells. Newer drugs have changed what rescue care looks like before transplant.

Radiation now has a narrower, more tailored role, aimed at leftover disease, small areas of relapse, or spots that stay active on scans. It looks most helpful around transplant for patients with bulky disease or weak early response. Modern shaped and guided methods let teams adapt dose to response. Proof for pairing radiation with the newest drugs stays thin and mostly rests on small past studies.
pmc-13320809:
Yiwen Huang and colleagues report a rare stomach tumour in a child in a 2026 case report and literature review. Gastric lipomas, benign fatty growths, account for only about 1 percent of stomach tumours in children, and just six childhood cases had been reported before. The review places the new case beside those earlier ones.

The patient was a 10-year-old boy with repeated black stools over 10 days, plus dizziness and tiredness. Blood tests showed a sharp drop in haemoglobin to 8.4 grams per decilitre, and scans showed a large fatty mass, 9.0 by 6.7 centimetres at its widest. The authors use the case to weigh diagnosis and surgical choices for such growths.
pmc-13321009:
Sabri Saeed Sanabani reviews the skin microbiome from its early study to new treatments in a 2026 narrative review. Human skin hosts bacteria, fungi, viruses, and mites that defend the barrier, train the immune system, and carry out metabolic work. The review blends classic work with modern gene reading and multi-omic studies.

Germ mixes differ across oily, moist, and dry skin sites, and their jobs include blocking invaders and making useful compounds. Imbalance is tied to eczema, acne, psoriasis, and slow healing wounds. Treatments that feed, add, or engineer helpful germs are presented as promising personal options. As a narrative review, the piece may carry selection bias and gives no pooled numbers.
pmc-13321309:
Yaqun Tang and Haijun Chen write a 2026 letter on blood markers for predicting new heart failure. A review by Noordermeer and others had gathered proof linking heart, stress, and scarring markers to later heart failure. The writers agree the proof is strong but argue the field must now show that markers change real decisions.

One large test of 28 markers in over 160,000 people lifted a standard accuracy score only from 0.812 to 0.819 when the best marker was added, a tiny gain. A major trial of marker guided care also failed to cut hospital stays or deaths. Heart failure subtypes may further split marker value, a point the letter presses.
pmc-13321809:
Jin Lin and a large team design a light driven catalyst for hydrogenation in a 2026 chemistry study. Frustrated Lewis pairs can turn inert supports into active sites, but their random placement and weak hydrogen activation limit use. The team anchored single rhodium atoms on cerium oxide to create ordered interface sites.

The catalyst hydrogenated styrene at 35 percent per hour, far above plain cerium oxide at 2.74 percent per hour in the report. Interface sites split hydrogen into reactive parts, and light pushed those parts toward pair sites while also creating fleeting new pair sites on the surface. Similar boosts appeared on other semiconductor supports, which suggests a general design route.
pmc-13322909:
Lijiao Wang and Tingshu Jiang present an advanced case of follicular dendritic cell sarcoma in a 2026 report. Their patient was a 51-year-old woman with six months of cough, sputum and chest tightness, worse breathlessness over the last month, and sharp weight loss.

Scans found a mass in the mediastinum, between the lungs, with spread to multiple sites and enlarged lymph nodes. Such tumours arise from follicular dendritic cells and are rare, hard to diagnose and often aggressive in course. Care combined immune therapy and targeted therapy in an integrated plan. The authors draw lessons from the diagnostic difficulty and the mixed treatment approach for clinicians who may meet this uncommon cancer.
pmc-13323509:
Yirui Dai and colleagues report a spinal cord disorder mistaken for mental illness, in a 2026 case report on subacute combined degeneration. A 39-year-old man had nine months of tingling, dizziness and emotional distress, with normal brain scans and electrical tests at first checks.

Doctors diagnosed somatic symptom disorder and anxiety, and several psychiatric drugs failed as leg weakness and unsteady walking grew. Specialist review found absent knee reflexes and lost vibration sense, and blood tests showed critically low vitamin B12, with spinal imaging changes running from neck to mid-back. B12 replacement plus escitalopram for leftover distress brought strong recovery, and at five months he walked fully with near-normal test scores.
pmc-13324309:
Dong Ruan and co-authors build a smart alloy scaffold that treats infected bone defects in timed stages, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Lasting bacterial infection over-fires the immune system and blocks bone growth, so single-target grafts often heal such defects poorly.

Their scaffold answers acidity changes in sequence. During the infection phase it releases copper ions for strong antibacterial action plus plant-derived vesicles that calm the early cytokine storm. Later it switches to steady magnesium release with low vesicle output, drawing stem cells in, speeding bone differentiation, improving the immune setting and growing blood vessels. Pathway checks point to blocking of the AGEs/RAGE/NF-kB route as part of the joint effect.
pmc-13324509:
Yoonsuk Huh and co-authors test whether scout images alone can predict a patient body outline for radiotherapy setup in a 2026 study. Surface-guided breath-hold treatment needs a free-breathing outline for baseline matching, which today means an extra CT scan.

The team trained a deep learning model on 173 chest CT simulation cases with front and side scout views. Test results on 26 held-out cases matched the true outlines closely, with a Dice score of 0.979 on average. Surface error averaged about 1.05 mm across the test group. Larger, more even torso shapes predicted best. Skipping the extra scan could cut dose and time, though live clinic checks must come first.
pmc-13325109:
Rizwan Rafique and co-authors study light resonances in bare silicon nanowires in a 2026 physics paper. Earlier work covered wires wrapped in an oxide shell, which itself bends the local light field.

Conical and cylindrical wires of varied length, stripped of any shell, were probed with electron energy-loss spectroscopy inside a scanning transmission microscope. Wires sat in vacuum or on carbon film. Every group showed periodic signals, and the resonance energy tracked wire length far more than surroundings. A strong sideways resonance appeared in all cases. The results suggest wire shape alone can tune these resonances, which eases design of silicon light devices.
pmc-13327609:
Furong Chen and colleagues reveal a two-way role for a bacterial toxin pair in a 2026 study. In Pseudomonas bijieensis strain 2P24, the toxin Fic-1 blocks DNA copying by adding an AMP mark to the gyrase subunit GyrB, and its partner AntF normally restrains it. Few enzymes known can remove such marks.

Joined together, the pair itself removes the mark, returning gyrase to its plain state, and lab and gene tests pinpointed one AntF residue, Glu28, as vital for that cutting action. AntF thus both brakes the toxin and helps it undo its own work. The finding adds a fresh control scheme for toxin systems and hints at how multi-part enzymes evolve.
pmc-13327909:
Jose Eric Mella Lacsa writes a 2026 letter to the editor on the hidden wounds of veterans. He responds to a recent review of the polytrauma clinical triad, the linked trio of chronic pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, and traumatic brain injury in military patients. The letter praises that work's joined-up treatment picture, then widens the lens.

From Seoul to São Paulo, he argues, veterans fight a second war at home: pain that outlasts the battlefield, trauma returning in dreams, and brain injury quietly eroding memory, balance, and identity. Care split into silos cannot meet that mix, so pain, brain, mental health, and rehabilitation teams must act as one under a whole-person approach. How societies answer, he writes, tests compassion as much as science.
pmc-13328509:
Jiayue Wu and co-authors compare two closely related melon lines in a 2026 study of fruit quality. One line, called 109, differs from its sister line 108 in firmness, sweetness, acidity, and other traits. The team measured basic fruit traits and used wide-ranging chemical profiling to map small molecules in the fruit.

Line 109 was firmer and had more soluble solids and acidity, but a lower sugar to acid balance than line 108. Profiling found 2,101 compounds, with 246 differing between the lines. Changed groups included sugar-related, acid-related, and amino-acid-derived compounds. Pathway checks pointed to sugar handling and terpenoid building routes. The results give breeders candidate compounds for better melon quality.
pmc-13328809:
Morris and colleagues analyzed in 2026 what drives dietary self-management in chronic kidney disease, where eating rules are strict and hard to keep. Rather than run a new survey, they reworked a published synthesis of 92 studies covering 2,924 adults in 23 countries. They sorted its themes into a standard framework of behavior domains and a wheel that links those domains to intervention types.

Twelve of fourteen domains played a role, showing that diet control rests on knowledge, skills, emotion, social life, and setting, not facts alone. Clashing advice and thin practical guidance were key barriers, while trust in professionals and learning by doing supported adherence. Two domains, optimism and intentions, were absent. Judged for cost, ease, and fairness, education and enablement ranked as the most workable intervention routes, while training and system changes scored as harder. The authors urge multi-part diet support that builds skills and confidence.
pmc-13330109:
Yanrui Cai and co-authors test automatic measurement of brain ventricle size after bleeding around the brain in a 2026 study. The Evans index guides choices about fluid drainage, but hand measurement is slow and varies by reader. Admission scans from 364 patients with sudden bleeding were read by an open deep learning pipeline and by two experts.

Repeat runs by the program agreed almost perfectly, and expert readers agreed closely too in the reported values. Program and expert readings matched well overall, and better once cases with frontal blood were removed. The program flagged more cases above the set cut point than experts did. pmc-13350009:

After the study came out, readers flagged faults in its reference list. One cited source had already been retracted before the study appeared. Two more cited sources were retracted after it appeared.

Several other cited sources do not seem to back the claims they were attached to. Taken together, the faults led the editors to warn readers formally. They advise reading the study with caution. The notice does not retract the study, but it puts its grounding in doubt. Journals use such flags when worries are real yet a final call is pending.
pmc-13395509:
Tasuku Miyake and co-authors describe, in 2026, a guided operation for a rare bone cyst in a young archer's elbow. The 19-year-old had two years of pain from a tiny cyst under the joint surface of the upper arm bone. Reaching it through the joint would harm cartilage, so the team planned a path from outside the joint. A patient-specific three-dimensional plan steered the tools.

The cyst was drilled out as a neat cylinder and the hole filled with a bone substitute. Later scans confirmed full removal. Pain faded over months and was gone by fourteen months. The authors present the method as a cartilage-sparing fix for deep cysts in hard spots.
pmc-13395909:
Kinza Degerlund-Maldi and co-authors check, in 2026, whether a standard health survey measures life quality well in psoriatic arthritis. Swedish register data held 13,105 patients with the joint and skin illness. The survey, EQ-5D-3L, and its single health scale were set against other measures. Tests covered group gaps, shared movement, and response to change.

Both tools matched partner measures fairly to strongly and split groups as expected. Most validity guesses held up. Change tracking fared worse: many response guesses failed, and the health scale missed who improved. Gains outside pain may slip past the survey, the authors note. Trial teams should pair it with wider tools.
pmc-13396309:
Aws Saudi and co-authors staged a direct contest between two scan types for men newly diagnosed with high-risk prostate cancer, in a 2026 phase II study. The question was whether a SPECT/CT tracer scan could match the PET/CT scan now favored for finding spread before treatment.

Each patient, aged 50 to 79, received three scans, including a bone scan and the PSMA-targeted PET used as the yardstick. Readers recorded spread to lymph nodes and bones, and the team compared sensitivity and accuracy across methods. They also checked whether treatment plans built on the SPECT result would match plans built on PET, which matters where PET scanners are scarce.
pmc-13396409:
Ezra Ben-Abu and co-authors built concrete formwork that unfolds itself on site, aiming to cut one of construction's most wasteful steps. Their 2026 report describes tubes that rest in more than one stable shape, shipped compact and then snapped into full-size molds with steel reinforcement already inside.

The team raised a steel-reinforced structure 2.36 meters tall in 14 seconds from its packed state. Tests showed the polymer shell of the tubes is not dead weight: it tripled the strength of the finished element. Because the mold deploys itself and carries its own reinforcement, the system could slash the labor, material, and setup time that poured concrete usually demands.
pmc-13396509:
Mark A. Faghy and co-authors published an author correction in 2026 to a Communications Medicine review of long COVID. The review, first issued in April 2026, surveyed how the condition works and what may come next. The correction fixes the record rather than the science, though one change does touch advice.

One contributor, a lived-experience expert, had been listed with a third affiliation that was not his, and that extra line is removed. The section on fatigue and post-exertional malaise now states plainly that physical therapy should be used with great caution in people with that symptom. It should focus on avoiding crashes, since proof of benefit is lacking. Both fixes appear in the online and PDF versions.
pmc-13397609:
Di Muraglia and team explore, in 2026, a gut-microbe compound that shields muscle cells from ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, bearing on Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Comparing fecal samples, they found dystrophic mdx mice and human DMD patients both carried reduced levels of commensal Bacteroides species. These include Bacteroides vulgatus, a producer of the endocannabinoid-like lipid commendamide. Mdx muscle also showed biochemical signs of ferroptosis risk.

The team found the molecule switches on the nuclear receptors PPAR-alpha and PPAR-gamma, with PPAR-alpha driving transcription of the antioxidant genes Gpx4 and Nrf2 that defend against ferroptosis. The authors propose gut-derived signaling as a side strategy alongside dystrophin-focused therapies for Duchenne patients, pending preclinical tests.
pmc-13398409:
L H Khiem and a large team squeeze a layered mineral crystal to watch its structure and vibrations shift. Their 2026 study works on Ca2FeCoO5, a brownmillerite compound made by a sol-gel route, using X-ray diffraction and Raman scattering up to 24 GPa of pressure. Pressure can flip complex oxides into new phases with fresh properties, a hunting ground for both physics and applications.

Above roughly 6 GPa the crystal began a gradual transition, visible in lattice measures, squeezing behaviour and odd bends in vibration modes. The team tracked cell size and mode frequencies for both the starting and the pressure-born phase. They link the change to tetrahedra in the structure rotating and rearranging under load.
pmc-13398909:
James Tran and colleagues report a fatal liver failure tied to hepatitis B waking up during lymphoma treatment. Their 2026 case concerns a woman in her sixties with follicular lymphoma on maintenance rituximab, last dosed a month before she fell ill. She arrived with deepening malaise and jaundice. Blood tests showed her liver enzymes, ALT and AST, at 2,500 and 2,400 units per litre in the values reported. Bilirubin stood at 20 mg per dL alongside those readings.

Tests found active hepatitis B, with surface antigen and viral DNA present, while records of screening or preventive antivirals before rituximab could not be found. Other causes were excluded, leaving viral reactivation under immune suppression as the judged cause. The authors press the lesson: screen and protect before rituximab starts.
pmc-13399109:
Xiaowei Ma and a large team of co-authors examined what controls cotton fiber growth in this 2026 study, focusing on a protein named GhTTLL12. Cotton fibers are single cells that sprout from the seed coat and lengthen fast. They make a handy model for studying how plant cells expand. Microtubules, the cell's internal scaffolding, help drive that elongation.

The team found GhTTLL12 most active during the fast elongation stage. Plants engineered to make extra GhTTLL12 grew taller, with longer roots, more fiber protrusions, and longer fibers. Plants with the gene knocked out by CRISPR showed the opposite pattern and poorer fiber quality. Tests showed the protein binds microtubules directly and helps them assemble into orderly crosswise arrays. Two more regulators complete the picture. GhMML3 switches the gene on to boost fiber cell division, while GhMYB86 switches it off and slows elongation.
pmc-13399409:
Yi-Qing Gao and colleagues report an unusual case, published in 2026, of papillary thyroid cancer that resurfaced in the skin of a patient's neck eight years after her thyroid surgery. A 29-year-old woman came to dermatology with a dark patch on the right side of her neck, noticed for two years. She had undergone radical surgery for a left-sided thyroid tumor at about age 21.

A biopsy removed a fragment of skin less than half a centimeter across. Under the microscope the tissue matched metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. Staining tests supported that verdict: the tumor cells were positive for TTF-1 and PAX-8, markers consistent with thyroid origin. Skin spread accounts for only a small share of thyroid cancer metastases, which usually go to lymph nodes, lungs, or bone. The report warns clinicians to biopsy new skin lesions in thyroid cancer survivors rather than dismiss them as benign.
pmc-13399509:
Sajama Nepali argues, in a 2026 essay, that spirituality deserves a working place inside mental health frameworks rather than a decorative mention. Drawing on theory, studies, and lived experience from several cultures, the essay treats spiritual practice as a coping resource. Practices named include surrender, mindfulness, detachment, yoga, dietary and hygiene rituals, and selfless service to others.

Nepali connects these practices to emotional regulation, resilience, and a sense of purpose, the very capacities modern definitions of mental health emphasize. The World Health Organization's 1998 proposal to add a spiritual dimension to its definition of health is cited as an early institutional signal. The essay is careful about limits: the link with well-being is context-dependent and not always positive. Spiritual beliefs can be read in harmful ways or used to avoid needed treatment. The proposed settlement is balance: spirituality as a complementary pathway alongside evidence-based care.
pmc-13399809:
Sahr and co-authors evaluate, in 2026, ultrasound-guided injections aimed at pain that persists after hip arthroscopy. The injections target three extra-articular sites at once: the hip capsule, the rectus femoris tendon origin, and the iliopsoas bursa. Their retrospective series covered 52 injections in 52 hips performed from 2015 to 2024, at a median of 308 days after the original impingement surgery, once joint-internal pain sources had been excluded.

Pain dropped sharply on the spot: the average visual analog score fell from 3.5 before injection to 0.4 immediately afterward in the recorded assessments. At the next follow-up visit, 36 patients, 69 percent of the series, reported at least some improvement, with 18, or 35 percent, calling it marked. Fourteen patients, 27 percent, reported no benefit at follow-up. The authors conclude that patients with adequately treated joint problems but lingering post-arthroscopy pain can benefit from this triple-site injection strategy.
pmc-13400209:
Hadeel Y Alghanim and colleagues scoped the literature on how rotator cuff patients feel and how much they move before and after surgical repair, in a 2026 scoping review. Searching five databases, the team screened 11,026 records and kept thirteen studies that measured psychological well-being or physical activity around rotator cuff repair. .

Depression symptoms were the most studied factor, appearing in ten studies, followed by anxiety in seven, with kinesiophobia and negative thoughts in two each. The consistent direction was that worse depression and anxiety tracked with worse pain, poorer function, and lower quality of life both before and after repair. The review's most pointed finding is an absence: not one included study measured physical activity in rotator cuff patients across the surgical episode. Activity is a plausible bridge between mood and recovery. The authors call for research on how activity and psychology interact around repair.
pmc-13400309:
Rasmus Michael Sandsdal and a large team report, in 2026, a planned follow-up look at the S-LiTE trial on keeping weight off. The trial enrolled 130 adults with obesity who first lost weight by diet. They were then assigned for one year to exercise, the drug liraglutide, both, or neither.

Exercise alone, and exercise with the drug, thinned the wall of the neck artery and lowered two blood markers of inflammation. The combined plan also improved markers tied to blood vessel lining health. Liraglutide alone showed no such gains. The authors conclude that regular activity stays central for vessel health after weight loss, with or without this drug class.
pmc-13400609:
Ryota Tsuruga and co-authors watch, in 2026, dopamine signals in a deep brain area of mice as they learn to balance threat and reward. Animals must often seek food while danger lurks nearby. The team focused on the tail of the striatum, a region tied to defensive behavior.

Mice learned that one odor predicted an air puff and another predicted water. Early on they blinked in anticipation, then shifted to licking as they adapted to the puff. Dopamine responses to the puff and its odor started high and faded with repetition. Removing dopamine cells in that area blocked avoidance learning but sped reward learning, while forcing the signal to stay high blocked adaptation. The fading signal, it seems, lets animals move from defense to reward seeking.
pmc-13401409:
Laura Cif and a large team of co-authors wrote a 2026 proof-of-concept study on using ordinary clinic videos and deep learning to phenotype hyperkinetic movement disorders. These conditions involve excess involuntary movement, and several often overlap in one patient. Sorting out which movement types a patient has guides treatment.

Videos from 21 patients and 4 healthy controls at one centre were processed with YOLOv8 pose estimation, which tracks body points without markers. Two-dimensional keypoint paths were converted into kinematic readouts covering statistical, timing, frequency, and complexity features. Ten-second windows were matched to expert labels for eight movement types. Standard models trained on those readouts produced window-level calls, which were combined into patient-level multi-label results, with decision thresholds tuned only on training members.
pmc-13402309:
Su-Bon Kim and co-authors designed stretchable display panels that grow evenly in all directions, so pictures stay true when pulled. Ordinary stretchable screens distort because the base shrinks sideways when stretched lengthwise. Frames with a negative Poisson ratio, which widen as they lengthen, fix that on paper, yet their hole-filled build cannot carry a display alone.

The team bonded such frames to smooth stretchy sheets at carefully chosen points only, so the frame could still rotate while the sheet stayed calm. A new yardstick, the isotropic expansion factor, measured distortion across scales from local patches to the whole panel. Panels built this way expanded evenly without visible image warp and kept working through repeated stretching. The work speaks to wearables and soft devices that must flex without bending the picture out of shape.
pmc-13402909:
Souza and colleagues test how far children with asthma can walk, and propose reading results through the World Health Organization's functioning framework, not as a bare distance. Lung tests can look near normal while activity quietly shrinks. Their 2026 study puts thirty nine children, age nine, through spirometry, asthma control and quality of life questionnaires, and a shuttle walk test. Walk performance is sorted into mild to moderate or severe limitation using the qualifiers.

The gap was stark: lung function averaged four fifths of predicted, yet walking reached two fifths. Nearly three quarters of the children landed in the severe category. Walk performance matched none of the measures, not lung function, not symptom control, not quality of life, and it slipped with age. A child can pass the tests, the authors argue, while unable to keep up, and walk tests scored this way make that limit visible.
pmc-13404109:
Pier-Valerio Mari and co-authors reported real-world use in 2026 of an antibody drug for a swelling-driven form of chronic lung disease. Twelve older patients at a Rome hospital got the drug every two weeks under a mercy-use plan. All had repeated flare-ups despite triple inhaler therapy, plus high counts of one white cell type.

Severe flare-ups fell sharply over six months of care. Lung airflow rose by about 120 milliliters at that point in their paired checks. Symptom scores dropped from near 23 to about 12.5 overall, with phlegm and chest tightness easing most. Higher starting symptom scores predicted bigger flare gains.
pmc-13404209:
Emma Davies and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a giant resistance plasmid helps a poultry Salmonella strain shrug off disinfectants inside biofilms. The strain ranks fourth among Salmonella types tied to human illness and lingers across poultry sites. Strains came from the United Kingdom and Austria, with gene checks across both sets.

Biofilm growth varied by strain and ran stronger on smooth, non-porous surfaces than on rough ones. Three common poultry disinfectants were tested on free cells and on biofilms. Carrying the plasmid, or its exact gene mix, made no clear difference to biofilm growth or disinfectant tolerance. What drives the strain's staying power remains an open hunt.
pmc-13404409:
Michael K Sheng headed a 2026 study warning that one lab tumor line can fool tests of engineered immune cell therapy. Such therapies train T cells to hunt a target tag on cancer cells. The Raji lymphoma line is a favorite stand-in for that work.

T cells from many donors attacked Raji cells even when the target tag was knocked out. Plain unedited T cells reacted much the same way. Blocking the cells' natural target sensors dulled the attack, which points to a mistaken-identity response. Other tumor lines did not trigger the effect. Trial models using Raji may thus overstate how well a therapy works.
pmc-13405109:
Zhiwei Gao and co-authors judge how well large language models fit Japanese workplace culture, in a 2026 study. Politeness levels and indirect communication carry heavy weight in Japanese offices, making them a stiff test for chatbots. Five multilingual models, including a Japanese-built one, faced typical workplace scenarios.

Native Japanese raters scored outputs across 1,718 valid evaluation sessions, producing a cultural alignment score for each model. Sub-scores separated language form, social values and social action. Phi and GLM matched or beat the home-grown LLM-jp model overall in the reported scores. Hofstede's six cultural dimensions frame the analysis, and the authors argue static Western benchmarks miss this kind of social fit.
pmc-13407009:
Wissem Dhahbi and colleagues ask, in a 2026 narrative review, how scientists can protect time for deep thought amid constant digital interruption. Notifications, media multitasking, and now AI tools that invite mental offloading all compete with the sustained attention that hard problems demand.

Searching literature from 2010 to September 2025, the authors link frequent interruption to disturbed coordination between brain networks for focus and for inward thought, with changes that can weaken sustained attention. Fragmented attention, they argue, erodes exactly the operations behind complex analysis and creative insight. Their remedy works at three levels: personal habits, institutional policies, and firmer technological boundaries, treating protected thinking time as a biological need rather than a perk.
pmc-13407409:
Domniki M. Karagianni and co-authors argue, in a 2026 commentary, that mental health belongs inside routine rheumatology care. Across conditions from lupus and rheumatoid arthritis to fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis, patients carry heavy psychological loads that clinics still address poorly, the authors say.

Reported rates run strikingly high: depression reaching up to 90 percent over a lifetime in some groups, anxiety between 18 and 65 percent, and frequent sleep trouble, fatigue, and difficulty naming feelings. Mood and disease feed each other, with psychological strain tracking pain, flare activity, and lost function, and quality of life falling below that of many other chronic illnesses. Their proposal, psychorheumatology, joins psychological screening, targeted treatment, and shared care between rheumatologists and mental health professionals.
pmc-13407809:
Qichen Liu and co-authors separate, in 2026, the two ways light can drive a chemical reaction on a catalyst surface. The team used a purpose-built copper and titanium oxide model catalyst. With it they pulled apart two effects during methanol breakdown. One is true photochemistry, where light's energy moves electrons. The other is heat from absorbed light warming the surface.

Advanced in situ spectroscopy, including synchrotron-based measurements, watched charge transfer directly. Simulations tracked molecular behaviour alongside. The division of labour proved tidy. Light-driven action boosted hydrogen output from methanol. The heating effect helped formaldehyde escape the surface. It left before it could be over-oxidised and wasted. The pairing delivered high hydrogen output, excellent formaldehyde selectivity, and long-term steadiness using no precious metals, a design lesson for solar fuel systems.
pmc-13410709:
Roland Christel Sonounameto and colleagues model in 2026 how well seasonal malaria prevention worked for young children in northern Benin. Under-fives there face heavy malaria each rainy season, so preventive drug rounds run yearly since 2019. Funding cuts now threaten the program, which makes solid proof of value urgent.

Routine health data from six treated zones were matched against stand-in comparison zones built from nine untreated ones. After the rounds began, severe malaria fell by about 41 percent in treated zones while rising in the comparison group. Milder cases rose in both groups, far less where drugs were given. The authors argue the program earns its keep and should be protected.
pmc-13410809:
Rodrigo Dillenburg and a large team show in 2026 that adding phosphate tags can reroute a brain protein from harmful clumps into tiny harmless balls. The protein, TDP-43, forms toxic deposits in ALS and a form of dementia. One loose region of the protein drives that clumping.

Computer models predicted that twelve phosphate tags would split the region into a water-shy half and a charged half, favoring small clusters over big sheets. Lab tests bore that out: tagged protein formed round particles about 20 to 50 nanometers wide instead of sheets that ripen into fibers. Salt levels could stretch those balls into worms or rods. Tagging may thus protect cells by capping cluster size.
pmc-13411009:
Haiyan Wang, Jiwei Hao, Jun-Hyun Bae, and Gregory Cartee examine in 2026 where inside muscle cells an energy-sensing enzyme wakes up after dieting or exercise in old rats. The enzyme, AMPK, guards cell fuel and sits in several compartments of the cell. Which spots respond in old age was largely unknown.

Old male rats either ate a restricted diet for eight weeks or swam once. Dieting raised enzyme activation in whole muscle but not in the three compartments tested, hinting at other active spots. Exercise switched the enzyme on in the cell's main fluid and raised its partner signal everywhere measured. One enzyme subunit also grew richer near the cell's power plants after dieting.
pmc-13411609:
Fang-Ching Liu and colleagues trace in 2026 eighteen years of deep neck infections in Taiwanese children, a condition that can close airways and kill. Data came from the island's largest medical system, covering hospitalized patients under 18 from 2006 to 2023. Germs, treatments, and outcomes were compared across two nine-year halves.

Of 1,743 cases, treatment shifted toward antibiotics alone, with surgery falling from about 9 to 6 percent. Intensive care admissions and chest complications also declined, while deaths stayed near zero. Germ patterns moved too: staphylococcus rose as streptococcus fell, drug-resistant staph became the leading aerobe, and one anaerobe species replaced another at the top. First-choice antibiotics should follow those shifts.
pmc-13411809:
Dario Colacurci and colleagues review in 2026 why twins who share one placenta can still differ sharply at birth. Both babies inherit the same genes and share one blood supply, yet one may carry a birth defect the other escapes. Forty-eight studies covering 441 twin pairs were gathered under standard review rules.

Reported gaps spanned heart defects, chromosome faults, sex growth problems, imprint errors, and brain, kidney, and bone conditions. Lab tools ran from chromosome spreads to full genome reading and chemical mark checks. Blame may fall on changes arising after the egg split, uneven sharing of the placenta, and chance in early growth. The list helps counselors explain such gaps to parents.
pmc-13412109:
Zeinab Fagheei Aghmiyuni and colleagues review in 2026 two living treatments for a drug-proof germ that infects burn wounds. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, shrugs off most drugs, even the carbapenem class kept in reserve. The review pulls from four databases to weigh phages, which are viruses that hunt bacteria, and probiotics as drug-free options.

Phages strike drug-proof strains with care, sparing much of the body's normal flora. Probiotics fight germs too, and they may calm swelling and help skin heal, the surveyed studies suggest. Used side by side, the pair may cut the germ load more than either one can alone. The authors call the pairing a strong next step for burn care, while proof in patients stays thin.
pmc-13412209:
Wenyan Huo and colleagues present in 2026 the complete genome of a fungus that helps a prized medicinal orchid sprout. Cremastra appendiculata seeds carry almost no food reserves, so they must partner with a fungus to germinate. The team assembled the genome of Coprinellus disseminatus from telomere to telomere, producing fifteen gapless chromosomes spanning 54.41 million bases with 98.80 percent completeness on standard checks.

In sprouting trials the fungus outperformed two close relatives at building orchid protocorm mass. All three shared much the same set of carbohydrate-cutting enzymes, ruling that out as the edge. Gene family growth in this species clustered in pathways for protein handling and cell junctions, which the authors propose explains its superior partnership.
pmc-13413009:
Shiyi Xu, Mohan Xu, and Erjin Zhou introduce HypEReg in 2026, a fix for a subtle flaw in AI-based brain scan alignment. Transformer models warp one brain MRI onto another accurately, yet their predicted warps sometimes fold tissue locally, breaking the smooth one-to-one mapping that later analyses assume. Their regularizer penalizes folding directly during training, using the warp's Jacobian determinant at every voxel, and adds nothing to the model's running cost.

On the IXI benchmark of 115 test subjects, overlap accuracy held steady while folding voxels fell from about one in sixty-six to near one in sixty-six thousand. Tested cold on a different dataset, folds stayed roughly a hundred times rarer than the plain model. Atlas label fusion, a downstream use, improved with the cleaner warps.
pmc-13415809:
Fuchs and colleagues used eye tracking in 2026 to study how people judge oral hygiene in teenagers wearing braces. Some photos used a dye that reveals plaque. Eye movements were recorded while each person evaluated the images.

Dental students judged hygiene most accurately of the three groups. Parents judged more strictly, and adolescents judged their own hygiene most leniently. Students also scanned the photos with significantly shorter eye paths than laypeople, suggesting trained, efficient looking. Using the plaque dye improved accuracy for all groups. The authors suggest dye use and hygiene feedback could help brace wearers and families assess cleaning honestly.
pmc-13418409:
Francesca Musumeci and colleagues refine a family of compounds that block SIRT2, an enzyme linked to cancer and brain disease, in a 2026 modelling and assay study. Computer screening of pyrazolo-pyrimidine relatives filtered a new series with stronger action than the group's earlier leads. Predicted contacts matched those of known reference blockers.

Lab assays confirmed the strategy. Two compounds stood out with very low concentrations needed for half inhibition, in the sub micromolar range. SIRT2 helps cancer cells in several settings, so selective blockers are sought as research tools and drug leads. Further biological work on the two leads is planned.
pmc-13418609:
Christos Costa and colleagues report keyhole surgery for a congenital bladder pouch in a young child, in a 2026 case report. A male infant first showed a widened urine tube on ultrasound after birth, and imaging later suggested a bladder diverticulum, an outpouching that traps urine. By age three he had repeated severe urine infections and poor bladder emptying.

Surgery confirmed a large pouch with the urine tube inserting into its middle. The pouch was removed laparoscopically and the tube reimplanted into the bladder. Symptoms resolved and emptying improved by three months. The case shows minimally invasive repair suits even complex childhood urinary anatomy.
pmc-13418809:
Zhonghan Xu and colleagues test whether gut microbes from mice with gum disease can disturb blood sugar control on their own. Gum disease has been linked to diabetes, yet the chain between mouth, gut, and sugar control stayed unclear. The team worked with germ-free mice raised in sterile housing, so any microbes present came only from the transfer itself.

One group received gut microbes from donor mice with induced gum disease, while a matched group got microbes from healthy donors. The gum-disease transfer shifted blood sugar handling in the receiving mice. Measures of short-chain fatty acids, the helpful products gut microbes make from fiber, dropped in the same animals. Inflammation markers rose alongside the sugar changes, sketching a path from mouth disease through the gut to wider body harm.
pmc-13419309:
Yunkao Zeng and colleagues measure immune-like cells on the retinal surface in branch retinal artery occlusion, a sudden blockage that starves part of the retina. Flat-view OCT scans can now count these cells and grade the brightness of injured tissue, yet the pattern in this condition was unmapped. The study drew on 17 patients, each with the blockage in one eye only.

Cell density ran higher where the blockage struck than in the spared region of the same retinas. Brightness ratios were taken from several retinal layers to grade the injury in numbers rather than by eye. A firm count of surface cells could help doctors judge damage and track recovery after treatment. The work extends earlier findings from the more severe central form of this blockage.
pmc-13419409:
Margarita Bellon and colleagues compare two ways to finish treating drug-resistant E. coli urinary infections: staying on a strong IV drug or stepping down to pills. The resistant germs behind these infections are classed as a serious public health threat. Their study spans six hospitals in one large health system and looks back at completed cases.

One group received IV carbapenem drugs for the whole course, while the other switched to oral therapy once stable. The main measure was days spent with a venous line in place for antibiotics, at hospital and at home. Fewer line days mean fewer line infections and earlier discharge for patients. The comparison gives stewardship teams real-world backing for safe step-down choices in a hard-to-treat infection.
pmc-13419609:
Alyssa Milton and colleagues set out the protocol for a trial of peer-delivered digital coaching for young Australians leaving early psychosis care. The move from intensive early services to lighter support is a fragile step that research has largely skipped. Their tool, MyBRANCHES, puts trained peers behind a digital self-management program for that transition window.

The hybrid trial judges two things at once: whether young people recover better, and whether the program can truly run in services. Recovery is scored on a standard scale, while feasibility uses an implementation measure, as joint primary outcomes. A cost study will weigh spending against quality-adjusted life years gained. More than a hundred youth mental health centers operate nationally, so a workable model could spread widely.
pmc-13420109:
Melanie Ardelt and colleagues analyze nearly fifty thousand hospital cases of spinal bone infection in Germany, comparing death rates under drug-only care against surgery. Hospital registry data from 2019 to 2023 supplied 49,951 cases of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, identified by diagnosis codes. Overall in-hospital mortality stood at 6.7 percent across the national set.

In raw comparisons, surgery lined up with higher death rates in patients aged 65 years and older, with odds of 1.47 in that band, and 1.56 in those aged 80 years and above in the reported figures. The authors warn that surgery goes to sicker patients, so the raw gap cannot be read as harm from operating. Their caution is the point: national numbers mislead when case mix is ignored, and risk factors need the adjusted view.
pmc-13420709:
Yu Wu and colleagues report a nasopharyngeal cancer patient whose emergency treatment for massive nose bleeding ended with both carotid arteries blocked. Radiation for this throat cancer can weaken artery walls until they burst, a complication with death rates reported as high as 76 percent when the carotid ruptures in the cited work. The woman lost consciousness after bleeding episodes that grew from 100 to 800 milliliters across days in the account given.

Doctors sealed the right carotid with embolization to stop the bleeding, yet scans later showed strokes on both sides of the brain and blockage of the left carotid as well. Emergency vessels were narrowed by spasm, leaving few good options in the moment. The case exposes how lifesaving bleeding control in an irradiated neck can still cost the brain its blood supply.
pmc-13421109:
Erica Blenda da Silva and colleagues build a score to predict death in hospital after surgery for hip fracture in older patients at a Brazilian trauma center. Hip fractures carry heavy illness and death rates in this age group, and a dynamic score could flag the frailest patients early. Their cohort covers 1,509 patients aged 60 years and above treated between 2013 and 2023.

Personal, clinical, bone, lab, and in-hospital course variables all fed the model building. The final score separated outcomes well, with an accuracy measure of 0.819 on the standard curve in the reported validation. A score that updates during the stay fits how risk truly evolves after fracture surgery. Ward teams can use it to trigger closer watch and family talks at the right time.
pmc-13421209:
Abtin Ijadi Maghsoodi and four colleagues introduce REACH in a 2026 paper, a machine-learning model that flags older hospital patients whose care is likely to become complex. The model was built in New Zealand, a country where older Māori and Pasifika people, and other underserved groups, face unequal access to care. Fairness shaped the design from the start.

REACH combines routine electronic health record data with standardised interRAI assessments to estimate each patient's probability of complexity. Hospitals can then use those estimates, alongside bed and staffing limits, to prioritise patients and route them into older-person care pathways. Tested on seven years of hospital data, the model identified complex geriatric cases better than existing approaches, and the authors present it as transferable to similar health systems.
pmc-13421609:
Suzanne Hill, Yobelli Alexandra Jimenez, Sarah Lewis and Dania Abu Awwad run, in a 2026 study, an expert consensus exercise on infection control during CT scans that use intravenous contrast dye. Practice varies between departments, and the team sought agreed recommendations on training, compliance and the handling of contrast systems.

A modified electronic Delphi process put nineteen statements to experienced CT radiographers and nurses across Australia over three rounds. Eighteen statements reached the agreed consensus threshold, covering training principles, the order of contrast administration, single- and multi-use systems, and hygiene in the CT room. A few statements about dripped contrast and tubing connections never settled. The authors offer the agreed set as a standardising baseline.
pmc-13421809:

pmc-13427609:

pmc-13428309:
