pmc-13451209:
Maxim Kovalev and co-authors share in 2026 lessons from two offshore farms of giant kelp, a fast-growing seaweed with farm promise. Seaweed breeding lags far behind crop breeding, so the team grew hundreds of varied kelp plants at sea in 2019 and 2020. They logged growth traits and scanned the kelp genes for links to yield.

Planting season and farm layout both shaped final biomass, while genes explained a fair share of carbon content and total mass. Three gene marks tied to those traits, near genes for sugar handling and cell frame work. Forecast models built on gene marks reached fair accuracy, a base the authors offer for breeding kelp lines with farm-ready traits.
pmc-13451809:
Hao-Sheng Ni and co-authors test in 2026 whether a blood count of allergy-linked cells can stand in for counts inside nose tissue. Their study drew 1,047 patients with long-term sinus swelling and nasal polyps who had sinus surgery at three hospitals in Jiangsu, China. Counts were paired at three time points across 2008 to 2016, and city wealth and air grit data were layered in.

Blood counts tracked tissue counts only weakly and sorted cases poorly. Levels also swung by hospital and year with no steady trend. City wealth, though, tracked both counts in a clear way. The authors warn that a cheap blood count cannot replace tissue checks, and they urge care for place and wealth gaps in allergy care.
pmc-13451909:
Wenjian Mao and a large team probe in 2026 a blood enzyme clash that worsens pancreas death in sudden pancreas attacks. A clot-trimming enzyme keeps a sticky blood factor in check, and white cell bursts free a second enzyme thought to block the trimmer. The team read both enzymes in 30 patients, then tested the link in dishes and in mice with made pancreas attacks.

Patients whose pancreas death passed a third of the organ showed low trimmer activity and high levels of the blocking enzyme. Blocking the blocker, adding the trimmer back, or breeding mice without either gene shifted the harm in line with the claim. The work names a fresh drug target for the worst pancreas attacks.
pmc-13452209:
Chul Hyun and Rong Wang chart in 2026 when stomach cancer risk, outside the stomach's top zone, turns real for United States groups by ancestry. Rates differ by race, yet age-set totals hide when risk climbs. The team read case counts from California and New York for 2010 to 2022, by age band and ancestry.

Risk sat higher in Hispanic and Asian groups at every age, with wide spread among Asian ancestries. Korean adults at sixty-something carried rates twelve times the white peer rate. Several Asian groups hit, up to twenty years early, the rate white adults reach in their sixties. The authors argue for earlier, risk-based checks in high-rate groups.
pmc-13452409:
Yiye Luo and nine co-authors track how fermenting a black truffle extract changes its flavor, aiming to lift the value of lower grade Chinese truffles. Their 2026 study pulled the flavor compounds out with water, then let the extract ferment while tasters and lab tests followed the change. The truffle in question is Tuber indicum, a species sold widely in China.

Early on the extract smelled earthy and leathery, but the scent shifted toward buttery and fruity notes as fermentation ran. Day six stood out as the peak point, when scent chemicals also reached their highest level. Tests flagged 24 key aroma chemicals, mostly alcohols and esters, and tied flavor growth to a few core body pathways. Makers of truffle seasonings can use the timing and the pathway map to steer flavor on purpose.
pmc-13452909:
Jingjie Fu, Fang Chen, Wenfeng Yang, Ting Chen, and Jian Xu ask whether tight spacing between machine liver treatments saves more lives in severe liver failure. The patients had acute on chronic liver failure tied to hepatitis B, a fast decline on top of long term liver disease. Their 2026 study looks back at 149 patients who got an artificial liver support system, a machine that does part of the liver's cleaning work.

Liver blood tests improved after treatment in both the tight spacing and wide spacing groups. By day seven after the last session, two bile pigment measures sat lower in the tight spacing group. Death within 90 days without a transplant hit 12.8 percent of that group against 29.6 percent of the wide spacing group. A worse starting liver score also meant a higher risk of death, and the authors call for planned trials to confirm the gap.
pmc-13453009:
Wang and colleagues showed in 2026 that mycoplasma infection, a common and often silent cell culture contaminant, can make lung cancer cells resist targeted EGFR drugs. These drugs block a growth signal many lung cancers depend on, but resistance almost always emerges. The team found the germ itself helps cells shrug off the drug osimertinib.

Infected cells kept growth and survival signals switched on and pulled the drug's target inside the cell more slowly, blunting its effect. Clearing the infection with antibiotics partly restored drug sensitivity, which pins the germ as a cause, not a bystander. Gene profiles pointed to shared pathways between infection and resistance. Blocking two support routes at once suppressed infected cells better. Patient data agreed: infection and high levels of a key enzyme tracked with shorter survival.
pmc-13453609:
Mercanoglu and colleagues showed in 2026 that breaking a sugar-coating step in pancreatic cells speeds the growth of Kras-driven pancreatic cancer, the mutation that starts most cases of this deadly disease. Many of these tumors carry stunted sugar chains on their surface proteins, ending in a marker called Tn. Whether that stunting is a byproduct or a driver was unclear.

In human tumors, the Tn marker appeared often and tracked with higher stage. The team then deleted the helper gene Cosmc in the pancreases of mice carrying mutant Kras. The altered mice developed precancerous lesions earlier and more widely, with more cell growth, more scarring, and mucin changes, though no spread to distant organs appeared in the study window. Protein profiling tied the loss to matrix and scar remodeling.
pmc-13453809:
Bao Lin and four co-authors track how a blood ratio moves after rectal cancer surgery and what its path says about survival. The ratio, platelets over lymphocytes, hints at body wide swelling and immune strength. Their 2026 study reviews patients who had keyhole radical surgery at one Chinese hospital between 2016 and 2020, with the ratio read at five points through early chemotherapy.

A grouping method found three paths: steadily rising, rising then falling, and steadily falling, with 67, 90, and 89 patients. Serious complications hit 7.9 percent of the falling group against 20.9 percent of the rising group. Five year survival for the whole group was 68.3 percent, with both non rising paths ahead of the rising one. Age over 65, deeper node spread, and poor cell grading stood as risk factors on their own.
pmc-13454309:
Qiang Zhang leads a fifteen-author team reporting a 2026 effort to predict low blood sugar during hospital stays for adults with a slow form of autoimmune diabetes. Such patients face sharp sugar swings, yet few risk tools target them. The team built three machine learning models from routine records at five hospitals in China, using one hospital as an outside check.

The study covered 752 patients treated between 2019 and 2025. Low sugar struck about 45 percent of patients in the main group and about 54 percent in the check group. Six factors carried most of the signal, led by the size of sugar swings and past low-sugar episodes. No model beat the others clearly in the outside check, and the authors add charts that show which factors drive each prediction.
pmc-13454609:
Jean-Paul Noel, Ruiyi Zhang, Xaq Pitkow, and Dora E. Angelaki report, in 2026, that monkeys skip decent rewards on purpose to win more across a whole session. Male macaques roamed a virtual world and could abort offers, passing up sure gains. Each animal settled into its own stable style of skipping, hinting that they tracked their long-run earnings.

Learning models fit the behavior with a two-part system: a policy module that values the long run, plus quick value updates for fast tweaks. The models predicted that the decision to skip should be readable in brain activity the moment an offer appears. Recordings confirmed this in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a front brain area, but not in two comparison areas. The authors cast that region as the brain's long-horizon policy keeper during ongoing behavior.
pmc-13454709:
Myrmel and colleagues ask whether the source of dietary protein changes how easily mice become obese in this 2026 study. Dairy and seafood proteins seem less fattening than land-meat proteins, but the pathways involved are unclear. The team fed mice high-fat, high-protein diets built on casein, cod, or chicken. Some mice lived at room temperature and others at warmer thermoneutral conditions. The team then profiled blood lipids and gene activity in several tissues.

Protein source changed obesity development regardless of housing temperature, and each diet left a distinct fingerprint in blood lipids and in gene activity in liver and fat tissue. One-carbon metabolism, a network handling building blocks for DNA and other molecules, stood out as a likely affected pathway. A growth-control complex called mTOR emerged as a predicted upstream regulator tying the diet differences together.
pmc-13454809:
Vanmathi C and five colleagues present, in 2026, a plant disease detector that reads leaves together with written symptoms and local weather. Photo-only systems falter in real fields, where signs blur and conditions vary. Their system, AgriFusionNet, fuses three streams: an image network reads the leaf, a language model reads the symptom notes, and a small network weighs temperature, humidity, rain, and soil moisture.

Training used an enriched public dataset covering 38 plant diseases plus healthy classes. The fused model reached an overall accuracy near 99 percent on its test data. Error patterns showed the text and weather streams rescued cases that photos alone confused. The authors frame the design as a step toward field-ready tools that help farmers act early, cut spray waste, and protect yields under changing farm conditions.
pmc-13455009:
Zhang and colleagues assemble the genome of a sexually deceptive Australian orchid that lures male wasps with fake scent and form, giving the species its genetic blueprint. Chiloglottis trapeziformis is a model for studying deception's evolution, but orchid genomes, especially from ground orchids, are scarce. Their 2026 study combines two long read sequencing methods with chromosome contact mapping to build parental copies of the genome, chromosome by chromosome.

Each copy resolved into twenty chromosomes, and scored high on completeness checks. The genome proved repeat rich, with jumping gene families filling most of it, and carried sixteen thousand protein coding genes per copy. Set against relatives, the species landed as sister to a jewel orchid, with gene order conserved. The surprise sat between the two copies: several inversions, flipped segments holding genes, without raised mutation rates. Structural change, the authors argue, may drive orchid diversity more than gene change itself.
pmc-13455409:
Dezhi Shen and five colleagues study, in a 2026 records analysis, whether body weight and nutrition shape early kidney injury in older patients with sepsis. The team drew on a large intensive care database, keeping 4,238 patients over the standard older age range who arrived without advanced kidney disease. Kidney injury arising within 48 hours was the outcome.

About half the group developed the injury that fast. Extra weight raised the odds in clear steps: overweight patients faced about 1.4 times the odds of normal-weight peers, rising to roughly double for obesity and above. Each added point of body mass index nudged risk up about four percent. Two nutrition risk scores were weighed alongside weight in the models. The authors argue that weight deserves a place in early kidney risk checks for older septic patients.
pmc-13456709:
Bang and colleagues measure how the front and back heights of one spinal bone change as women age. The bone is the twelfth thoracic vertebra, T12, where the rib cage spine meets the lower back. Their 2026 study reads MRI scans from 409 women aged 20 to 90. It measures both heights on side view images, then compares six age bands, from young adults to women over eighty.

The front height averaged lower than the back height in every band. Both heights shrank with age, and the front shrank faster, losing about a quarter of its young adult height by the oldest band, against about a fifth at the back. That uneven loss helps explain the wedge shapes seen in aging spines. The authors offer the values as a normal aging reference, useful when doctors judge whether a short vertebra reflects disease or age alone.
pmc-13457309: Why do some teens become targets of online harassment? Da Dong, Xinyi Lu, and others test an mixed theory. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is cyber-victimization research. It combines rational choice and situational convergence perspectives to examine adolescent cyber victimization, asking which circumstances and decisions put young people in harm's way.
pmc-13459409:
Dan Liu and co-authors ran a standard nursing program to stop hospitalized older adults from inhaling food or liquid into their lungs, a dangerous event called aspiration. Their 2026 project at a tertiary hospital in China's Shanxi Province, translated a national nursing standard into twenty two audit criteria covering screening, feeding plans, and oversight. It used an established audit and feedback system. Nurses' knowledge, how well they spotted high risk patients, and actual aspiration rates were compared before and after the rollout.

Aspiration incidence fell from 27.72 percent at baseline to 13.59 percent after the program, roughly halving in this ward population. The improvement survived statistical adjustment, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.359 for aspiration after the program. Nurses' knowledge scores and their spotting of high risk patients also improved across the audit cycles. Structured audit and feedback can make prevention consistent rather than nurse dependent, the authors say.
pmc-13460209:
Yichen Guo, Ruilin Li, and Wenhui Zhao compared in 2026 two emergency department tests for acute coronary syndrome: CT angiography of the heart arteries and high-sensitivity troponin blood testing. Their meta-analysis pooled twenty-one studies covering 4,239 patients with acute chest pain, mostly at low to intermediate risk, of whom about a fifth truly had the syndrome. Study quality was graded with a standard diagnostic tool.

Imaging outperformed the blood test on accuracy, with sensitivity in the mid-nineties percent and a summary accuracy measure clearly above troponin's. Troponin results varied much more between studies. The authors conclude that scanning is better at ruling the syndrome out in lower-risk chest pain, while warning that moderate specificity and uneven study results demand cautious use.
pmc-13460709:
Saber Delpasand Khabbazi and colleagues review in 2026 what is known about drought stress in Cannabis sativa, a crop valued for fiber, seed, and medicinal cannabinoids. Dry spells are growing more frequent with climate change, threatening yield and the plant's chemical profile. The review gathers evidence across plant shape and body function, its chemistry, gene control, and links with soil microbes around the roots.

Cannabis answers water shortage with coordinated changes across all those layers, yet big gaps remain. Root-driven adjustment is poorly charted, small RNA regulation is barely explored, and inherited chemical marks on DNA that could carry drought memory are almost unstudied. The authors chart future directions aimed at breeding and managing cannabis that keeps producing under dry conditions.
pmc-13461309:
Meijian Yang and colleagues report a lung cancer patient whose spinal cord failure turned out to be autoimmune myelitis, not tumour spread. The 65-year-old man had extensive-stage small cell lung cancer and arrived with bladder failure, then fast-rising leg paralysis.

Scans showed long inflamed stretches inside the cord with no crushing mass, and spinal fluid held inflammation but no cancer cells. Blood and fluid tested strongly positive for AQP4 antibodies, pinning the diagnosis on neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. High-dose steroids plus immune globulin steadied him, and a maintenance drug, satralizumab, followed during steroid tapering. Yang urges prompt antibody testing in such cases, since mistaking myelitis for metastasis delays the right treatment.
pmc-13461609:
Hao Wu and a large team review evidence in 2026 on whether fumes and pollutants called aromatic hydrocarbons help drive prostate cancer. Benzene and related compounds found in traffic fumes, tobacco smoke, workplace air, and cooking smoke are the focus. The authors gather work from population studies, animal tests, lab-grown mini tissues, and cell studies. Their aim is to judge whether a cancer link is biologically believable.

Human studies show modest links between long exposure and higher prostate cancer risk, with clearer patterns in some jobs. One compound in the group damaged genes in prostate tissue, stirred harmful oxygen reactions, altered hormone signals, and helped tumor cells survive and spread. The reviewers stress that proof of cause is still limited by rough exposure measures and mixed pollutants. They call for studies that pair exact exposure records with prostate-focused lab work and long-term follow-up.
pmc-13461709:
Kamine Julie Jacobsen leads a 2026 study of how hearing decline in older men relates to brain and thinking changes. Hearing loss is common with age and may be a risk factor care can change. The men came from a birth cohort studied across lives with thinking tests and brain scans. At ages 70 and 71 they took hearing tests covering tones, contrast, and speech in noise.

Fifty-one men took part. An earlier visit near age 63 gave baseline thinking scores. Machine learning sorted the men into four paths of thinking change. Two hearing measures best predicted which path a man followed: a tone test and a speech-in-noise test. Brain features also tied to hearing, with temporal lobe size linked to one hearing skill and lower areas to another. The authors read the pattern as a tangled three-way link among hearing, brain, and thinking
pmc-13462209:
Jonathan Massie and colleagues examine, in a 2026 letter, the hidden advice work of blood specialists in the United Kingdom, called liaison haematology. Such work includes formal and informal guidance to other clinicians, plus help reading lab results, for patients not under the specialist's own care. The labor is skilled and in demand, yet rarely counted in planning. Other fields, such as microbiology and psychiatry, have tried to measure similar loads.

The team used a mixed approach, starting with stakeholder interviews to learn what data mattered most. Survey and workload elements drawn from those talks measured demand and barriers across the country. Their letter frames the problem: a large, valued service runs largely unseen, with little record of its time cost or worth. Naming and defining the work is a first step. The authors aim to ground future staffing decisions in real evidence about this advice burden.
pmc-13463709:
Yingxin Wang and eight co-authors validate a stool PCR test for Helicobacter pylori, a stomach germ tied to ulcers and cancer. The standard breath test needs special gear and carries small radiation concerns. A stool test would be easier to run if it proved just as exact.

Four hospitals enrolled 866 patients, and 777 gave valid stool checks for the head-to-head trial. The new Cellrun test flagged positives at nearly the same rate as the breath test and a rival kit. Agreement with the breath test was near perfect, and accuracy in spiked control checks reached one hundred percent. Misses clustered where germ counts sat near the test floor.
pmc-13463809:
Khanate Sayasit and seven co-authors design one PCR test meant to catch a whole genus of mosquito-borne viruses. The Orthoflavivirus genus holds dengue, Zika, West Nile, yellow fever, and Japanese encephalitis viruses, whose gene codes differ sharply. The team skipped classic sequence alignment and mined short code chunks called k-mers instead.

Across 11,846 virus genomes the search found a conserved six-hundred-letter stretch in one gene, fit for primer design. The test sensed most target viruses at one to ten copies per microliter, though West Nile needed far more. On stored patient material the test reached high overall accuracy and matched dengue calls exactly. The method offers a template for broad tests against fast-changing virus groups.
pmc-13465509:
Jia Sun leads a team that knocks out the Adcy5 gene in Nile tilapia to probe pigment control. The gene makes cAMP, a cell messenger downstream of hormone signals, yet its pigment role was murky. Gene-edited fish lost their black vertical bars and paled across the body.

Pigment cell counts stayed normal, which clears cell birth and points at cell function. Inside black and red pigment cells, the granules clumped at the center and refused to spread, a transport failure. Melanin-making genes quieted and total melanin fell in several tissues. Flooding cells with cAMP partly restored spreading, while an upstream hormone push helped little, which places the gene mid-cascade. Red cell involvement widens its role past black pigment alone.
pmc-13466809:
Carson Peters and colleagues evaluate Facebook advertising as a recruitment tool for clinical research, with attention to messages tailored for a key population, in a 2026 study. The design mixed numbers with voices: ad performance data on one side, and in-depth interviews with fifteen recruiters on the other. Targeted ads were compared against general ones on equal footing.

People who saw tailored ads joined at a higher rate than those who saw general ads, about a third versus about a quarter, and expressed interest more often too. Interview themes explained what recruiters believe makes targeting work. The combined display of both strands is meant to guide teams planning sign-up drives.
pmc-13466909:
Mıdık and a wide team of Turkish cancer doctors read in 2026 the charts of 32 patients with liver cancer that could not be cut out. All had a twin immune drug plan as first care. The plan, called STRIDE, pairs two drugs that free the immune system to hunt tumors. A world trial had shown a life gain, but proof from Türkiye was thin. The cases came from 18 hubs.

The mid point of time with no growth was just past seven months. Mid life span sat near eleven and a half months, with the top end not yet reached in the count. Half the group had liver harm not tied to a virus, and two in five had the B virus form. Grave side effects hit fewer than one in ten patients. The authors call the plan workable, and urge a bigger, head to head test.
pmc-13467309:
Simab Kanwal and colleagues describe in 2026 how they reworked a photosynthetic bacterium to make more of a key building block for natural pigments. The organism, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, can be pushed to produce geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, a starting material for carotenoids and other valuable compounds used in food and health products. The team blocked storage pathways so more carbon flowed toward pigment production.

Two engineered strains were compared with the normal strain under varied conditions, including added carbon and ultraviolet light. Cutting both glycogen and a bioplastic storage pathway gave the strongest gains in pigment buildup. The work points toward growing pigments and related compounds in sunlight-driven microbes instead of extracting them from plants or making them by chemistry.
pmc-13467709:
Sylvia Waschke and colleagues validate in 2026 a cheap handheld device for sorting recycled fishing net plastics at the point of collection. Good recycling needs correct polymer identification, but the precise laboratory method requires fixed equipment that coastal collection points do not have. Their device, called Melting Box 1.0, repurposes the controlled heater of a commercial vaporizer to watch small samples soften and melt.

Test plastics from Vietnamese fishing net recycling, including polyethylene, polypropylene, polyamide, and blends, were scored on a simple three-step visual scale. Agreement with the laboratory-grade Kofler hot bench was good, with an average offset of only 2.9 degrees on melting start across the comparisons. A field tool that sorts nets on the beach could raise the quality of recycled plastic before it ever reaches a factory.
pmc-13468209:
Ma and colleagues mapped the genes behind maize resistance to Fusarium ear rot in 2026, a fungal disease that cuts grain yield and quality worldwide. They crossed a resistant line with a susceptible one and followed 257 offspring lines over three years, scanning their genomes with over 6,800 markers.

Five resistance regions were found on five different chromosomes, each explaining a modest share of the variation in disease. The strongest region, on chromosome 5, explained about thirteen percent and held two candidate genes. Those genes behaved differently in the resistant and susceptible parents, supporting their role. No maize line is fully resistant, so the authors present these regions as breeding material for stacking partial protection into commercial varieties.
pmc-13468409:
Junpeng Wu, Yaoyang Zhang, Hancheng Zhang, Ning Bai, Yajin Ye and Kunrong He published this 2026 study of drought-response genes in pecan trees. The XTH gene family helps plants remodel their cell walls, which matters under water shortage, but its pecan members were unmapped. The team searched the pecan genome, catalogued the family, and then tested one standout gene by inserting it into a model plant.

They found 34 XTH genes in pecan, falling into four evolutionary groups. Several responded to drought, and one, CiXTH18, switched on strongly and stayed on. Arabidopsis plants carrying CiXTH18 grew longer roots under laboratory drought stress made with a water-binding chemical. Their detached leaves lost water more slowly, and their tissue held less hydrogen peroxide, a damage marker. The inserted gene also boosted two known drought-response genes after stress. The authors nominate CiXTH18 as a candidate for breeding hardier nut trees.
pmc-13469409:
Jannatul Ferdous and colleagues build TL-RL-FusionNet in 2026, a ransomware detector that learns which training cases deserve the most attention. Modern ransomware behaves in mixed ways, some of them harmless looking, and it spreads fast through linked business systems. Older signature tools miss these shifting patterns.

The system turns sandbox behavior reports into color grids, then reads them with two pretrained image networks whose features are merged. A small learning agent adjusts the weight of each training case during learning, much like a gambler favoring better bets. Fresh scoring tables in each test round prevent information leakage. On the team dataset the detector scored above 99 percent accuracy. On a public benchmark it reached about 90 percent, showing a harder test.
pmc-13469609:
Hankare and colleagues in India told in 2026 of fifteen children with stiff one side cerebral palsy whose leg faults were fixed in one operation day. Such palsy warps the leg at three heights: the calf pulls the foot down, a thigh cord pulls the knee in, and toe cords curl the toes. Fix one height alone, and the rest still spoil the gait. Their single event plan cut all three in one go for each child.

The gains were broad. Ankle bend swung from a down pull to a sound up reach. Knee bend at walk fell to a quarter of its start mark, and toe curl cleared in each child. Gait grew more even, steps grew longer, and skill class rose for most. Snags were few: one over fix and one weak leg. The authors back the three cut plan as safe and strong for walk ready children.
pmc-13469909:
Xiaona Song and colleagues introduce BEV-Nexus in 2026, a fusion system that helps self driving cars detect objects in three dimensions from a bird eye view. Merging camera images with laser point clouds often stumbles on wrong depth guesses and poorly aligned features. Their design lets the point cloud guide the image branch as it predicts depth, using true depth data and projected points as anchors.

A second module weighs the two feature streams window by window, according to how well they agree, which reduces alignment errors. A third block widens the view of each feature while adding a light attention step. On the nuScenes benchmark the system beat its base model on both main detection scores, by close to two points on the validation set. Speed stayed nearly unchanged, which the authors count as a practical advantage.
pmc-13470009:
Mohammad Mahdi Kariminejad and colleagues analyze in 2026 how errors grow in a cheap motion sensor that sits perfectly still. A smartphone carrying a MEMS inertial unit was fixed at a surveyed point, giving a zero motion reference. Seventy five half minute recordings, taken ten times per second, fed a statistical workup of both raw readings and the positions computed from them.

The team checked whether the data looked normal, steady over time, and even in spread, then fitted time series models and examined the frequency content. A joint estimation method assigned error shares to each computed state at once. Acceleration and rotation readings on all three axes behaved like steady white noise. The study offers a baseline for judging how much drift such sensors add before any real movement begins.
pmc-13470809:
Xiang Cheng and colleagues formulate in 2026 a modified cement grout for shoring up crushed sandstone deep in mines. Grouts must flow well into broken rock yet harden into strong support, a balance that water content controls. Their blend uses ultrafine cement with a waterborne polyurethane modifier plus additives for flow, expansion, and fast setting, tested across a range of water to cement ratios.

A small polyurethane dose shortened setting, cut shrinkage, and raised strength. As water rose, the slurry flowed better and set slower, while strength climbed then fell, peaking at a middle ratio. Grouted crushed sandstone at that ratio reached a peak strength about thirty nine percent above the plain control after twenty eight days. Microscopy and heat measurements tied the gain to how the polymer coats and bridges grains at each water level.
pmc-13471209:
Richard Daly and co-authors compile in 2026 the first national picture of venous thromboembolism rates in Ireland across eight years. These blood clots, in legs or lungs, burden patients and health systems worldwide, yet Ireland lacked solid national counts. Hospital discharge records from 2015 to 2022 supplied the cases, sorted into clots that caused the admission, clots arising during it, and hospital acquired events.

More than fifty one thousand adult cases were recorded, giving a mean yearly incidence near one hundred seventy two per hundred thousand people. Primary clots averaged about ninety eight per hundred thousand. Hospital acquired clots ran near ten per thousand discharges. Pregnancy related clots came to about two and a half per thousand births. The authors offer the figures as a baseline for prevention policy and for judging the pandemic years.
pmc-13471409:
Huang and co-authors tested whether migraine weakens the ear's built-in protective reflexes, which are run from the brainstem. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 143 people in four matched groups: 44 healthy controls, 49 with tinnitus only, 25 with migraine only, and 25 with both conditions.

Migraine patients showed raised thresholds for the middle-ear muscle reflex, the tiny muscle flinch that guards against loud sound, on the opposite-side test. They also showed weaker suppression of otoacoustic emissions, faint sounds the inner ear itself makes, pointing to a faulty medial olivocochlear reflex. Having tinnitus on top of migraine added no further deficit, so the authors propose the reflex measure as an objective marker of migraine-related hearing pathway involvement.
pmc-13471509:
Le Moigne and co-authors grew twenty side-by-side lake-water bacterial groups under identical starting conditions to test whether chance alone shapes what a microbiome can do. Their 2026 metagenomics study focused on cellobiose, a plant sugar, and whether missing genes explained why some communities never used it.

The dispersal-limitation idea failed: several communities held every gene needed for cellobiose processing yet never touched the sugar. The team reconstructed 122 bacterial genomes with a median completeness of 94.67% across the microcosms, and found functional redundancy, many species able to do the same job, mirrored the random draw of genomes. That overlap was lower within groups than between them, a signature of similar species competing.
pmc-13471709:
Patrick Bedard and colleagues use brain and muscle recordings in 2026 to locate the source of rapid fatigability in myalgic encephalomyelitis, also called chronic fatigue syndrome. Fifteen patients and nineteen matched healthy volunteers squeezed a grip device, holding half their maximum force in alternating half minute blocks. Force, forearm muscle electricity, and brain activity from scalp electrodes and scanners were recorded together, with fatigue onset set person by person.

Patients matched the healthy group on maximum force yet tired much sooner. Healthy volunteers ramped muscle and brain activity up until fatigue, then let it drift down. Patient muscles and brains, by contrast, barely fluctuated across the whole task. The flat central response points the authors toward the brain and its drive signals, rather than the muscle itself, as the seat of fatigability.
pmc-13473309:
Kumar and colleagues modelled in 2026 how layered graphene materials respond when heat and load act together. Such graded materials shift their make-up gradually from one face to the other, mixing strength with low weight. The team studied two pairings, graphene with copper and titanium with zirconium, formed as a spherical shell. They applied two theories of thermoelasticity, the coupled physics of heat and strain.

Laplace transforms removed the time dependence from the equations, and finite element methods handled the spatial variation. The authors compared results across both theories and both pairings, presenting field values as graphs. The comparison showed where the graphene pairing behaved differently and where the numerical method mattered. The authors argue the finite element approach is needed for dependable design values in these coupled problems.
pmc-13474509:
Bor surveyed 274 agro-pastoralist households in Ethiopia's Gambella region on how they fight crop pests without synthetic chemicals. The 2026 mixed-methods study combined questionnaires, key informant interviews, focus groups, and field observation across chosen villages, achieving a 100% questionnaire response rate.

Ash was the workhorse practice, used by nearly half of farmers (49.6%). Crop rotation and intercropping followed at roughly one in six households. Botanical extracts, hand removal of pests, planting-time shifts, and chili or tobacco sprays rounded out the list. Fall armyworm, maize stem borer, and African bollworm topped the pest list the practices target. The author reads the toolkit as generations-deep farming knowledge worth building into extension programs rather than replacing with purchased inputs these farmers largely lack.
pmc-13474609:
Tahvilian and co-authors pooled the randomized trial evidence on whether vegetarian diets calm C-reactive protein, the blood marker clinicians use to gauge body-wide inflammation. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered trials of at least three weeks comparing lacto, lacto-ovo, or vegan diets against omnivorous eating in adults.

The answer was a near-perfect null. Across 11 eligible comparisons totaling 545 participants, vegetarian diets shifted CRP by a weighted mean difference of just −0.04 against controls, with a confidence interval spanning −0.23 to 0.15 and a p value of 0.683 for the pooled test. Heterogeneity was literally zero, with an I-squared of 0.0% across the trials, and no subgroup rescued an effect. The authors grade the evidence moderate and call for larger, better-designed trials before the question is settled.
pmc-13474709:
Swain and co-authors investigated the July 2024 Chandipura virus outbreak in Gujarat, India, where a sandfly-borne virus caused explosive brain inflammation in children. Their 2026 matched case-control study confirmed 54 cases across 20 of the state's 33 districts, in children with a median age of four years, 59% of them boys.

The illness killed half its victims: the case fatality rate was 50% among confirmed cases, with fever in 87% of children, convulsions in 74%, and altered consciousness in 57.4% as it raced through multiple organ systems. Two risk factors stood out in adjusted analysis: severe underweight carried an odds ratio of 4 for becoming a case, and poor housing conditions carried 2.66 on the same measure. Rural homes made up 81% of cases, and the team urges stronger surveillance and diagnostics before the next monsoon season.
pmc-13474909:
Resano-Zuazu and co-authors studied back pain in 20 police horses in Madrid in 2026, combining hands-on examination with camera-based gait analysis and a behavior checklist. Myofascial pain syndrome, pain arising from tight, tender spots in muscle called trigger points, is common in horses but hard to measure. The team scored each horse by touch along the back, filmed movement in hand and under a rider, and tallied pain behaviors shown while ridden.

Every horse had at least one trigger point along the back, 85 percent showed a jump reaction when the spot was pressed, and 80 percent had restricted movement in the region. Behavior scores averaged 7.2 on the ridden checklist, and 40 percent of horses met the pain threshold of eight or more behaviors. Yet touch scores matched neither gait measures nor behavior tallies, so the authors keep palpation as the primary diagnostic tool.
pmc-13476209:
Christoph Boesecke and co-authors analyze in 2026 a two-drug cure for fresh hepatitis C infection in people who had the virus before. The eight-week course had already proven itself in first-time infections. Among 286 trial members, fifty-two had a prior infection history. Those members carried higher rates of HIV co-infection and recent risk exposures.

No true drug failures occurred in either group once non-drug dropouts were set aside. Side effect rates looked alike across groups. Prior infection should not bar people from the short course.
pmc-13477509:
Ruth Brookman and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review of how researchers measure results in psychosocial dementia care studies. Such programs use activities, therapy, and support rather than drugs, yet studies measure success in very uneven ways. The review maps reported measures against an international dementia outcome set, plus an added domain for caregiver wellbeing.

The team found 136 studies covering arts therapies, memory approaches, education, movement programs, sensory work, and robot or animal assistance. Symptom measures appeared 205 times and thinking tests 146 times, while social functioning and quality of life appeared far less often. Dozens of different tools measured the same domains, which makes studies hard to compare. The authors highlight a gap between what studies measure and what people with dementia and families say matters most.
pmc-13479709:
Muneebah Vaid and coauthors present a 2026 review on skeletal muscle as an overlooked target of bisphenol A, the plastic chemical found in most human samples worldwide. BPA mimics hormones and disrupts endocrine, metabolic, and heart systems. Its effects on reproduction, brain, liver, and fat are well studied, yet muscle, the body's main glucose sink, drew little attention.

Experimental studies surveyed here show BPA altering muscle structure, energy handling, and insulin response in cells and animals. Direct human evidence tying exposure to muscle function remains thin, a gap the authors state openly. The review assembles what exists and argues that muscle outcomes belong in BPA risk assessment, since small metabolic insults in so large a tissue could matter at population scale.
pmc-13479809:
Hengcheng Zhu and coauthors published a 2026 exploratory analysis of how rainfall and storms relate to malaria cases in Mozambique, which carries the world's fifth highest malaria burden. Climate change is intensifying storms there and disrupting the national control program. Monthly district case counts came from the national malaria program, and rainfall data came from NASA earth observation archives.

Rainfall was aggregated to districts and months to match the case data. The central question is timing: how many weeks or months after heavy rain do cases climb, as mosquito breeding sites fill and parasites complete their cycles. Knowing the lag tells control teams when to surge spraying, bed net distribution, and clinic supplies after storms. The analysis is framed as preparedness guidance rather than causal proof.
pmc-13479909:
Chaohui Wang and coauthors published a 2026 study of how sour jujube trees resist witches' broom disease, a germ sickness that twists growth and blocks fruit. The setup used a living contrast: healthy resistant branches grafted onto sick trees had lived seven years beside diseased branches on the same roots. Leaves from both branch types were set side by side.

Hardy leaves showed stronger sun-food measures, including water loss and net carbon gain. Carbon use patterns differed, and joint gene and protein maps traced the control layers behind the gap. Because both branch types share one tree, genes and setting stay the same, singling out the defense response itself. The authors aim to hand breeders solid cell-level leads for guarding a fruit tree with real market worth.
pmc-13480809:
Tom J. Smak and co-authors report a 2026 route for turning polyethylene waste into dual-acid building blocks for new plastics. Oxygen plus nitrogen oxide gases chew the chain ends into dicarboxylic acids such as the feedstocks for nylon. With tuned conditions and no catalyst at all, the team reached near twenty-nine percent yield in molecule terms while burning little carbon to gas.

High nitrogen oxide pressure kept gas losses down across several polyethylene grades, giving strong carbon recovery. Adding a copper-vanadium catalyst pushed dual-acid yield past half, with the acid share of product weight above ninety percent. Even a dirty mix of post-consumer polyethylene and polypropylene gave a like product slate. Keeping plastic carbon in the loop as monomers beats burning it, and the tolerance for real waste streams matters for scale-up.
pmc-13482309:
Cao and colleagues improve a chaos-based search algorithm in 2026 for plotting three-dimensional drone routes through obstacle-filled airspace. Planners must thread safe, smooth paths through terrain and buildings while respecting flight limits, and older optimizers often settle too early on mediocre routes. Their upgraded method seeds the search with evenly spread starting points, remembers past search gradients to steer, and adds random long jumps modeled on Lévy flight to escape dead ends.

On the standard CEC benchmark functions, a public test suite for optimizers, the method matched strong rivals for precision and stayed stable across repeated runs of the tests. In simulated three-dimensional flight scenarios it produced routes that were feasible under all the coupled constraints, smooth to fly, and comparatively short. The authors offer the algorithm for constrained trajectory planning generally, with drones facing cluttered environments as the motivating case for the work.
pmc-13482609:
Wu and colleagues build a two-stage neural system in 2026 for direction-of-arrival estimation, the radar and sonar task of pinpointing where a signal comes from. It works without first modeling the antenna flaws that usually wreck such systems. Real arrays suffer shifted elements, coupling between neighbors, and mismatched gains, and labeled training data for every flaw is impractical. Their cascade cleans the signal with adaptive filters, then feeds a self-taught network imitating the classic MUSIC spectrum method.

The filter stage uses four layers tuned on signal statistics, while the spectrum stage stacks eight layers trained without human-provided direction labels. Because the stages train in parallel and correct errors inside the pipeline, no explicit model of the array's flaws is ever needed. Across unseen test scenarios it beat current methods, holding up especially when signals were faint or snapshots few.
pmc-13483709:
Heather Lusby, Stacy G Beal, and Kenneth H Rand profile hospital patients whose diarrhea tests detect a specific gut bacterium often studied in infants. Their 2026 review covers 792 hospitalized adults and children with symptoms who tested positive on a rapid multi-pathogen panel, compared with symptomatic patients whose panels found nothing. Length of stay and past medical history receive close attention.

Stay length patterns ran in opposite directions for adults and children, with positive adults tending to stay longer and positive children tending to stay shorter, though only the child pattern reached significance. Among adults, a history of autoimmune disease appeared in 31.4 percent of positive patients versus 19.2 percent of controls. The authors flag the autoimmune link, not previously reported, as a lead for follow-up work on gut imbalance.
pmc-13483909:
Hejazi Yekta and colleagues tested whether releasing the diaphragm muscle by hand eases chronic low back pain that has no clear structural cause. The diaphragm links breathing to trunk stability, so tightness there might feed back pain. Their 2026 trial randomly assigned 24 adults to three sessions of real or sham diaphragm release, with both groups also receiving standard electrical nerve stimulation. Pain, reach, balance, and disability were scored after treatment and one week later.

The real-release group reported a significantly larger pain drop than the sham group across the sessions measured. Disability scores also improved more with real treatment, by an amount the authors judge clinically meaningful. Reach toward the floor trended better right after treatment but faded by the one-week check. Balance gains were mixed. Hejazi Yekta presents the brief therapy as a useful add-on needing longer trials.
pmc-13486309:
Kazuki Nozawa reports what happens when a flagship breast cancer drug is given a second run after a break. Published in 2026, the post-hoc analysis draws 26 patients who received trastuzumab deruxtecan again from a nationwide Japanese cohort of 664 with HER2-positive metastatic disease. Survival without progression, time to treatment failure, overall survival, and response rate are tracked in the real world.

Median time without progression reached 6.5 months, treatment failure came at 4.9 months, and overall survival reached 14.2 months, with 27 percent of tumors shrinking measurably. Patients who had stopped the first course for reasons other than progression fared numerically better on the second run. No lung inflammation, the drug's feared side effect, appeared during retreatment. Carefully chosen patients may gain a useful extra option.
pmc-13486509:
Joudah and colleagues compared custard apple seeds against its pulp and peel to see which part carries the stronger medicine-like activity. The fruit, Annona squamosa, is used in folk medicine, but its parts are rarely benchmarked head to head. Their 2026 study profiled the chemistry of seed and fruit extracts, then ran antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cancer-cell tests in the laboratory.

Seed extract led on most measures, topping the peroxyl-radical scavenging assay and strongly blocking two inflammation enzymes. It even beat standard comparison drugs on selectivity for one of those enzymes in the assays reported. Fruit extract fought back on two classic antioxidant tests, where it outperformed the seed extract. Seeds also killed liver, breast, and colon cancer cells more potently in dish tests. Joudah argues the usually discarded seeds deserve attention as a source of active compounds.
pmc-13486709:
Moghanloo and Vaghefi measured swirling water flow around a bridge pier fitted with a protective collar inside a sharply bending laboratory channel. Rivers bend, and the spiral secondary flows in bends dig dangerous holes around bridge supports. Their 2026 experiment used a 180-degree channel with an oblong pier, testing collars of several thicknesses while a three-dimensional velocity probe mapped the currents over a stabilized bed.

The fastest surface current hugged the convex bank, where the pressure gradient steepens in the bend. Thickening the collar from the thinnest to the thickest setting cut peak secondary flow strength by about 30 percent in the measurements taken. The strongest swirl appeared near the 70-degree section of the bend for thin collars. Vorticity peaked at a different section, showing protection shifts rather than erases the swirl. Moghanloo offers the maps for engineers armoring piers in real river bends.
pmc-13487709:
Ryan LaGrone reports a 2026 case of an infected aortic bulge that came back after repair, with two rare germ foes at once. Infected aortic bulges, called mycotic aneurysms, make up under five percent of all aortic bulges. Klebsiella germ cases fill just three past reports, with one repeat case. A threadworm, Strongyloides, joins the mix here for the first time in such a report.

The worm can ferry gut germs into the blood as it moves through the body. That path may have reseeded the aorta with Klebsiella. Care cut out infected chest and belly tissue in full. A bypass graft then ran from armpit to both groins, far from the tainted field. Open repair stays the top choice in such cases. How long drug care should last stays an open point.
pmc-13487909:
Jingmei Xiao and co-authors revisit trial data in a 2026 post-hoc analysis of people taking antipsychotic medicines for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Volunteers had received a probiotic, dietary fiber, both together, or placebos for twelve weeks, with blood levels of short-chain fatty acids measured over time.

Higher levels of two gut-related acids, propionate and butyrate, were linked with lower weight, lower body mass index, and better insulin measures in the combined treatment context. The links were modest and come from a secondary analysis, so they suggest a mechanism rather than prove one. Still, the findings point to gut products as a possible route to ease metabolic harm.
pmc-13488209:

Women patients fare worse after cardiac surgery on average, and some fields report benefits when doctor and patient sex match. The registry held 57,729 adults having one of four common first-time heart operations between 2012 and 2022, treated by 239 surgeons, of whom about a fifth were women.

Female patients had higher rates of the combined bad outcome, covering death, readmission, or complications within thirty days, regardless of surgeon sex in the reported figures. Surgeon sex alone showed no independent link with outcomes, and pairing mattered no more than chance. The authors direct improvement efforts toward clinical risk preparation instead.
pmc-13488609:

Nickel dust at work has long been tied to lung cancer, but its many forms, from salts to nano grains, act in unlike ways. The team sized and coated checked each form, then tracked cell uptake with fine scopes and metal gauges over two days.

One form, a nickel sulfur mix, did the most harm by far, and it also shed the most nickel ions into the broth. A plain nickel salt shed less and ranked next in harm, while one oxide form did no harm at all. All gritty forms showed up inside cells, tucked in sacs. Oddly, uptake rank and harm rank did not line up. The authors say harm springs from a tangle of uptake, ion shed, and form.
pmc-13490709:
Karakurt and two colleagues in Türkiye surveyed in 2026 how worn out health science students felt by online classes. The group came from one university in the east of the country, and most had taken theory courses online in the prior school year.

The mean score sat near the mid point of the five point scale, so the group showed average levels of strain, not extreme ones. Scores ran higher for students who found distance study harder than face to face study. The same held for those who had trouble reaching course sources or using the tech. The authors urge active learning methods in online theory courses and easier access to class materials for all students.
pmc-13491709:
Lauren He and five co-authors ask in 2026 what women's health providers know about rheumatic diseases, which often strike during the childbearing years and complicate pregnancy choices. A national online questionnaire tested 200 providers, mostly at universities, on new disease presentations, contraception, and drug management around pregnancy.

Scores were weakest for spotting new rheumatic disease around and after birth, where barely a quarter of answers were correct. Contraception counseling earned the best scores and the highest confidence, though gaps remained there too. Seven in ten respondents said the web was their main resource. Most wanted guidance as websites, printed guidelines, or phone apps. The authors call for shared resources built with rheumatology colleagues.
pmc-13491809:
Febe Hertveldt leads an eleven-author team listening in 2026 to families in crisis whose babies cannot settle, sleep, or feed normally long past the usual age. Persistent regulatory problems strain the bond between parent and infant, sometimes to breaking point. Six couples who had received specialist infant mental health treatment were interviewed in depth, and their accounts were analyzed thematically.

Parents described the experience as a rupture of everyday life rather than ordinary tiredness. Fathers often escaped into work while mothers stayed trapped in round-the-clock care, an imbalance that deepened exhaustion on both sides. Outside dismissal and inward shame cut families off from help, leaving them isolated on what felt like an island. Long after the worst phase, vulnerability and resilience coexisted in different mixes, and the authors press for recognition and accessible support.
pmc-13492109:

From an initial pool of over sixty thousand records, 465 studies qualified.

Seventy studies with non-overlapping data anchored the synthesis, most using X-ray video of swallowing. Every study that measured safety found thicker liquids safer than thinner ones, since thin drinks slip toward the airway more easily. Smaller sips limited leftover residue when liquids were thickened, while solid textures rarely entered the airway but left more residue in patients. The reviewers stress tailoring texture changes to each person's measured swallowing.
pmc-13493809:

In the 2026 trial, 80 young rabbits received one of five diets, from a plain basal feed up to 20 grams of leaf meal per kilogram. The team tracked weight gain, feed efficiency, antioxidant enzymes in muscle, and inflammatory signals in blood and liver.

Rabbits on the highest dose finished far heavier than the control group, ending above 2,400 grams against roughly 2,085 grams for the unsupplemented animals. They also converted feed more efficiently, and their muscle antioxidant enzymes rose while a marker of fat damage fell. A key inflammatory messenger in the liver dropped steeply, from just under 289 to about 81 units, while a calming immune signal climbed. The authors recommend the two highest doses, while noting no cool-condition control group existed.
pmc-13493909:

Some tanks included sediment, the mud layer at the bottom of real waterways, and others held water alone.

Communities in open water changed fastest, while sediment buffered the shift and kept communities steadier. Cadmium provoked bigger changes than arsenic at the same dose, marking it as the more disruptive contaminant here. pmc-13495509:

Single aerobic exercise and exercise paired with thinking tasks each beat control conditions. Programs of five to eight weeks beat very long ones. Rankings pointed to a sweet spot: sessions near forty minutes, twice a week, over five to eight weeks, at low intensity. The authors offer the recipe as a guide for school and clinic programs.
pmc-13499709:
Ross, with Tatta and Bezner, argues that pain care for LGBTQIA+ people needs a new base. Rates of long-term pain run about twice as high in this group. Past care has stressed flaws and weak spots in the person. That view can hide bias, stress from stigma, and blocks to kind care. The authors call for care built on strength instead. It should back coping skills, free choice, and pride in who a person is. Ties to community count as part of care too.

Physical therapists sit in a strong place to lead this shift. They can build trust and safe sessions. They can plan movement around what each person values most.
pmc-13499909:

Both dementias look similar at mild stages, with overlapping thinking profiles, yet correct naming increasingly guides treatment. Their prospective study enrolled 121 patients with probable disease at mild stages, all supported by disease-specific biomarkers, for clinical, thinking, and perception testing.

Memory loss ran deeper in Alzheimer disease across recall tests, while thinking scores otherwise overlapped heavily. Minor hallucinations appeared in over half the Lewy body group against a small minority in the other group in the reported shares. Seeing patterns in noise, called pareidolia, was also far more frequent, the strongest split among the perception tests. The authors argue that routinely asking about these experiences sharpens early diagnosis.
pmc-13500709:

Two studies compared pairs choosing together against individuals choosing alone, probing fairness instincts, preference overlap, and worries about how each chooser appeared to the other.

Pairs sought more variety than solo choosers in the reported findings. Reciprocity drove the effect, with partners taking turns indulging each other's favourites across rounds, which naturally diversifies the basket. When both partners loved the same option, pair variety dropped, making preference alignment a brake on the process. Impression concerns mattered only through the gap between partners' scores, not their absolute levels, refining how marketers should think about group choice.
pmc-13500809:

Treatment slowed the progression of symptoms such as low body weight and lactic acidosis, a buildup of lactic acid in the blood. pmc-13501309:
Fang and colleagues presented SlotDeconv, a method for estimating which cell types occupy each spot in spatial transcriptomics data, in a 2026 paper. Fang split the problem in two: a reference module learns distinctive signature vectors for each cell type, trained with a diversity constraint that pushes similar types apart. A spatial module first estimates proportions spot by spot, then smooths them using neighborhood consistency. Removing the diversity constraint cut accuracy sharply, and using average profiles instead of learned signatures collapsed it entirely. Against four rivals on a twenty-seven-cell-type mouse brain dataset, SlotDeconv achieved the highest correlations, with the biggest gains exactly on the confused cortical neuron subtypes. It validated on human pancreatic cancer and mouse olfactory bulb tissues.
pmc-13501609:

The median age of the deficient group was 73 years. Among all twenty patients, female sex and severe stomach lining atrophy were associated with the deficient status in single-variable analysis, with a wide confidence interval reflecting the tiny sample. Checkpoint molecule patterns differed from case to case rather than following one signature. The authors present the work as hypothesis-generating groundwork for understanding why checkpoint blockade helps only some of these patients.
pmc-13501709:

Cytology, the Pap test approach, remained the primary method in 80.5 percent of countries, while visual inspection with acetic acid led in low-development settings and few countries had adopted HPV testing as the main screen.

pmc-13501809:

The authors offer the six as leads for breeding higher-yielding cane.
pmc-13502309:

The authors argue the formula is early diagnosis plus a plan fitted to the individual break, balancing stability for healing against preserving the tooth's structure.
pmc-13503409:

Doctors' experience often diverged from official shortage lists.

Psychiatry and kidney medicine ran close behind, and general practice was not far back. The authors argue official reporting should match what practices actually experience. They present the specialty and drug breakdowns as a map for where stockpiling and communication fixes would pay off fastest.
pmc-13505009:
Yumiko Saito-Nakano leads a team tracking how long an amoeba keeps the virulence that animal passage gave it, in a 2026 study. The parasite Entamoeba histolytica causes gut disease and liver abscesses. Lab strains lose their bite over time unless they pass through an animal host now and then.

All three began highly virulent, making abscesses over a third of the liver's weight. Each clone lost that power on its own schedule, gone by six, twelve, or eighteen months. pmc-13506209:
Karipidis and Karipidis proposed a mechanism for post-exertional malaise, the crash after activity that defines some long COVID patients, in a 2026 hypothesis paper. Karipidis proposes the virus leaves the vessel lining inflamed and drains its supply of a helper molecule the enzyme needs. When exercise raises blood flow friction, the starved enzyme produces a damaging oxidant instead of nitric oxide, fueling an injury cycle. Their two-threshold model separates the exertion level that triggers malaise from a tolerance threshold for vessel stress. They specify blood markers and vessel tests, timed a day or two after a challenge, that could confirm or refute it.
pmc-13506509:

The team then checked surgical specimens for spread patterns that matter for smaller, organ-saving surgery.

Nineteen patients reached the ypT0 to ypT2 range that could suit local excision. Most showed a solid shrink pattern, no spread beyond the visible tumor, and no lymph node disease. The widest hidden spread measured 8 mm. Such detail can help surgeons set safe margins and choose who can keep the rectum.
pmc-13507309:

Higher income brackets predicted risk too, an unusual direction hinting at diet and lifestyle shifts. The authors urge Ghana's health service to fund earlier screening and pre-pregnancy education for high-risk women.
pmc-13508109:
Luca De Simone Carone leads a ten-author team describing two unusual sugar-based coatings found on a gut bacterium, in 2026 work. The results recast gut bacterial coatings as active peacekeepers, not mere triggers.
pmc-13508309:

Spread causes most deaths in this hard-to-treat cancer type. A surface protein called PZR helps cancer cells move, invade, and travel. The team made antibodies against PZR and measured how they bind. Cell dish tests checked whether the lead antibody slowed movement and how the protein partners with a known adhesion molecule.

The lead antibody bound PZR and entered cancer cells that carry the protein. It cut migration and spread in dish tests and a mouse model of metastasis. PZR turned out to grip an adhesion partner that anchors cells to the protein mesh around them, switching on a growth signal. The humanized antibody kept its binding strength and anti-spread effect. The results support PZR as a fresh target in this cancer.
pmc-13508409:
Dorothy Hung and seven co-authors examine whether lean management helped American primary care practices weather the post-pandemic years, in 2026 work. Lean methods, borrowed from manufacturing, streamline work and cut waste in clinics. Data came from a national survey of 1,245 physician practices. They then compared lean and non-lean practices on crisis response, finances after the pandemic, and how workforce shortages hit patient care.

Lean practices tended to be larger, tied to health systems or community health centers, and heavier users of value-based payment deals. After accounting for those traits, lean practices were far more likely to run an incident command system during the pandemic. They were also more likely to act on clinician burnout. The authors argue that habits of structured problem solving double as crisis readiness. For small practices, the study frames lean adoption as resilience building, not mere efficiency chasing.
pmc-13508809:
Tripathy applied machine learning in 2026 to predict infant deaths in India, using data from the NFHS-5 national family health survey. Spotting the strongest risk signs could help target aid where infant deaths stay high. Newer computer methods may catch patterns that standard models miss.

Five models were trained and scored on how often they were right and how well they ranked risk. Random forest and decision tree models reached about 74 percent accuracy. That clearly beat the classic regression model at about 65 percent, and the tree models also scored higher on ranking skill. Six factors stood out as the strongest predictors: birth order, the mother's schooling, twin birth, household wealth, cooking fuel type, and the mother's age at her first birth. Tripathy argues such tools can guide focused programs for high-risk families.
pmc-13510209:
Yufeng Xie and eight co-authors test a plant compound called phellodendrine in a zebrafish model of inflammatory bowel disease, in 2026 work. The disease brings lasting gut inflammation, and current drugs often work weakly or carry heavy side effects. The team triggered bowel inflammation in zebrafish with a chemical irritant, then measured immune cell entry, gene activity, gut barrier strength, microbes, and oxidative stress with and without the compound.

Treated fish showed less immune cell invasion and a shift in immune cells toward a calmer state, with inflammatory genes turned down and protective ones turned up. The gut barrier held better, with more mucus protein, more mucus-making cells, and less leaking. Harmful microbes fell while helpful ones rose, and oxidative stress eased. Computer pathway work pointed to a few inflammatory routes and six candidate target genes for follow-up.
pmc-13511309:
María Casares-Jimenez and fourteen co-authors describe the clinical load of symptomatic hepatitis E virus genotype three infection in southern Spain, in 2026 work. This virus type is a leading cause of sudden liver inflammation in Europe. Ten hospitals sent suspected cases for central testing between 2022 and 2025, using a standard two-step check of antibodies and viral RNA, with viral typing for positive cases.

Of 1124 people tested, 267 infections were confirmed, and the positive share stayed high across the study years. About two fifths of patients needed hospital admission, a small share developed severe liver failure, and three died, each with major other illness. Major comorbidity on its own predicted both admission and severe disease. The authors say host health, more than viral differences, drove bad outcomes in routine care.
pmc-13511909:
Reeja Raj and eleven co-authors present an infant case of a life-threatening overreaction of the immune system, in 2026 work. The syndrome, called HLH, floods the body with inflammatory signals and can shut down organs. An eight-month-old girl with influenza A arrived with seizures, a swollen liver and spleen, and low blood cell counts. Her ferritin and two immune signals ran very high, all pointing toward the syndrome.

Treatment aimed at the syndrome and at the virus began, yet she died of heart and lung failure. Gene testing found single-copy changes in two genes tied to immune control, hinting at a built-in predisposition. The team stresses how hard it is to separate inherited forms from infection-triggered ones at the bedside. Early gene and signal profiling, they argue, could steer how hard to suppress immunity in each case.
pmc-13515109:
Ding Li and five colleagues compare gut microbes in grazing yaks and feedlot Holstein cattle living at high altitude, in a 2026 study from the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Yaks evolved for thin air and sparse forage, while imported Holsteins often struggle there. Twenty animals of each type provided samples for gene surveys and deep DNA profiling, backed by lab fermentation tests, digestive enzyme tests, and blood measures.

Yak microbes were richer in enzyme families that attack plant carbohydrates, and lab cultures from yak dung digested dry matter more completely with stronger enzyme activity. Blood profiles diverged too, with yaks showing higher levels of several immune signals and Holsteins higher IgG antibody levels. Li's team links the contrasting microbes to the animals' different digestion and immune profiles, while cautioning that diet and management differed alongside species.
pmc-13516009:
Kanokwan Suwannarong and ten colleagues survey wildlife contact and eating habits in Thailand's border provinces in a 2026 One Health study. These rural, ethnically mixed communities live close to animals, and such contact is a known route for new infections. Between late 2020 and mid 2022 the team interviewed four hundred villagers face to face and tested blood for melioidosis, a soil-borne disease.

Wildlife eating was near universal over a lifetime, and almost two-thirds had eaten wildlife in the past six months. Wild boar led the menu, followed by rice-field rats. Most participants were women, many worked in farming, and understanding of zoonotic risk and immunity was thin. One subdistrict stood out, with about a fifth of its tested villagers carrying melioidosis antibodies. Suwannarong's team urges stronger health education for staff, village volunteers, and residents on the risks of wildlife contact and consumption.
pmc-13517209:
Zhen Liu and co-authors test in this 2026 study whether a coated feed additive helps young White King pigeons through weaning. Weaning is the stressful switch from parent-fed pigeon milk to eating on their own at about one month old. The additive is sodium butyrate, a gut-friendly acid salt, in a protective coating.

Birds receiving the supplement grew better and showed healthier intestines than unsupplemented birds at the same stage. Their gut lining developed more fully, and the mix of microbes in the intestine shifted in favorable ways, alongside improved immune measures. The coating also removes the additive's sharp smell and lets it blend evenly with the grit pigeons need. The authors recommend it as a tool for easing the weaning transition in meat pigeon production.
pmc-13518309:
Chunwei Li and Panfeng Zhao clone and measure a self-incompatibility gene across tomato species in a 2026 study. Many flowering plants reject their own pollen, a system steered by S-RNase genes in the style. The pair gathered partial copies of a relative gene, named ZS, from four tomato species. The lines mixed self-rejecters with self-accepters. They tracked where and how strongly each copy switched on.

The ZS genes spoke only in styles, never elsewhere. Volume differed sharply by species. One self-accepting clade, S habrochaites, ran its copies louder than the self-rejecting S chilense, an upset of the tidy expectation that expression level simply follows the mating system. Li and Zhao frame the atlas as groundwork: knowing which copies exist and how they behave is the step before anyone can explain, or breed around, tomato self-incompatibility at the molecular level.
pmc-13518809:
Yuxing Cai, Yuxuan Zhang, Hanyu Gao, and Yong Huang report a 2026 recipe for ring-shaped biaryl molecules, paired aromatic rings whose twist gives them handedness. Such ring-constrained structures interest drug designers, yet making them with adjustable ring sizes had few good methods. Medium rings are notoriously hard to close.

Their twist-expand-seal plan first opens a flat ring with a chiral carbene catalyst to set the twist. Alcohols of varying chain length then widen the ring, and a final bond-forming step seals it shut. Across 49 examples they reached yields up to 99 percent and near-perfect handedness control. Ring sizes ran from 9 to 14 members, widening the design space.
pmc-13518909:
Na Wei leads a seven-author study in 2026 asking whether circular economy practices cut production-based carbon emissions in six leading circular economies: Austria, Belgium, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, and the United States. The team used municipal waste generation and treatment as a stand-in measure for circularity, an angle earlier work had barely tested.

Data from 1991 to 2020 passed through several econometric methods, including pooled and country-level lag models plus causality checks. Circular economy activity linked to long-run emission reductions across the panel and in most individual countries. Spain was the exception. Wei and colleagues say the pattern supports circular strategies as climate policy, with room to learn why Spain diverged.
pmc-13519009:
Norbert Solymosi leads a nine-author team sequencing DNA from an ancient Egyptian corn mummy in 2026. Corn mummies are human-shaped ritual figures sprouted from grain, soil, and water for the Khoiak festival. The Budapest specimen dates to the later third century BC, and the team asked whether any ancient DNA survived inside it.

Metagenomic reads mixed obvious modern contaminants with material that could plausibly be ancient. Spore-forming Bacillus relatives dominated the bacterial traces. Wheat fragments matched ancient emmer wheat from Egypt and the southern Levant most closely, while moth traces resembled hawk moth genomes. Human fragments carried mitochondrial and Y-chromosome lineages common in Africa today, consistent with the object's origin.
pmc-13520409:
Belal Al-zu'bi and colleagues screen in 2026 bone tumours for a vitamin A processing enzyme called CYP26A1, which is raised in many cancers yet had not been mapped in bone tumours. Tissue staining covered 95 tumours spanning benign, intermediate and malignant types, plus normal bone.

Normal bone showed no staining, while about one third of tumours stained positive. Intermediate tumours stained most often, especially giant cell tumours, whereas bone-forming cancers such as osteosarcoma generally showed none. Rare chordoma and adamantinoma cases stained strongly despite tiny numbers. Protein network analysis adds context on what the enzyme may interact with in tumour tissue.
pmc-13520509:
Cevher İlhan Cevheri tests in 2026 whether mixing composted farmyard manure with mineral fertiliser lifts cotton yield and profit under semi-arid, irrigated conditions. Low soil organic matter and rising fertiliser prices squeeze growers of the Candia variety in chalky soils.

Nine feeding plans varied phosphate, urea and manure doses. Manure plus urea at the middle manure rate gave the highest seed cotton yield, about one third above the unfertilised control, with heavier bolls and better fibre output. Fibre quality traits stayed unchanged across plans. Tallest plants came from the highest phosphate plan. Economic results begin in the opening summary, supporting manure integration for profit.
pmc-13520609:
Christine Li, Julia Rogers, Haya Raef, and Laura Aspey present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 54-year-old man with advanced cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This is a skin-homing blood cancer. His severe itching had resisted many standard treatments. His mycosis fungoides covered most of his skin. He was receiving palliative chemotherapy. Dermatology was consulted during a hospital admission for infected skin wounds.

He was started on nemolizumab. This antibody drug blocks the receptor for interleukin-31, a key itch signal. Within seven days of a single loading dose, his itching resolved completely. The relief held at about six months. No side effects were reported. The authors offer this as support for this new use.
pmc-13522509:
Na Ju and colleagues report a battery study, published in 2026. It uses a single crystal as the electrode of a water-based proton battery. Most work on these safe, cheap batteries designs molecules. This team asked how molecular stacking changes proton storage. They studied a naphthoquinone compound. Diffraction, microscopy, and calculations were used.

Stacked molecular pairs formed a reinforced crystal face. It had the lowest energy cost for taking up protons. The electrode used nearly all of its theoretical capacity. A full cell built from the material performed accordingly. Crystal engineering matters as much as molecular design in these batteries, the study argues.
pmc-13523209:
Marwan Sheikh-Taha audits medication safety in older adults with heart failure in a 2026 retrospective study. Home medication lists for five hundred twenty-four patients aged sixty-five or older admitted to two hospitals were checked against the 2023 Beers Criteria. That list names medicines that can be risky in older adults. Medicines were sorted into categories such as generally inappropriate, risky interactions, and dose problems in kidney impairment.

Nine in ten patients were taking at least one flagged medicine, and about a quarter of all home medicines met the criteria. Stomach, heart, and brain medicines were the commonest flagged groups. Kidney disease, depression, prostate enlargement, and a higher total number of conditions each predicted a heavier flagged burden. The author recommends targeted medication review and careful deprescribing in such patients.
pmc-13523309:
Joshua Onyango and colleagues analyze risk factors for udder infection in Nigerian dairy cows in a 2026 multilevel study. A cross-sectional survey covered two hundred ninety-eight farms in Plateau State, collecting farm, animal, housing, milking hygiene, and treatment information. Infection was counted at herd level from farmer-reported cases in the current lactation, a definition the authors note could misclassify some herds without laboratory confirmation.

Nearly six in ten herds reported mastitis in the current year. Large herds had markedly higher odds, and the presence of working bulls also mattered. Post-milking teat dipping was strongly linked to lower odds, as were aspects of milking hygiene such as separate cleaning cloths. Treatment practices also entered the final models. The authors offer the layered analysis as a guide for targeted control on diverse farms.
pmc-13523509:
Marilyn Macdonald and others map, in a 2026 scoping review, models of publicly funded home care for older adults living in the community across six high-income countries. Home care supports aging in place, yet funding, governance, and delivery differ sharply between systems. Evidence about those models was scattered and hard to compare.

The review covered Canada, England, Denmark, Sweden, Australia, and New Zealand, searching three databases from 2005 onward plus grey literature. Nineteen sources were included.
