Five models emerged, ranging from provincially organized Canadian care and Australia's consumer-directed packages to municipal universal welfare in Denmark and Sweden, direct payments in England, and nationally framed services in New Zealand. Review evidence was uneven and mostly descriptive, with relational care and workforce conditions prominent in noted experience.
pmc-13524709:
Devika Nair and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 longitudinal study, symptom burden after starting dialysis and its link with hospitalization. Symptoms weigh heavily on people with kidney failure, yet which symptom patterns best predict hospital use was unclear. The team used a kidney disease quality-of-life questionnaire in people beginning hemodialysis in the United States.

Latent transition analysis sorted patients into low, moderate, and high symptom burden groups. The high group combined severe symptoms with strong disease impact. Nearly every questionnaire scale, adjusted for patient characteristics, predicted higher hospitalization hazard. High overall burden raised the hazard by about one fifth. Worsening pain interference and fatigue each added measurable risk on their own. The authors propose symptom tracking as a practical prognostic tool at dialysis start.
pmc-13527109:
Zhao and colleagues separate two miserable sensations in this 2026 mouse study of visceral pain, aching from the internal organs, and itch, asking how one brain region tells them apart. The basolateral amygdala was the suspect. Tagging whichever neurons fired during each sensation, the team traced their wiring and read their gene activity cell by cell.

Two distinct neuronal populations answered the two stimuli, and they projected to different targets: visceral pain neurons wired to the ventromedial hypothalamus, itch neurons to the dorsomedial striatum, forming separate control circuits. The populations also carried signature genes, Fgf2 in the pain-labeled cells and Notch2 in the itch-labeled ones. Knocking down each gene selectively dulled only its own sensation, leaving the other intact. The authors argue the amygdala sorts these aversive signals by dedicated circuit and molecule, offering two precise drug targets for conditions that resist current treatments.
pmc-13527509:
Meng and colleagues reported a 2026 case of stubborn lower-leg ulcers linked to cabozantinib, in a man with kidney cancer that had spread widely. Cabozantinib is a targeted cancer drug that blocks blood vessel growth signals. His cancer had first been treated with immunotherapy, stopped for a severe skin reaction, and he switched to cabozantinib in 2022 after radiation failed, with a good tumor response.

Meng describes how a small spontaneous ulcer appeared on his right leg about six months into cabozantinib treatment, on a background of untreated poor vein circulation. It worsened into a painful, treatment-resistant wound by mid-2024. The drug was paused on suspicion of toxicity, swabs found only normal skin bacteria. A biopsy showed an inflammation pattern resembling pyoderma gangrenosum, an ulcer disease driven by immune cells. The authors discuss how vessel-blocking drugs impair wound healing and outline management lessons for similar patients.
pmc-13528109:
Syeda Humaida Hasan and six colleagues chart birth defects in a Bangladeshi newborn intensive care unit in a 2026 study. The unit at Chittagong Medical College Hospital admitted 5,223 babies from August to December 2020. Careful exams found defects in 183 babies, about three and a half percent. Defects were sorted with a standard disease code system.

Muscle and bone problems were the most common group, with sixty-seven cases. Cleft lip and palate came next, then heart and circulation faults. Sadly, about thirty-one percent of affected babies died. Their death risk ran about 1.6 times that of babies without defects. Mother's high blood pressure and diabetes each linked with far higher odds. Too much or too little fluid around the baby also linked strongly. The authors urge antenatal screening and routine newborn checks.
pmc-13530109:
Tian Niu, Qicong Li, and Ao Zhang search in 2026 for RNA-binding proteins that forecast survival in papillary kidney cancer. Such proteins control how gene messages get used inside cells, yet their role in this kidney cancer type was unclear. Data came from a large public cancer atlas.

From hundreds of altered proteins, seven stood out for their link to patient survival. A risk score built from those seven separated patients into groups with clearly different outcomes in both test sets. Lab checks on kidney cell lines confirmed changed levels for several proteins, supporting a scoring tool for treatment planning.
pmc-13530209:
Lu Weihua and co-authors devise a 2026 method for moving color schemes from paintings onto consumer products through felt emotion. Shoppers increasingly want goods that stir a feeling, yet product shapes leave little room for novelty. Color carries that emotional load across cultures without words.

Painting colors were grouped, product color plans were mapped by part and function, and volunteer ratings tied each group to emotion words. Matching emotion labels then bridged a painting group to a product plan. A coffee machine test using Chinese paintings showed richer color and stronger perceived design value.
pmc-13531809:
Xiaohai Luo and colleagues link belly-fat chemistry to poor bone healing in a 2026 hospital study of leg fractures. Records covered 485 adults whose thigh or shin shaft fractures were fixed with internal rods between 2022 and 2025. A visceral fat index combined waist size, body mass, and blood fat measures.

About 12 percent showed delayed union or nonunion at six months. The fat index ran clearly higher in that group, and each unit rise lifted the odds of poor healing by roughly 60 percent after full adjustment. The index beat plain body mass and waist measures at telling groups apart.
pmc-13531909:
Diederick BH Verheijen leads a 2026 tissue study of a risky heart anatomy where a coronary artery runs inside the aortic wall before exiting. That buried segment may act like a flap valve linked to sudden death. Fifteen surgical patients from several centers donated the removed wall segment for staining and review.

All segments showed a two-layered middle wall with no outer layer between artery and aorta. The aorta side carried dense fibrous tissue matching the nearby valve junction. The artery side showed widespread degeneration: elastic fiber damage, cell loss, and matrix buildup. Damage grew with age, informing risk judgment.
pmc-13536709:
Lijun Zhou and co-authors track repeat flu infections across Sichuan Province in a 2026 population study covering more than 2.8 million cases from 2023 to 2025. Follow-up lasted up to three years after a first infection. Statistical models estimated how repeat risk grows over time and which age, job, and residence groups face the highest risk of catching flu again.

Repeat risk rose in yearly steps and reached a modest share by the third year. Most repeat infections clustered 9 to 12 months after the first illness. Children and teens faced notably higher repeat risk than middle-aged and older adults, and work and residence patterns also mattered. The authors suggest that vaccine and prevention plans focus more tightly on young people and heavily exposed jobs.
pmc-13536809:
Barik and colleagues map son preference across India's districts and show its drivers change with geography, a fact national averages flatten away. Son preference, wanting boys over girls, fuels skewed sex ratios and unequal care. Using survey data on over a hundred thousand married women from the 2019-2021 national family health survey, their 2026 analysis applied geographically weighted regression. That method lets each predictor's strength vary place by place, after confirming the pattern was genuinely non-uniform.

Reported son preference ranged from under a tenth of women in some districts to over two fifths in others, clustering strongly across the northern and central belts. The local models showed the leading factors, mothers' illiteracy and large households, biting hard in the north and centre while barely mattering in the south. Local explanatory power peaked in the northern districts.
pmc-13537909:
Kim and colleagues published a 2026 study on a flu vaccine idea aimed at killer T cells. Seasonal flu vaccines chase surface parts that the virus keeps changing. Internal virus parts stay nearly the same across strains, though. The team loaded those steady parts onto tiny biodegradable carriers.

The carriers wore display molecules that present cargo to killer T cells. Two internal flu pieces, from mouse and human sets, held on best. In mice, loaded carriers raised flu-specific killer T cell responses. The human display version also loaded cleanly, hinting at use in people. A carrier vaccine could someday cover many flu strains at once. Steady internal targets sidestep the yearly vaccine redesign cycle entirely.
pmc-13538709:
Jay B Bisen and colleagues compare tiny retinal infarct marks across stroke patients and healthy controls in a 2026 imaging study. The marks, seen on retinal scans, may mirror small vessel health in the brain. Scans from 64 patients scanned near a cortical stroke were set against 65 controls with clean heart calcium scores. Mark counts were compared by timing, stroke circulation, and eye side, with risk factor adjustment.

Patients scanned before and after stroke both carried clearly more marks than controls. Counts did not differ between pre- and post-stroke groups, between circulation territories, or between the eye on the stroke side and its partner. Adjustment erased the post-stroke link. The authors read the marks as signs of long-standing vessel strain from risk factors rather than fresh stroke damage.
pmc-13542009:
Yixi Chen and co-authors investigate in 2026 whether high levels of CD74, a protein that helps display immune markers on cell surfaces, signal a worse outlook in acute myeloid leukemia. They mined public cancer databases rather than running new lab experiments.

CD74 was much higher in leukemia tissue than in healthy controls, especially in subtypes rich in monocytes and in patients whose white cell counts ran high. Patients with high CD74 survived less well overall. Its level also tracked with more memory B cells, monocytes, and a calming type of macrophage inside tumors, and with pathways for antigen display and immune response. The authors propose CD74 as both a prognostic marker and a possible target for immune-based treatment.
pmc-13543509:
Zhilong Wang's team ran a 2026 feeding study testing a blend of three probiotic bacteria in weaned yaks, whose immature rumens and unsettled microbes make weaning a risky, growth-stalling transition. Sixteen eight-month-old yaks were split into two groups of eight; one got the blend of Bacillus and Lactobacillus species at 0.2 percent of dietary dry matter, the other ate the basal diet alone. Growth, blood readings, and rumen microbes and their products were tracked.

Probiotic yaks grew clearly better. Their blood urea nitrogen fell, a protective antioxidant enzyme rose, and a pro-inflammatory signal dropped, indicating relief of weaning stress. Inside the rumen, ammonia nitrogen fell while microbial protein and useful fermentation acids rose, showing a more productive microbial community. The authors present combined probiotics as a handy lever for guiding rumen growth at weaning.
pmc-13543609:
Chen and colleagues uncover an alliance driving the deadliest turn in prostate cancer: its transformation into the neuroendocrine subtype, which shrugs off hormone therapy and most targeted drugs. Their 2026 work fingers SUCLG2, a mitochondrial energy enzyme, moonlighting in the nucleus. When growth signals arrive, SUCLG2 travels into the nucleus, teams with the activated EGFR receptor, and they switch on the VEGFA gene, launching the neuroendocrine programme and resistance to EGFR-blocking drugs.

Forcing SUCLG2 up made cancer cells resistant to the drug erlotinib, while removing it restored sensitivity and slowed tumours in mice, effects reversible by restoring VEGFA. A computer screen for compounds that erase the SUCLG2 signature found phenethyl isothiocyanate, a mustard-family plant chemical, which synergised with erlotinib against patient-derived tumour organoids and shrank grafts in animals. The authors propose dual targeting as a biomarker-guided strategy for this subtype.
pmc-13545709:
Akihiro Tobe and a large international team examined in 2026 whether early complications after a catheter-based aortic valve replacement cast a shadow over the following year. Their analysis drew on the LANDMARK trial, which compared one valve family against two established rivals in patients with severe aortic narrowing. Complications counted were nonfatal events in the first 30 days, such as stroke, major bleeding, kidney injury, or a new pacemaker.

Of 742 patients alive at 30 days, about a quarter had suffered at least one such event. That group died at roughly twice the rate of the complication-free group over the rest of the year, while quality of life among survivors looked similar. The authors label the analysis exploratory and warn about bias from studying only survivors.
pmc-13546709:
Naimat Ullah Khan led a 2026 survey of Cryptosporidium infection in goats across three districts of southern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan. The parasite causes diarrhea, dehydration, and losses on goat farms. Stool samples from 360 goats were stained and examined under the microscope, and infection rates were compared by district, season, age, and sex.

About one goat in five carried the parasite, with the highest rate in Kohat district. Summer brought a clear peak, near 30 percent, and the youngest kids, under about two weeks old, were hit hardest at roughly a third infected. Rates barely differed between males and females. The authors recommend farmer training, timed deworming, early screening, and cleaner water and housing.
pmc-13547109:
Aisan Nouri, Lisa Jamieson, and Seyed Kian Haji Seyed Javadi made a policy case in 2026 for silver diamine fluoride, a liquid painted onto tooth cavities to stop them without drilling. Drawing on reviews, trials, cost studies, and guidelines, they weighed the treatment across clinical, workforce, economic, and fairness angles. The liquid is cheap, quick to apply, and workable in community settings for children, older adults, and people who struggle to reach a dentist.

Uptake still lags because of unclear rules, weak payment routes, training gaps, worries about the black stain it leaves, and patchy follow-up. The authors propose a six-part framework covering financing, regulation, training, patient communication, research, and governance. Their bottom line: evidence is no longer the barrier; systems are.
pmc-13547209:
Desalegn Berhanu Katiso and co-authors measured in 2026 how many newborns die in their first week at a general hospital in central Ethiopia, and which factors drive the risk. Records for 400 babies admitted up to seven days old between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed with a standardized checklist. The early death rate came to about 16.5 percent of admissions.

Infection starting early in life, breathing distress, oxygen deprivation around birth, prematurity, and a low five-minute vitality score each raised the odds of death several-fold. Two treatments pointed the other way: breathing support with continuous positive airway pressure and light therapy for jaundice were linked with lower mortality. The authors call for stronger intensive care, skilled birth attendance, and infection control.
pmc-13547309:
Tingyu Xu and colleagues designed in 2026 a blockchain-based system for guarding data from connected medical devices, whose current centralized setups invite hacking, forgery, and unauthorized access. Their design spreads records across a permissioned network of hospital nodes in five layers. A voting protocol commits entries, and standard hashing and digital signatures prove records are untampered and traceable. Access follows job roles, and an index speeds up searches.

Tests with ten thousand health transactions across four to ten nodes processed a few hundred transactions per second, and indexed lookups answered in under 65 milliseconds even as the network grew. The authors note that real deployment still needs testing for energy use, storage growth, and recovery from node failures.
pmc-13547609:
Huseong Lee and colleagues measured methane-making microbes in the rumens of young crossbred calves in 2026, looking for early links between microbe load and how the animals eat, grow, and ferment feed. Twenty-three male Japanese Black and Holstein cross calves were raised identically from one to nine weeks of age, then split into high and low methanogen groups by DNA counts.

Daily weight gain matched between the groups. Calves in the high group ate more starter feed at six weeks, and their rumens made proportionally less propionate, a useful fermentation product. The high group's rumen favored the classic methane genus, while the low group carried more bacteria tied to propionate production. Starter intake across all calves rose with methanogen counts. The authors frame the patterns as early-life signatures worth following.
pmc-13548709:
Cansu Mine Aydın, Özlem Karabulutlu, and Tuğba Kavas survey older adults with chronic illness in Kars, eastern Turkey, about three intertwined states of mind, in a 2026 correlational study. Climate change anxiety is rising even among older generations, and its interplay with death anxiety and resilience was unmapped in this group. Between March and November 2025, 386 participants completed online scales for all three constructs.

Average scores sat in the middle range for each scale. Climate anxiety correlated weakly and negatively with resilience, while resilience correlated positively in a weak way with one pairing and moderately negatively with death anxiety, as the authors report the pattern. Women scored higher than men on both climate and death anxiety. The team recommends support programs that respect income, social circumstances, and gender differences to protect resilience in chronically ill older adults.
pmc-13550409:
Vansh Aggarwal and colleagues build a real-time yoga coach that watches through a camera and corrects posture, designed for people with lower-body disabilities, in a 2026 study. Guided practice is often out of reach for this group, and earlier pose systems ignored disability entirely. Their system uses a fast pose estimation model, in its Thunder variant, feeding deep neural networks that compare the user's joints against proper form, with chair yoga as the practice setting.

The pipeline judges video input on the fly and flags posture errors as they happen, aiming to prevent the injuries that bad form can cause. The team also curated a dataset of chair yoga poses, which they describe as the first of its kind. The authors position the work as a step toward home wellness tools that include bodies usually left out of fitness technology.
pmc-13551709:
Negash Wakgari, with four colleagues, published a 2026 mixed-methods study building the first questionnaire tools to capture women's own experience of abortion care in Ethiopia. No patient-reported measures existed for this care anywhere, the authors note. Items came from a systematic review and from Ethiopian women's accounts, then passed through two expert Delphi rounds that cut weak items and cognitive interviews with women who checked clarity.

Seventy-two draft items shrank to thirty: twenty-one covering care experience and nine covering outcomes. Women in interviews found instructions, wording, response options, and the recall period clear and relevant. The authors present the paired tools as a step toward person-centered, rights-based abortion care that services can actually measure.
pmc-13551909:
Yehualashet Belayneh, leading four colleagues, published a 2026 case-control study of precancerous cervical lesions among women screened at public facilities in Debre Markos town, Ethiopia. Such lesions can progress to cervical cancer, a major concern in lower-income countries. The study compared 85 women with lesions against 255 without, using interviewer questionnaires and chart review, then applied logistic regression.

Eight factors stood as determinants in the final model, led by HIV positivity, genital mutilation, and having two or more lifetime partners, each raising odds several-fold in the reported estimates. Rural residence, living alone, sexually transmitted infection history, early sexual debut, and age above forty also raised odds. The authors use the list to target screening and prevention in the town's facilities.
pmc-13552609:
Gonzalo Solís-García leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 Spanish interview study on counsel before very early birth. Parents of babies born between twenty-three and just under twenty-seven weeks took part. Fifteen families spoke after their babies left newborn intensive care. All had received advice before birth at a large referral hospital during 2023 and 2024.

Four themes came out of the talks. Parents worked to grasp hard facts, weighed how and where news was given, and rode strong feelings. Most were pleased with the counsel, yet they wanted plainer, kinder help that fit their own values. Needs for detail varied widely between families. The authors call for counsel that arms parents for choice while tending to their distress.
pmc-13554109:
Nihat Arslan leads a four-author team building a learning model that spots diseases on wheat leaves in a 2026 study. Wheat feeds much of the world, and leaf diseases cut harvests hard. Hand checks are slow and lab tests take time, while plain photo models stumble in messy field light. Their model blends a network strong on local detail with one strong on whole-leaf context, plus a step that sharpens faint marks.

An attention block spotlights the most telling regions, and a gate weighs local against global clues for each leaf. Tests ran on three photo sets, from tidy lab shots to rough field images. Scores hit perfect marks on balanced sets and stayed above ninety-nine percent in field trials. The authors back early, sharp diagnosis to trim spray use.
pmc-13558609:
Nadine Wehbe and five colleagues tested in 2026 whether an extract of the seagrass Halodule uninervis can calm inflamed immune cells. Seagrasses carry bioactive compounds, yet this species had never been checked for anti-inflammatory action. The team treated mouse macrophages with a bacterial toxin that reliably triggers inflammation. They added the alcohol extract of the plant. Measurements covered inflammatory messengers, cell movement, and the signalling pathways that switch inflammation on.

The extract dialled down two hallmark inflammatory enzymes and cut output of nitric oxide and two inflammatory cytokines. Treated cells also migrated less, a sign of a quieter response. Three master signalling routes inside the cell were suppressed in parallel. The authors conclude that the seagrass shows genuine anti-inflammatory activity in the dish. It deserves study as a gentler alternative to synthetic drugs. Cell results, they stress, are an early step.
pmc-13558709:
Shu Yang and four colleagues charted in 2026 how weather shapes outbreaks of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Yichun. That city carries China's heaviest burden of this rodent-borne disease. Weekly case and weather records from 2005 to 2023 were fed into random forest models to pick time lags. Lag-aware statistical models then let risk curve with temperature, humidity, and rainfall.

Risk peaked at a mild temperature near fourteen degrees, humidity showed a right-skewed pattern, and rainfall traced an inverse J shape. Effects arrived months later, with temperature's strongest echo at about half a year. Temperature swung between protective and harmful phases across its lag window, while rain and humidity mostly protected. Formal tests found no interplay among the three factors. City officials gain a calendar for timing rodent control and vaccination drives.
pmc-13559109:
Shi and colleagues published a 2026 study on spotting infection risk in preterm babies. A germ called Ureaplasma can infect newborn airways without clear early signs. The team studied 430 preterm infants at one hospital in Jinjiang, China. They built a scoring chart from mother and baby facts available early.

Ninety-two babies tested positive for the germ in airway samples overall. A mother's own genital infection with the germ raised risk most sharply. Early water-breaking and womb inflammation also raised the odds strongly. The chart sorted babies with high accuracy in the study's checks. Early flagging could focus monitoring and spare antibiotics for low-risk babies. All five risk inputs come from routine records, not special tests.
pmc-13559809:
Aaron Machen, Muhammad Rizwan Sardar, and Gilbert Aidinian report the case of a 72-year-old man found to have a wire retained inside his left internal carotid artery. Their 2026 case report explains that the wire remained from an endovascular procedure performed more than a year earlier at another facility. The man came to attention with dizziness, and duplex imaging revealed the foreign body.

Angiography showed the wire's tip curled inside the carotid, with the wire trailing down toward the descending aorta. Because so much time had passed, the team feared the tip had embedded in the vessel wall, making snare retrieval through a catheter risky. They chose open surgery instead, removing the wire and repairing the artery with a patch angioplasty, without complications. The authors place the case against a thin literature on open retrieval, noting most retained objects come out percutaneously when caught early.
pmc-13561209:
Subedi and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of macrophage activation syndrome in a thirteen-month-old boy with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a rare inflammatory childhood disease. The syndrome is a life threatening overreaction of the immune system that often masquerades as severe sepsis. He arrived two months after steroids were stopped, with high fever, rash, and lethargy.

Blood counts fell across all lines while inflammation markers soared, so he was first treated empirically for sepsis with antibiotics. Fever persisted and clotting failed progressively, with ferritin climbing to a markedly elevated level that pointed away from infection. Subedi found blood cultures negative and bone marrow showed none of the cell eating pattern often expected in this syndrome. High dose intravenous steroids produced rapid clinical and laboratory improvement, and he stayed well at three months.
pmc-13561709:
Cheng Yang and colleagues describe their first two cases of robot-assisted single-port surgery to clear inguinal and pelvic lymph nodes in penile cancer. Their 2026 case report introduces a suprapubic antegrade approach through one concealed incision. Node dissection remains the cornerstone for controlling this rare cancer's spread, yet open surgery brings skin death, infection, and swelling at high rates.

The first patient, aged sixty-one, had node-positive squamous cancer and underwent the robotic dissection two weeks after radical penectomy. The second, aged fifty-three, had both operations in one sitting. Neither man suffered major complications, and neither showed recurrence at six and two months of follow-up respectively. Cosmetic results benefit from the single hidden cut. The authors call the technique feasible in this tiny preliminary series, while stressing that cancer outcomes need larger cohorts and longer follow-up.
pmc-13562209:
Yutong Cheng and colleagues chart the global burden of inflammatory bowel disease from 1990 to 2021 through the Global Burden of Disease database, sorting patterns by development level and sex. Their 2026 analysis tracks incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability rates, then breaks down what drives change in each stratum. Gene-based tests of candidate exposures ride along as an exploratory strand.

Global incidence crept upward year by year while prevalence, death, and disability rates eased downward across the period. Wealthy regions still carried the heaviest standardized burden in 2021, yet mid-level regions posted the fastest incidence and prevalence gains. Aging drove change in rich countries, population growth in poor ones. The disability gap between countries ran wider among women than men. Every genetic link vanished after correction for multiple testing. The authors press for locally fitted strategies against an unevenly shared burden.
pmc-13563909:
Ömer Faruk Öz and five colleagues look for a fingerprint of overactive bladder in women's urine, focusing on two acids. Overactive bladder is diagnosed by symptoms alone, urgency and frequency without infection, and its biology stays fuzzy. Their 2026 study recruited 186 women, excluding anyone with heart or metabolic disease or related medication. An eight-question score split them into 81 with probable overactive bladder and 105 controls. Urine succinate and malate were measured by mass spectrometry and scaled to creatinine.

Both acids ran higher in the bladder group, who were older and more often postmenopausal. After adjusting for age, body mass, births, and menopause, the link held for succinate at a ratio of 1.69, and weakly for malate at 1.25. Succinate discriminated the groups, with an accuracy area of 0.678. The authors call the finding hypothesis-generating: a sign that the bladder's energy handling may differ, pending studies that track diet and urinary microbes.
pmc-13566409:
Carsten A. Wagner, John A. Sayer, and Michael Straub review, in a 2026 article for a European endourology section, when genetic testing helps people with kidney stones. More than forty genes can cause single-gene forms of stone disease, often with early onset, frequent recurrence, kidney damage, and problems outside the kidneys.

Recent studies found a likely single-gene cause in up to about a third of affected children and in a smaller share of unselected adults. The authors recommend testing for patients under twenty-five and for those with high-risk metabolic profiles. A precise genetic answer can guide personal treatment, diet advice, and screening of relatives who may share the risk.
pmc-13572409:
Marco Antonio Barroca, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 study that runs chemistry calculations partly on a quantum computer. The test case is oxygen reduction at a battery electrode surface, a step that sets how well lithium batteries work. Exact math for such systems is out of reach, so the team picked a small active space of key orbitals.

A density-based screen chose the orbitals, and a quantum method called sample-based quantum diagonalization did the hard part. Circuits ran on up to 80 qubits of an IBM Heron R2 chip. For spaces up to 12 orbitals, results matched a trusted classic method. At 27 orbitals, the extended version beat the classic methods that could still run at that size. The work hints at quantum help for hard reaction problems.
pmc-13572509:
Alessia Manganaro, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of two drugs given just before a sharp bout of social stress. One bout of social defeat does not cause lasting low mood on its own, yet it primes mice to react strongly to a mild stress a week later. The team asked whether a dose right before the first bout can block that priming.

Male mice got a single shot of propranolol, a heart drug that blocks adrenaline signals, or of corticosterone, a stress hormone, or of salt water. After defeat and a later mild stress, social tests gauged the outcome. Propranolol partly blocked the priming effect. The design isolates a narrow window: treatment at the first stress, not during the later one. Results may hint at ways to blunt stress effects early, before patterns set in.
pmc-13573309:
Junfeng Lu, with six colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of how protons move through protic ionic liquids, salts that are liquid and carry spare protons. Proton flow drives fuel cells and green chemistry, and its path in water is well mapped. In these thicker, water-free liquids, the path was murky.

The team joined machine-learned force fields, advanced motion simulations, and proton NMR measures on choline amino acid liquids. Protons crossed a range of fleeting setups, most often a shared pair form called Zundel-like, more than the single form common in water. Free energy checks showed that chain flex and bulk jointly set the hop barriers. Heat sped up exchange by reshuffling hydrogen bonds, and quantum effects lowered the barrier further. The map links liquid structure to proton speed for design work.
pmc-13575209:
Anurag Srivastava and six colleagues study rust-like corrosion in 3D-printed nickel-titanium alloy in a 2026 paper. This shape memory alloy returns to its set form after bending, and laser melting can print complex parts from it. Print settings leave pores and surface flaws that may invite corrosion.

Samples printed at two power levels and two hatch spacings soaked for 72 hours in a salt solution that mimics body fluid. The low-power set, cut along the build direction, held the most pores at 5.4 percent and pitted deepest, up to 110 micrometres. Wider hatch spacing gave better resistance on the face tested. Surfaces with fewer defects formed thin, compact protective films. The authors stress build direction and surface finishing over bulk settings alone.
pmc-13576009:
Katherine Staab, Noah Johnson, and Ana Chiddington report a pilot project that changed how continuing medical education gets planned, in a 2026 paper. At Southern California Permanente Medical Group, course planning had run in silos, with stakeholders joining late. The redesign brought key people together from the first consultation.

Eighteen faculty and planners who had worked under both the old and new models answered a survey. Support ran high under both systems. Views on how well people communicated, coordinated, and reached resources were more consistently positive under the shared model. Views on preparedness, efficiency, and teaching value were mixed. The authors read the results as early support for starting with collaboration, and call for larger studies with stronger measures.
pmc-13576109:
Tian Chao, Wang WenHui, and Zhao JinTao model land use and carbon flows for the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region in a 2026 study. Land serves production, living, and ecological roles, each with its own carbon emissions and uptake. The region faces heavy emission pressure from fast urban growth.

From 2000 to 2020 total emissions rose sharply, with a pattern of high values in the southeast and low in the northwest. Carbon uptake by land weakened overall, strongest in the northwest. The team then built a 2035 planning scenario using optimisation tools. Their plan beat the original land plan on economic benefit, reduction efficiency, compactness, and access, while cutting projected emissions by 19.04 percent. Prediction accuracy reached 82.24 percent. The authors offer the framework for regional carbon policy.
pmc-13576309:
Elif Seren Tanrıverdi and three colleagues hunt for hidden microbes in patients whose urine shows white cells yet grows nothing in culture, a pattern called sterile pyuria, in a 2026 study. Standard culture misses organisms that grow poorly in the lab. The team ran a DNA test for 14 candidate pathogens on samples from two university hospitals.

Urine came from 201 patients with the pattern and 180 controls without it. The DNA test found at least one candidate organism in 50.2 percent of patients against 10 percent of controls. Ureaplasma urealyticum led the list, ahead of Mycoplasma hominis and Gardnerella vaginalis, mostly in adult women. Higher white cell counts linked strongly to positive tests and to doctors starting treatment. The authors say these organisms deserve clinical attention, judged case by case.
pmc-13576509:
Agathe Chabassier and colleagues report a real-world study, published in 2026. It uses data from connected scales and blood pressure cuffs. It measures what changes after people start GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Users were matched to similar non-users. Causal inference methods did the matching. Body composition was followed in about two thousand adults. Blood pressure was followed in a smaller group.

Starting a GLP-1 drug was associated with weight loss. The median loss was just under ten percent over the following year. Most of the loss was fat. Muscle loss was much smaller. Small drops in blood pressure were sustained. The starting ratio of muscle to fat best predicted the quality of weight loss. Lower-ratio users lost more fat while sparing muscle.
pmc-13578209:
Yujiao Wang and co-authors report a 2026 field study on how height above sea level and nitrogen feed shape wheat yield and grain quality. Six winter wheat types, classed as strong, medium, or weak in gluten, grew for two seasons at three sites in China. The sites ranged from near sea level to Lhasa, high on the Tibetan plateau.

High ground cut mean yield sharply compared with Beijing, mainly through fewer spikes and lighter grains. Grain protein rose at Lhasa, yet bread-making quality did not improve, and strong gluten types lost dough strength there. Weak gluten wheat held up best. Nitrogen needs split by gluten type, so the authors advise matching both the seed choice and the feed rate to the site height.
pmc-13579909:
Brenda J Tittlemier and colleagues interview Canadians who do rehabilitation research side by side with the people who use its results, in a 2026 study. Partnered research brings clinicians, managers, and clients into study decisions, with hopes of making findings stick in practice. Talks were held with seven researchers alongside six knowledge users, most of them women, about how they judge such teamwork.

None had run a formal check on their partnership, citing time above all, though most saw value in one. Partners still named wide effects: studies shaped from the first question to the final share out, plus personal growth in skills and confidence. Many forces drove those effects, from trust to meeting habits. The authors warn that skipping evaluation leaves the field guessing about what partnering truly buys.
pmc-13583209:
Fatima Alnaimat and colleagues offer the first portrait of systemic sclerosis in Jordan in this 2026 study. Systemic sclerosis is a rare autoimmune disease that hardens skin and can damage inner organs. Fifty-seven patients from a single clinic at Jordan University Hospital in Amman took part, answering questions on symptoms, mood, hand use, and daily quality of life.

Most patients were women, and just over half had the limited form of the disease. A color change in cold fingers, called Raynaud's phenomenon, appeared in 49 patients, and nearly half had finger ulcers. Lung scarring and high pressure in the lung arteries were each found in a large share. Scores for body and mind were equally lowered in both disease forms, which points to a heavy daily burden.
pmc-13587509:
Shubham Pandey and colleagues explore the microbes of India's solar salterns, shallow ponds where seawater dries into salt. Such ponds are stable yet extreme, and their salt-loving microbes hold enzymes and compounds of industrial interest. Their 2026 study paired old-style culture growing with whole-community gene reading at four salterns spread across the country, tracking how salt, acidity, and conductivity sorted the life present.

At the saltiest sites, archaea, an ancient branch of microbes, took over, while milder sites held a more even mix with bacteria. The team also grew 42 hardy isolates in the lab. Gene reads brimmed with tools for ion pumping, sun-proofing, and DNA repair, plus clusters that could make new germ-killing compounds. Resistance genes stayed rare and patchy. The authors frame salt itself as the master filter shaping these communities.
pmc-13588209:
Sakoon Saggu and colleagues report a movement pattern never before tied to a slow measles brain disease. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, is a fatal brain inflammation that can surface years after measles, bringing mental decline and rhythmic jerks. Their case concerns a 14-year-old boy who had measles at age seven and came in with a year of falls and trouble standing.

On standing, his legs shook and his knees buckled without warning as the thigh muscles briefly lost their tone, a pattern classed as orthostatic hyperkinetic disorder with negative myoclonus. Sitting, lying, and walking freed him of the shaking, though the buckling could interrupt his steps and caused his falls. Scans showed frontal brain lesions, and his disease sat at an early-middle stage. The authors say this standing-linked pattern widens the known face of the disease.
pmc-13591809:
Zahra Bagheri-Hosseinabadi and four colleagues check, in 2026, how often metabolic syndrome appears in people with lupus, an autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own tissues. The syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor sugar and fat control. Their clinic group held 200 lupus patients, classed by standard rules for both conditions.

Just over a quarter of the lupus patients also met the bar for metabolic syndrome. Their disease activity scores, though, were no worse than those of lupus patients without the syndrome. One inflammation marker ran higher in the combined group. Weight, waist size, blood sugar, and most blood fats all ran worse there too. The team says heart and metabolic screening deserves a firm place in lupus care.
pmc-13591909:
Rui Wang and three colleagues link, in 2026, a simple blood ratio to low muscle mass in people with type 2 diabetes. The ratio sets C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, against albumin, a sign of nutrition. Their study held 1,009 patients whose muscle was measured by X-ray scanning. Low muscle mass was classed by Asian working group rules.

One in five men and about one in seven women had low muscle mass. In men, a higher ratio paired with higher odds of low mass, and the link held after age, fats, blood pressure, and body size were weighed. In women no such link appeared. Wang and the team suggest the cheap ratio may flag men who need muscle checks.
pmc-13592209:
Joseph Carver and three colleagues teach a computer to design silver nanoparticle recipes backward from a wanted size. Particle size rules how silver specks perform in sensors, catalysts, and medicine, yet cooks still find recipes by trial and error. Their team pooled lab data from batch pots and flow reactors, then trained five prediction models. A Gaussian process model won, calling sizes with high accuracy.

Working backward, the system proposed recipes for target sizes from 20 to 70 nanometers, ranked by expected error, spread, and doubt. Fresh lab runs landed within a few percent of target in batch pots and close behind in flow rigs. Carver and the team call the validated loop a shortcut past blind recipe hunting.
pmc-13592409:
Min Su Kang and six colleagues tune, in 2026, a selector switch for dense phase change memory arrays. In crosspoint grids, stray current leaks through unchosen cells, so each cell needs a guard that opens only past a threshold voltage. Their guard uses a germanium tellurium sulfur glass mixed by sputtering, then dosed with nitrogen. The gas ties up weak bonds, trims traps, and evens the switching voltage.

The doped device endured around ten billion cycles, switched in under twenty nanoseconds, and leaked very little current while off. It also withstood heat far above working needs. Paired with a memory cell, it blocked current cleanly under voltage control. Kang and the team pitch the balance of speed, endurance, and low threshold for packed memory grids.
pmc-13599709:
Lovisa Hellsten and six colleagues published this 2026 population study of sexual and reproductive healthcare use among young people with autism or ADHD in Stockholm County, Sweden. These groups may face barriers to services such as contraception advice and testing. Digital care is expanding as an alternative. Using registry data from 2018 to 2022, the authors compared service use in 12- to 22-year-olds with and without these diagnoses.

The study covered 454,405 young people, including 11,850 autistic youth and 31,144 with ADHD. Young people with ADHD used services more than peers in both digital and in-person care; for in-person visits, odds were about double in females. Autistic youth used services less, especially males, whose in-person odds were 0.45 relative to controls. Autistic females who did enter care used it as intensively as peers, suggesting the barrier is getting through the door. Gaps were smaller for digital care, hinting it may ease access.
pmc-13609509:
Wangxin Li and five colleagues build a generative system to fake microbial colony photos for training detection software. Deep learning can count colonies on Petri dishes, but it needs many labeled images, and real colony photos take time to produce. Their Double Deep Convolutional GAN creates synthetic colonies in two moves, overlapping small single colonies into composites and generating complete plates. It then tunes how many synthetic images to add using several quality metrics at once.

Starting from 236 real samples, the optimized recipe added 1,320 synthetic images. The realism score improved from 38.9 to 37.1, lower being better, and downstream detectors validated the approach: colony detection accuracy reached 0.975. The authors present the composite adversarial design as a practical answer to data scarcity in microbiology imaging. Labs could expand small photo collections into training sets for automated colony analysis, cutting manual counting in medical and food-safety testing.
pmc-13612609: Karel Allegaert and five colleagues issued this correction to their Pediatric Nephrology study of kidney function in cooled, birth-asphyxiated newborns. The notice is a correction only. Formulas in the original article were printed wrong in three places, the abstract, page 3, and the graphical abstract, missing a time term. The notice supplies fixed formulas so readers compute the estimated glomerular filtration rate across the first ten days of life. No data, results, or conclusions change.
pmc-13612809:
Boers and colleagues published a 2026 review on calcium given around childbirth to cut bleeding. Heavy bleeding after birth is a top cause of mother deaths worldwide. Calcium helps the womb muscle grip and keep contracting after delivery. The team pooled studies testing calcium given around the time of birth.

Pooled results linked calcium with less blood loss after delivery overall. Mothers given calcium also needed fewer extra womb-tightening drugs afterward. The womb's failure to contract drives most heavy bleeding cases after birth. Standard first drugs sometimes fail or cannot be used safely for all. Calcium may serve as a cheap helper beside them, they conclude. More trials must firm up dose and timing before routine use.
pmc-13615109:
Takuro Ariga and colleagues compare in 2026 the cost-effectiveness of chemoradiotherapy against surgery for stage I cancer of the oesophagus in Japan, the earliest stage of the disease. Their model combined survival figures from a Japanese trial with quality-of-life scores mapped from standard cancer questionnaires, counting only direct medical costs from the public health system's view. Future costs and life years were discounted at 2 percent per year.

The drug and radiation route cost about 26,313 United States dollars more than surgery, while adding 0.630 quality-adjusted life years, giving a ratio near 41,742 dollars per such year. Checks on the model's weak points showed which inputs moved the answer most. For a health system weighing two good treatments, the study prices the gentler, organ-keeping option in terms officials can judge.
pmc-13616909:
Rodney Alan Long and a large multi-institution team report a 2026 approach that uses large language models to speed up biomedical data standardization. Research groups describe their variables in incompatible ways, which blocks pooling of studies. Their system drafts common data elements, the shared definitions that let datasets line up, for clinical and research dictionaries.

The team processed thirty-one datasets through a GPT-4 based pipeline and had experts check the output. Most generated fields needed no revision, and accuracy was highest on well-structured sources. Tests on Alzheimer and Parkinson datasets mapped about a third of unseen variable names onto existing elements automatically. The authors argue that automating this tedious groundwork lowers barriers to collaboration across studies.
pmc-13618809:
Jaiden Townsend and four colleagues report a case where a heart blood test accidentally exposed infective endocarditis hiding behind a chest infection. Their patient, a woman with a permanent pacemaker, had persistent fever, pleuritic pain, and a productive cough and was being treated for right-sided pneumonia. Blood cultures stayed negative, but a markedly raised NT-proBNP, a heart strain marker drawn because of breathlessness and fluid on her chest film, pushed the team to scan her heart.

Ultrasound revealed a large, irregular, independently mobile mass clinging to the pacemaker lead inside the right atrium and flopping across the tricuspid valve with each cycle. A probe passed down the esophagus confirmed it. That picture, in context, meant infection of the device itself, and she was referred to a specialist center for complete extraction. The authors highlight culture-negative endocarditis as a diagnostic trap and echocardiography as the decisive tool.
pmc-13618909:
Sayida Al-Jamei and eight colleagues measure medication burden and quality of life in Yemeni cancer patients on chemotherapy. Their cross-sectional study ran at the National Oncology Centre in Sana'a from December 2025 to February 2026. Two hundred thirty-four adults were interviewed and their records reviewed. Polypharmacy meant five or more non-cancer medications, a common situation because chemotherapy demands many supportive drugs.

The burden was near-universal: about ninety-five percent met the polypharmacy threshold and over half took ten or more non-cancer medicines. Average global quality of life sat below fifty on a hundred-point scale, with financial difficulty the worst-scoring problem, ahead of fatigue and pain. Surprisingly, heavier medication burden did not independently predict worse quality of life. Being female did, predicting both lower quality of life and higher medication use, while older age and illiteracy showed borderline links to poorer scores.
pmc-13620009:
Wagner Bettiol, Roberto Lanna-Filho, and Cristiano Limberger chart how Bacillus bacteria became the backbone of biological crop protection in Brazil. These spore-forming microbes fight plant diseases, help crops grow, and ease stress, which makes them attractive farm products. The team compiled registrations from national databases and drew market estimates from farmer surveys across two crop seasons, the later one covering more than sixteen thousand interviews.

By December 2025, Brazil had 297 Bacillus-based products built on 126 strains, led by four main species. Farmers apply them by seed treatment, soil drench, furrow, or leaf spray against fungal, bacterial, and nematode diseases. Treated area grew nearly fivefold between the two surveys, and sales value more than tripled, giving these products roughly half the national biocontrol market. The authors credit microbial science, regulation, and farmer trust for the climb.
pmc-13621409:
Saja A Althobaiti and Ola G Hussein built a green sensing platform from iron-copper nanoparticles that imitate an enzyme. Their particles act like peroxidase, the enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide to drive color changes, turning a clear reagent blue in proportion to what is present. That single trick lets the platform measure peroxide itself, glucose after a coupled reaction, and toxic hexavalent chromium.

Testing showed clean straight-line responses across wide ranges for all three targets, with good selectivity against common interfering substances. Glucose readings in real human serum samples worked, proving the method outside pure lab water. To free the test from bench instruments, the team added smartphone photo analysis of the color and a small electronics board for data capture. Green chemistry scorecards rated the approach kindly. The authors present it as a template for bedside and field testing built on cheap, water-made materials.
pmc-13621609:
Claire Yu and Joan Gluch use two dental cases to show how stigma shapes LGBTQ+ oral health, in a 2026 case-based review. A nonbinary patient, repeatedly misgendered at the dentist, delayed care until cavities went untreated. A transgender man ground his teeth under stress tied to staff calling him by his deadname. Both stories trace clinical harm back to ordinary office interactions rather than the dentistry itself.

The authors pair the cases with a literature review of barriers: higher substance use, postponed visits, scarce culturally competent providers, and bisexual adults facing especially poor outcomes. Simple practices made the difference in their telling: correct pronouns, chosen names, and communication that signals safety. They press for provider training, nondiscrimination policies, and clinic structures that earn trust before treatment starts. Affirming care, they argue, is not decoration; it changes whether patients return and whether treatment succeeds.
pmc-13623409:
Chloe E Coulter, Samuel J Hopper, and Gina D Jefferson describe a demanding salvage operation where a patient regained the ability to eat by mouth against steep odds. The woman had oesophageal cancer treated earlier with chemoradiation, then surgery that joined her throat to her stomach. When cancer returned beside that join, standard options ran out.

The recurrence sat in the pyriform sinus, a groove beside the voice box, touching the rebuilt food passage. Surgeons removed the larynx and throat and rebuilt the missing circle of tissue with a flap of thigh tissue carrying its own blood vessels, sewn to the stomach conduit. Scarred, irradiated tissue and poor blood supply made failure likely. Even so, healing held and she returned to oral intake. The authors present the case as proof that careful salvage reconstruction can restore eating in medically complex patients, and she remained free of disease.
pmc-13623509:
Alexander Muacevic and colleagues review how juvenile-onset Huntington's disease differs from the adult form at the level of mechanism. Huntington's is an inherited brain disease caused by an overlong repeat in the huntingtin gene, and it brings movement, thinking, and psychiatric symptoms. Onset before age twenty counts as juvenile, and those patients carry far longer repeats.

The review contrasts the two forms across several fronts. These include gene expression errors and faulty message splicing in striatal neurons, disturbed building of synapses, the behaviour of protein clumps, and the failing of the cell's protein clean-up systems. Ongoing brain development is the thread tying the differences together, since the young brain is still wiring itself when the disease strikes. Symptoms differ too, with stiffness and slowness dominating in the young rather than the jerky movements of adults. The authors argue for diagnoses and treatments designed for juveniles specifically.
pmc-13624009:
Akke de Lange, Luc H W T Geelen, and W Daniel Kissling study when fallow deer are active across the day in a managed Dutch coastal dune system. Camera traps reveal daily rhythms, but pooling all deer can hide differences between the sexes and seasons. The site has heavy daytime recreation, no large predators, and culling aimed at females.

Forty-nine camera sites logged more than four thousand sexed detections across three seasons: the rut, the period after it, and the birthing season. As a herd, the deer favoured twilight and night, above all in and after the rut. Splitting by sex changed the story. Females stayed strongly nocturnal, especially after the rut, while males added twilight and daytime activity in spring, driving the herd's daytime rise. Overlap between the sexes peaked during the rut, then shrank. The authors urge managers to read activity by sex and season.
pmc-13624709:
Panumas Sun-Arlee and a broad team dissect which mutations weaken a dengue virus type 3 vaccine candidate. The candidate, built from a virus softened by long passage through animal kidney cells, carries seven changes spread across its shell and inner proteins. The researchers built swapped versions of the virus, putting parent or candidate parts in one at a time, then measured plaque size in cell culture and illness in mouse brains.

Swapping the inner, nonstructural parts back to the parent form restored parent-like plaques and strength, which marks that segment as a main weakening factor. Changing only shell parts also shifted behavior, so softness seems to come from mutation mixes rather than single changes. Such maps help vaccine makers tune live dengue vaccines with more care.
pmc-13625809:
Marko Mirza Sahinovic and co-authors test whether a blood pressure drug dripped into a vein also moves the body's sleep hormone. Norepinephrine is a stress chemical the body makes itself, and it prods melatonin production in the brain, yet its effect as a medicine was unclear. In a crossover study, thirty-six healthy volunteers received rising doses while awake and again under general anesthesia, giving 417 paired blood readings.

More norepinephrine in the blood went with clearly higher melatonin, and levels ran higher while awake than under anesthesia. That state did not break the link between the two chemicals, and people who started with more melatonin responded the most. The finding matters for intensive care, where round-the-clock drips may quietly shift patients' body clocks.
pmc-13626309:
Lucie Ráčková leads an eleven-author team testing a desk-friendly antidote to acute stress. Their device, called ÉOS, pairs slow coherent breathing at six breaths a minute with blue light exposure. In a double-blind crossover trial, twenty-nine people endured a standard laboratory stress test. Then they either used the device or rested quietly, swapping on another visit. Stress, sleepiness, mood, heart rhythm, and brain waves were tracked throughout.

Subjective stress fell by nearly a third after the device session, sleepiness eased, and positive mood rose, all compared with plain rest. Body measures such as heart rate variability did not budge, and negative mood stayed put. The authors pitch the pairing for workplaces, while calling for tests that split the two parts and follow workers longer.
pmc-13630209:
Lorenzo D. Stafford and four colleagues ran a preliminary study of whether presenting food differently can restore some eating pleasure for people with smell and taste disorders. Thirty-three participants with smell loss took a standardised smell test, then tasted foods varied by colour, shape, or accompanying music mood, rating enjoyment and sensory qualities.

The ratings showed no clear effect of any presentation change, a null result the authors report plainly. Interviews told a richer story: since losing smell, participants most often reached for stronger textures and extra herbs and spices to make food interesting again. The mismatch between numbers and testimony leads the authors to call for more carefully designed studies rather than claiming the idea dead.
pmc-13630409:
Shuqi Wang and colleagues built a silicon battery anode coated and bound in one carbon-baking step, aiming to tame silicon's swelling problem. Silicon can hold far more charge than graphite, but micro-sized silicon swells by about 300 percent as it charges, cracking electrodes apart.

The process left a uniform carbon skin on the particles and through the whole electrode, with no added glue or conductive filler. First-cycle efficiency reached about 87 percent, a strong start for silicon anodes. After 400 cycles the electrode still held 84 percent of its capacity, and a graphite blend kept 91 percent after 500 cycles. A full pouch cell matched with a standard cathode also worked, supporting real-world use.
pmc-13630809:
Jan Reubens and twenty-one colleagues tell the story of the European Tracking Network, the collaboration that follows tagged fish and other aquatic animals across a continent. Published in 2026, the account explains how Europe lagged North America and Australia in coordinated tracking infrastructure until the network formed as a grassroots effort in 2017.

It has since grown into a durable system with a central database, shared dashboards, and partners deploying receivers nationally while feeding one platform built on open data principles. The network supports cross-border studies of movement, habitat links, and behaviour, while wrestling with familiar strains: patchy funding, incompatible gear, false detections, and ownership questions. The authors position it within a coming global aquatic observatory.
pmc-13632009:
Sol Hooy Oh and five colleagues published this 2026 cohort study linking heart health scores to later emergencies in Korea. The score, called Life's Essential 8, grades four habits, namely diet, activity, smoking, and sleep, plus four body measures. Earlier work tied the score to death rates, mostly in Western and Chinese groups. The Korean team asked whether it also predicts first major cardiovascular events in their own population.

They linked national health survey records from 2014 through 2018 with insurance claims that track hospital events over time. After removing people with prior heart attacks or strokes and those missing score parts, they kept just over twenty-one thousand adults for analysis. Korean eating patterns and body shapes differ from Western ones, so a local test matters. The study design lets readers judge how well a United States score travels to East Asia.
pmc-13634409:
Shourui Niu and eight colleagues studied a tiny RNA molecule that calms brain inflammation after stroke in rats. Ischemic stroke blocks blood flow to part of the brain, and the returning blood triggers inflammatory injury on top of the original damage. Sequencing of rat cortex pointed the team to the molecule miR-125a-5p, which sat inside inflammation-related pathways. They raised its levels in rats and measured brain damage, movement problems, and cell death.

Treated rats showed smaller damaged areas, fewer dying cortex cells, and better neurological scores. The molecule works by reining in a protein called TRAF2, a switch in an inflammatory chain. Levels of that switch and its downstream partners fell in the cortex. Inflammatory messengers in the blood fell as well. The authors conclude that this small RNA protects the injured brain by quieting a central inflammation pathway, marking a possible direction for stroke therapy research.
pmc-13635209:
Lorenzo Vilizzi published this 2026 dataset paper to support tools that screen species for invasion risk. Managers use screening kits to judge whether a non-native species might turn invasive, and those kits need honest calibration data. Calibration requires species already labeled invasive or non-invasive on solid evidence. Vilizzi assembled such labels for more than nineteen hundred taxa drawn from over two hundred screening applications across hundreds of regions and more than two decades.

Each taxon's label was rebuilt from scratch through a standard checking workflow that leaned on authoritative databases and the scientific literature. Every verification step and evidence source is recorded inside the dataset itself. That transparency lets later users reproduce why each species earned its label. The author offers the collection as a shared reference for calibrating screening tools and comparing how they perform across regions, strengthening the preventive side of biosecurity.
pmc-13635609:
Montezuma and colleagues wrote in 2026 a practical guide, issued by a European digital pathology society, for laboratories choosing digital pathology systems before they buy. Scanning glass slides into images is spreading through pathology, but the systems are costly and shape a lab's work for years. Advice on how to judge them before purchase was scarce, so the society drew on experience from many institutions.

The guide walks through each part of the setup: slide scanners, image management software, workstations, storage, and links to laboratory information systems. It stresses testing with a lab's real workload rather than vendor demos, checking that systems talk to each other, and planning for growth. The authors aim the advice at pathologists, IT teams, and managers matching a system to local needs.
pmc-13642909:
Jee Eun Choi and eleven colleagues present a 2026 mouse study on how stress-related signaling steers a class of immune cells inside breast tumors. Type 2 innate lymphoid cells can either help or hinder tumors, and the switch behind that split was unclear.

The team focused on the beta2-adrenergic receptor, a receiver for stress hormones. Removing or blocking it in these cells enriched a more active form, raised helpful T cell entry into tumors, and slowed tumor growth. The receptor's absence reprogrammed the cells toward stimulating immunity. The authors suggest blocking this pathway could strengthen cancer immunotherapy.
pmc-13643609:
Gareth Lingham and eleven colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional analysis from the Busselton Healthy Ageing Study in Western Australia asking whether eye signs of past sun exposure track with skin cancer history. Three eye findings, pterygium, a glowing ultraviolet marker, and myopia, all reflect earlier sun dose.

Of 3,829 participants with cancer history data, about a fifth had keratinocyte skin cancer. A current pterygium, a fleshy eye growth, and past pterygium removal each linked with that cancer history after adjustment. The glow marker and myopia showed no link, and melanoma links were absent. The authors advise warning pterygium patients about skin risk.
pmc-13645609:
Jiajie Yan and ten colleagues review records of 202 patients who had keyhole surgery to repair a torn shoulder tendon at one hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The team measured how much nursing care each patient needed in the first forty-eight hours after surgery. They then compared that workload score with shoulder function three months later. Their idea is that early nursing load may reflect how complex a patient's recovery will be.

Patients who needed more early nursing care had worse shoulder scores at three months, and the link followed a graded pattern across workload levels. Links with unplanned clinic visits or readmission were too imprecise to judge. The authors propose the workload score as an early warning sign worth testing in advance-looking studies. For now, they present it as a research lead rather than a tool ready for routine care.
pmc-13645709:
Burhanettin Ozdemir and three colleagues survey medical students at Alfaisal University in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, about how they judge their learning environment. The questionnaire used is called DREEM, a standard tool for rating medical school settings. The sample held 411 first- and second-year students taught mainly through team-based learning. The team checked whether the tool's five-part structure held up and how scores linked with students' views of their own academic ability.

The five-part structure received mixed but broadly supportive evidence from the statistical checks. Links differed by year: first-year students tied self-views to teaching and social scores, while second-year students tied them to all parts of the environment. Patterns also differed between male and female students. No overall score gaps appeared between years or genders. The authors advise schools to read subscale patterns, not just one total score, when improving courses.
pmc-13649409:
Maryam N. ALNasser surveyed 112 faculty members at a Saudi science college about everyday slips of mind, such as lost focus or missed tasks. Staff juggle teaching, research, and office duties, and heavy loads may strain the mind. She used a standard survey form that asks how often such slips occur.

Nearly half of the staff rated their slips as moderate, and a large share rated them as severe. Women reported more slips than men. Teaching loads of 31 to 40 hours a week also linked to more slips. In contrast, more research work and a fair share of office duties linked to fewer slips. The author urges balanced loads and follow-up work with direct tests of thinking.
pmc-13649509:
Feiyan Ju and seven colleagues tested sprays that help wheat cope with heat during grain filling. Heat at that stage cuts both growth and yield in winter wheat. Field plots got one of two growth regulators, a nutrient salt, or a blend of all three, and the team tracked genes, leaf action, and yield.

The sprays kept leaf photosynthesis strong and lifted the leaf's own defence enzymes. Harmful oxygen by-products and membrane damage fell as a result. The blend worked best of all: it curbed biomass loss and raised grain yield the most. Gene reads showed joint control of light capture and defence paths. The authors offer the blend as a farm-ready lead for hot spells, backed by a clearer picture of how it works.
pmc-13649709:
Brittany T. Rupp and eight colleagues built a cell atlas from nose swabs that can tell long-term nose inflammation from nose cancer, in a 2026 study. The two states share symptoms, so cancer is often found late. Their platform uses deep learning to read shape traits of single cells in plain microscope images.

The base atlas held more than six hundred thousand immune cell images, joined with over two and a half million swab images from health, chronic sinus disease, and cancer. Cancer samples showed more of one immune cell class and busier grain-like cells. Some cell clusters in cancer bore shape marks never seen in the other states. The authors back swab tests for early, point-of-care screening.
pmc-13650009:
Thomas Nguyen and one colleague lay out a roadmap for computer models of activity-dependent myelination. That is the process by which brain cells adjust the fatty coating on nerve fibers in response to how active those fibers are. Adjusting the coating changes how fast signals travel, so timing between brain areas can be tuned alongside signal strength.

The authors compare existing models by how each one links neural activity to changes in the coating, and they weigh what each model assumes, does well, and leaves out. The hard part is that the biology runs on many time scales at once, from quick electrical events to slow structural change. Their perspective argues that careful modeling can guide experiments and help place this timing-based learning beside the better-known learning that happens at synapses.
pmc-13650809:
Shelby M Royal and four colleagues, publishing in 2026, ask what actually limits growth in captive-reared eastern hellbenders: crowding or food. Young rearing programs for this threatened giant salamander often guess at stocking densities and feeding rates, and wrong guesses waste animals and money.

Two experiments ran for seven and eight months. The first compared growth across low, medium, and high densities and found no differences. The second crossed three densities with three food levels in a full factorial design. Food availability drove growth clearly, with the highest feeding level producing growth roughly a quarter to nearly a half greater than the lower levels. Density and its interaction with food showed no effect. The authors advise programs to feed generously and to house animals at the higher tested densities without fear of stunting, yielding larger animals for release.
pmc-3237409:
Schloss, Gevers, and Westcott address how PCR and sequencing artefacts distort studies based on the 16S rRNA gene. Next-generation sequencing sparked growth in research on microbial communities and their roles in health. Copying DNA before sequencing, though, introduces errors that can look like rare microbes.

The authors show how such artefacts inflate apparent diversity and how to reduce their effects. Cleaner pipelines protect studies of the gut, soil, and other communities from chasing phantom species. Their guidance shaped standard practice in microbiome analysis worldwide.  Mock communities with known contents let the authors measure the artefacts directly themselves.
pmc-5605509:
The GBD 2016 team reported in 2017 on illness and injury that do not kill, across the whole world. As death rates fall, life spans grow, and populations age, non-fatal outcomes form a larger share of the total burden of disease. Pain, disability, and mental illness shape daily life for huge numbers of people.

The study gives complete estimates of how often hundreds of diseases and injuries occur. It also counts how many people live with each one, and the years lived with disability, for nearly two hundred countries from 1990 to 2016. Such counts show where health systems must shift focus from saving lives to keeping people able and well. They guide plans for rehab, mental health, and chronic care.
pmc-6298009:
Nicole Davis, Diana Proctor, Susan Holmes, and coauthors presented a statistical fix for contaminant DNA in 2018. Microbe surveys often pick up DNA that was never in the sample. Contaminants sneak in from kits and lab reagents.

Their method, built into the decontam tool, spots sequences whose pattern matches contamination rather than biology. Sequences that appear more in blank controls or in dilute samples are flagged. Removing them sharpens results, above all for samples with few real microbes. The approach gave the field a shared, testable way to clean data instead of hand-waving the problem.
pmc-7026709:
The GBD 2017 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Collaborators published this global analysis in 2019. The burden of inflammatory bowel disease is rising worldwide. Levels and trends vary sharply between countries and regions.

The study reports cases and deaths for Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis across nearly two hundred countries. Rates remain highest in North America and Europe but climb fast in newly industrialized regions. An aging patient pool adds disability even where rates level off. Understanding that geography helps governments plan specialist care and drug budgets. The authors note that health systems in fast-growing regions face a double burden of old and new diseases.
pmc-7067809:
Johnny Fares, Mohamad Fares, Hussein Khachfe, and coauthors revisited the molecular principles of metastasis in 2020. Metastasis, the spread of cancer to distant organs, causes most cancer deaths. For all its importance, the process remains poorly understood.

The review follows cancer cells through escape, travel in blood, and colonization of new tissue. New views stress that spread can start early and that dormant cells can wake years later. Immune evasion and organ-specific niches get detailed treatment. Readers see why stopping spread, not just shrinking tumors, is oncology's hardest problem. Each stage of spread is paired with the therapies now being tested against it.
pmc-7619509:
Richard Durbin presents a new data structure that makes pangenome search structures able to grow and change. The graph Burrows-Wheeler transform lets researchers search huge sets of genome paths, yet existing versions are static and awkward to build. Durbin's design adapts the skiplist, a probabilistic list structure with fast search, to run-length-compressed data. So common operations scale with the number of runs in the data rather than its raw size.

A dynamic version supports inserting new material at comparable speed, which static structures cannot do. The paper applies the structure to paths through a graph built from closed syncmers, a sparse way of sketching genome similarity. Working code ships inside an open software package. For pangenome projects that keep adding samples, a searchable index that updates in place removes a costly rebuild from every analysis.
pmc-8262709:
Guanghui Xiong and colleagues launched ADMETlab 2.0 in 2021, an online platform that predicts how a candidate drug will behave in the body. Most drug projects fail because a compound is absorbed poorly, breaks down badly, or proves toxic. Testing those properties early, even by computer prediction, saves years and money.

The platform predicts the full set of such properties, known by the initials ADMET: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity. The authors describe the models behind the predictions and how the second version widened and sharpened them. Freely available tools of this kind let even small labs screen compounds before committing to costly experiments.
pound-exultations-1909:
Ezra Pound, a young American poet in London, published Exultations in 1909. It was his third small book in little more than a year. Pound was teaching himself poetry by raiding the past, and this collection leans hard toward the medieval troubadours of Provence.

The poems include translations and imitations of troubadour songs, full of spring mornings, distant ladies, and formal praise. Early original lyrics stand beside them, already showing Pound's drive toward exact, musical speech. The medievalist and the modernist in Pound are both visible here, side by side. Exultations is a workshop book: readers can watch a revolutionary poet gathering his tools from a thousand years of verse.
pound-personae-1909:
Ezra Pound published Personae in London in 1909, his first substantial collection and his bid for poetic mastery. The title means masks in Latin, and Pound explained that each poem speaks through an adopted character or voice. He was twenty-three, freshly arrived from America, and determined to remake English poetry.

The poems move from troubadour translations to dramatic monologues and sharp lyrics. Pound tries on Provençal singers, Italian courtiers, and his own brash modern self. The technique is already dazzling, though the great Imagist manifestos still lay ahead. Critics took notice of the young American at once. Personae is the root from which Imagism and much of modern poetry grew.
prince-zaleski-pg10709:
Matthew Phipps Shiel set three mottoes over his Prince Zaleski of 1895: Isaiah's come now, and let us reason together. Cervantes on the knight who imitated the penance of Beltenebros in the Sable Mountain. And a line of Sophocles in Greek, that all things may be told and all things dared. The epigraphs are the detective's coat of arms. Zaleski reasons like a prophet, keeps his penance like a mad knight, and dares any conclusion the facts demand.

The three tales, the Race of Orven, the Stone of the Edmundsbury Monks, and the S.S., unfold in the prince's decaying palace. Where the narrator brings him the world's locked-room griefs and watches that just and passionate mind work without leaving its couch. This printing shows the full title apparatus of 1895, the year of Holmes's absence and Zaleski's brief, incense-heavy reign as the decadent answer to Baker Street.
recherches-sur-le-systeme-nerveux-en-gen: French title pages alone open this work, whose title promises studies of the nervous system in general.
